Significant Risks and Uncertainties Nature of Operations We operate predominantly in the midstream energy industry, which includes gathering, transporting, processing, fractionating and storing natural gas, NGLs, crude oil, and petrochemical and refined products. As such, changes in the prices of hydrocarbon products and in the relative price levels among hydrocarbon products could have a material adverse effect on our financial position, results of operations and cash flows. Changes in prices may impact demand for hydrocarbon products, which in turn may impact production, demand and the volumes of products for which we provide services. In addition, decreases in demand may be caused by other factors, including prevailing economic conditions, reduced demand by consumers for the end products made with hydrocarbon products, increased competition, adverse weather conditions, public health emergencies and government regulations affecting prices and production levels. The natural gas, NGL and crude oil volumes currently transported, gathered or processed at our facilities originate primarily from existing domestic resource basins, which naturally deplete over time. To offset this natural decline, our facilities need access to production from newly discovered properties. Many economic and business factors beyond our control can adversely affect the decision by producers to explore for and develop new reserves. These factors could include relatively low crude oil and natural gas prices, cost and availability of equipment and labor, regulatory changes, capital budget limitations, the lack of available capital or the probability of success in finding hydrocarbons. A decrease in exploration and development activities in the regions where our facilities and other energy logistics assets are located could result in a decrease in volumes handled by our assets, which could have a material adverse effect on our financial position, results of operations and cash flows. Even if crude oil and natural gas reserves exist in the areas served by our assets, we may not be chosen by producers in these areas to gather, transport, process, fractionate, store or otherwise handle the hydrocarbons extracted. We compete with other companies for such production on the basis of many factors, including, but not limited to, geographic proximity to the production, costs of connection, available capacity, rates and access to markets. Credit Risk We may incur credit risk to the extent counterparties do not fulfill their obligations to us in connection with our marketing of natural gas, NGLs, crude oil, and petrochemicals and refined products and under long-term contracts with minimum volume commitments or fixed demand charges. Risks of nonpayment and nonperformance by customers are a major consideration in our businesses, and our credit procedures and policies may not be adequate to sufficiently eliminate customer credit risk. Further, adverse economic conditions in our industry, such as those experienced in connection with the COVID-2020 pandemic in 2020, may increase the risk of nonpayment and nonperformance by customers, particularly customers that have sub-investment grade credit ratings or small-scale companies. We manage our exposure to credit risk through credit analysis, credit approvals, credit limits and monitoring procedures, and for certain transactions may utilize letters of credit, prepayments, net out agreements and guarantees. However, these procedures and policies do not fully eliminate customer credit risk. F-68 ENTERPRISE PRODUCTS PARTNERS L.P. NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS The primary markets for our services are the Gulf Coast, Southwest, Rocky Mountain, Northeast and Midwest regions of the U.S. We have a concentration of trade receivables due from independent and major integrated oil and gas companies and other pipelines and wholesalers operating in these markets. These concentrations may affect our overall credit risk in that these energy industry customers may be similarly affected by adverse changes in economic, regulatory or other factors. In those situations where we are exposed to credit risk in our derivative instrument transactions, we analyze the counterparty’s financial condition prior to entering into an agreement, establish credit and/or margin limits and monitor the appropriateness of these limits on an ongoing basis. Generally, we do not require collateral for such transactions nor do we currently anticipate nonperformance by our material counterparties. Insurance Matters We participate as a named insured in EPCO’s insurance program, which provides us with property damage, business interruption and other insurance coverage, the scope and amounts of which we believe are customary and prudent for the nature and extent of our operations. While we believe EPCO maintains adequate insurance coverage on our behalf, insurance may not fully cover every type of damage, interruption or other loss that might occur. If we were to incur a significant loss for which we were not fully insured, it could have a material adverse impact on our financial position, results of operations and cash flows. In addition, there may be timing differences between amounts we accrue related to property damage expense, amounts we are required to pay in connection with a loss, and amounts we subsequently receive from insurance carriers as reimbursements. Any event that materially interrupts the revenues generated by our consolidated operations, or other losses that require us to make material expenditures not reimbursed by insurance, could reduce our ability to pay distributions to our unitholders and, accordingly, adversely affect the market price of the Partnership’s common units. Involuntary conversions result from the loss of an asset due to some unforeseen event (e.g., destruction due to a fire). Some of these events are covered by insurance, thus resulting in a property damage insurance recovery. Amounts we receive from insurance carriers are net of any deductibles related to the covered event. We record a receivable from insurance to the extent we recognize a loss from an involuntary conversion event and the likelihood of our recovering such loss is deemed probable. To the extent that any of our insurance claim receivables are later judged not probable of recovery (e.g., due to new information), such amounts are expensed. We recognize gains on involuntary conversions when the amount received from insurance exceeds the net book value of the retired assets. In addition, we do not recognize gains related to insurance recoveries until all contingencies related to such proceeds have been resolved, that is, a non-refundable cash payment is received from the insurance carrier or we have a binding settlement agreement with the carrier that clearly states that a non-refundable payment will be made. To the extent that an asset is rebuilt, the associated expenditures are capitalized, as appropriate, on our Consolidated Balance Sheets and presented as “Capital expenditures” on our Statements of Consolidated Cash Flows. Under our current insurance program, the standalone deductible for property damage claims is $ 30million. We also have business interruption protection; however, such claims must involve physical damage and have a combined loss value in excess of $ 30million and the period of interruption must exceed 60days. With respect to named windstorm claims, the maximum amount of insurance coverage available to us for any single event is $ 200million, after applying the appropriate deductibles. A named windstorm is a hurricane, typhoon, tropical storm or cyclone as declared by the U.S. National Weather Service. Beginning in April 2023, we maintain insurance coverage for general liability, excess liability, automotive liability and workers’ compensation that is separate from EPCO’s insurance program. For these policies, we are responsible to the extent that losses are within policy limits. We have reserves for both open claims asserted, and an estimate of claims incurred but not reported (“IBNR”). The IBNR reserve is estimated based on actuarial assumptions and analysis and is updated annually. Future events, such as the number of new claims to be filed each year, the average cost of disposing of claims, as well as the numerous uncertainties surrounding litigation and possible state and national legislative measures could cause the actual costs to be higher or lower than estimated. Accordingly, these claims, if resolved in a manner different from the estimate, could have a material adverse impact on our financial position, results of operations and cash flows. Our reserve balance, which is a component of “Other current liabilities” on our Consolidated Balance Sheets, was $ 39million and $ 22million at December 31, 2024 and 2023, respectively. question: Analyzing the Partnership's 2024 and 2025 10-K filings, how do the qualitative risks associated with its voluntary ESG disclosures and aspirational targets, including the use of credits or offsets, influence the perceived operational integrity and strategic adaptability of the firm?
answer: The Partnership's voluntary ESG disclosures are based on expectations, assumptions, and hypothetical scenarios, leading to inherent uncertainties and potential for misinterpretation given the long timelines and lack of an established single reporting approach [1, 2]. These voluntary ESG targets are aspirational, and the Partnership acknowledges it may face unforeseen costs, technical difficulties, or operational obstacles in meeting them [1, 2]. Furthermore, achieving these targets might involve contractual arrangements, such as purchasing credits or offsets, which could draw scrutiny from certain constituencies, potentially affecting perceived operational integrity [1, 2]. The anticipation of pressure from investors and lenders to adopt more aggressive climate or ESG-related goals, without a guarantee of implementation due to costs or technical issues, highlights a strategic adaptability challenge [1, 2]. This blend of uncertain reporting, aspirational targets, and potential for external scrutiny on mitigation methods implies a qualitative risk to how the Partnership's operational integrity and long-term strategic adaptability are viewed by the market and key stakeholders.

question: Given the Partnership's sensitivity to commodity price fluctuations, as indicated by the 'Effect of Hypothetical 10% Change' in its NGL/Refined Products Forwards/Swaps from FY23 to FY24, quantify this change and discuss how evolving ESG pressures on hydrocarbon demand could influence future volatility in this financial risk metric.
answer: For NGL/Refined Products Forwards/Swaps in the non-trading or mark-to-market category, the 'Effect of Hypothetical 10% Change' increased from $43 MM as of December 31, 2023 [3] to $58 MM as of December 31, 2024 [4]. This represents a quantitative increase of $15 MM in the estimated impact from a 10% price change. From a governance perspective, the Partnership acknowledges that its voluntary ESG targets are aspirational and that it may face "unforeseen costs or technical difficulties" or "potential costs or technical or operational obstacles" in implementing more aggressive climate goals [1, 2]. Heightened ESG scrutiny, particularly from investors and lenders pushing for more aggressive goals, could lead to significant shifts in hydrocarbon demand or increased regulatory costs, thereby increasing the volatility and magnitude of the "Effect of Hypothetical 10% Change" on its commodity derivative portfolios [1, 2]. This increased scrutiny directly impacts the underlying commodity prices, affecting the value-at-risk for these instruments and potentially influencing the firm's financial stability (ROA, ROE, NPM).

passages.text: Moreover, while we create and publish voluntary disclosures regarding ESG matters from time to time, many of the statements in those voluntary disclosures will be based on expectations, assumptions and hypothetical scenarios. Such expectations, assumptions and hypothetical scenarios are necessarily uncertain and may be prone to error or subject to misinterpretation given the long timelines involved and the lack of an established single approach to identifying, measuring, and reporting on many ESG matters. Additionally, while we may have or may announce various voluntary ESG targets in the future, such targets are often aspirational. We may not be able to meet such targets in the manner or on such a timeline as initially contemplated, including, but not limited to as a result of unforeseen costs or technical difficulties associated with achieving such results. To the extent we meet such targets, it may be achieved through various contractual arrangements, including the purchase of various credits or offsets that may be deemed to mitigate our ESG impact instead of actual changes in our business operations. Some of these arrangements may receive scrutiny from certain constituencies. Also, despite any aspirational goals, we may receive pressure from investors, lenders, or other groups to adopt more aggressive climate or other ESG-related goals, but we cannot guarantee that we will be able to implement such goals because of potential costs or technical or operational obstacles.

To the extent that we do meet such targets, we may consider the acquisition of various credits or offsets that may be deemed to assist in the achievement of such targets or otherwise mitigate our ESG impact instead of actual achievements of such targets or actual changes in our ESG performance. question: Given the inherent uncertainties in the Partnership's ESG reporting, the aspirational nature of its targets, and external stakeholder pressures, evaluate the cumulative impact these governance factors have on ET's long-term financial metrics, such as ROCE and EPS, and its overall competitive positioning within the midstream sector.
answer: The Partnership's reliance on expectations, assumptions, and hypothetical scenarios for ESG disclosures, coupled with the aspirational nature of its targets, introduces significant uncertainty into its operational and financial outlook [1, 2]. This ambiguity can lead to a perceived lack of clear commitment or tangible progress, potentially increasing capital costs and affecting investor confidence, which could negatively impact key financial metrics like ROCE by increasing the cost of capital and potentially reducing returns on employed capital. The challenge in meeting ESG targets due to unforeseen costs or technical difficulties could directly impact operating expenses, thereby compressing Net Profit Margins (NPM) and consequently earnings per share (EPS) [1, 2]. Furthermore, the stated strategy of using contractual arrangements, including purchasing credits or offsets, to achieve ESG targets may face 'scrutiny from certain constituencies' [1, 2]. Such scrutiny could escalate reputational risks, leading to potential divestments by ESG-focused funds, affecting the firm's stock price (AVGSHAREPRICE, MBR, PS) and potentially its ability to raise capital on favorable terms. Moreover, persistent pressure from investors and lenders to adopt more aggressive ESG goals, which the Partnership may struggle to implement due to 'potential costs or technical or operational obstacles,' could further strain financial resources and limit strategic flexibility [1, 2]. Cumulatively, these governance factors could undermine the Partnership’s long-term competitive positioning by increasing operational costs, hindering access to capital, and eroding stakeholder trust, thereby placing downward pressure on ROCE and EPS and potentially impacting shareholder returns.

Analyze the broader impact of these governance-related challenges on ET's competitive positioning within the oil and gas midstream sector, considering market perception and strategic adaptability.

passages.text: Moreover, while we create and publish voluntary disclosures regarding ESG matters from time to time, many of the statements in those voluntary disclosures will be based on expectations, assumptions and hypothetical scenarios. Such expectations, assumptions and hypothetical scenarios are necessarily uncertain and may be prone to error or subject to misinterpretation given the long timelines involved and the lack of an established single approach to identifying, measuring, and reporting on many ESG matters. Additionally, while we may have or may announce various voluntary ESG targets in the future, such targets are often aspirational. We may not be able to meet such targets in the manner or on such a timeline as initially contemplated, including, but not limited to as a result of unforeseen costs or technical difficulties associated with achieving such results. To the extent we meet such targets, it may be achieved through various contractual arrangements, including the purchase of various credits or offsets that may be deemed to mitigate our ESG impact instead of actual changes in our business operations. Some of these arrangements may receive scrutiny from certain constituencies. Also, despite any aspirational goals, we may receive pressure from investors, lenders, or other groups to adopt more aggressive climate or other ESG-related goals, but we cannot guarantee that we will be able to implement such goals because of potential costs or technical or operational obstacles.

Moreover, while we create and publish voluntary disclosures regarding ESG matters from time to time, many of the statements in those voluntary disclosures will be based on expectations and assumptions. Such expectations and assumptions are necessarily uncertain and may be prone to error or subject to misinterpretation given the long timelines involved and the lack of an established single approach to identifying, measuring, and reporting on many ESG matters. Additionally, while we may also announce various voluntary ESG targets in the future, such targets are aspirational. We may not be able to meet such targets in the manner or on such a timeline as initially contemplated, including, but not limited to as a result of unforeseen costs or technical difficulties associated with achieving such results. To the extent that we do meet such targets, we may consider the acquisition of various credits or offsets that may be deemed to assist in the achievement of such targets or otherwise mitigate our ESG impact instead of actual achievements of such targets or actual changes in our ESG performance. Also, despite these aspirational goals, we may receive pressure from investors, lenders, or other groups to adopt more aggressive climate or other ESG-related goals, but we cannot guarantee that we will be able to implement such goals because of potential costs or technical or operational obstacles.

question: Analyze the trend in the fair value of ET's Mark-to-Market (Trading) Natural Gas Basis Swaps IFERC/NYMEX from December 31, 2023, to June 30, 2024, and evaluate the implications of the corresponding changes in sensitivity to hypothetical 10% price movements for the company's risk exposure.
answer: The fair value of ET's Mark-to-Market (Trading) Natural Gas Basis Swaps IFERC/NYMEX shifted from a $16MM asset at December 31, 2023 [2], to a $5MM liability at June 30, 2024 [3]. Concurrently, the sensitivity to a hypothetical 10% price change for these derivatives shifted from a $4MM asset to a $5MM asset, indicating an increased potential impact from price fluctuations [2, 3]. This trend suggests a significant change in market expectations for natural gas basis spreads or a strategic adjustment in ET's trading positions, which could materially alter the company's profit and loss from these speculative positions.

question: Analyze the significant shift in the fair value of ET's Fair Value Hedging Derivatives for Natural Gas Fixed Swaps/Futures from Dec 31, 2023, to Dec 31, 2024, and discuss the implications of the change in sensitivity to hypothetical price movements.
answer: ET's Fair Value Hedging Derivatives for Natural Gas Fixed Swaps/Futures experienced a substantial change, shifting from a $45MM asset at Dec 31, 2023, to a $4MM liability at Dec 31, 2024 [1]. Concurrently, the disclosed sensitivity to a hypothetical 10% price change for these instruments nearly doubled, increasing from $9MM in 2023 to $15MM in 2024 [1]. This dramatic reversal from an asset to a liability position, coupled with heightened price sensitivity, indicates either a fundamental change in the hedged exposure, a strategic adjustment in the hedging instruments themselves, or a significant shift in the natural gas forward curve. Such a change could materially impact future earnings stability if commodity prices move unfavorably.

question: Which executive officers are required to provide certifications under Section 302 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 for ET's 2025 10-K?
answer: For ET's 2025 10-K, the Co-Chief Executive Officers and the Chief Financial Officer are required to provide certifications pursuant to Section 302 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 [1]. These certifications are a crucial aspect of regulatory compliance, ensuring the integrity of financial reporting and overall corporate governance.

question: Considering ET's voluntary ESG targets and potential scrutiny, how might compliance with regulatory bodies like FERC and PHMSA influence the company's operational flexibility and strategic decisions regarding ESG initiatives?
answer: ET acknowledges that its voluntary ESG targets are aspirational and subject to scrutiny, with potential pressure from various groups for more aggressive goals [2]. Compliance with regulatory bodies such as the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), which oversee aspects of the energy industry, could influence operational flexibility by imposing standards for environmental impact or safety. This could lead to unforeseen costs or technical difficulties, affecting the feasibility, cost, and timeline of achieving ESG targets, thereby impacting strategic decisions in the midstream sector [2, 3].

passages.text: Moreover, while we create and publish voluntary disclosures regarding ESG matters from time to time, many of the statements in those voluntary disclosures will be based on expectations, assumptions and hypothetical scenarios. Such expectations, assumptions and hypothetical scenarios are necessarily uncertain and may be prone to error or subject to misinterpretation given the long timelines involved and the lack of an established single approach to identifying, measuring, and reporting on many ESG matters. Additionally, while we may have or may announce various voluntary ESG targets in the future, such targets are often aspirational. We may not be able to meet such targets in the manner or on such a timeline as initially contemplated, including, but not limited to as a result of unforeseen costs or technical difficulties associated with achieving such results. To the extent we meet such targets, it may be achieved through various contractual arrangements, including the purchase of various credits or offsets that may be deemed to mitigate our ESG impact instead of actual changes in our business operations. Some of these arrangements may receive scrutiny from certain constituencies. Also, despite any aspirational goals, we may receive pressure from investors, lenders, or other groups to adopt more aggressive climate or other ESG-related goals, but we cannot guarantee that we will be able to implement such goals because of potential costs or technical or operational obstacles.

QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK. General In the normal course of our business operations, we are exposed to certain risks, including changes in interest rates and commodity prices. In order to manage risks associated with assets, liabilities and certain anticipated future transactions, we use derivative instruments such as futures, forward contracts, swaps and other instruments with similar characteristics. Substantially all of our derivatives are used for non-trading activities. We assess the risk associated with each of our derivative instrument portfolios using a sensitivity analysis model. This approach measures the change in fair value of the derivative instrument portfolio based on a hypothetical 10% change in the underlying interest rates or quoted market prices on a particular day. In addition to these variables, the fair value of each portfolio is influenced by changes in the notional amounts of the instruments outstanding. The sensitivity analysis approach does not reflect the impact that the same hypothetical price movement would have on the hedged exposures to which they relate. Therefore, the impact on the fair value of a derivative instrument resulting from a change in interest rates or quoted market prices (as applicable) would normally be offset by a corresponding gain or loss on the hedged debt instrument, inventory value or forecasted transaction assuming:

Changes in U.S. trade policy and the impact of tariffs may have a material adverse effect on our business and results of operations. Our business and results of operations may be adversely affected by uncertainty and changes in U.S. trade policies, including tariffs, trade agreements or other trade restrictions imposed by the U.S. or other governments. These actions have caused uncertainty and volatility in financial markets, may result in retaliatory measures on U.S. goods and may adversely impact both the U.S. and global economies. Our business requires access to steel and other materials to construct and maintain our pipelines. While our practice is to source steel through domestic producers in the U.S. in most instances, any imposition of or increase in tariffs on imports of steel or other materials, as well as corresponding price increases for such materials available domestically, could increase our construction costs and our costs to maintain our assets. To the extent that we are unable to pass all or any such cost increases on to our customers, such cost increases could adversely affect our returns on investment. Higher materials costs could also diminish our ability to develop new projects at acceptable returns, particularly during times of economic uncertainty, and limit our ability to pursue growth opportunities. Tariffs or other trade restrictions may lead to continuing uncertainty and volatility in U.S. and global financial and economic conditions and commodity markets, inflation, and reduced demand for our and our customers’ products and services. Such conditions could have a material adverse impact on our business, results of operations and cash flows. Also, disruptions and volatility in the financial markets may lead to adverse changes in the availability, terms and cost of capital. Such adverse changes could increase our costs of capital and limit our access to external financing sources to fund acquisitions, capital projects, or refinancing of debt maturities on similar terms, which could in turn reduce our cash flows and limit our ability to pursue growth opportunities. 65 ITEM 2. question: Given the data from the past two fiscal years, what is the change in ET's total financial exposure to a hypothetical 10% movement in commodity prices across all Mark-to-Market (Trading) and Non-Trading derivative categories, including Natural Gas, Power, Crude, and NGL/Refined Products, from YE 2023 to YE 2024? Further, how has this change in exposure impacted the firm's overall risk profile concerning commodity price volatility?
answer:
ET's total financial exposure to a hypothetical 10% movement in commodity prices across all Mark-to-Market (Trading) and Non-Trading derivative categories increased by $28 MM from YE 2023 to YE 2024 [1, 2]. This indicates a higher sensitivity to commodity price volatility, potentially increasing the firm's overall risk profile concerning these fluctuations [1, 2].

**Detailed Calculation:**
**For YE 2023 (from ET-10-K-2024, page 53):**
*   **Mark-to-Market Derivatives (Trading):**
    *   Natural Gas (Basis Swaps IFERC/NYMEX): $4 MM [1]
    *   Power (Futures): $1 MM [1]
    *   Total Trading = $4 MM + $1 MM = $5 MM
*   **(Non-Trading) Derivatives:**
    *   Natural Gas (Basis Swaps IFERC/NYMEX): $1 MM [1]
    *   Natural Gas (Swing Swaps IFERC): $1 MM [1]
    *   Natural Gas (Fixed Swaps/Futures): $2 MM [1]
    *   Natural Gas (Forward Physical Contracts): $1 MM [1]
    *   NGL (Forwards/Swaps): $43 MM [1]
    *   Crude (Forwards/Swaps): $5 MM [1]
    *   Refined Products (Futures): $38 MM [1]
    *   Total Non-Trading = $1 MM + $1 MM + $2 MM + $1 MM + $43 MM + $5 MM + $38 MM = $91 MM
*   **Fair Value Hedging Derivatives (Non-Trading):**
    *   Natural Gas (Basis Swaps IFERC/NYMEX): $1 MM [1]
    *   Natural Gas (Fixed Swaps/Futures): $9 MM [1]
    *   Total Hedging = $1 MM + $9 MM = $10 MM
*   **Total YE 2023 Exposure:** $5 MM (Trading) + $91 MM (Non-Trading) + $10 MM (Hedging) = $106 MM

**For YE 2024 (from ET-10-K-2025, page 51):**
*   **Mark-to-Market Derivatives (Trading):**
    *   Natural Gas (Fixed Swaps/Futures): $3 MM [2]
    *   Natural Gas (Basis Swaps IFERC/NYMEX): $3 MM [2]
    *   Power (Futures): $1 MM [2]
    *   Crude (Forward/Swaps): $39 MM [2]
    *   NGL/Refined Products (Forwards/Swaps): $58 MM [2]
    *   NGL/Refined Products (Futures): $13 MM [2]
    *   Total Trading = $3 MM + $3 MM + $1 MM + $39 MM + $58 MM + $13 MM = $117 MM
*   **Fair Value Hedging Derivatives:**
    *   Natural Gas (Basis Swaps IFERC/NYMEX): $2 MM [2]
    *   Natural Gas (Fixed Swaps/Futures): $15 MM [2]
    *   Total Hedging = $2 MM + $15 MM = $17 MM
*   **Total YE 2024 Exposure:** $117 MM (Trading) + $17 MM (Hedging) = $134 MM

**Change in Total Exposure (YE 2023 to YE 2024):**
$134 MM - $106 MM = $28 MM increase.

question: Analysts are keen to understand the implications of ET's voluntary ESG targets. Can management elaborate on the potential risks associated with not meeting these aspirational goals as initially contemplated, considering the long timelines and technical difficulties involved?
answer: ET's voluntary ESG targets are aspirational and based on inherently uncertain expectations, assumptions, and hypothetical scenarios, especially given the long timelines and the absence of a single established reporting methodology [3, 4]. The company acknowledges the risk of not achieving these goals due to unforeseen costs or technical difficulties [3, 4]. Additionally, while ET may utilize various contractual arrangements, including credits or offsets, to mitigate its ESG impact, such methods might face scrutiny from certain constituencies [3, 4]. Furthermore, ET could face pressure from investors, lenders, or other groups to adopt more aggressive climate or ESG-related objectives, which might not be implementable due to potential costs or operational/technical obstacles [3, 4].

question: Can you discuss ET's strategy for managing commodity price risk, specifically detailing the types of derivative instruments utilized for non-trading activities and how these instruments help mitigate risks associated with assets, liabilities, and forecasted transactions?
answer: ET actively manages its commodity price risk through a strategy primarily involving non-trading derivative instruments such as futures, forward contracts, and swaps [1, 2]. These instruments are deployed to hedge exposures tied to the firm's assets, liabilities, and anticipated future transactions [1, 2]. For Natural Gas, ET utilizes Basis Swaps (IFERC/NYMEX), Swing Swaps (IFERC), Fixed Swaps/Futures, and Forward Physical Contracts [1, 2]. Similarly, for NGL, Crude, and Refined Products, the company employs Forwards/Swaps and Futures [1, 2]. This approach allows ET to offset the potential impact of hypothetical price movements on their hedged exposures, thereby mitigating overall commodity price volatility risk [1, 2].

##### PART I. FINANCIAL INFORMATION
#### ITEM 3. QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
###### EOG RESOURCES, INC.
EOG's exposure to commodity price risk, interest rate risk and foreign currency exchange rate risk is discussed in (i) the "Financial Commodity Derivative Transactions," "Financing" and "Outlook" sections of "Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations - Capital Resources and Liquidity" included in EOG's Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2023, filed on February 22, 2024 (EOG's 2023 Annual Report); and (ii) Note 12, "Risk Management Activities," to EOG's Consolidated Financial Statements included in EOG's 2023 Annual Report. For updated information regarding EOG's financial commodity and other derivative contracts and physical commodity contracts, see (i) Note 12, "Risk Management Activities" to EOG's Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements in this Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q; (ii) "Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations - Results of Operations - Operating Revenues" in this Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q; and (iii) "Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations - Capital Resources and Liquidity - Financial Commodity and Other Derivative Transactions" in this Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q.

General In the normal course of our business operations, we are exposed to certain risks, including changes in interest rates and commodity prices. In order to manage risks associated with assets, liabilities and certain anticipated future transactions, we use derivative instruments such as futures, forward contracts, swaps and other instruments with similar characteristics. Substantially all of our derivatives are used for non-trading activities. We assess the risk associated with each of our derivative instrument portfolios using a sensitivity analysis model. This approach measures the change in fair value of the derivative instrument portfolio based on a hypothetical 10% change in the underlying interest rates or quoted market prices on a particular day. In addition to these variables, the fair value of each portfolio is influenced by changes in the notional amounts of the instruments outstanding. The sensitivity analysis approach does not reflect the impact that the same hypothetical price movement would have on the hedged exposures to which they relate. Therefore, the impact on the fair value of a derivative instrument resulting from a change in interest rates or quoted market prices (as applicable) would normally be offset by a corresponding gain or loss on the hedged debt instrument, inventory value or forecasted transaction assuming:

question: Analyze the total net fair value change of ET's commodity-related financial derivative instruments (both assets and liabilities) from Dec 31, 2024 to June 30, 2025. Quantify the change and explain how it could influence the company's `EVEBITDA` multiple and ultimately `AVGSHAREPRICE`.
answer: The total net fair value of ET's commodity-related financial derivative instruments shifted from a net liability of $30 MM at Dec 31, 2024 [1] to a net asset of $79 MM at June 30, 2025 [3], representing a positive change of $109 MM. This significant improvement in the net fair value of derivatives could positively impact ET's reported earnings and cash flows, thereby enhancing its `EVEBITDA` multiple. A higher `EVEBITDA` generally signals stronger financial performance and can lead to a rise in the `AVGSHAREPRICE` as investors perceive reduced risk and improved profitability.

question: How might ET's approach to voluntary ESG disclosures and aspirational targets, as outlined in its 2025 10-K, influence investor sentiment and potentially affect valuation metrics such as its `MBR` and `AVGPE`?
answer: ET's voluntary ESG disclosures and aspirational targets, as noted in its 2025 10-K, rely on uncertain expectations, assumptions, and hypothetical scenarios, which may be prone to error [4]. The company acknowledges potential unforeseen costs or technical difficulties in meeting these targets, and may use credits or offsets, which could face scrutiny [4]. Furthermore, ET anticipates potential pressure from investors to adopt more aggressive ESG goals, which could be challenging due to costs or operational obstacles [4]. This inherent uncertainty and the possibility of external scrutiny regarding ESG initiatives could lead to mixed investor sentiment. While transparent ESG reporting can attract capital and improve `MBR` by signaling long-term sustainability, any perceived shortcomings or reliance on offsets without fundamental operational changes might deter ESG-focused investors, potentially impacting the company's `AVGPE` multiple and overall `MBR` negatively.

Such expectations, assumptions and hypothetical scenarios are necessarily uncertain and may be prone to error or subject to misinterpretation given the long timelines involved and the lack of an established single approach to identifying, measuring, and reporting on many ESG matters. Additionally, while we may have or may announce various voluntary ESG targets in the future, such targets are often aspirational. We may not be able to meet such targets in the manner or on such a timeline as initially contemplated, including, but not limited to as a result of unforeseen costs or technical difficulties associated with achieving such results. To the extent we meet such targets, it may be achieved through various contractual arrangements, including the purchase of various credits or offsets that may be deemed to mitigate our ESG impact instead of actual changes in our business operations. Some of these arrangements may receive scrutiny from certain constituencies. Also, despite any aspirational goals, we may receive pressure from investors, lenders, or other groups to adopt more aggressive climate or other ESG-related goals, but we cannot guarantee that we will be able to implement such goals because of potential costs or technical or operational obstacles.

question: Analyze the key revenue and expense drivers across ET's Transmission & Gulf of America and NGL & Refined Products T&S segments for the six months ended June 30, 2025. How do these operational aspects qualitatively inform a perspective on the company's ability to generate strong `ROCE` and sustain `AVGSHAREPRICE`?
answer: For the six months ended June 30, 2025, ET's Transmission & Gulf of America segment generated total revenues of $2,584 MM, with service revenues being the dominant component at $2,311 MM external and internal, and product sales contributing $223 MM [5]. Its Modified EBITDA was $1,749 MM [5]. The NGL & Refined Products Transportation and Services (T&S) segment reported total revenues of $12,850 MM, primarily from external customer revenues of $11,063 MM, with product sales reaching $1,940 MM [5]. This segment achieved a Modified EBITDA of $3,581 MM [5]. Both segments demonstrate strong revenue generation, with NGL & Refined Products T&S showing significantly higher revenue and EBITDA. The growth in service revenues indicates stable, fee-based income, which generally signals lower business risk and consistent cash flows. Strong and growing Modified EBITDA from these core segments suggests efficient operations and profitability. Qualitatively, these operational aspects highlight ET's capacity to generate robust earnings, which are crucial for a healthy `ROCE`. Sustained high `ROCE` is a key indicator of efficient capital allocation and profitability, which typically underpins a favorable `AVGSHAREPRICE` and long-term shareholder value.

question: Compute the year-over-year growth rate in refined products sales for MPC's Refining & Marketing segment for the three months ended June 30, 2025, compared to the same period in the prior year.
answer: For the three months ended June 30, 2025, MPC's Refining & Marketing segment reported refined products sales of $29,945 million [1]. The year-over-year growth rate is calculated as (($29,945 MM - $34,094 MM) / $34,094 MM) * 100%, which results in a decrease of approximately 12.17%.

question: Analyze MPC's strategic approach to managing its diverse portfolio of investments across Refining & Marketing, Midstream, and Renewable Diesel, and qualitatively assess how the forward-looking statements regarding market conditions and commodity prices could influence the valuation and future performance of these segments.
answer: MPC manages a diverse portfolio of investments across its Refining & Marketing, Midstream, and Renewable Diesel segments [4]. For example, in R&M, it holds a 50% ownership in The Andersons Marathon Holdings LLC with a carrying value of $190 MM. In Midstream, notable investments include 45% in BANGL ($281 MM), 41% in LOOP LLC ($310 MM), and 50% in Sherwood Midstream LLC ($488 MM). The Renewable Diesel segment includes a 50% interest in Martinez Renewables LLC with a carrying value of $1,184 MM [4]. MPC characterizes its forward-looking statements as subject to risks, contingencies, or uncertainties, emphasizing that actual outcomes may differ materially from expectations [3]. Key commodity price benchmarks and products relevant to MPC's operations include WTI crude oil, NGLs, and refined products traded on exchanges like NYMEX [5]. Qualitatively, significant changes in WTI prices could directly impact the profitability of the Refining & Marketing segment by affecting crude input costs and refined product margins. Similarly, fluctuations in NGL prices would influence both the Midstream and potentially Renewable Diesel segments, depending on feedstock costs or product sales. According to MPC, these market risks and other uncertainties could cause actual results to vary materially from anticipated outcomes, thereby influencing the valuation and future performance across its segments [3].

We assess the risk associated with each of our derivative instrument portfolios using a sensitivity analysis model. This approach measures the change in fair value of the derivative instrument portfolio based on a hypothetical 10% change in the underlying interest rates or quoted market prices on a particular day. In addition to these variables, the fair value of each portfolio is influenced by changes in the notional amounts of the instruments outstanding. The sensitivity analysis approach does not reflect the impact that the same hypothetical price movement would have on the hedged exposures to which they relate. Therefore, the impact on the fair value of a derivative instrument resulting from a change in interest rates or quoted market prices (as applicable) would normally be offset by a corresponding gain or loss on the hedged debt instrument, inventory value or forecasted transaction assuming:

answer: MPC discloses internal corporate governance policies such as a 'Trading of Securities Policy' and a 'Marathon Petroleum Corporation Officer Compensation Clawback Policy' as exhibits. These policies aim to maintain market integrity, reduce potential financial and reputational risks, and align management incentives with long-term shareholder returns, thereby positively influencing firm value and investor confidence [2].

question: Analyze the diverse ownership structures within MPC's Midstream segment, specifically distinguishing between entities marked as VIEs and other joint ventures, and discuss what these structures generally imply for financial reporting and the company’s DER.
answer: Within MPC's Midstream segment, the ownership structures vary significantly. For entities such as MarkWest EMG Jefferson Dry Gas Gathering Company, L.L.C. (67% owned) and MarkWest Utica EMG, L.L.C. (59% owned), both explicitly marked as VIEs, MPC holds a controlling financial interest. This generally implies these entities would be fully consolidated onto MPC's financial statements, meaning their total assets and liabilities, including debt, would be reflected on MPC's balance sheet. Conversely, other JVs like BANGL (45% owned) and Illinois Extension Pipeline Company, L.L.C. (35% owned) are not marked as VIEs and have less than 50% ownership, suggesting they are typically accounted for using the equity method. Under this method, only MPC's share of net income (loss) flows through its income statement, and the investment is recorded on the balance sheet, but the full assets and liabilities, including debt, of these JVs are not. These varied structures allow MPC to manage different levels of control and risk exposure, directly influencing how total debt and equity are reported, which in turn impacts the company’s Debt-to-Equity Ratio (DER) [3].

With regards to commodity derivatives, our Level 3 fair values primarily consist of the following commodity derivative instruments used to hedge various inventories and transportation capacities: (i) NGL, crude, natural gas, refined products and commercial energy-based contracts with terms greater than 36 months; (ii) over-the-counter options; and (iii) exchange traded options with terms greater than one year. In addition, we often rely on price quotes from reputable brokers who publish price quotes on certain products and compare these prices to other reputable brokers for the same products in the same markets whenever possible. These prices, when combined with data from our commodity derivative instruments, are used in our models to determine the fair value of such instruments. Our nonrecurring fair value estimates are generally based on the income approach to fair value and reflect various Level 3 inputs. In many cases, there are no active markets (a Level 1 fair value measure) to rely on or other similar recent transactions (a Level 2 fair value measure) to compare to. Our nonrecurring fair value estimates often include management’s expectations of the residual market values for the underlying assets based on their knowledge and experience in the industry (a Level 3 fair value measure). Other examples of Level 3 inputs used in the valuation models include anticipated gross operating margins, throughput or processing volumes, utilization factors, sustaining capital expenditures, discount rates and business growth rates. When probability weights are used in cash flow modeling, the weights are generally obtained from management personnel having oversight responsibilities for the assets being tested.

question: Analyze the YoY change in MPC's Q2 share repurchase program activity from 2024 to 2025, considering the total number of shares purchased and the avg price paid per share.
answer: MPC's Q2 share repurchase activity saw a significant decrease from 2024 to 2025. In Q2 2024, MPC purchased a total of 15,743,304 shares at an average price of $183.91 per share [1]. By Q2 2025, the total number of shares purchased dropped to 4,762,547, with an average price paid per share of $145.32 [2]. This represents a (4,762,547 - 15,743,304) / 15,743,304 = -69.7% decrease in the total number of shares repurchased, and a ($145.32 - $183.91) / $183.91 = -21.0% decrease in the average price paid per share.

ITEM 7A. QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK. General In the normal course of our business operations, we are exposed to certain risks, including changes in interest rates and commodity prices. In order to manage risks associated with assets, liabilities and certain anticipated future transactions, we use derivative instruments such as futures, forward contracts, swaps and other instruments with similar characteristics. Substantially all of our derivatives are used for non-trading activities. We assess the risk associated with each of our derivative instrument portfolios using a sensitivity analysis model. This approach measures the change in fair value of the derivative instrument portfolio based on a hypothetical 10% change in the underlying interest rates or quoted market prices on a particular day. In addition to these variables, the fair value of each portfolio is influenced by changes in the notional amounts of the instruments outstanding. The sensitivity analysis approach does not reflect the impact that the same hypothetical price movement would have on the hedged exposures to which they relate. Therefore, the impact on the fair value of a derivative instrument resulting from a change in interest rates or quoted market prices (as applicable) would normally be offset by a corresponding gain or loss on the hedged debt instrument, inventory value or forecasted transaction assuming:

question: How do MPC's insider trading policies and officer compensation clawback policies align with the company's overall risk management framework, particularly regarding forward-looking statements and potential financial misconduct?
answer: MPC's 'Trading of Securities Policy' and 'Marathon Petroleum Corporation Officer Compensation Clawback Policy' are integral to its risk management framework, aiming to uphold financial integrity and mitigate misconduct [3]. The Trading of Securities Policy likely governs how employees and officers can trade MPC securities, preventing the use of material non-public information, while the Clawback Policy enables the company to recover erroneously awarded compensation in cases of misconduct or misstated financial results. These policies bolster the company's commitment to ethical conduct and transparency. MPC's forward-looking statements include cautionary language that highlights risks, contingencies, or uncertainties, identified by words such as “anticipate,” “believe,” “commitment,” and “expect” [4, 5]. By enforcing strict insider trading rules, MPC aims to ensure fair markets and prevent information asymmetry. The Clawback Policy serves as a disincentive for financial misrepresentation, aligning executive incentives with accurate financial reporting and long-term value creation. Together, these policies enhance corporate governance by addressing potential areas of financial misconduct, safeguarding shareholder interests, and reinforcing the reliability of its disclosures amidst the inherent risks outlined in its cautionary statements [3-5].

question: Evaluate how MPC's various executive and director compensation plans, including severance, deferred compensation, and thrift plans, are structured to incentivize long-term value creation and mitigate excessive risk-taking, particularly in light of industry competition and market risks.
answer: MPC's compensation framework, including the 'Marathon Petroleum Corporation Senior Leader Change in Control Severance Benefits Plan,' 'Marathon Petroleum Corporation Deferred Compensation Plan for Non-Employee Directors,' and the 'Marathon Petroleum Thrift Plan,' aims to align executive incentives with long-term value creation while managing risk [3, 6]. These plans are designed to attract and retain key talent in a competitive industry. The severance plan provides security in change-of-control scenarios, potentially allowing executives to focus on company performance rather than personal job security during transitions. Deferred compensation plans for directors encourage long-term commitment and ownership, as payouts are typically tied to future company performance or tenure. Thrift plans, often retirement savings vehicles, also foster long-term financial planning. MPC's financial statements also refer to general 'Incentive Programs' [7]. The design of these programs implicitly considers the competitive landscape in the Oil & Gas Refining & Marketing industry and external market risks such as commodity price volatility, as detailed in the 'Market Risks' section of its financial filings. By linking compensation to performance metrics over extended periods and incorporating various plan types, MPC endeavors to discourage short-term, high-risk endeavors that could jeopardize sustained company health, thereby mitigating excessive risk-taking and fostering strategic decision-making in a challenging market environment [3, 6, 7].

question: Based on MPC's 2024 10-K, elucidate the company's inventory costing method, referencing the relevant abbreviation and discussing its implications for financial reporting.
answer: MPC utilizes the LIFO (Last in, first out) inventory costing method, as explicitly stated in its 2024 10-K glossary [3]. The LIFO method assumes that the latest inventory purchased is the first one sold. While the qualitative implications are not detailed in this definitional entry, typically, during periods of rising costs, LIFO results in a higher cost of goods sold (COGS) and lower taxable income, thus reducing tax liabilities. Conversely, in periods of declining costs, LIFO would lead to lower COGS and higher taxable income [3].

question: Assess the evolving commodity price exposure risk for MPC's Refining & Marketing (R&M) segment by calculating the percentage contribution of Refined Products revenue to total R&M segment revenue for the three months ended June 30, 2025, June 30, 2024, and September 30, 2024. Analyze the trend and discuss the implications for MPC's overall R&M market risk profile.
answer:
For the three months ended June 30, 2025, MPC's R&M segment reported Refined Products revenue of $29,945 MM and total R&M revenue of $31,828 MM [1]. This yields a percentage contribution of Refined Products to total R&M revenue of ($29,945 / $31,828) * 100% = 94.08%.

For the three months ended June 30, 2024, the R&M segment reported Refined Products revenue of $34,094 MM and total R&M revenue of $36,654 MM [2]. This results in a percentage contribution of Refined Products of ($34,094 / $36,654) * 100% = 93.02%.

For the three months ended September 30, 2024, the R&M segment reported Refined Products revenue of $31,462 MM and total R&M revenue of $33,775 MM [3]. This gives a percentage contribution of Refined Products of ($31,462 / $33,775) * 100% = 93.16%.

Analysis of Trend:
The percentage contribution of Refined Products to total R&M segment revenue showed a slight increase over these periods: 93.02% in Q2 2024, rising marginally to 93.16% in Q3 2024, and further to 94.08% in Q2 2025. This trend indicates a consistent, and even slightly increasing, dominance of refined product sales within the R&M segment's revenue mix.

Implications for MPC's R&M market risk profile:
This sustained high reliance on refined product revenues suggests that the R&M segment's market risk profile is predominantly influenced by factors affecting the demand and pricing of refined products, such as consumer behavior, economic conditions, and refining margins (crack spreads), rather than direct crude oil price volatility. While crude oil is a key input, the segment's exposure is more to the differential between input and output prices. The slight upward trend in refined product contribution could imply a marginal shift towards a more integrated refining model, potentially aiming to optimize crack spreads and capture more value downstream, which inherently carries its own set of market risks related to processing costs, operational efficiency, and regional demand dynamics for various refined fuels [1-3].

question: Discuss the regulatory environment and its associated risks influencing MPC's Renewable Diesel segment, specifically considering the impact of programs like RFS2 and the market for RINs.
answer:
MPC's Renewable Diesel segment operates within a regulatory framework significantly influenced by programs like RFS2 (Revised Renewable Fuel Standard program) and the market for RINs (Renewable Identification Numbers) [4, 5]. The RFS2 program, as required by the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007, mandates minimum volumes of renewable fuels to be blended into the U.S. transportation fuel supply [4, 5]. To demonstrate compliance, refiners and importers must acquire RINs, which are credits generated by producing or importing renewable fuels [4, 5].

This regulatory structure introduces inherent risks to MPC's renewable diesel operations. Fluctuations in RIN prices, driven by supply and demand for these credits, can directly impact the profitability and competitiveness of producing and selling renewable diesel. Significant changes to RFS2 mandates, either through legislative amendments or EPA rulings, could alter the demand for renewable fuels and, consequently, the value of RINs, leading to increased compliance costs or reduced margins for MPC's Renewable Diesel segment [4, 5]. Furthermore, the broader political and environmental policy landscape surrounding renewable fuels is dynamic, presenting ongoing uncertainty and potential for regulatory shifts that could either create opportunities or pose challenges to MPC's investments and strategic direction in this area. Managing these regulatory complexities, including potential enforcement actions by bodies like the EPA, is a critical component of MPC's risk mitigation strategy for its Renewable Diesel business [4, 5].

OVERVIEW

We are an independent oil and gas company engaged in the development, exploration and production of oil, natural gas and NGLs. Our operations are focused in the Permian Basin in Texas and New Mexico, the Marcellus Shale in Pennsylvania and West Virginia and the Anadarko Basin in Oklahoma. Our business strategy is to develop our resource base in these areas and to optimize the value of our assets by focusing on returns, generating free cash flow and maintaining a strong balance sheet. We actively manage our portfolio, prioritizing projects with the highest returns and adjusting our activity levels based on commodity price outlooks, service costs, capital availability and other market dynamics. We also continue to evaluate opportunities to enhance our inventory of drilling locations through acquisitions, trades, leasing and other transactions that align with our strategy.

Our revenues, profitability and future growth are substantially dependent upon prevailing prices for oil, natural gas and NGLs, which are influenced by factors beyond our control, including the supply of and demand for oil, natural gas and NGLs, the level of inventory and storage capacity, economic growth, weather conditions, transportation constraints, export capacity, geopolitical events, production and export quotas established by OPEC and other producing countries, and the value of the U.S. dollar. Because natural gas comprised a significant portion of our production in the most recent periods, natural gas prices have a greater impact on our results than oil prices. Natural gas prices are historically cyclical and can be volatile. Changes in natural gas prices may materially affect our cash flows, profitability and levels of activity.

We seek to mitigate our exposure to commodity price volatility by entering into derivative financial instruments. We utilize these instruments to hedge a portion of our forecasted production, which provides a degree of predictability to cash flows and supports our planned capital program. Our hedging activities are designed to protect a portion of our projected cash flows, reduce the impact of commodity price fluctuations and support our ability to execute our development plans. However, our hedging program is not without risk and is intended to provide partial protection against future price volatility; it is not intended to, and will not, eliminate all price-related risks.

We maintain a disciplined approach to capital allocation. Our capital program is focused on optimizing returns by allocating capital to projects with attractive rates of return and by maintaining a balance between growth and free cash flow generation. We continue to invest in infrastructure, technology and operational efficiencies to improve well performance, reduce costs and enhance safety and environmental performance. Our capital program is funded primarily through operating cash flows, supplemented by our cash on hand and, when appropriate, borrowings under our revolving credit facility. We believe this approach provides flexibility to adjust our activities and spending based on market conditions.

Operationally, we continue to prioritize safety, environmental stewardship and regulatory compliance. We are committed to minimizing environmental impacts and reducing emissions through the application of best practices, investing in emissions-reducing technologies, and engaging with stakeholders. We have initiatives focused on reducing flaring, improving water management practices, minimizing methane emissions, and increasing transparency in our reporting.

We also focus on maintaining a strong liquidity position and balance sheet. Our financial position provides flexibility to manage through commodity price cycles, invest in our core operating areas and pursue opportunities that enhance shareholder value. We continually assess our leverage, liquidity and capital structure and may opportunistically refinance or repay debt to reduce interest costs and extend maturities. We believe our current liquidity and financial strength, combined with our asset base and operating capabilities, position us to continue executing on our strategy and delivering long-term value to our shareholders.

Our operating results for the period reflect the influence of commodity price volatility, cost inflation and supply chain constraints, as well as efficiencies gained from ongoing optimization of drilling and completion designs. We continue to monitor market conditions, including the availability and cost of services, inflationary pressures, and potential changes in regulations. We may adjust our development plans in response to these and other factors to maintain capital efficiency and protect returns.

We remain focused on generating sustainable free cash flow and returning capital to shareholders through dividends and, when appropriate, share repurchases, while maintaining operational flexibility and a strong balance sheet. Our long-term strategy is to deliver returns-focused growth by developing our high-quality resource base in the Permian Basin, Marcellus Shale and Anadarko Basin.

question: Mgmt view on further CapEx in E&P?
answer: CTRA management maintains a disciplined 2025 CapEx program of $2.0–$2.3 billion, fully funded from operating cash flow, with the Permian Basin as the clear priority. Activity levels are broadly consistent with prior-year execution, and the company expects 175–205 net wells to be brought online. While the plan is anchored in annual guidance, management retains flexibility to adjust spending in response to commodity price conditions.

Outlook
Our 2025 full year capital program is expected to be in the range of approximately $2.0 billion to $2.3 billion. We expect to fund these capital expenditures with our operating cash flow. We expect to turn-in-line 175 to 205 total net wells in 2025 across our three operating regions. We expect to invest approximately 67 percent of our capital expenditures in the Permian Basin, 14 percent in the Marcellus Shale, 11 percent in the Anadarko Basin and the remaining eight percent for gathering systems infrastructure, saltwater disposal and other capital expenditures.

In 2024, we drilled 313 gross wells (159.4 net) and turned-in-line 294 gross wells (153.0 net). For the three months ended March 31, 2025, our capital program focused on the Permian Basin, Marcellus Shale and Anadarko Basin, where we drilled 50.7 net wells and turned in line 37.3 net wells. Our capital program for the remainder of 2025 will focus on execution of our 2025 plan presented in our annual guidance. In the normal course of our business, we will continue to assess the oil and natural gas price macro environments and may adjust our capital allocation accordingly.

We strive to maintain an adequate liquidity level to address commitments, both short-term and long-term. We believe that we have sufficient capacity to repay our debt and other obligations as they become due over the next 12 months and, based on current expectations, for the longer term.

Our primary sources of liquidity are cash on hand, net cash provided by operating activities and availability under our revolving credit agreement. As of December 31, 2023, we had no borrowings outstanding under our revolving credit agreement, our borrowing base and aggregate elected commitments were $1.5 billion, and we had unrestricted cash on hand of $956 million. We may from time to time access the capital markets to supplement our liquidity and for other corporate purposes, which could include the issuance of debt or equity securities, repurchases, redemptions, exchanges or other adjustments of outstanding debt, acquisitions, investments, working capital, capital expenditures and other general corporate purposes. The timing and amount of any such transactions will be subject to market conditions and other factors.

We expect our cash on hand, net cash provided by operating activities and availability under our revolving credit agreement to be sufficient to fund our operations, service our debt, pay our dividends and meet our other obligations as they become due for at least the next 12 months and, based on current expectations, for the longer term.

Public Policy and Government Regulation

Our industry is subject to a wide range of governmental regulations and policies that are continuously changing. These regulations and policies affect, among other things, exploration and development operations, production, handling, storage, transportation and disposal of oil, gas and NGLs, environmental and safety matters, the emission and discharge of materials into the environment, and the acquisition of properties and mineral rights. Governmental actions can also affect demand for our products and services and may, among other things, impose taxes, fees and other costs, restrict access to, and use of, various lands, and increase compliance and operating costs. We cannot predict the nature or extent of future legislative and regulatory changes, and such changes could materially affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.

The following are significant areas of government control and regulation affecting our business:

Exploration and Production Regulation

Our operations are subject to various federal, state, tribal and local laws and regulations that affect exploration and production activities, including with respect to:

acquisition of seismic data;

design, location, drilling and casing of wells;

hydraulic fracturing;

well production, and the gathering and transportation of such production;

spill prevention plans;

emissions and discharge permitting;

use, transportation, storage and disposal of fluids and materials incidental to exploration and production; and

funding of plugging and abandonment obligations.

These and other laws and regulations can require us to obtain permits before commencing drilling and other operations, restrict the substances that can be released, require remedial measures to mitigate pollution from past and ongoing operations, and impose substantial liabilities for pollution resulting from our operations. Failure to comply with these laws and regulations may result in the assessment of administrative, civil and criminal penalties, the imposition of remedial obligations, and the issuance of orders enjoining some or all of our operations.

Environmental Regulation

We are subject to complex and changing environmental laws and regulations that may result in increased costs, restrictions on operations and delays in the permitting of projects. Areas of particular focus include the regulation of air emissions, water discharges, waste management and disposal, and protection of natural resources. Certain air emissions from oil and gas operations are regulated by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and by state environmental agencies. The EPA has adopted and proposed regulations that limit emissions of methane and volatile organic compounds from certain oil and gas operations, and additional regulations may be adopted in the future.

Other environmental regulatory matters include the Clean Water Act, which regulates discharges into waters of the United States, and the Safe Drinking Water Act, which regulates underground injection activities, including the disposal of produced water and hydraulic fracturing fluids. Additional federal or state measures to further regulate hydraulic fracturing, including restrictions on water sourcing or disposal, could increase the costs of drilling and completion activities and delay or curtail our operations.

In addition, we are subject to laws and regulations governing the handling, storage, transportation and disposal of solid and hazardous wastes, as well as releases of hazardous substances. These laws impose strict, joint and several liability for the costs of investigation and cleanup of contaminated sites, and such costs can be substantial.

Because the adoption, implementation and enforcement of new laws and regulations, or changes to existing laws and regulations, may occur over time and at different levels of government, we cannot predict the ultimate cost of compliance. Changes in laws and regulations, or the interpretation thereof, could result in significant increases in our operating or capital expenditures or otherwise adversely affect our business, financial condition or results of operations.

question: CTRA assessment of unproved O&G properties?
answer: CTRA capitalizes acquisition costs of unproved oil and gas properties but expenses ongoing carrying and exploration costs. These unproved assets are evaluated periodically on an aggregate basis for impairment, considering lease terms, drilling success, and likelihood of conversion to production. If leases are unlikely to be developed or expire, their value is written down. Overall, the carrying amount of unproved properties depends heavily on acreage life, exploration activity, and the company’s ability to convert leases into producing assets.

passages.text:
Oil and Gas Properties

The Company uses the successful efforts method of accounting for oil and gas producing activities. Under this method, acquisition costs for proved and unproved properties are capitalized when incurred. Exploration costs, including geological and geophysical costs, the costs of carrying and retaining unproved properties and exploratory dry hole drilling costs, are expensed. Development costs, including the costs to drill and equip development wells and successful exploratory drilling costs to locate proved reserves are capitalized.

Exploratory drilling costs are capitalized when incurred pending the determination of whether a well has found proved reserves. The determination is based on a process which relies on interpretations of available geologic, geophysical and engineering data. If a well is determined to be successful, the capitalized drilling costs will be reclassified as part of the cost of the well. If a well is determined to be unsuccessful, the capitalized drilling costs will be charged to exploration expense in the Consolidated Statement of Operations in the period the determination is made. If an exploratory well requires a major capital expenditure before production can begin, the cost of drilling the exploratory well will continue to be carried as an asset pending determination of whether reserves have been found only as long as: (1) the well has found a sufficient quantity of reserves to justify its completion as a producing well if the required capital expenditure is made and (2) drilling of an additional exploratory well is under way or firmly planned for the near future. If drilling in the area is not under way or firmly planned or if the well has not found a commercially producible quantity of reserves, the exploratory well is assumed to be impaired and its costs are charged to exploration expense.

Development costs of proved oil and gas properties, including estimated dismantlement, restoration and abandonment costs and acquisition costs, are depreciated and depleted on a field basis by the unit-of-production method using both proved developed and proved reserves.

Costs of sold or abandoned properties that make up a part of an amortization base (partial field) remain in the amortization base if the unit-of-production rate is not significantly affected. If significant, a gain or loss, if any, is recognized and the sold or abandoned properties are retired. A gain or loss, if any, is also recognized when a group of proved properties (entire field) that make up the amortization base has been retired, abandoned or sold.

The Company evaluates its proved oil and gas properties for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate an asset’s carrying amount may not be recoverable. The Company compares expected undiscounted future cash flows to the net book value of the asset. If the future undiscounted expected cash flows, based on estimates of future commodity prices, operating costs and anticipated production from proved reserves and risk-adjusted probable and possible reserves, are lower than the net book value of the asset, the capitalized cost is reduced to fair value. Commodity pricing is estimated by using a combination of assumptions management uses in its budgeting and forecasting process as well as historical and current prices adjusted for geographical location and quality differentials, as well as other factors that management believes will impact realizable prices. Fair value is calculated by discounting the future cash flows. The discount factor used is based on rates utilized by market participants that are commensurate with the risks inherent in the development and production of the underlying oil and natural gas.

Unproved oil and gas properties are assessed periodically for impairment on an aggregate basis through periodic updates to the Company’s unproved acreage amortization based on past drilling and exploration experience, the Company’s expectation of converting leases to held by production and average property lives. Average property lives are determined on a geographical basis and based on the estimated life of unproved property leasehold rights.
