Lease Terms and Expiration

Our leases typically have primary terms ranging from three to five years, with options for renewal or extension in certain cases. Lease terms may also include drilling or continuous operations provisions which, if satisfied, can extend the lease beyond the primary term. The expiration of undeveloped leases can impact our development plans and inventory of future drilling locations. We manage our lease expiration profile by prioritizing development activities in areas with near-term expirations and by selectively pursuing lease extensions or renewals where economic returns are attractive. We also seek to reduce lease expiration risk by securing drilling commitments or undertaking timely operations where appropriate.

We intend to continue to evaluate our leasehold position and development plans to ensure that we are allocating capital to the highest-return opportunities and managing lease expiration risks in a disciplined manner. We believe that our inventory of undeveloped acreage, combined with our development capabilities and operational efficiencies, positions us to continue to create long-term value for our shareholders.

Oil and Gas Assets Accounting, Classification, Reserves & Valuation

Successful Efforts Method of Accounting and Classification

We utilize the successful efforts method of accounting for our oil and gas exploration and production activities. Under this method, costs of acquiring properties are capitalized when incurred and are amortized over the expected life of the reserves. Costs of exploratory wells are capitalized pending the determination of whether proved reserves have been discovered and are charged to expense if the well is determined to be non-productive. Development costs are capitalized as assets and include costs incurred to access proved reserves and ready them for production. We also classify capitalized costs as either developmental or exploratory based on the nature of the activities undertaken. This classification affects the timing and method of amortization as well as impairment testing.

Exploration costs, including geological and geophysical costs and delay rentals, are expensed as incurred. Leasehold acquisition costs, including bonuses and other consideration paid to acquire mineral interests, are capitalized. Costs associated with drilling exploratory wells are capitalized pending the determination of whether proved reserves have been found and are expensed if no proved reserves are established. Development costs are capitalized as incurred and include expenditures for drilling and equipping development wells, constructing facilities and other activities required to access and produce proved reserves. Upon first production, capitalized costs are transferred to the depletable base and amortized using the units-of-production method based on proved reserves. Depletion rates can vary based on changes in reserve estimates, production mix, development timing and other factors.

Impairment of Long-Lived Assets

Proved oil and gas properties are reviewed for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate the carrying amount may not be recoverable based on estimated future undiscounted cash flows. If the carrying amount is not recoverable, the asset is written down to fair value using discounted cash flows, quoted market prices or other valuation techniques. Unproved properties are assessed periodically for impairment and are amortized based on the expiration of lease terms or as facts and circumstances indicate a reduction in value. The frequency and magnitude of impairment charges can vary depending on commodity prices, reserve revisions, well performance, development plans and other market factors.

Fair Value Measurements

Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. We prioritize valuation inputs based on the observability of the inputs used in the valuation techniques (Level 1, Level 2 and Level 3). Level 3 inputs include unobservable inputs that are supported by little or no market activity and reflect our own assumptions about the inputs that market participants would use in pricing the asset or liability. In certain cases, internally developed models are used to estimate fair value where observable market data is not available. The fair value hierarchy gives the highest priority to Level 1 inputs and the lowest priority to Level 3 inputs. When measuring fair value, we maximize the use of observable inputs and minimize the use of unobservable inputs.

Asset Retirement Obligations

We record the fair value of our asset retirement obligations (“ARO”) in the period in which the legally enforceable obligation is incurred. The ARO is estimated based on current costs, expected timing of abandonment and a credit-adjusted risk-free rate. ARO liabilities are accreted over time and the associated asset is depreciated over the useful life of the asset. Actual abandonment costs incurred can differ from estimates due to changes in laws and regulations, cost estimates, timing of abandonment, and other factors. Revisions to the estimated obligation are recorded in the period in which the estimate changes.

Business Combinations

We account for business combinations using the acquisition method of accounting, which requires identifiable assets acquired and liabilities assumed to be recorded at their acquisition date fair values. Any excess of the purchase price over the fair value of net assets acquired is recorded as goodwill. Transaction costs are expensed as incurred. The fair values of oil and gas properties are determined using a combination of market data, comparable transactions and discounted cash flow techniques, which include significant estimates such as expected production, commodity prices, operating costs and capital expenditures.

Goodwill

Goodwill is not amortized but is tested for impairment at least annually or more frequently if indicators of impairment are present. If the carrying amount of a reporting unit exceeds its fair value, an impairment loss equal to the amount by which the carrying value exceeds the fair value is recognized, not to exceed the carrying amount of goodwill. We use a combination of income and market approaches to estimate the fair value of our reporting units.

Financial and Operating Overview
Financial and operating results for the year ended December 31, 2024 compared to the year ended December 31, 2023 reflect the following:

• Net income decreased $504 million from $1.6 billion, or $2.14 per share, in 2023 to $1.1 billion, or $1.51 per share, in 2024.

• Net cash provided by operating activities decreased $863 million, from $3.7 billion, in 2023 to $2.8 billion in 2024.

• Equivalent production increased 4.1 MMBoe from 243.5 MMBoe, or 667.1 MBoe per day, in 2023 to 247.6 MMBoe, or 676.5 MBoe per day, in 2024.

◦ Oil production increased 4.7 MMBbl from 35.1 MMBbl, or 96 MBbl per day, in 2023 to 39.8 MMBbl, or 109 MBbl per day, in 2024.

◦ Natural gas production decreased 28.0 Bcf from 1,052.7 Bcf, or 2,884 MMcf per day, in 2023 to 1,024.7 Bcf, or 2,800 MMcf per day, in 2024.

◦ NGL volumes increased 4.1 MMBbl from 32.9 MMBbl, or 90 MBbl per day, in 2023 to 37.0 MMBbl, or 101 MBbl per day, in 2024.

• Average realized prices (including impact of derivatives):

◦ Oil was $74.22 per Bbl in 2024, 2 percent lower than the $76.07 per Bbl price realized in 2023.

◦ Natural gas was $1.75 per Mcf in 2024, 28 percent lower than the $2.44 per Mcf price realized in 2023.

◦ NGL price for 2024 was $19.95 per Bbl, 2 percent higher than the $19.56 per Bbl price realized in 2023.

• Total capital expenditures for drilling, completion and other fixed assets were $1.8 billion in 2024 compared to $2.1 billion in 2023.

Other financial highlights for the year ended December 31, 2024 and subsequent periods include the following:

• Issued $500 million aggregate principal amount of 5.60% senior notes due March 15, 2034. We used the net proceeds, and cash on hand, to repay the $575 million of 3.65% weighted-average private placement senior notes that matured in September 2024.

• Amended our revolving credit agreement to increase our aggregate commitments from $1.5 billion to $2.0 billion and extend the maturity date from March 2028 to September 2029.

• Entered into a $1.0 billion delayed draw term loan agreement consisting of two tranches of $500 million each, which was fully drawn in January 2025 to partially fund the FME and Avant acquisitions that both closed in January 2025.

• Issued $750 million aggregate principal amount of 5.40% senior notes due February 15, 2035 and $750 million aggregate principal amount of 5.90% senior notes due February 15, 2055. The net proceeds were used to partially fund the FME and Avant acquisitions which both closed in January 2025.

• Completed our previously announced acquisitions of FME and Avant in January 2025 for an aggregate consideration of approximately $4.0 billion, subject to certain post-closing adjustments.

• Increased our quarterly base dividend from $0.20 per share to $0.21 per share in February 2024, and in February 2025 our Board of Directors approved an additional increase of our quarterly base dividend from $0.21 per share to $0.22 per share.

• Repurchased 17 million shares of our common stock during 2024 for $464 million.

 Market Conditions and Commodity Prices
Our financial results depend on many factors, particularly commodity prices and our ability to find, develop and market our production on economically attractive terms. Commodity prices are affected by many factors outside of our control,

including changes in market supply and demand, which can be impacted by pipeline capacity constraints, inventory storage levels, basis differentials, weather conditions, and geopolitical, economic and other factors.

Oil prices were relatively steady in 2024 compared to 2023 as demand has continued for oil supply. Following global conflict and supply chain disruptions that drove high oil prices in 2022, OPEC+ reacted with supply reductions which helped to stabilize oil price levels in 2023. U.S. oil production was relatively flat from 2023 to 2024, which, when combined with OPEC+’s reductions, contributed to relatively steadier oil prices in 2023 and 2024. Additionally, while OPEC+ previously announced gradually increasing oil production over the course of 2025, several key members of OPEC+ have indicated their intent to delay such increases until the second half of 2025 and into 2026.

Natural gas prices trended down in 2024 compared to 2023 as strong production and relatively weak demand drove inventory levels above the five-year average. While natural gas prices have recovered from their lows in early 2024, natural gas prices in 2024 still trended lower overall compared to 2023. In response to the weakness of natural gas prices, we reduced our capital expenditures in the Marcellus Shale and also strategically curtailed our natural gas production in the basin from August 2024 through November 2024, resulting in an estimated curtailment of 232 MMcf per day of net production during that period. Natural gas prices increased slightly during the last quarter of 2024 and so far have continued to increase into early 2025 due to, among other factors, colder temperatures resulting in increased seasonal demand. Meanwhile, basis differentials became more divergent in 2024, in part due to constrained pipeline capacity and oversupply in certain geographic areas, and at times have resulted in negative spot market pricing for natural gas during 2024, such as the Waha Hub in the Permian Basin. While such issues have abated so far in 2025 in part due to the opening of the Matterhorn Express Pipeline in the fourth quarter of 2024, basis differentials may increase in magnitude again in 2025 due to a variety of factors we cannot predict. Looking to 2025, forward pricing indicates the recent increase in natural gas prices overall is expected to continue through the remainder of 2025, partially as a result of, among other factors, an expected increase in demand driven by LNG exports. However, LNG exports may be impacted by retaliatory tariffs (including China’s recently announced LNG tariffs), which could reduce the expected demand for LNG in 2025. Nevertheless, we expect natural gas prices overall to be stronger in 2025 compared to 2024.

Although the current outlook on oil and natural gas prices is generally favorable and our operations have not been significantly impacted in the short-term, in the event further disruptions occur and continue for an extended period of time, our operations could be adversely impacted, commodity prices could decline, and our costs may increase. We expect commodity price volatility to continue, including as a result of conflicts in the Middle East, actions of OPEC+ (including the ability of OPEC+ to successfully coordinate production quotas), and potentially swift near- and medium-term fluctuations in supply and demand. While we are unable to predict future commodity prices, at current oil, natural gas and NGL price levels, we do not believe that an impairment of our oil and gas properties is reasonably likely to occur in the near future. However, in the event that commodity prices significantly decline or costs significantly increase from current levels, our management would evaluate the recoverability of the carrying value of our oil and gas properties.

In addition, the issue of, and increasing political and social attention on, climate change has resulted in both existing and pending national, regional and local legislation and regulatory measures, such as mandates for renewable energy and emissions reductions. Changes in these laws or regulations may result in delays or restrictions in permitting and the development of projects, may result in increased costs and may impair our ability to move forward with our construction, completions, drilling, water management, waste handling, storage, transport and remediation activities, or may result in renewable energy alternatives that become more competitive with traditional oil and natural gas-derived products (including government subsidies and incentives for electric vehicles), any of which could have an adverse effect on our financial results.

For information about the impact of realized commodity prices on our revenues, refer to “Results of Operations” below.

Environmental and Safety Regulations
General. Our operations are subject to extensive and stringent federal, state and local laws and regulations, including those governing the protection of the environment, the discharge of materials into the environment, waste disposal and characteristics, emissions into the air and water, the good neighbor statute, endangered and threatened species, protection of cultural and historical resources and the safety of our operations and our workforce. These laws and regulations may require us to obtain permits before we can conduct some activities, restrict the types, quantities and concentration levels of various substances that can be released into the environment in connection with our operations, limit or prohibit activities on lands lying within wilderness, wetlands and other protected areas and impose substantial liabilities for pollution resulting from our operations and on properties where our operations are conducted. Failure to comply with these laws and regulations may result in the assessment of administrative, civil and criminal penalties, imposition of investigative, remedial or corrective action requirements, the imposition of injunctive relief or, in some circumstances, payment of natural resource damages and other damages. Under these laws and regulations, we could be held jointly and severally liable for the full cost of remedial or corrective measures, the efforts of which also could have an adverse impact on our ability to use, extract hydrocarbons from, otherwise operate or enjoy our real property interests.

Benefits of self-auditing environmental compliance. Many states, including Oklahoma, Texas and Pennsylvania, have adopted laws and regulations regarding the conduct of voluntary environmental audits. These laws allow the entity owning or operating a facility to conduct a voluntary audit, report any violations detected as a result of such audit and correct these violations without the payment of material administrative, civil or criminal penalties. We have environmental compliance programs for our operations in Oklahoma, Texas and Pennsylvania that we believe are consistent with such laws and regulations, and, where appropriate, we have reported violations detected during such audits in accordance with these laws. We are unable to estimate or quantify the potential dollar amount that we could be required to expend in the event corrective action is required or administrative, civil or criminal penalties are applied, as a result of any audit we have conducted under the voluntary audit laws. If we fail to comply with these laws and regulations, such failure could have an adverse effect on our business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows.

Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act (“CERCLA”). CERCLA, also known as the Superfund law, imposes remediation and liabilities relating to releases of hazardous substances into the environment. Under CERCLA and similar state statutes, joint and several liability may be imposed on classes of persons generally defined to include the current and the past owners and operators of a site where a release or threatened release of hazardous substances has occurred and entities that disposed or arranged for the disposition of hazardous substances. Under CERCLA, such persons may be held liable for amounts paid to clean up a site, to reimburse the government for costs incurred by the government on behalf of a third party in cleaning up a site, or to compensate third parties for damages, including natural resource damages, resulting from the release of hazardous substances from the site. CERCLA’s liability provisions also may apply to companies for the conduct of parties that were entirely separate from, and unrelated to, a company’s current or former operations. Although CERCLA generally excludes petroleum from its definition of a hazardous substance, claims have been brought based on the surrounding facts and circumstances to require remediation even where petroleum products are, by themselves, not considered hazardous substances. Although we do not currently maintain any ownership interests in Superfund sites, we cannot provide any assurance there will not be hazardous substances present on real properties where we conduct operations or at offsite disposal locations, or that we will not be included as a responsible party at a CERCLA site in the future.

Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (“RCRA”). RCRA, and comparable state statutes, affect oil and gas companies through regulation of the generation, transportation, treatment, storage and disposal of liquid and solid wastes. For example, drilling fluids, produced waters and other wastes associated with the development, production and/or processing of oil or gas are currently regulated by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) and state agencies with jurisdiction pursuant to RCRA, as “non-hazardous” wastes. Specially handled waste is any commercial and industrial waste that remains non-hazardous, which is subject to more stringent handling and disposal requirements than non-hazardous waste but less rigorous than those for hazardous waste. Certain petroleum refining and natural gas processing operations routinely produce large quantities of specially handled wastes that may require management and disposal at specially permitted facilities. It is possible some oil and gas and/or natural gas processing wastes now classified as non-hazardous could be reclassified as hazardous in the future. Any such reclassification of currently non-hazardous wastes as hazardous could subject the generators of such waste and/or the facility that manages the waste to more stringent handling, storage, treatment and disposal requirements and cause more inspection and enforcement action by the EPA or other regulatory agencies. For example, an EPA inspection of such facilities could result in the imposition of corrective action or remediation requirements as well as additional compliance requirements or monetary penalties for any operational standards not satisfied.

Air emissions and climate change. The Clean Air Act (“CAA”) and comparable state and local laws and regulations impose requirements for improving or maintaining air quality and impose limits on emissions from various industrial sources, including emissions from oil and gas production and processing facilities, as well as impose various operational, monitoring, reporting and record-keeping requirements. These laws and regulations are frequently changed and generally require difficult and costly compliance measures. These laws and regulations may require us to continuously evaluate, obtain and strictly comply with air permits, install emissions control equipment, use specific fuels, utilize specific pollution control technologies, adopt work and operational practices at our operations, satisfy stringent emissions control requirements, incur administrative, and sometimes capital, costs, and to do all of these things within specified time limits. In addition, the EPA and state agencies can require certain notifications to be made if a change in operations results in new emissions increased by more than a particular amount.

Methane regulation. On June 30, 2021, the President signed into law a joint resolution of Congress under the Congressional Review Act (the “CRA”) disapproving a 2020 final rule issued by the EPA under the previous administration that had effectively rescinded methane emissions standards for new, reconstructed and modified oil and gas sources governed by the agency’s 2012 and 2016 new source performance standards. As a result of that joint resolution, the 2020 rule reversed by Congress has no force or effect, and methane emissions from the oil and gas sector are regulated by the 2012 and 2016 new source performance standards. Subsequently, on November 2, 2021, the EPA issued a proposed rule, and on November 15, 2022, a supplemental proposal, that combined would establish comprehensive new and existing source standards of performance for methane and volatile organic compound emissions of certain facilities in the oil and natural gas source category, including new leak detection and repair standards as well as control requirements for certain types of process equipment. On December 2, 2023, the EPA announced a final rule that includes robust and flexible methane emissions reduction requirements for oil and gas facilities, including by establishing clear and consistent standards for reduction of fugitive emissions from new and existing oil and gas facilities as well as requiring capture of gas from most new and a significant number of existing wells. On March 8, 2024, the EPA supplemental rule was published in the Federal Register, kicking off the implementation process in which EPA begins to gather information from states to prepare state plans that are tailored to the needs of each respective state with plans to be submitted to the EPA in 24 months from the effective date of the rule—June 10, 2024—in addition to carrying out other aspects of rulemaking such as outreach with stakeholders and weapons to enforcement in certain situations.

Water. The federal Water Pollution Control Act, also known as the Clean Water Act (“CWA”), and similar state, local, and Canadian legal regimes impose restrictions and strict controls regarding the discharge of pollutants, including oil and refined products, into state waters and waters of the United States, as well as land areas with a hydrological connection to such waters. These controls have become more stringent and limiting over time. Permits must be obtained to discharge into jurisdictional waters and to conduct certain activities in these waters and wetlands. In addition, the CWA, along with analogous laws and regulations, require preparation and implementation of spill prevention, control and countermeasure plans in connection with on-site storage of significant quantities of oil. The scope of these plans has been expanded significantly after the Deepwater Horizon incident in the Gulf of Mexico.

Governmental Proceedings
From time-to-time, we receive notices of violation from governmental authorities asserting that our operations are not in full compliance with applicable environmental and safety laws and regulations. These notices may require us to take corrective action or to cease or modify certain operations. We also from time-to-time receive notices relating to alleged violations of environmental statutes and regulations. If we are unable to resolve these matters, we could be required to pay civil penalties, undertake corrective actions, and implement compliance measures. While we cannot predict the outcome of such actions, individually or in the aggregate, we do not currently believe these items will have a material effect on our financial position, results of operations or cash flows.

In June 2023, we received a Notice of Violation and Opportunity to Confer from the New Mexico Environment Department (“NMED”) alleging violations of the New Mexico State Implementation Plan (“NMSIP”) and certain other state and federal air quality regulations at certain of our facilities. We are working with the NMED to address the alleged violations, and are implementing corrective action plans to prevent future violations at those facilities. We do not believe these alleged violations will have a material adverse effect on our financial position, results of operations, or cash flows.

 ITEM 1A. Risk Factors
For additional information about the risk factors that affect us, see Item 1A of Part I of our Form 10-K.

 ITEM 2. Unregistered Sales of Equity Securities and Use of Proceeds
None.

 ITEM 3. Defaults Upon Senior Securities
None.

 ITEM 4. Mine Safety Disclosures
Not applicable.

 ITEM 5. Other Information
(a) None.
(b) During the quarterly period covered by this Report, none of the Company’s directors or officers has adopted or terminated a Rule 10b5-1 trading arrangement or non-Rule 10b5-1 trading arrangement, as each term is defined in Item 408 of Regulation S-K.
(c) Not Applicable.

Regulation
General. New or revised rules, regulations and policies may be issued, and new legislation may be proposed, that could impact the oil and gas industry. The oil and gas industry is heavily regulated at the federal, state and local levels, and these regulations are frequently subject to change. Any such changes could increase our costs, impose additional compliance obligations, limit our activities, or affect the economics of our operations. In addition, some jurisdictions have adopted, or are considering, regulatory requirements associated with methane emissions reductions; hydraulic fracturing; flaring and venting; water sourcing, use and disposal; induced seismicity; wildlife and habitat protection; and other environmental, health and safety matters.

Federal Regulation of Oil and Gas. The development, production, and sale of oil, natural gas and NGLs in the U.S. are subject to comprehensive federal laws and regulations. Various federal agencies, including the U.S. Department of the Interior, the EPA, and the U.S. Department of Transportation, regulate various aspects of our operations. For example, the Bureau of Land Management (“BLM”) and the Office of Natural Resources Revenue (“ONRR”) regulate development on federal lands and on the Outer Continental Shelf, including permitting, bonding, valuation of production, royalties and other matters. The EPA regulates air emissions, water discharges and waste management, among other things. The Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration regulates the design, construction, testing, operation and maintenance of natural gas and hazardous liquid pipelines.

State and Local Regulation. States regulate many aspects of oil and gas development and production, including permitting, spacing, pooling, drilling, completion, gathering, transportation, plugging and abandonment. States also regulate the handling and disposal of oil and gas wastes, oil and gas production taxes and severance taxes, and bonding requirements. Local governments may regulate or restrict the location of wells and related facilities, as well as noise, traffic, hours of operation and setbacks, through zoning ordinances and land use regulations.

Air Emissions and Climate Regulation. Federal, state and local laws regulate emissions of air pollutants, including methane and other greenhouse gases (“GHGs”). The EPA has established New Source Performance Standards for certain oil and gas facilities and has recently finalized more stringent requirements for methane and volatile organic compound emissions. Various states have adopted, or are considering, GHG reduction targets and cap-and-trade programs. These statutes and regulations may require installation of emissions control equipment, leak detection and repair programs, operational changes, recordkeeping and reporting, and other compliance measures.

Water Regulation. The CWA and analogous state laws impose restrictions and strict controls regarding the discharge of pollutants into waters of the United States and state waters, including wetlands. Certain activities in jurisdictional waters and wetlands require permits, and discharges of pollutants from point sources are subject to effluent limitations and monitoring requirements. The Safe Drinking Water Act and state laws regulate the underground injection of fluids, including for enhanced recovery and disposal of produced water. Our water sourcing, use and disposal practices are subject to these regulatory frameworks.

Hydraulic Fracturing. Hydraulic fracturing is a common completion technique for oil and gas wells. Various states regulate hydraulic fracturing activities, including disclosure of chemicals used, well construction standards, water management and seismic monitoring. The EPA has issued guidance and studies related to hydraulic fracturing and has regulatory authority over certain aspects, such as underground injection of fluids associated with disposal wells.

Endangered Species and Wildlife Protection. The ESA, the Migratory Bird Treaty Act and similar state laws protect certain species and their habitats. Compliance with these laws may result in limitations on where and when we can conduct operations and may require consultation with federal and state wildlife agencies. Designation of critical habitat areas and listing of additional species may impose further restrictions on our activities.

Occupational Health and Safety. The Occupational Safety and Health Act and comparable state laws regulate workplace health and safety, including hazard communication, process safety management and injury reporting. We are subject to these requirements across our operations and maintain programs designed to promote safe work practices, training and compliance.

Decommissioning and Abandonment. Federal and state laws require the proper plugging and abandonment of wells and the decommissioning of associated facilities. We are required to provide financial assurance and to perform plugging and abandonment activities in accordance with applicable regulations. Failure to properly plug wells and decommission facilities can result in enforcement actions and liabilities.

Compliance and Costs. Compliance with applicable federal, state and local regulations can be complex and costly. We incur capital and operating expenditures to comply with these regulatory requirements. Changes in laws, regulations and policies, or changes in their interpretation or enforcement, could increase our costs, delay or curtail our operations or otherwise negatively affect our business.

We monitor the evolving regulatory landscape and engage with regulators and stakeholders to understand and prepare for potential changes. We also maintain compliance programs and internal controls designed to promote adherence to applicable requirements across our operations.

Successful Efforts Method of Accounting

We follow the successful efforts method of accounting for our oil and gas producing activities. Acquisition costs for proved and unproved properties are capitalized when incurred. Judgment is required to determine the proper classification of wells designated as developmental or exploratory, which ultimately will determine the proper accounting treatment of costs incurred. Exploration costs, including geological and geophysical costs, the costs of carrying and retaining unproved properties and exploratory dry-hole costs are expensed. Development costs, including costs to drill and equip development wells and successful exploratory drilling costs to locate proved reserves, are capitalized.

Revenue Recognition

The Company’s revenue is typically generated from contracts with third parties. All revenue is recognized in accordance with Accounting Standards Update No. 2014-09, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (Topic 606). Revenue is recognized when the Company satisfies a performance obligation by transferring control of a good or service to a customer at an amount that reflects the consideration expected to be received in exchange for those goods or services. The Company identifies a contract with a customer, identifies performance obligations in the contract, determines the transaction price, allocates the transaction price to the performance obligations in the contract and recognizes revenue when (or as) control of a promised good or service is transferred to the customer. The Company applies the revenue recognition criteria to each contract unless the contracts are combined under the revenue standards. The Company considers the collectability of consideration when determining whether a contract exists and only recognizes revenue when it is probable that the consideration will be collected.

Revenue from oil, natural gas and NGLs sales is recognized at the amount of consideration expected to be received when control of the product is transferred to the customer. The Company’s oil, natural gas and NGLs contracts are typically short-term in nature with a term of one year or less. The Company satisfies its performance obligations upon delivery of the product at a contractual delivery point and records revenue when the customer obtains control of the product. Control is generally defined as the ability to direct the use of and obtain substantially all of the remaining benefits from the asset. The Company’s contracts with customers for oil, natural gas and NGLs generally specify the delivery of products at the wellhead, into a gathering system, at the inlet of a processing plant or at a downstream delivery point. When the Company sells at the wellhead, the Company typically recognizes revenue at that point as control transfers at the wellhead. When the Company sells at a point downstream of the wellhead, the Company evaluates whether it is acting as the principal or agent in the transaction by assessing whether it controls the products before they are transferred to the customer.

The Company recognizes revenue as a principal when it controls the product prior to transfer to the customer. In this situation, the Company records revenue on a gross basis with the gathering, processing or transportation costs presented separately as expenses within “Transportation, gathering and processing” on the Consolidated Statement of Operations. When the Company does not control the product prior to transfer to the customer and therefore acts as an agent, the Company recognizes revenue net of gathering, processing or transportation fees. The determination of the presentation of these fees is based on contracts and the point in the value chain at which control of the product transfers.

Oil sales contracts are typically priced at specified differentials to the applicable market index price, and revenue is recognized at a point in time when control of the oil transfers to the customer, which is generally when the product is delivered at the designated delivery point. Natural gas and NGLs sales contracts are frequently priced based on the applicable market index price adjusted for quality and transportation, and revenue is recognized when control of the product transfers to the customer, which generally occurs at the point of delivery. The Company’s revenue streams are presented net of any royalties due to landowners or other interest holders as the Company has determined that such royalty payments represent payments to collaborators and not customers under Topic 606.

The Company may also have contracts for the sale of residue gas and NGLs resulting from processing the Company’s natural gas. In these arrangements, the processor may retain a portion of the products as compensation for services, or the Company may pay a fee and retain title to all products. Where the Company retains title and control of the products through processing and subsequently sells to a customer, the Company recognizes revenue on a gross basis. Where the processor has title to a portion of the products, or the Company has determined that it does not control the products before they are transferred to the customer, the Company recognizes revenue net of processing fees or retained products.

The Company recognizes revenue from other sources such as gathering, transportation and processing services when these services are provided to third parties. Revenue from such services is recognized over time as the service is provided to the customer. The Company determines whether it is acting as the principal or as an agent in these arrangements based on whether it controls the service before it is transferred to the customer.

Contract balances related to revenue recognition primarily include receivables from contracts with customers, which are included in “Accounts receivable – oil, gas and NGLs” on the Consolidated Balance Sheet. The Company does not typically have contract assets or contract liabilities because the timing of billing and performance generally coincides and there are no significant financing components in the Company’s contracts with customers due to the short-term nature of the contracts.

Significant judgments and estimates are required in recognizing revenue from contracts with customers. These include determining whether the Company is acting as principal or agent, identifying performance obligations, determining the transaction price including variable consideration, and allocating the transaction price to the performance obligations. The Company’s policies and estimates may change as contracts evolve and as additional guidance is issued by standard-setting bodies.

The Company does not disclose the aggregate amount of revenue expected to be recognized in the future from remaining performance obligations with an original expected duration of one year or less, as permitted by the practical expedient in Topic 606.

The Company has elected to present all taxes assessed by a governmental authority that are collected from customers on a net basis in the Consolidated Statement of Operations.

The Company monitors customer credit risk and maintains allowances for doubtful accounts as necessary. The Company evaluates the creditworthiness of its customers based on a combination of qualitative and quantitative factors, including historical collection trends, current economic conditions and the financial condition of customers.

The nature and timing of the Company’s revenue recognition remain consistent across reporting periods, and there were no significant changes in judgments related to the recognition and measurement of revenue during the periods presented.

The Company’s revenue recognition policies are consistent with industry practices and the requirements of Topic 606. The Company continues to evaluate the impact of any future changes in accounting standards on the recognition of revenue from contracts with customers.

The Company may enter into marketing or other arrangements that involve the purchase and sale of commodities in which the Company acts as a principal or an agent depending on whether it controls the product before transfer to the customer. In such cases, the Company assesses whether it controls the product prior to transfer and recognizes revenue accordingly.

The Company has elected to use the practical expedient allowing the recognition of revenue at the amount of consideration to which it has a right to invoice when that amount corresponds directly with the value to the customer of the Company’s performance completed to date.
