Revenue Recognition

The Company’s revenue is typically generated from contracts with customers for the sale of oil, natural gas and NGLs and, to a lesser extent, from gathering, transportation and processing services provided to third parties. Revenue is recognized in accordance with Accounting Standards Codification Topic 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (Topic 606). The Company recognizes revenue when it satisfies a performance obligation by transferring control of a good or service to a customer at an amount that reflects the consideration to which it expects to be entitled in exchange for those goods or services. The Company identifies the contract with a customer, identifies the performance obligations in the contract, determines the transaction price, allocates the transaction price to the performance obligations in the contract and recognizes revenue when (or as) control of the goods or services is transferred to the customer.

For oil, natural gas and NGLs sales, the Company typically satisfies its performance obligations and recognizes revenue at a point in time when control of the product transfers to the customer, which generally occurs at delivery points specified in the contracts. The Company’s sales contracts are generally short-term in nature with pricing based on market indices, and any variable consideration is typically resolved within a short period following delivery. The Company assesses whether it is acting as principal or agent in each sales arrangement based on whether it controls the product prior to transfer to the customer. When the Company controls the product prior to transfer, revenue is recognized on a gross basis and gathering, processing and transportation fees are presented as expenses within “Transportation, gathering and processing” in the Consolidated Statement of Operations. When the Company does not control the product prior to transfer, revenue is recognized net of fees.

Revenue from gathering, transportation and processing services provided to third parties is recognized over time as the services are rendered. Consideration received for these services is typically based on volumetric fees and is recognized in proportion to the services provided. The Company does not have significant obligations for returns, refunds or warranties in its contracts with customers.

The Company’s contracts with customers do not typically include significant financing components due to the short-term nature of the arrangements and prompt settlement terms. The Company recognizes receivables from contracts with customers when its right to consideration becomes unconditional. Receivables are included within “Accounts receivable – oil, gas and NGLs” in the Consolidated Balance Sheet. The Company evaluates the collectability of receivables and maintains allowances for credit losses as necessary based on historical experience, current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts.

The Company presents taxes assessed by governmental authorities that are collected from customers, such as sales and excise taxes, on a net basis, excluding them from revenue.

The Company applies the practical expedient that permits the recognition of revenue in the amount to which it has a right to invoice when that amount corresponds directly with the value to the customer of the Company’s performance completed to date. The Company also applies the practical expedient to omit disclosure of remaining performance obligations with an original expected duration of one year or less.

The Company’s policies for identifying performance obligations, determining transaction prices and allocating those prices to performance obligations are based on contractual terms and customary business practices. The Company’s judgments include determining whether it acts as principal or agent and estimating variable consideration, including quality and transportation adjustments, which are generally resolved shortly after delivery.

The Company’s revenue recognition policies are consistent with industry practices and the requirements of Topic 606, and there were no significant changes in judgments that affect the timing or amount of revenue recognized during the periods presented.

The Company’s revenue is disaggregated by product type and geography to provide additional insight into the nature, amount, timing and uncertainty of revenue and cash flows. Disaggregation reflects management’s assessment of how revenue is affected by economic factors. The Company’s disaggregated revenue disclosures are included in the notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements.

The Company continues to monitor guidance issued by standard-setting bodies and evaluates the impact of such guidance on its revenue recognition practices. The Company does not expect the adoption of future guidance related to revenue recognition to have a material impact on its financial statements.

The Company recognizes revenue in the amount that reflects the consideration expected to be received when control of a promised good or service transfers to the customer in accordance with Topic 606.

Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates

The preparation of financial statements in conformity with U.S. GAAP requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the amounts reported in the consolidated financial statements and accompanying notes. These estimates and assumptions are based on historical experience and other factors that management believes to be reasonable under the circumstances and are evaluated on an ongoing basis. Actual results could differ from those estimates and such differences could be material.

Management considers certain accounting policies to be critical because they are both important to the presentation of the Company’s financial condition and results of operations and require management to make difficult, subjective or complex judgments. The following policies are considered critical accounting policies and estimates:

Reserve Estimates and Depletion

The estimation of proved oil and gas reserves is a complex process involving subjective judgment and a number of variables and uncertainties. Reserves estimates are used in the calculation of depletion, depreciation and amortization (DD&A) and the evaluation for impairment of oil and gas properties. The accuracy of reserves estimates depends on the quality of available geological, engineering and economic data, the interpretation of that data and the assumptions used regarding future commodity prices, operating costs, capital expenditures and other factors. As additional information becomes available, reserves estimates may change and could have a significant impact on the Company’s DD&A expense and impairment assessments.

Impairment of Long-Lived Assets

The Company evaluates its long-lived assets, including proved oil and gas properties, for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts of such assets may not be recoverable. The recoverability of long-lived assets is assessed by comparing the carrying value of the asset group to the undiscounted future net cash flows expected to be generated by the asset group. If the carrying amount exceeds the sum of the undiscounted future net cash flows, an impairment loss is recognized for the amount by which the carrying amount exceeds the fair value of the asset group. Fair value is estimated using assumptions that market participants would use in pricing the asset, including commodity prices, reserves quantities, expected production, operating costs and discount rates.

Asset Retirement Obligations

The Company records asset retirement obligations (AROs) for the estimated costs to retire oil and gas properties. AROs are recognized when a legal obligation to retire a long-lived asset is incurred and can be reasonably estimated. The ARO liability is initially measured at fair value and is accreted to its settlement value over time using the credit-adjusted risk-free rate. The associated asset retirement cost is capitalized as part of the carrying amount of the related long-lived asset and is depreciated over the asset’s useful life. Estimates of AROs are based on current regulatory requirements, estimated useful lives and historical experience, and are subject to change as new information becomes available.

Income Taxes

The Company accounts for income taxes under the asset and liability method. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are recognized for the expected future tax consequences of temporary differences between the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities for financial reporting purposes and the amounts used for income tax purposes. Deferred tax assets are reduced by a valuation allowance when it is more likely than not that some portion or all of the deferred tax assets will not be realized. The Company recognizes interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits as a component of income tax expense.

Derivatives and Hedging

The Company uses derivative instruments to manage exposure to commodity price risk. Derivative instruments are recorded at fair value on the Consolidated Balance Sheet, and changes in fair value are recognized in earnings unless specific hedge accounting criteria are met. The Company does not designate derivative instruments as hedges for accounting purposes and, therefore, recognizes all changes in fair value in earnings.

Revenue Recognition

Revenue from contracts with customers is recognized when control of the promised goods or services is transferred to the customer in an amount that reflects the consideration to which the Company expects to be entitled in exchange for those goods or services. The Company’s revenue recognition policies are described in more detail in the notes to the consolidated financial statements.

Management believes that the judgments and estimates involved in the critical accounting policies discussed above are reasonable; however, changes in facts and circumstances or the use of different assumptions could result in materially different amounts reported in the Company’s financial statements.

Successful Efforts Method of Accounting and Classification

We utilize the successful efforts method of accounting for our oil and gas exploration and development activities. Under this method, acquisition costs for proved and unproved properties, costs of successful exploration wells and development wells, and equipment and facilities costs are capitalized. Geological and geophysical costs and costs of unsuccessful exploration wells are expensed as incurred. Costs incurred to maintain reserves and to improve production are considered development costs and are capitalized. The classification of costs as exploration, development or acquisition is based on the nature of the activities and the stage of the project.

Property acquisition costs include costs to purchase or lease mineral rights. Costs to acquire proved properties are amortized on a unit-of-production basis over the life of the proved reserves of the properties. Costs to acquire unproved properties are assessed periodically to determine whether they have been impaired or have reached the end of their useful lives. When unproved properties are determined to be impaired, the costs are charged to expense. If the properties are subsequently developed and reserves are proved, the costs are reclassified to proved properties and amortized accordingly.

Exploration costs include geological and geophysical costs, costs of exploratory wells, and other costs incurred in the search for oil and gas. Geological and geophysical costs, including seismic studies, are expensed as incurred. Exploratory well costs are initially capitalized but are charged to expense if the well is determined to be unsuccessful. If an exploratory well finds reserves that cannot be classified as proved at the end of the reporting period, the costs may continue to be capitalized as long as certain criteria are met, including the intent to continue exploration or evaluation of the discovery and the availability of sufficient evidence that the reserves are likely to be proved in the future.

Development costs include the costs of development wells and related equipment and facilities, including costs to access proved reserves and to provide facilities for the extraction, treatment, gathering and storage of oil and gas. Development costs are capitalized and amortized on a unit-of-production basis over the life of the proved developed reserves.

Depreciation, depletion and amortization (DD&A) of capitalized costs of proved properties are calculated using the unit-of-production method based on the ratio of current period production to estimated total proved reserves. The estimates of proved reserves are revised periodically as additional information becomes available as a result of continued exploration and development activities and production history. Changes in proved reserves estimates may result in significant changes to DD&A expense.

Impairment of oil and gas properties is evaluated when events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts of the properties may not be recoverable. For proved properties, impairment is assessed on a field-by-field basis by comparing the carrying amount of the asset group to the undiscounted future net cash flows expected to be generated by the asset group. If the carrying amount exceeds the sum of the undiscounted future net cash flows, an impairment loss is recognized for the amount by which the carrying amount exceeds the fair value of the asset group. Fair value is estimated based on assumptions that market participants would use in pricing the asset, such as commodity prices, reserves quantities, expected production, operating costs and discount rates.

For unproved properties, impairment is assessed periodically based on the Company’s plans for the properties, the results of exploration activities, the terms of the leases and other relevant factors. Unproved properties that are individually significant are assessed individually for impairment, while the remainder are assessed in the aggregate.

Asset retirement obligations (AROs) are recognized for the estimated costs to retire oil and gas properties. AROs are initially measured at fair value in the period the legal obligation is incurred and are subsequently accreted to their expected settlement values over time using the credit-adjusted risk-free rate. The associated asset retirement costs are capitalized as part of the carrying amount of the related long-lived assets and are depreciated over the assets’ useful lives.

The Company classifies costs in the Consolidated Statement of Operations based on their nature and function. Exploration expenses include geological and geophysical costs and the costs of unsuccessful exploratory wells. Production expenses include costs of operating and maintaining wells and related equipment and facilities. Depreciation, depletion and amortization expense includes DD&A of the capitalized costs of proved properties, equipment and facilities, and other capital assets.

The determination of whether costs are classified as exploration, development or acquisition and the assessment of impairment require significant judgment by management. These judgments are based on the evaluation of geological, engineering and economic data and the Company’s plans and expectations for the properties. Changes in judgments or the availability of new information could result in changes in the classification of costs or the recognition of impairment losses.

1. Summary of Significant Accounting Policies

Use of Estimates. The preparation of financial statements in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (U.S. GAAP) requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the amounts reported in the financial statements and accompanying notes. Actual results could differ from those estimates.

Revenue Recognition. EOG recognizes revenue in accordance with Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) Topic 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers. Revenue is recognized when control of the promised goods or services is transferred to the customer in an amount that reflects the consideration to which EOG expects to be entitled in exchange for those goods or services. EOG’s revenues are primarily derived from the sale of crude oil, natural gas liquids (NGLs) and natural gas. Contracts with customers are generally short-term in nature with pricing based on market indices, and performance obligations are typically satisfied at a point in time when control transfers at the designated delivery point.

Oil and Gas Operations. EOG accounts for its crude oil and natural gas exploration and production activities under the successful efforts method of accounting. Acquisition costs for proved and unproved properties, costs of successful exploratory wells and development wells and the costs of acquiring support equipment and facilities are capitalized. Geological and geophysical costs, including seismic costs, and the costs of unsuccessful exploratory wells are expensed as incurred. Depreciation, depletion and amortization (DD&A) of capitalized costs of proved properties are computed using the units-of-production method based on estimated proved reserves. EOG evaluates its oil and gas properties for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts may not be recoverable. If the carrying amount exceeds the sum of the undiscounted future net cash flows expected to be generated by the properties, an impairment loss is recognized for the amount by which the carrying amount exceeds the fair value of the properties.

Asset Retirement Obligations. EOG recognizes asset retirement obligations (AROs) for the estimated costs to retire long-lived assets, such as plugging and abandoning wells and removing related equipment and facilities. AROs are initially measured at fair value in the period a legal obligation is incurred and are subsequently accreted to their settlement value over time using a credit-adjusted risk-free rate. The associated asset retirement costs are capitalized as part of the carrying amount of the related long-lived asset and are depreciated over the asset’s useful life.

Income Taxes. EOG accounts for income taxes under the asset and liability method. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are recognized for the future tax consequences attributable to differences between the financial statement carrying amounts of existing assets and liabilities and their respective tax bases. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured using enacted tax rates expected to apply to taxable income in the years in which those temporary differences are expected to be recovered or settled. The effect on deferred tax assets and liabilities of a change in tax rates is recognized in income in the period that includes the enactment date.

Derivatives. EOG uses derivative instruments to manage commodity price risk. Derivative instruments are recorded at fair value on the Consolidated Balance Sheets and are presented on a gross basis. Changes in the fair value of derivative instruments are recognized currently in earnings as gains or losses in operating revenues unless specific hedge accounting criteria are met. EOG does not currently designate derivative instruments as accounting hedges under ASC Topic 815, Derivatives and Hedging.

Fair Value Measurements. EOG follows ASC Topic 820, Fair Value Measurement, which defines fair value, establishes a framework for measuring fair value and expands disclosures about fair value measurements. Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date.

Leases. EOG accounts for leases in accordance with ASC Topic 842, Leases. At the inception of an arrangement, EOG determines whether the arrangement is or contains a lease. Right-of-use assets represent EOG’s right to use an underlying asset for the lease term and lease liabilities represent EOG’s obligation to make lease payments. Lease liabilities are measured at the present value of future lease payments at the commencement date. Right-of-use assets are measured at the amount of the lease liability, adjusted for any lease payments made at or before the commencement date and certain initial direct costs. Leases with terms of 12 months or less are not recognized on the balance sheet.

Recently Issued Accounting Pronouncements. EOG monitors recently issued accounting pronouncements and evaluates the potential impact of new standards on its financial statements. EOG does not expect that the adoption of recently issued standards will have a material impact on its consolidated financial statements.

Stock-Based Compensation. EOG accounts for stock-based compensation in accordance with ASC Topic 718, Compensation—Stock Compensation. The cost of employee services received in exchange for awards of equity instruments is measured based on the grant-date fair value of the awards and recognized over the period during which an employee is required to provide service in exchange for the award.

Comprehensive Income. Comprehensive income includes all changes in equity during a period except those resulting from investments by owners and distributions to owners. Comprehensive income is presented in the Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income.

Earnings Per Share. Basic earnings per share (EPS) is computed by dividing net income available to common stockholders by the weighted-average number of shares of common stock outstanding during the period. Diluted EPS reflects the potential dilution that could occur if securities or other contracts to issue common stock were exercised or converted into common stock.

Cash and Cash Equivalents. Cash and cash equivalents include cash on hand and short-term investments with original maturities of three months or less.

Accounts Receivable and Allowance for Credit Losses. Accounts receivable are recorded at the amount billed to customers and do not bear interest. The allowance for credit losses is based on historical experience, current economic conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts.

Inventories. Inventories consist primarily of materials and supplies and are stated at the lower of cost or net realizable value.

Property, Plant and Equipment. Property, plant and equipment are stated at cost. Expenditures for maintenance and repairs are expensed as incurred. Major renewals and betterments that extend the useful lives of assets are capitalized.

question: CTRA position regarding hydraulic fracturing?
answer: CTRA views hydraulic fracturing as essential to its business, since most wells would not be economical without it. At the same time, the company recognizes growing regulatory, environmental, and water management risks that could increase costs or disrupt operations. To mitigate these challenges, Coterra is emphasizing water recycling and monitoring evolving regulations, but stricter rules could still have a material adverse effect on its operations and financial condition.

passages.text: Hydraulic Fracturing. Substantially all of our exploration and production operations depend on the use of hydraulic fracturing to enhance production from oil and natural gas wells. Most of our wells would not be economical without the use of hydraulic fracturing to stimulate production from the well. Due to concerns raised relating to potential impacts of hydraulic fracturing on groundwater quality, legislative and regulatory efforts at the U.S. federal, state and local levels have been initiated to render permitting and compliance requirements more stringent for hydraulic fracturing or to restrict or prohibit the activity altogether. States in which we operate also have adopted, or have stated intentions to adopt, laws or regulations that mandate further restrictions on hydraulic fracturing, such as imposing more stringent permitting, disclosure and well-construction requirements on hydraulic fracturing operations and establishing standards for the capture of air emissions released during hydraulic fracturing. In addition to state measures, local land use restrictions, such as city ordinances, may restrict drilling in general or hydraulic fracturing in particular. Increased regulation and attention given to the hydraulic fracturing process could lead to greater opposition to oil and natural gas production activities using hydraulic fracturing techniques, which could have an adverse effect on oil and natural gas production activities, including operational delays or increased operating costs in the production of oil and natural gas, or could make it more difficult to perform hydraulic fracturing.

hard_negatives.text:
Hydraulic fracturing. A technology involving the injection of fluids, which typically include small amounts of several chemical additives and a proppant, into a formation to create fractures and fracture networks in low/middle permeability reservoirs that allow oil or natural gas to flow more freely to the wellbore.

MBbl. One thousand barrels of oil or other liquid hydrocarbons.

MBoe. One thousand barrels of oil equivalent.

Mcf. One thousand cubic feet of natural gas.

MMBbl. One million barrels of oil or other liquid hydrocarbons.

MMBoe. One million barrels of oil equivalent.

MMBtu. One million British thermal units.

MMcf. One million cubic feet of natural gas.

Natural gas. A hydrocarbon gas found in a gaseous form primarily composed of methane, or CH4.

Natural gas liquids. The heavier liquids that condense from the natural gas stream extracted from oil and gas wells that are processed into finished products such as ethane, propane, butane and natural gasoline; commonly referred to as “NGLs”.

Net acres or net wells. The percentage of total acres/wells in which we own a working interest.

Operating margin. Oil, natural gas and NGL sales, less transportation expense and LOE.

Operator. The individual or company responsible for the exploration, development, and/or production of an oil or gas well or lease.

Play. A geographic area with hydrocarbon potential.

Proved reserves. Quantities of oil and gas that, by analysis of geoscience and engineering data, can be estimated with reasonable certainty to be economically producible—from a given date forward, from known reservoirs and under existing economic conditions, operating methods and government regulations—prior to the time at which contracts providing the right to operate expire, unless evidence indicates that renewal is reasonably certain. If deterministic methods are used, the term “reasonable certainty” means a high degree of confidence that the quantities will be recovered. If probabilistic methods are used, then there should be at least a 90 percent probability that the quantities actually recovered will equal or exceed the estimate.

Proved developed reserves. Reserves that can be expected to be recovered through existing wells with existing equipment and operating methods; or in which the cost of the required equipment is relatively minor compared to the cost of a new well.

Proved undeveloped reserves. Proved reserves that are expected to be recovered from new wells on undrilled acreage or from existing wells where a relatively major expenditure is required.

PV-10 non-GAAP. The present value of estimated future net revenue to be generated from the production of proved reserves calculated in accordance with SEC guidelines and does not include future cash outflows associated with settling asset retirement obligations. Future cash inflows are computed by applying an unweighted 12-month first-day-of-the-month average of actual prices for the preceding 12 months, with consideration of quality, transportation and regional price differentials, over the estimated future production of the proved reserves. Future development and production costs are computed by applying the costs prevailing as of the date of the estimate based on year-end costs held flat for the life of the reserves and assumes continuation of reserve-to-production ratios used in the calculation. Future income taxes are computed by applying the appropriate year-end statutory tax rates, including consideration for estimated future statutory depletion benefits, to the future pretax net cash flows relating to proved oil and gas reserves, less the tax basis of the properties involved. PV-10 is then calculated by discounting the resultant future net cash flows at a 10% annual rate to determine their present value. PV-10 has been included in this report as a supplemental disclosure and because we believe it is useful to investors for evaluating the relative monetary significance of our oil and gas properties. Further, not all producers calculate PV-10 in the same manner. PV-10 is not a financial measure prescribed by GAAP and does not purport to represent the fair value of our oil and gas properties. PV-10 should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for the standardized measure of discounted future net cash flows as defined under GAAP and presented in the supplemental oil and gas disclosures in our consolidated financial statements.

Reserves. Estimated remaining quantities of oil and gas and related substances anticipated to be economically producible from known accumulations from a given date forward by application of development projects to known accumulations; the area of the reservoir considered a known accumulation is delineated by drilling and/or defined by water contact, if any, and the proved area must be delineated by drilling; also, the term "reserves" includes (1) quantities of oil and gas subject to delivered volumes under a sales agreement with purchasers for which the price is defined deterministically and in the same manner as quantities for which oil and gas sales are subject to a future prices as defined under the SEC guidelines, and (2) oil and gas that will be consumed as fuel in the operations of the properties in which the reserves exist.

Resource play. A general term for an accumulation of hydrocarbons known to exist over a large area.

Royalty interest. The interest that entitles the owner to receive its proportionate share of the gross proceeds from the sale of production, free of expenses for drilling, development, and operations, but subject to severance taxes.

SEC. U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

Standardized measure (GAAP). The present value (discounted at 10% per year) of estimated future net cash inflows related to proved reserves.

Working interest. The operating interest that gives the owner the right to drill, produce and conduct operating activities on the property and to incur the costs of exploration, development and operations according to its proportionate interest in the property.

Regulation
General. New or revised rules, regulations and policies may be issued, and new legislation may be enacted, that could materially affect the oil and gas exploration and production industry. Such changes could affect, among other things, our production levels, the way we operate, our environmental and safety practices, the costs of compliance, and our financial performance.

Federal, State and Local Regulation. Our operations are subject to extensive regulation by federal, state and local authorities. These regulations cover a broad range of matters including, but not limited to, drilling and completion practices, well construction, groundwater protection, air emissions, waste disposal, and surface land usage. The requirements can vary significantly between jurisdictions, and we must obtain and maintain numerous permits and approvals to conduct our activities. Failure to comply with these regulations could result in fines, penalties, or restrictions on operations.

Environmental and Safety Standards. We are subject to environmental laws and regulations that aim to protect air and water quality, manage waste, and ensure safe operations. Compliance with these standards may require significant expenditures for monitoring, reporting, equipment upgrades, and facility modifications. We continuously review and adapt our practices to meet evolving requirements and to support responsible development.

Hydraulic Fracturing. Our completion operations commonly utilize hydraulic fracturing. Regulators at various levels of government continue to evaluate and, in some cases, implement more stringent requirements related to well construction, chemical disclosure, water sourcing and disposal, and induced seismicity. We expect ongoing scrutiny and potential changes to the regulatory framework applicable to hydraulic fracturing. Additional restrictions or requirements could increase costs, limit the availability of services, or affect the timing of our projects.

Air Emissions and Methane. We are subject to regulations governing emissions of greenhouse gases, volatile organic compounds, and other air pollutants. Recent and pending rulemakings may result in additional monitoring, control technologies, and reporting obligations. We evaluate the applicability of these rules to our assets and implement measures designed to comply with current requirements and to prepare for potential future changes.

Water Management. Our operations require the sourcing, handling, storage, and disposal of water. We manage water through a combination of supply planning, transportation and storage infrastructure, treatment, and disposal methods. Regulatory requirements related to water use, discharge, and disposal wells can affect our costs and operational flexibility.

Waste and Spill Prevention. We maintain programs and procedures aimed at preventing spills and managing waste generated during drilling and production activities. Applicable regulations may require secondary containment, spill response planning, and the use of approved disposal methods for certain materials. We regularly review these programs to maintain compliance and to address any changes in regulatory expectations.

Focus on Safe, Responsible and Sustainable Operations. The safety and welfare of our employees, contractors and communities, and protection of the environment is foundational to our culture and operations. We are committed to achieving leading EHS performance through our programs, including initiatives focused on process safety, improving our safety culture, and pursuing operational excellence. We empower all employees and contractors to stop work they believe to be unsafe or unhealthy.

Code of Business Conduct and Ethics. We maintain and enforce a risk-based Code of Business Conduct and Ethics that is focused on a set of values, behaviors and principles to maintain the integrity and ethics of our organization. Our Code of Business Conduct and Ethics applies to all directors, officers and employees and ensures we are acting honestly and ethically in accordance with all applicable laws, and with integrity in our interactions with our stakeholders. Our Code of Business Conduct and Ethics also addresses such topics as conflicts of interest, insider trading, confidential information and the protection and appropriate use of company assets, among others. Our employees and directors are required to complete a Code of Business Conduct and Ethics certification annually. We intend to satisfy the disclosure requirement under Item 5.05 of Form 8-K regarding an amendment to, or release of material changes in, certain provisions of our Code of Business Conduct and Ethics that apply to our principal executive officer, principal financial officer, principal accounting officer or controller, or person performing similar functions, by posting such information on our website.

Workforce Training and Engagement. Our employees and contractors receive training on EHS procedures as well as on topics to enhance their implementation of our programs. We utilize internal and third-party programs and software to deliver and track training and maintain a record of training. In addition, we continue to seek continuous improvement through review of leading and lagging indicators and engage our workforce through safety observations.

Supply Chain and Human Rights. Our values and behaviors include ensuring all aspects of our business are conducted in accordance with international human rights principles. We set our expectations of suppliers through policies and expectations contained within our Functional Safety Management System, our Code of Business Conduct and Ethics, our Environmental Policy and our Human Rights and Child Labor Policy. In addition, our Third Party Risk Management (TPRM) program is designed to address enterprise risk by providing a comprehensive risk-based approach for third party risk management. The TPRM program is used to estimate the risk of engagement of a vendor through risk profiling across various risk domains. The risk profile is used to determine the level of due diligence and ongoing monitoring conducted for engagement of a third party. Our Third Party Code of Conduct reinforces our commitment to engaging third parties who support legal and ethical business practices. The Code communicates the minimum standards for suppliers or other third parties to conduct business with us and our expectation for suppliers and third parties to promote continuous improvement in their supply chain and to exceed minimum standards in pursuit of business engagement with us.

Human Capital Resources. As of December 31, 2024, we had 1,872 full-time employees working in the United States, with 1,037 employees located in the Southern Region, 793 located in the Marcellus Shale, and 42 employees located in Houston, Texas. None of our employees are covered by a collective bargaining agreement. Our ability to ensure that the labor and employee relations climate remains stable in both the short and long term is integral to consistently achieving our business objectives. We strive to attract and retain qualified persons to advance our business and replace those who retire or otherwise leave our company, such as our long-term employees and those who have had managerial positions.

Freedom of Association/Right to Organize. We respect our employees’ freedom of association and legal right to organize without fear of reprisal, interference or discrimination, and without the obligation of prior consultation. Employees have freedom of association and the right to organize or join associations or unions of their choice in compliance with applicable laws.

Available Information. Our website is accessible free of charge at www.coterra.com. Our Annual Reports on Form 10-K, Quarterly Reports on Form 10-Q, Current Reports on Form 8-K, Proxy Statements and amendments to those reports and statements filed or furnished pursuant to Sections 13(a) or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 are available on our website. The contents of our website and other information posted there could be deemed to be material; however, other than as specifically noted herein, such website is not part of, and is not incorporated into, this Annual Report on Form 10-K or any other report we may file with or furnish to the SEC.

question: CTRA view on competitive P&E landscape?
answer: CTRA operates in an intensely competitive oil & gas landscape where larger peers benefit from scale and resources. However, its concentrated acreage, secured service capacity, and access to both owned and third-party infrastructure provide a buffer against pricing pressure and logistical bottlenecks. These factors could position CTRA to sustain reliable operations and protect margins despite broader industry volatility.

passages.text:
Competition
The oil and gas industry is highly competitive, and we experience strong competition in the areas in which we operate. We primarily compete with integrated, independent and other energy companies for the sale and transportation of our oil and natural gas production to pipelines, marketing companies and end users. Many of these competitors have greater financial, technical and personnel resources and exploration and development budgets than we have. The effect of these competitive factors cannot be predicted.

Price, contract terms, availability of rigs and completion crews and related equipment and quality of service, including pipeline connection times, distribution efficiencies and reliable delivery record affect competition. For example, constrained pipeline capacity and oversupply in certain geographic areas in 2024 resulted in negative spot market pricing at times for natural gas, such as in the Permian Basin at the Waha Hub. We believe that our concentrated acreage positions and our access to both third-party and Company-owned gathering and pipeline infrastructure in our core operating areas, along with our expected activity level and the related services and equipment that we have secured for the upcoming years, enhance our competitive position.

ACREAGE
Our interest in both developed and undeveloped acreage depends on the extent and nature of our ownership position within a particular area. Acreage is described according to the nature of title acquired, such as fee ownership or various types of mineral leases. Management periodically reviews our undeveloped acreage for recoverability of these amounts and records impairment in the period the assessment is made.

• Developed Acreage – Developed acreage is acreage assignable to producing wells or wells capable of production.
• Undeveloped Acreage – Undeveloped acreage is acreage on which wells have not been drilled or where wells have been drilled but are not yet capable of production.
• Gross Acreage – Gross acreage and gross wells are the total acres and wells in which we have an interest.
• Net Acreage – Net acreage and net wells are determined by multiplying the gross acres and gross wells by our fractional working interest owned.

The following table presents information about our gross and net developed and undeveloped acreage by core area as of December 31, 2023:

|------|-----|------------|-----|-------------|-----|------------|

| Core | | (in acres) | | (in acres) | | (in acres) | (in acres) |
| | | | | | | | |
| Marcellus Shale | | | | | | | |
| Permian Basin | | | | | | | |

| Total | | | | | | | |

Acreage Expirations

Certain of our undeveloped acreage will expire at the end of the applicable primary term unless we exercise our contractual rights to extend the terms of some of such leases or establish production from the acreage prior to lease expiration. In addition, our leases typically provide that expiring leases can be extended under certain circumstances such as the commencement of a dry hole, drilling operations or production. The following table presents our net undeveloped acreage scheduled to expire during the next three years and thereafter as of December 31, 2023.

| | | Net Undeveloped Acreage Scheduled to Expire |
|-----|-----|----------------------------------------------|
| | | 2024 | 2025 | 2026 | Thereafter | Total |
| | | | | | | |

We endeavor to manage our lease expiration profile by prioritizing drilling and completion activities on acreage nearing expiration, entering into lease extensions when economically justified and selectively acquiring additional interests. We also evaluate acreage trade opportunities that may optimize our position, consolidate working interests, reduce noncore leasehold and improve capital efficiency. However, there is no assurance we will be able to retain all of our undeveloped acreage in the future, and the extent to which leases may be extended depends on the terms of the leases and current market conditions, including commodity prices and availability of services.

Royalty Interests and Working Interests

Our working interest ownership varies by well and by area, and our net revenue interest after royalties and other burdens will differ accordingly. Royalty burdens are governed by lease terms and mineral ownership and can impact our net recoveries from production. We continuously assess our working interest and royalty structures as part of our broader development planning, including potential farm-in and farm-out transactions, joint ventures and participation agreements which can affect our net acreage and drilling obligations.

Environmental and Operational Considerations

We are subject to a wide range of environmental regulations that may affect our ability to develop certain acreage. In addition, access to infrastructure, surface use restrictions, spacing requirements, pooling and unitization, and other operational considerations may impact the timing and extent of development on specific leases. We actively manage these factors to maintain compliance and optimize development plans.

Additional information about our properties, including reserves, wells and production, is included elsewhere in this report.

Market Conditions and Commodity Prices
Our revenues, operating results and cash flows are highly dependent upon the prices of the commodities we produce—oil, natural gas and NGLs. Commodity prices are subject to significant volatility and are influenced by global and domestic supply and demand, geopolitical developments, macroeconomic conditions, changes in production by OPEC+ and other producing nations, regional differentials, transportation constraints, refining capacity, inventory levels, weather, regulatory policies and market speculation, among other factors. We do not have control over the market prices for the commodities we sell, and we cannot predict future price movements with certainty.

Oil and NGL prices are primarily influenced by global supply and demand dynamics, geopolitical events and refining economics, while natural gas prices are driven largely by domestic supply and demand, weather patterns, storage levels, LNG export capacity and pipeline takeaway constraints in producing regions. Regional basis differentials can also have a material impact on the realized prices we receive relative to benchmark indices, reflecting transportation costs, quality and location differentials and local market conditions.

We utilize a combination of physical sales arrangements and financial derivative instruments to mitigate a portion of our exposure to commodity price volatility. Our risk management activities are designed to provide a degree of price certainty and support our capital program and dividend framework; however, such activities can also limit upside participation during periods of rising prices and may expose us to potential non-cash mark-to-market gains and losses. The extent and timing of our hedging activities may vary based on our view of market conditions, risk tolerance and other factors.

Sustained periods of lower commodity prices could result in reductions to our planned capital expenditures, slower growth in production, increased evaluation of potential impairments of oil and gas properties and other assets, and could adversely affect our ability to access capital markets on favorable terms. Conversely, periods of higher commodity prices may positively impact our cash flows and allow for increased investment and shareholder returns, although service cost inflation and supply chain constraints can offset some of these benefits.

We continuously monitor market conditions and adjust our development plans, portfolio allocation and marketing strategies in response to changing price environments. We remain focused on operational efficiency, capital discipline and maintaining a strong balance sheet to navigate commodity price volatility.

Marketing Activities

Oil, Gas and NGL Marketing

The spot markets for oil, gas and NGLs are subject to volatility that can materially impact our realized prices and cash flows. We market our production using a combination of term and spot sales, as well as through transport arrangements to multiple end markets, including refineries, petrochemical plants, utilities, marketers and other purchasers. We sell oil, gas and NGLs under a variety of arrangements, including month-to-month agreements and short-term (less than one year) agreements at prices negotiated monthly or quarterly, and under longer-term contracts with formulas based on market indices adjusted for location and product quality differentials.

Oil is typically sold at or near the lease location or delivered to purchase points on gathering systems or pipelines with pricing based on regional differentials to published benchmarks. Natural gas production is sold at the wellhead, to gathering systems or processors that extract NGLs and return residue gas to the market, or transported on interstate pipelines. NGLs are generally sold to petrochemical, refining and other industrial customers at prices tied to Mont Belvieu or Conway benchmarks.

Our ability to obtain favorable pricing and secure adequate takeaway capacity is influenced by the availability of transportation infrastructure, including gathering systems, processing facilities, fractionation capacity, storage and pipelines in the regions where we operate. In certain areas, pipeline or processing capacity may be limited, and we may experience curtailments, increased basis differentials or the need to secure alternative transportation, including trucking or third-party arrangements, which may increase costs.

We also may enter into marketing or trading activities, including the purchase and resale of commodities, to optimize transportation capacity, fulfill contractual commitments and manage location and quality differentials. These activities can result in gains or losses depending on market conditions, price differentials and our ability to efficiently manage logistics. Our marketing activities are conducted in accordance with applicable regulations and risk management policies, and we monitor counterparty credit exposure and require appropriate credit support where necessary.

Delivery Commitments

We have various delivery commitments for oil, gas and NGLs under transportation, processing and sales contracts. These commitments are designed to provide reliable access to end markets and improve price realizations. Failure to deliver volumes under such agreements may subject us to deficiency payments or other contractual remedies. We regularly evaluate these commitments in light of our production forecasts, market conditions and available alternatives, and we may renegotiate, assign or terminate obligations where contract terms allow.

Marketing
In 2024, EOG continued its diversified approach to marketing its production with the objective of maximizing price realizations while maintaining flexibility to respond to changing market conditions. We sell crude oil, natural gas and NGLs to a broad range of customers, including refiners, marketers, integrated oil companies, power generators, local distribution companies and industrial users. Our marketing strategy includes a combination of spot and term sales, utilization of transportation options and management of basis differentials through physical and financial arrangements.

Crude Oil. We market crude oil using pipeline, gathering systems, rail and, where appropriate, trucking to reach multiple end markets. The majority of our crude oil is sold under market-indexed pricing arrangements with adjustments for location and quality differentials. We seek to access premium markets and optimize netbacks by leveraging transportation agreements and optionality across regions, including the Gulf Coast. We also manage price exposure through the use of financial derivatives in accordance with our risk management policies.

Natural Gas. Our natural gas is sold at the wellhead, to gathering systems or to third-party processors, with pricing based on market indices such as Henry Hub or regional hubs adjusted for basis differentials. We may enter into firm transportation and processing agreements to ensure access to end-use markets and to reduce exposure to takeaway constraints in key producing areas. Our strategy emphasizes balancing contracted capacity with operational flexibility to manage seasonal and regional variability in demand and pricing.

NGLs. NGLs are marketed primarily to petrochemical, refining and other industrial customers at prices referencing Mont Belvieu or other regional benchmarks, with adjustments for product composition and delivery location. We may utilize fractionation agreements and storage capacity to manage product streams and seasonal demand patterns, and we work with processors and midstream providers to optimize NGL value.

Basis Differentials and Transportation. Regional price differentials can significantly impact our realized prices. We actively manage basis exposure by securing transportation capacity, expanding access to sales points and, where appropriate, utilizing financial instruments. We monitor market conditions and consider opportunities to shift sales to higher-value markets or adjust transportation commitments. In areas where pipeline or processing capacity is constrained, we may experience wider basis differentials or curtailments, and we evaluate alternatives to mitigate these effects.

Counterparty Credit and Risk Management. We have established credit policies and procedures to manage counterparty exposure in our marketing activities. These include ongoing credit evaluations, monitoring of receivables and, when appropriate, the use of credit support arrangements such as letters of credit. Our risk management program includes limits and controls designed to monitor and govern marketing activities and derivative positions.

Regulatory Considerations. Our marketing operations are subject to federal, state and local regulations, including those governing pipeline transportation, market transparency, trading practices and environmental protection. We monitor regulatory developments and adjust our marketing practices as needed to ensure compliance and to adapt to changes that could affect market dynamics, transportation availability or pricing mechanisms.

Forward-Looking Information
This Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q contains certain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Forward-looking statements are based on our current expectations, estimates and projections about our industry, management’s beliefs and certain assumptions we have made. Words such as “anticipates,” “expects,” “intends,” “plans,” “believes,” “seeks,” “estimates,” “targets,” “should,” “could,” “would,” “will,” “may” and variations of such words and similar expressions are intended to identify such forward-looking statements. These statements are not guarantees of future performance and are subject to risks, uncertainties and other factors, some of which are beyond our control, that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied by such forward-looking statements.

Important factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those in the forward-looking statements include, among others: changes in commodity prices and basis differentials; fluctuations in supply and demand for oil, natural gas and NGLs; the availability of, and costs associated with, drilling rigs, completion crews, equipment, materials, labor and other oilfield services; transportation constraints, gathering and processing availability and costs; the pace of infrastructure development in our operating areas; weather conditions, including hurricanes and winter storms; regulatory and legislative developments affecting our industry; actions by OPEC+ and other producing nations; the availability and cost of capital; the performance of our hedging program; drilling results and reserve estimates; the timing and amount of future production; the availability and timing of regulatory approvals; and other risks described in our filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including the “Risk Factors” section of our Annual Report on Form 10-K.

You should not place undue reliance on forward-looking statements contained in this report, which speak only as of the date hereof. We undertake no obligation to publicly update or revise any forward-looking statements, whether as a result of new information, future events or otherwise.

question: Impact of decline in oil prices on quarterly base dividend?
answer: Despite an 8% drop in realized oil prices, strong production growth and higher gas and NGL prices drove a sharp increase in earnings and cash flow. This resilience allowed the company to raise its quarterly base dividend from $0.21 to $0.22 per share, signaling confidence in sustaining shareholder returns even amid commodity price volatility.

Financial and Operating Overview
Financial and operating results for the six months ended June 30, 2025 compared to the six months ended June 30, 2024 reflect the following:

• Net income increased $455 million from $572 million, or $0.77 per share, in 2024 to $1.0 billion, or $1.35 per share, in 2025.

• Net cash provided by operating activities increased $666 million, from $1.4 billion in 2024 to $2.1 billion in 2025.

• Equivalent production increased 15.2 MMBoe from 123.3 MMBoe, or 677.7 MBoe per day, in 2024 to 138.5 MMBoe, or 765.4 MBoe per day, in 2025.

◦ Oil production increased 7.8 MMBbl from 19.1 MMBbl, or 104.9 MBbl per day, in 2024 to 26.9 MMBbl, or 148.4 MBbl per day, in 2025.

◦ Natural gas production increased 24.5 Bcf from 522.3 Bcf, or 2,869.9 MMcf per day, in 2024 to 546.8 Bcf, or 3,021.1 MMcf per day, in 2025.

◦ NGL volumes increased 3.4 MMBbl from 17.2 MMBbl, or 94.5 MBbl per day, in 2024 to 20.6 MMBbl, or 113.6 MBbl per day, in 2025.

• Average realized prices (including impact of derivatives):

◦ Oil was $66.52 per Bbl in 2025, 14 percent lower than the $77.25 per Bbl realized in 2024.

◦ Natural gas was $2.74 per Mcf in 2025, 56 percent higher than the $1.76 per Mcf realized in 2024.

◦ NGL price was $20.66 per Bbl in 2025, two percent higher than the $20.28 per Bbl realized in 2024.

• Total capital expenditures for drilling, completion and other fixed assets were $1.1 billion in 2025 compared to $927 million in the corresponding period of the prior year.

Other financial highlights for the six months ended June 30, 2025 include the following:

• Closed two acquisitions in January 2025 in the Delaware Basin in New Mexico for total consideration of $3.3 billion in cash and the issuance of 28,190,682 shares of our common stock valued at $785 million based on the closing price of our common stock on the closing date of the transactions.

• Increased our quarterly base dividend from $0.21 per share to $0.22 per share in February 2025.

• Repaid $350 million of the Tranche A Term Loan.

• Repurchased 2 million shares for $47 million.

Derivative Instruments and Risk Management Activities

Our commodity price risk management strategy is designed to reduce the effect of price volatility on our cash flows by limiting our exposure to declines in commodity prices while also allowing for participation in commodity price increases. From time to time, we may hedge a portion of our expected future oil, natural gas liquids ("NGLs") and natural gas production volumes. We also may use basis swaps to reduce basis risk and collars to limit price risk through a combination of floor and ceiling prices. We do not enter into derivative contracts for trading purposes.

We evaluate our commodity price risk management activities on an ongoing basis and, where appropriate, adjust our positions in response to changes in market conditions, our operating plans and other factors, including counterparty credit considerations. The extent to which we engage in commodity price risk management activities remains at our discretion and may vary from time to time. The use of commodity derivative instruments exposes us to credit risk from our counterparties and to the risk of financial loss if our production and sales volumes are less than our hedged volumes or if there is a significant, sustained increase in the prices of the commodities we produce.

Periodically, we enter into financial commodity derivatives, including swaps, collars and basis swaps, with a number of counterparties. Under swap contracts, we receive a fixed price for a specified notional volume of commodities in exchange for paying a variable price based on a market-based index. Collars provide price protection through the combination of purchased put options (which set a floor price) and sold call options (which set a ceiling price) for specified notional volumes. Basis swaps are used to mitigate differences between the index price at which we sell our production and the NYMEX price used for hedging.

We are exposed to market risk on the open positions of these commodity derivative contracts and we monitor and manage our exposure by establishing and enforcing risk limits and monitoring compliance with those limits. We also monitor counterparty credit exposure and collateral arrangements. Our derivative contracts typically contain provisions that allow for netting of cash settlement amounts with the same counterparty and may include collateral provisions that require the posting or receipt of collateral depending on the fair value of the positions and the counterparty’s creditworthiness.

question: Natural gas impact on operating rev?
answer: Natural gas was the main driver of the overall decline in operating revenues in 2024. Revenues fell by $599 million (–26%), largely due to lower realized prices (–$538 million) and to a lesser extent reduced volumes (–$61 million) from strategic curtailments in the Marcellus Shale. While higher production in the Permian and Anadarko partially offset the decline, the sharp drop in gas prices accounted for the majority of the negative impact.

MARKETING
Substantially all of our oil and natural gas production is sold under both long-term (more than one year) and short-term (less than one year) agreements at prices negotiated with third parties or based on market indices. The terms of these sales contracts vary by commodity and potential credit exposure may be limited to the duration of the agreement.

We are reasonably assured of market access for all of our oil and natural gas production in the current commodity price and infrastructure environment. We sell our production under various contract terms to customers that include gas marketers, pipeline companies, oil refineries and midstream companies. We sell NGLs primarily to petrochemical facilities and NGL marketing and transportation companies. The majority of our production is sold at variable, or market-sensitive, prices. Oil and spot market prices for North American natural gas and NGLs are primarily influenced by the supply and demand for these products. Potential impacts from OPEC policy decisions, world and United States (U.S.) inventories and U.S. crude oil and NGL exports may cause volatility in commodity prices for oil, NGLs and natural gas. Changes in these prices have a direct effect on our operating results.

We also incur gathering and transportation expenses when we move our natural gas from wellhead markets to other downstream markets. At times, we use large volume gas transaction points along the major pipelines to move our natural gas to more favorable markets. We are currently unaware of any potential production curtailments related to potential state or federal regulation in any of the areas we operate; however, we cannot guarantee that we will always be able to transport and market all of our production.

 Delivery Commitments
We have entered into various firm sales contracts to deliver and sell natural gas in our areas of operation, including firm processing and pipeline transportation agreements to move volumes to market. Firm sales contracts generally do not require the delivery and sale of fixed and determinable quantities. However, since these contracts take advantage of our firm capacity on pipeline and gathering systems, we may experience a shortfall in pipeline system delivery capability at fluctuating delivery levels from time to time. To address this situation, we may purchase natural gas to balance excess pipeline system delivery demands from time to time. As of December 31, 2024, we were not committed to deliver fixed quantities of oil or NGLs for the years subsequent to 2024. For natural gas commitments, we may utilize the spot market or purchase to satisfy shortfalls, should they occur. The required volumes under the following sales contracts represent our expected level of firm sales under the contracts and may change as the contractual delivery levels and our own production and purchases change over the next five years. We believe we will have sufficient production quantities to meet these commitments, and we also expect to use some of our firm transportation capacity to deliver third party natural gas to various markets.

ITEM 3. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk
In the normal course of business, we are subject to a variety of risks, including commodity price risk and interest rate risk. We may use derivative instruments to manage the commodity price risk for our oil, natural gas and NGL production and interest rate risk inherent in our outstanding debt obligations. All of our derivative instruments and any gains or losses resulting from changes in fair value are recorded at fair value and included in our Consolidated Financial Statements. These derivatives do not qualify for hedge accounting. Accordingly, gains and losses associated with changes in the fair value of these derivative instruments, including unrealized gains and losses resulting from changes in the fair value of the derivative instruments, are recorded in earnings as a component of other (income) expense, net. The fair value of our derivative instruments is based on estimates provided by counterparties, which are reviewed for reasonableness by us.

 Commodity Price Risk
Our most significant market risk exposure is pricing applicable to our oil and natural gas production. We expect commodity prices to remain volatile. Our realized prices are mainly driven by the worldwide price for oil and spot market prices for North American natural gas and NGLs. Our realized prices are also impacted by basis differentials for natural gas, which are defined as the difference in the quoted market prices of natural gas at different geographic market locations. Differentials can vary by region and time period. We also incur gathering and transportation expenses when we move our natural gas from wellhead markets to other downstream markets. At times, we use large volume gas transaction points along the major pipelines to move our natural gas to more favorable markets.

Derivative Instruments and Risk Management Activities

Our commodity price risk management strategy is to reduce, over time, a portion of our exposure to commodity price volatility by using derivative arrangements to protect what we believe to be acceptable returns on our investment. In addition, we enter into forward contracts to sell natural gas to limit exposure to regional basis risk. We do not enter into derivative instruments for speculative or trading purposes.

We believe our derivative arrangements have decreased the volatility of our average realized prices and cash flows from operating activities. Marketing Activities

Oil, Gas and NGL Marketing

The spot markets for oil, gas and NGLs are subject to volatility and cyclicality and we expect this will continue in the future. Oil and spot market prices for North American natural gas and NGLs are primarily influenced by the supply and demand for these products. Crude oil prices are strongly impacted by estimates of worldwide demand expectations for such commodities and economic uncertainty is likely to be reflected in crude oil prices. Natural gas spot market prices are strongly impacted by rationalization of supply and demand of natural gas, industry drilling and completion activity and consumer demand/housing usage. NGL prices are primarily affected by demand for petrochemical feedstocks as the key drivers are the strength of the economy and its relationship to the demand for petrochemical products, as well as the relative balances between feedstocks for ethylene production. Potential impacts from OPEC policy decisions, world and United States (U.S.) inventories and U.S. crude oil and NGL exports may cause volatility in commodity prices for oil, NGLs and natural gas in 2025. Changes in these prices have a direct effect on our operating results, as they are reflected in our product revenues.

Under market-sensitive contracts, the price we receive for production from the majority of our oil, natural gas and NGL volumes is tied to a market index, with various adjustments for, among other things, product quality and location. As a part of managing our oil, natural gas and NGL price risk, we may utilize both long-term and short-term marketing agreements to sell a portion of our future production. Under those agreements, we obtain market prices by negotiating index and basis adjustments. Although our natural gas supplies are sold to a variety of purchasers, the sales are principally to marketers, midstream processors and co-generation and utility companies. Oil and NGLs are principally sold to marketers and refiners. Sales are generally made under short-term (less than one year) agreements at prices negotiated with third parties.

Additionally, we may enter into financial hedging arrangements or use derivative financial instruments (such as swaps, collars, options and basis swaps) to manage our exposure to price fluctuations for our commodity purchases and sales and our oil and natural gas. Marketing
In 2024, EOG continued its diversified approach to marketing its production.

In 2024, EOG's average realized U.S. NGL price was $22.77 per barrel as compared to the monthly average Mont Belvieu, Texas, NGL price of $18.77 per barrel. EOG's per-barrel average U.S. NGL price premium to Mont Belvieu, Texas, was $4.00, compared to a premium of $2.41 per barrel for 2023.

Based on these factors, the Company generally elects to sell unprocessed gas when natural gas prices are high relative to NGL prices.

In EOG's foreign operations, purchase and sale contracts are usually based on fixed supply positions while transportation and processing are integrally tied to long-term contracts. The Company's sales prices are based on fixed or market indices in the various countries where EOG operates, which we believe reduces the risk arising from commodity price changes.

EOG has secured some long-term U.S. crude oil and NGL transportation and natural gas, crude oil and NGL export capacity to diversify market access confirmations. The transportation and export capacities utilized in EOG's commercial portfolio are expected to be sourced from future production of available reserves.

Based on these factors, the Company generally elects to sell unprocessed gas when natural gas prices are high relative to NGL prices.

question: CTRAs 24 cap investment strategy & outlook + marketing arrangements for O&G sales?
answer: CTRAs 2024 plan reflects capital discipline, with a 12% lower budget than 2023 while still advancing 132–158 wells. The strategy emphasizes the Permian Basin for oil-driven growth, balanced by gas exposure in the Marcellus and Anadarko. Marketing remains diversified across contract types and customers, with manageable transportation costs and no current constraints, positioning CTRA to capture value while maintaining flexibility in dynamic commodity markets.

2024 OUTLOOK
Our 2024 capital program is expected to be approximately $1.75 billion to $1.95 billion, a decrease of 12 percent (at the mid-point) from $2.1 billion in 2023. We expect to turn-in-line 132 to 158 total net wells in 2024 across our three core operating areas. Approximately 60 percent of our drilling and completion capital will be invested in the Permian Basin, 23 percent in the Marcellus Shale and 17 percent in the Anadarko Basin (at the mid-point).

MARKETING
Substantially all of our oil and natural gas production is sold under both long-term and short-term sales contracts at market-sensitive prices. We sell oil, natural gas and NGLs to a broad portfolio of customers, including industrial customers, local distribution companies, oil and gas marketers, major energy companies, pipeline companies and power generation facilities.

We also incur gathering and transportation expenses when we move our oil and natural gas production from wellhead markets to other downstream markets.

To date, we have not experienced significant difficulty in transporting or marketing our production as it becomes available; however, there is no assurance that we will always be able to transport and market all of our production.
