Liquidity and Capital Resources
We strive to maintain an adequate liquidity level to address commitments, both short-term and long-term. We believe that we have sufficient capacity to repay our debt and other obligations as they become due over the next 12 months and, based on current expectations, for the longer term.

Our primary sources of liquidity are cash on hand, net cash provided by operating activities and availability under our revolving credit agreement. As of December 31, 2024, we had no borrowings under our revolving credit agreement and our borrowing base and aggregate elected commitments were $2.25 billion. We also had $1.7 billion of unrestricted cash on hand at December 31, 2024. In addition, we may access the capital markets to supplement our liquidity, which may include the issuance of debt or equity securities, repurchases and exchanges of existing debt securities, or other transactions.

We continue to actively manage our liability profile and pursue options designed to enhance financial flexibility and optimize our capital structure. During 2024, we completed various financing activities, including the issuance of senior notes and an amendment to our revolving credit agreement. We may, from time to time, seek to retire, redeem, repurchase or exchange our outstanding debt through open market purchases, privately negotiated transactions, tender offers, redemptions, exchanges or otherwise. The amount and timing of such activities, if any, will depend on market conditions, our liquidity position, contractual restrictions and other factors.

We may also pursue acquisitions and dispositions of assets in order to align our portfolio with our long-term business strategy. We regularly evaluate acquisition and divestiture opportunities and may, from time to time, acquire or dispose of assets or business units when we believe it is appropriate. The amount and timing of any such activities, if any, will depend on a number of factors, including market conditions, commodity prices, valuations and the availability of attractive opportunities and potential counterparties.

Our ability to obtain capital on acceptable terms depends in part on our credit ratings. As of December 31, 2024, our senior unsecured debt was rated investment grade by all three major ratings agencies. Although the ratings agencies do not provide formulas or methodologies for determining credit ratings, the agencies consider a number of qualitative and quantitative factors associated with our business and operations in evaluating our credit ratings.

While there are no “rating triggers” that would require an immediate acceleration of amounts due or termination under any of our debt agreements or financial instruments, a downgrade in our credit ratings by one or more rating agencies could negatively impact our access to capital markets and our balance sheet. While there are no “rating triggers” that would require an immediate acceleration of amounts due or termination under any of our debt agreements or financial instruments, a downgrade in our credit ratings could increase our cost of capital and adversely affect our ability to execute our business strategy.

As of December 31, 2024, our total long-term debt was $7.3 billion. We had no borrowings outstanding under our revolving credit agreement and had $2.25 billion of available capacity under that facility. We were in compliance with all covenants under our debt agreements at December 31, 2024. None of our debt agreements include covenants that we believe would materially restrict our ability to incur additional indebtedness, make investments or undertake other activities that are important to the successful execution of our business strategy.

We intend to continue to use our cash flows and other sources of liquidity to fund our operations, capital program, dividends and potential debt repurchases, redemptions, exchanges, tender offers or otherwise. We expect that our cash on hand, cash flow from operations and available borrowings under our revolving credit agreement will be sufficient to meet our obligations and fund our planned activities over the next 12 months and, based on current expectations, for the longer term.

Our working capital is substantially influenced by the variables of commodity prices, operating costs and the timing of cash collections and disbursements. While we cannot predict future commodity prices with certainty, we believe our financial position, liquidity and planned activities will allow us to meet our working capital requirements over the next 12 months.

In February 2024, our Board of Directors approved a $3.0 billion share repurchase program. The repurchase program authorizes share repurchases of our common stock in the open market or through privately negotiated transactions. The timing and amount of share repurchases will be determined by management based on market conditions, share price and other factors.

In addition to the repurchase program, our Board of Directors authorized an increase in our quarterly dividend. Future dividend payments are subject to approval by our Board of Directors and will depend on, among other factors, cash flows from operations, our financial condition, market conditions and the capital requirements of our business.

We may also pursue strategic alternatives to enhance stockholder value, including asset sales, joint ventures, mergers, acquisitions, recapitalizations and other transactions. Any such transactions could materially affect our capital structure, liquidity and financial condition, and there can be no assurance that any such transactions will be consummated or, if consummated, will be successful.

In the ordinary course of business, we enter into commitments, contracts and contingencies. These primarily relate to purchase obligations, contractual obligations for drilling services and other operating activities, firm transportation and processing commitments, leases, asset retirement obligations and legal matters. We believe our cash flows and available sources of liquidity are sufficient to meet these obligations as they become due.

We also use derivative instruments to manage commodity price risk and, to a lesser extent, interest rate risk. These derivatives include swaps, collars and options. Our derivative activities are subject to our risk management policies and are designed to provide a degree of price certainty to our future cash flows, reduce volatility and support our capital program and dividend strategy. We do not enter into derivative instruments for speculative or trading purposes.

We may, from time to time, enter into joint ventures, partnerships and other investment arrangements with strategic partners to develop assets, share in capital requirements and create additional financial flexibility. These arrangements can provide access to capital and expertise, strengthen our balance sheet and enhance returns. The terms of any such arrangements will be based on market conditions and the specific attributes of the opportunities at hand.

We continually assess our liquidity and capital resources and may modify our business plans in response to changes in commodity prices, capital markets, regulatory developments and other factors. We believe our financial flexibility, liquidity position and operating capabilities will allow us to successfully execute our business strategy and create long-term value for our stockholders.

We maintain strong relationships with lenders, investors and other stakeholders and believe we have sufficient access to capital to fund our operations and strategic initiatives. We will continue to monitor market conditions and adjust our financing plans as necessary to support our business objectives.

We will also continue to evaluate our capital structure and may pursue opportunities to optimize our balance sheet, including potential refinancing of existing debt, extension of maturities and reduction of overall borrowing costs. The timing and terms of any such transactions will depend on market conditions and our financial objectives.

We believe that our current liquidity position, together with anticipated cash flows from operations, will be sufficient to fund our planned operations, capital program, dividends and other obligations for the next 12 months and, based on current expectations, for the longer term.

Cash and Cash Equivalents

The Company considers all highly liquid short-term investments with a maturity of three months or less when purchased to be cash equivalents. Cash and cash equivalents may, at times, exceed federally insured limits or include deposits in money market funds that are not insured or guaranteed by the U.S. government. The Company mitigates credit risk by selecting financial institutions with high credit ratings and limits exposure to any one financial institution. The Company monitors the financial condition of such institutions and considers any possible credit risk to be minimal.

Restricted Cash

Restricted cash includes cash that is legally or contractually restricted as to withdrawal or use. Restricted cash primarily consists of cash deposited in escrow accounts that are restricted for use.

Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

The Company records an allowance for doubtful accounts based on management’s assessment of the collectability of accounts receivable, which includes consideration of historical credit loss experience, current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts that affect the collectability of the reported amount. The Company evaluates the adequacy of the allowance for doubtful accounts at each reporting date and recognizes adjustments to the estimate of future expected credit losses on outstanding receivables as necessary.

Inventories

Inventories are primarily comprised of tubular goods and well equipment and are stated at the lower of cost or net realizable value. Cost is determined using the weighted-average cost method. Inventories are assessed periodically for obsolescence.

Properties and Equipment

Oil and Gas Properties

The Company uses the successful efforts method of accounting for its oil and gas activities. Under this method, acquisition costs of proved and unproved properties, development costs and successful exploration costs are capitalized. Costs relating to unsuccessful exploration efforts are expensed as incurred. Costs not directly associated with acquiring or discovering proved reserves are also expensed as incurred. Capitalized costs of proved oil and gas properties are depleted by field using the unit-of-production method based on estimates of proved developed reserves, and capitalized costs of wells and related equipment and facilities are depleted by field using the unit-of-production method based on estimates of total proved reserves. The provision for depletion of capitalized costs of oil and gas properties is calculated using estimated future cash flows, which are based on estimated future production of proved reserves and estimated future prices and costs. The estimates of proved reserves are determined by the Company’s internal reservoir engineers and are reviewed by independent petroleum engineers. The Company’s reserve estimates are prepared in accordance with guidelines established by the SEC and the FASB. The Company’s estimates of proved reserves are based on many factors, including but not limited to, geological and engineering estimates of oil and gas in place, economic recoverability of reserves, production experience and historical trends, operating costs, development costs and commodity prices. The Company’s estimates of proved reserves are subject to revision as additional information becomes available as a result of drilling, testing, reservoir studies, changes in prices and costs, technology, and other factors. Such revisions are often positive or negative and may be substantial. The Company’s reserve estimates may change, either positively or negatively, in the future, which could have a significant impact on the Company’s results of operations and financial condition.

The Company evaluates its proved oil and gas properties for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the assets may not be recoverable from future undiscounted net cash flows expected to be generated by the assets. If the carrying amount exceeds the sum of the undiscounted future net cash flows, the excess is recognized as an impairment loss for the amount by which the carrying amount exceeds the fair value of the assets. Fair value is estimated using discounted cash flow models and other valuation techniques, which require assumptions about future prices, production levels, operating costs, capital costs and other factors. The Company’s impairment assessments are based on the Company’s best estimates and assumptions, which are inherently subjective. Changes in the Company’s estimates and assumptions could result in changes in the impairment assessments and impairment charges in the future.

Unproved properties are assessed periodically for impairment on a property-by-property basis based on factors such as the Company’s drilling plans, the results of exploration activities, the terms of the leases and other relevant factors. Impairment of unproved properties is included in exploration expense.

Other Properties and Equipment

Other properties and equipment are recorded at cost and depreciated on a straight-line basis over their estimated useful lives. The Company reviews the carrying amount of other properties and equipment for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the assets may not be recoverable. If the carrying amount exceeds the sum of the undiscounted future net cash flows expected to be generated by the assets, the Company recognizes an impairment loss for the amount by which the carrying amount exceeds the fair value of the assets.

Capitalized Interest

The Company capitalizes interest on expenditures for significant investments in unproved oil and gas properties and on the construction of facilities. Capitalized interest is included in the carrying amount of the related assets and is amortized over the estimated useful lives of the assets.

Asset Retirement Obligations

The Company recognizes asset retirement obligations (AROs) for its legal obligations to retire long-lived assets, including plugging and abandoning wells, removing equipment and facilities, and restoring land at the end of the life of the assets. The Company records the fair value of AROs in the period in which the obligations are incurred. The fair value of AROs is estimated using discounted cash flow techniques and the Company’s credit-adjusted risk-free rate. The associated asset retirement costs are capitalized as part of the carrying amount of the related long-lived assets and depreciated over the assets’ useful lives. The ARO liability is accreted to its settlement value over time using the Company’s credit-adjusted risk-free rate.

Leases

The Company accounts for leases in accordance with ASC 842, Leases. At the inception of an arrangement, the Company determines whether the arrangement is or contains a lease. Right-of-use assets represent the Company’s right to use an underlying asset for the lease term and lease liabilities represent the Company’s obligation to make lease payments. Lease liabilities are measured at the present value of future lease payments at the commencement date. Right-of-use assets are measured at the amount of the lease liability, adjusted for any lease payments made at or before the commencement date and certain initial direct costs. The Company recognizes lease expense for operating leases on a straight-line basis over the lease term. The Company has elected practical expedients to not separate lease and non-lease components and to not recognize assets and liabilities for leases with terms of 12 months or less.

Fair Value Measurements

The Company measures certain assets and liabilities at fair value on a recurring basis and recognizes certain other assets and liabilities at fair value on a nonrecurring basis. Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. The Company leverages observable market data or assumptions that market participants who are independent, knowledgeable and willing to transact would use in pricing the asset or liability. The Company classifies fair value measurements within the fair value hierarchy based on the nature of the inputs used in the valuation techniques. The fair value hierarchy prioritizes inputs into three broad levels, with Level 1 inputs consisting of quoted market prices for identical assets and liabilities in active markets, Level 2 inputs consisting of observable inputs other than quoted market prices included in Level 1, and Level 3 inputs consisting of unobservable inputs. The Company discloses the fair value of financial instruments for which it is practicable to estimate fair value.

Recently Issued Accounting Pronouncements

The Company monitors recently issued accounting pronouncements and evaluates the potential impact of new standards on its financial statements. The Company does not expect the adoption of recently issued standards to have a material effect on its consolidated financial statements.

2. Acquisitions
Cimarex Energy Co.

On October 1, 2021, the Company and Cimarex completed the Merger pursuant to the Agreement and Plan of Merger, dated as of May 23, 2021, by and among the Company, Double C Merger Sub, Inc., a wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, and Cimarex (“the Merger”). The Merger was accounted for as a business combination under ASC 805, Business Combinations, with the Company treated as the accounting acquirer. Under the terms of the Merger, each share of Cimarex common stock outstanding immediately prior to the effective time of the Merger was converted into the right to receive 4.0146 shares of the Company’s common stock. The Company issued approximately 408 million shares of common stock to Cimarex stockholders in connection with the Merger. The total purchase price consideration was measured at fair value as of the closing date of the Merger and consisted of the fair value of the shares of the Company’s common stock issued to Cimarex stockholders. The Company incurred transaction costs in connection with the Merger that were expensed as incurred and recorded in “Merger-related expenses” in the Consolidated Statement of Operations.

The preliminary allocation of the purchase price consideration to the assets acquired and liabilities assumed was based on estimates of their fair values as of the closing date and was subject to revision as additional information became available. The fair values of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed were determined using valuation techniques, including discounted cash flow models and market-based valuations, which required management to make significant estimates and assumptions with respect to future commodity prices, production volumes, operating and development costs, and other factors. The Company finalized the purchase price allocation within the measurement period in accordance with ASC 805.

The results of Cimarex’s operations have been included in the Company’s consolidated financial statements since the closing date of the Merger. The Company’s Consolidated Statement of Operations includes the revenues and expenses of Cimarex since October 1, 2021. The Company’s Consolidated Balance Sheet includes the assets acquired and liabilities assumed in the Merger at their respective fair values as of the closing date. The Merger was accounted for as a tax-free reorganization for U.S. federal income tax purposes.

Acquisitions and Divestitures

Grayson Mill Acquisition On June 26, 2024, Devon entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Grayson Mill Energy’s Williston Basin business for total consideration of approximately $5.0 billion, subject to customary purchase price adjustments, consisting of $3.25 billion of cash and approximately 37 million shares of Devon common stock. The transaction was approved by the Boards of Directors of both companies and is subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals and the expiration or termination of the applicable waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act. The acquisition is expected to add high-margin, low-risk oil production and significant inventory depth to Devon’s Williston Basin position. The purchase price was determined based on negotiated terms between the parties and reflects the fair value of the assets to be acquired and liabilities to be assumed at closing. The acquisition is expected to close in the first quarter of 2025. The Company intends to finance the cash portion of the purchase price with a combination of cash on hand and borrowings under its revolving credit facility.

Divestitures of Non-Core Assets During 2024, Devon completed divestitures of certain non-core assets in the Eagle Ford and other areas for total proceeds of approximately $1.1 billion, net of customary purchase price adjustments. The Company recognized gains and losses on divestitures based on the difference between the proceeds received and the carrying value of the assets divested, net of transaction costs. The divestitures are consistent with Devon’s strategy to high-grade its asset portfolio and allocate capital to its highest-return opportunities. Proceeds from divestitures were used to reduce debt, fund the Company’s capital program and repurchase shares of common stock.

Accounting for Acquisitions and Divestitures The Company accounts for acquisitions that meet the definition of a business under ASC 805, Business Combinations, using the acquisition method of accounting. Under this method, the Company recognizes, separately from goodwill, the identifiable assets acquired, the liabilities assumed and any noncontrolling interest in the acquiree at their acquisition-date fair values. The excess of the fair value of the consideration transferred over the fair value of the net assets acquired is recognized as goodwill. Transaction costs related to acquisitions are expensed as incurred and are not included in the consideration transferred. For transactions that do not meet the definition of a business, the Company accounts for the transactions as asset acquisitions and capitalizes transaction costs as part of the cost of the assets acquired. The Company recognizes divestitures when control of the assets is transferred to the buyer and derecognizes the carrying amount of the assets and liabilities divested. Gains or losses on divestitures are recognized in earnings and are measured as the difference between the proceeds received and the carrying amount of the assets and liabilities divested, net of transaction costs.

Pro Forma Financial Information The following unaudited pro forma financial information presents the Company’s results of operations as if the Grayson Mill acquisition had occurred on January 1, 2023. The pro forma financial information is provided for illustrative purposes only and is not necessarily indicative of the results of operations that would have been achieved if the acquisition had occurred on the date indicated, nor is it indicative of future results of operations. The pro forma financial information includes adjustments to reflect the allocation of the purchase price, adjustments to depreciation, depletion and amortization, and adjustments to interest expense and income taxes, among other items. The pro forma financial information does not reflect potential synergies, cost savings or other benefits that may be realized as a result of the acquisition.

Regulatory Approvals and Closing Conditions The closing of the Grayson Mill acquisition is subject to customary regulatory approvals, including the expiration or termination of the applicable waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act, and other customary closing conditions. There can be no assurance that the acquisition will be completed as currently contemplated or at all. If the acquisition is not completed, the Company’s business, financial condition and results of operations could be adversely affected.

Acquisitions of Property and Equipment

During the third quarter of 2024, Devon entered into a definitive agreement to acquire certain oil and gas properties and related equipment located in the Williston Basin for total consideration of approximately $5.0 billion, subject to customary adjustments. The transaction consisted of $3.5 billion of cash and approximately 37 million shares of Devon common stock, based on a fixed exchange ratio. The acquisition is expected to enhance Devon’s oil-weighted production mix, extend the Company’s inventory life and provide opportunities for operational synergies and cost efficiencies. The closing of the transaction is subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals and the expiration or termination of the applicable waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act. The Company expects to finance the cash portion of the purchase price with available liquidity, including cash on hand and borrowings under its revolving credit facility.

The acquired properties include interests in approximately 500,000 gross (300,000 net) acres with an average working interest of 60% and net production of approximately 150,000 Boe per day, of which approximately 70% is oil. The acquisition also includes interests in gathering and processing infrastructure and other related midstream assets. The Company expects to integrate the acquired properties into its existing Williston Basin operations and plans to continue to optimize development plans to maximize returns on investment. The Company believes the acquired properties have significant remaining drilling inventory with attractive economics at current commodity prices.

The Company accounts for the acquisition in accordance with ASC 805, Business Combinations, as the acquired set of activities and assets meets the definition of a business. Accordingly, the Company will recognize the assets acquired and liabilities assumed at their acquisition-date fair values. The Company will record the excess of the fair value of the consideration transferred over the fair value of the net assets acquired as goodwill. The Company will expense transaction costs related to the acquisition as incurred.

Purchase Price Allocation The purchase price will be allocated to the assets acquired and liabilities assumed based on their estimated acquisition-date fair values. The Company expects to use a combination of valuation techniques, including discounted cash flow models and market-based approaches, to estimate the fair values of the identifiable assets acquired and liabilities assumed. The Company’s estimates of fair value will be based on assumptions about future commodity prices, production volumes, operating and development costs, discount rates and other factors. The Company expects to finalize the purchase price allocation within the measurement period provided by ASC 805.

Pro Forma Financial Information The following unaudited pro forma financial information presents the Company’s results of operations as if the acquisition had occurred on January 1, 2023. The pro forma financial information is provided for informational purposes only and does not purport to represent what the Company’s results of operations would have been had the acquisition occurred on the date indicated, nor does it purport to project the Company’s results of operations for any future period. The pro forma financial information includes adjustments for depreciation, depletion and amortization, interest expense, income taxes and other items directly attributable to the acquisition.

question: CTRA health and safety standards for P&E workers?
answer: CTRA embeds health and safety as a core value, emphasizing personal responsibility, safety leadership, and contractor inclusion. Its EHS management system governs the entire operating lifecycle, reinforced by a Stop Work Authority program that empowers workers to prevent unsafe operations. Compliance with OSHA, EPA, CERCLA, and state laws ensures rigorous oversight of hazardous substances and workplace exposure. Overall, CTRAs framework reflects a proactive, prevention-oriented approach to protecting P&E workers.

passages.text: Health and Safety. The health and safety of our employees is one of our core values for sustainable operations. This value is reflected in our strong safety culture that emphasizes personal responsibility and safety leadership, both for our employees and our contractors that are on our worksites. Our safety programs are built on a foundation that emphasizes personal safety and includes a Stop Work Authority program that empowers employees and contractors to stop work if they discover, or even suspect, a dangerous condition or other serious EHS hazard. Our comprehensive EHS management system establishes a corporate governance framework for EHS compliance and performance and covers all elements of our operating lifecycle.

hard_negatives.text:
Occupational Safety and Health Act and Other Laws and Regulations. The Occupational Safety and Health Act, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (“OSHA”) regulations issued thereunder and comparable states laws and regulations are intended to protect the health and safety of workers, including those engaged in performing drilling and transportation activities. In addition, OSHA’s hazard communication standard, the EPA’s community right-to-know regulations under Title III of the federal Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act, comparable state statutes and any implementing regulations require that information be maintained about hazardous materials used or produced in our operations and that this information be provided to employees, other potentially affected persons and governmental authorities. In addition, our operations at times include work in confined spaces. We work to comply with the OSHA permit-required confined spaces in general industry standard and also work to ensure contractors performing work at our facilities utilize a confined space entry plan and have a permit that lists the hazards in the spaces and the methods of effectively isolating, controlling or in other ways mitigating the hazards.

Regulation of GHG Emissions. The EPA previously finalized a series of GHG monitoring, reporting and emissions control rules for certain sources, including by adopting the Clean Power Plan to reduce CO2 emissions from existing electrify generation facilities, the validity of which has been subject to both litigation and attempted rescission by the Trump administration. The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the Affordable Clean Energy Rule adopted by the Trump administration, and, in June 2022, the U.S. Supreme Court held that Congress did not grant the EPA the authority to devise emissions caps based on the generation shifting approach of the Clean Power Plan. As a result, the EPA in May 2023 proposed a rule to reduce CO2 from new fossil fuel-fired stationary combustion turbines and existing coal, oil and gas fuel-fired steam generating units through heat rate improvements, carbon capture and storage, green hydrogen co-firing and other measures. In April 2024, EPA issued final rules for electric generating units to limit CO2 emissions from existing coal- and new natural gas-fired power plants, requiring control technologies such as hydrogen and carbon capture and sequestration (“CCS”). The new regulations are likely to be challenged in rulemaking and litigation and thus remain subject to potential modification or rescission. The endangerment finding, and such GHG rules, if implemented, could, in either case, adversely affect our operations, as well as limit the extent to which some of our strategic business plans succeed by increasing our operational costs and compliance burdens. Still, considerable uncertainty remains with respect to future emission reduction requirements for GHGs, in particular with respect to existing industrial and related sources of GHG emissions.

In addition, the Paris Agreement entered into by nearly 200 countries in December 2015 sets a goal to keep the average global temperature from rising more than 2 degrees Celsius over pre-industrial levels, and to pursue maximum efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius. Although the U.S. withdrew from the Paris Agreement in November 2020, President Biden issued an executive order to rejoin the Paris Agreement in January 2021, which became effective for the U.S. in February 2021. Following the U.S. re-entry into the Paris Agreement, President Biden announced in April 2021 that the U.S. would set a new emissions reduction target to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions 50% to 52% below 2005 levels by the year 2030 and set the goal of reaching net-zero economies no later than 2050. As of January 2025, the specific measures to be taken by the U.S. to achieve this target have not been established, but could include the imposition of aggressive new emissions reduction requirements affecting a substantial part of the U.S. economy that could adversely affect demand for the energy we produce.

Employee. As of December 31, 2023, we had 1,872 full-time employees working in the United States, 1,037 of whom were located in the Southern Region, 793 of whom were located in the Marcellus Shale and 42 of whom were located in Houston, Texas. None of our employees are covered by a collective bargaining agreement. Our ability to ensure the labor and employee relations climate remains stable in both the short and long-term is integral to consistently achieving our business objectives. We seek to attract and retain qualified persons to advance our business and replace those who retire or otherwise leave our company, such as our long-term employees and those who have held managerial positions.

Employee Safety and Wellness

We prepare our workforce to work safely with comprehensive training and our Stop Work program, and we take measures to keep our workforce healthy. We continue to emphasize personal responsibility for safety and encourage our workforce to be actively involved in developing a proactive safety culture at Devon. We also encourage our workforce to ThinkRisk and conduct operations and activities that identify and mitigate risks through the use of our life saving rules. In addition to personal responsibility for safety, leadership accountability at the highest levels of the Company helps ensure our workforce puts safety first.

We collect and monitor safety metrics and statistics to reduce injury and illness and promote an injury-free workplace.

We are prepared to respond to emergencies across the organization. The focus of emergency preparedness is to limit impacts to our people and our neighbors and to minimize effects on the environment. Our business unit teams rehearse safety procedures on a routine basis, including gridwide incident command. These teams include a collaboration of our operations, EHS and support staff who work to ensure our processes are prepared and ready to respond to a wide variety of issues.

Devon also prioritizes the physical, mental and financial wellness needs of our workforce and offers a variety of programs and resources to support our employees’ and their eligible dependents’ physical, mental and financial well-being. We provide benefits and programs to support employees in all stages of their lives that help guide them on their financial journey and improve overall financial capabilities.

Our wellness program empowers eligible employees to work towards increasing positive lifestyle habits by focusing on nutrition, movement, sleep and mental well-being. We also offer a comprehensive employee assistance program, including 24-hour live access to master’s-level counselors and other licensed professionals, access to financial experts, staff attorneys, elder-care consultants and other professionals.

Human Capital Management
As of December 31, 2024, EOG employed approximately 3,150 persons, of which approximately 2,800 were based in the U.S. and 350 were based outside of the U.S. EOG also utilized approximately 1,900 third-party contractors to support its operations in the U.S. and 85 third-party contractors to support its operations outside of the U.S. EOG’s Human Capital Management function is led by EOG’s Chief Human Resources Officer, who reports to the CEO and the Board and focuses on various areas, including the following:

Culture; Recruiting; Retention . EOG's culture is key to its success and includes a sense of stewardship, a performance-driven culture and a simple focused game plan. EOG seeks to hire individuals who share these principles and to promote from within based on performance, which EOG believes aids in retention and reduces costs and training time. EOG's recruiting staff focuses on attracting and retaining the best talent with a balanced approach to experienced candidates and new graduates. EOG believes that it offers an attractive work environment and a wellearned reputation that supports its ability to recruit and retain highly qualified employees. EOG has a strong college recruiting program and offers a wide range of internships and new graduate positions across multiple disciplines.

Employee Engagement and Development . EOG seeks to foster a work environment that promotes alignment of employees with its goals, collegiality and inclusion, teamwork and esprit de corps. EOG regularly conducts a company-wide employee engagement and satisfaction survey. Based on the results of this survey, focus discussions are held throughout the company and action items are developed to implement continuous improvements supporting EOG’s employee engagement. EOG seeks to provide high-quality training and development opportunities for its employees through on-the-job training, leadership development, mentoring, continuing education, specialty training and other programs.

Diversity, Equity and Inclusion . EOG values the gender, racial, ethnic and cultural backgrounds and perspectives of its employees. EOG believes a workforce that represents diverse perspectives and experiences contributes to the success of the organization and creates value for EOG’s shareholders. EOG seeks to hire and develop the best talent by creating a fair and balanced work environment. EOG provides employees with training and development opportunities, including on-the-job training, mentoring and continuing education programs and practices.

We are subject to numerous possible disruptions from unexpected events and circumstances beyond our control, including natural disasters, extreme weather conditions, war, violent conflict, geopolitical events and local security concerns, public health crises such as outbreaks of pandemic or contagious diseases and misinformation related to these events. The occurrence of any of such events or issues, as well as a sustained disruption to the capital markets, could cause damage or reduce demand for our products or cause us to incur significant losses.

We are constantly pursuing new technologies and practices in order to minimize hazards and risks in our operations. Despite these efforts, unexpected events may occur that cause personal injury and widespread and significant property damage or other harm resulting in disturbance or cessation of our operations. Our insurance and indemnities may not be adequate or enforceable to cover all risks and liabilities we may sustain. For example, oil and gas properties are typically not fully insured against all risks, because of the economic limits of available coverage. The occurrence of an event not fully covered by insurance could have a material adverse effect on our operations and financial condition. In addition, insurance coverage may not be available in the future at current levels of cost or coverage, which could adversely affect our ability to maintain insurance coverage after liability for a catastrophic event.

Our proved reserves are estimates. Any material inaccuracies in those estimates or underlying assumptions will materially affect the quantities and present value of our reserves.

Reserves engineering is a subjective process of estimating underground accumulations of oil and natural gas that cannot be measured in an exact manner. The process relies on interpretations of available geologic, geophysical, engineering and production data. The extent, quality and reliability of this data can vary. The process also requires many assumptions relating to current and future economic and regulatory conditions and commodity prices. Any significant inaccuracy of these assumptions causes the relevant quantities and present value estimates of the reserves to be inaccurate.

question: Accounting method for O&G activities & treatment of dry hole costs?
answer: CTRA applies the successful efforts method, capitalizing acquisition and development costs but expensing geological, geophysical, lease carrying, and exploratory dry-hole costs. Exploratory drilling costs may be capitalized temporarily until the well’s outcome is known, but if determined unsuccessful, they are written off to exploration expense. This approach ensures only costs leading to proved reserves are capitalized, while unsuccessful exploration is immediately reflected in earnings.

Successful Efforts Method of Accounting

We follow the successful efforts method of accounting for our oil and gas producing activities. Acquisition costs for proved and unproved properties are capitalized when incurred. Judgment is required to determine the proper classification of wells designated as developmental or exploratory, which ultimately will determine the proper accounting treatment of costs incurred. Exploration costs, including geological and geophysical costs, the costs of carrying and retaining unproved properties and exploratory dry-hole costs are expensed. Development costs, including costs to drill and equip development wells and successful exploratory drilling costs to locate proved reserves, are capitalized.

Oil and Gas Reserves

The process of estimating quantities of proved reserves is inherently imprecise, and the reserves data included in this document are only an estimate. The process relies on interpretations and judgment of available geological, geophysical, engineering and production data. The extent, quality and reliability of this technical data can vary. The process also requires certain economic assumptions, some of which are mandated by the SEC, such as commodity prices. Additional assumptions include drilling and operating expenses, capital expenditures, taxes and availability of funds. Any significant variance in the interpretations or assumptions could materially affect the estimated quantity and value of our reserves and can change substantially over time. Periodic revisions to the estimated reserves and future cash flows may be necessary as a result of reservoir performance, drilling activity, commodity prices, fluctuations in operating expenses, technological advances, new geological or geophysical data or other economic factors. Accordingly, reserves estimates are generally different from the quantities ultimately recovered.

The reserves estimates of our oil and gas properties have been prepared by our reservoir engineering staff and certain of our reserves are subject to an evaluation performed by an independent third-party petroleum consulting firm. In 2024, greater than 90 percent of the total future net revenue discounted at 10 percent attributable to our proved reserves were subject to this evaluation. For more information regarding reserves estimation, including historical reserves revisions, refer to the Supplemental Oil and Gas Information included in Item 8.

Our rate of recording DD&A expense is dependent upon our estimate of proved reserves, which are utilized in our unit-of-production calculation. If the estimates of proved and proved developed reserves were to be reduced, the rate at which we record DD&A expense would increase, reducing net income. Such a reduction in reserves may result from lower market prices, which may make it uneconomic to drill and produce higher cost fields. A five percent positive or negative revision to proved reserves would result in a decrease of $0.33 per Boe and an increase of $0.37 per Boe, respectively, on our DD&A rate. This estimated impact is based on current data, and actual events could require different adjustments to our DD&A rate.

In addition, a decline in proved reserves estimates may impact the outcome of our impairment test under applicable accounting standards. Due to the inherent imprecision of the reserves estimation process, risks associated with the operations of proved producing properties and market sensitive commodity prices utilized in our impairment analysis, we cannot determine if an impairment is reasonably likely to occur in the future.

Oil and Gas Properties

We evaluate our proved oil and gas properties for impairment on a field-by-field basis whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate an asset’s carrying amount may not be recoverable. We compare expected undiscounted future cash flows to the net book value of the asset. If the future undiscounted expected cash flows, based on our estimate of future commodity prices, operating costs and anticipated production from proved reserves and risk-adjusted probable and possible reserves, are lower than the net book value of the asset, then the capitalized cost is reduced to fair value. Commodity pricing is

48

estimated by using a combination of assumptions management uses in its budgeting and forecasting process, historical and current prices adjusted for geographical location and quality differentials, as well as other factors that we believe will impact realizable prices. Given the significant volatility in oil, natural gas and NGLs prices, estimates of such future prices are inherently imprecise. In the event that commodity prices significantly decline, we would assess whether the decline constitutes a triggering event that would require us to test the recoverability of the carrying value of our oil and gas properties and, if necessary, record an impairment charge. Fair value is calculated by discounting the future cash flows. The discount factor used is based on rates utilized by market participants that are commensurate with the risks inherent in the development and production of the underlying oil and natural gas.

Unproved oil and gas properties are assessed periodically for impairment on an aggregate basis through periodic updates to our unproved acreage amortization based on past drilling and exploration experience, our expectation of converting leases to held by production and average property lives. Average property lives are determined on a geographical basis and based on the estimated life of unproved property leasehold rights. Historically, the average property life in each of the geographical areas has not significantly changed and generally ranges from three to five years. The commodity price environment may impact the capital available for our drilling activities. We have considered these impacts when determining the amortization of our unproved acreage. If the average unproved property life decreases or increases by one year, the amortization would increase by approximately $12 million or decrease by $8 million, respectively, per year.

As these properties are developed and reserves are proved, the remaining capitalized costs are subject to depreciation and depletion. If the development of these properties is deemed unsuccessful and the properties are abandoned or surrendered, the capitalized costs related to the unsuccessful activity are expensed in the year the determination is made. The rate at which the unproved properties are written off depends on the timing and success of our future exploration and development program.

Oil and Gas Properties

The Company uses the successful efforts method of accounting for oil and gas producing activities. Under this method, acquisition costs for proved and unproved properties are capitalized when incurred. Exploration costs, including geological and geophysical costs, the costs of carrying and retaining unproved properties and exploratory dry hole drilling costs, are expensed. Development costs, including the costs to drill and equip development wells and successful exploratory drilling costs to locate proved reserves are capitalized.

Exploratory drilling costs are capitalized when incurred pending the determination of whether a well has found proved reserves. The determination is based on a process which relies on interpretations of available geologic, geophysical and engineering data. If a well is determined to be successful, the capitalized drilling costs will be reclassified as part of the cost of the well. If a well is determined to be unsuccessful, the capitalized drilling costs will be charged to exploration expense in the Consolidated Statement of Operations in the period the determination is made. If an exploratory well requires a major capital expenditure before production can begin, the cost of drilling the exploratory well will continue to be carried as an asset pending determination of whether reserves have been found only as long as: (1) the well has found a sufficient quantity of reserves to justify its completion as a producing well if the required capital expenditure is made and (2) drilling of an additional exploratory well is under way or firmly planned for the near future. If drilling in the area is not under way or firmly planned or if the well has not found a commercially producible quantity of reserves, the exploratory well is assumed to be impaired and its costs are charged to exploration expense.

Development costs of proved oil and gas properties, including estimated dismantlement, restoration and abandonment costs and acquisition costs, are depreciated and depleted on a field basis by the unit-of-production method using both proved developed and proved reserves.

Costs of sold or abandoned properties that make up a part of an amortization base (partial field) remain in the amortization base if the unit-of-production rate is not significantly affected. If significant, a gain or loss, if any, is recognized and the sold or abandoned properties are retired. A gain or loss, if any, is also recognized when a group of proved properties (entire field) that make up the amortization base has been retired, abandoned or sold.

The Company evaluates its proved oil and gas properties for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate an asset’s carrying amount may not be recoverable. The Company compares expected undiscounted future cash flows to the net book value of the asset. If the future undiscounted expected cash flows, based on estimates of future commodity prices, operating costs and anticipated production from proved reserves and risk-adjusted probable and possible reserves, are lower than the net book value of the asset, the capitalized cost is reduced to fair value. Commodity pricing is estimated by using a combination of assumptions management uses in its budgeting and forecasting process as well as historical and current prices adjusted for geographical location and quality differentials, as well as other factors that management believes will impact realizable prices. Fair value is calculated by discounting the future cash flows. The discount factor used is based on rates utilized by market participants that are commensurate with the risks inherent in the development and production of the underlying oil and natural gas.

Unproved oil and gas properties are assessed periodically for impairment on an aggregate basis through periodic updates to the Company’s unproved acreage amortization based on past drilling and exploration experience, the Company’s expectation of converting leases to held by production and average property lives. Average property lives are determined on a geographical basis and based on the estimated life of unproved property leasehold rights.

Sales Revenue

Revenues from the sale of oil, natural gas and NGLs are recorded when control of the product transfers to the customer and in an amount that reflects the consideration we expect to receive in exchange for the product. The point at which control of the product transfers to the customer is based on existing contract terms, which may result in recognition of revenue at the time the product is produced and delivered at the lease or when the product is delivered to a receipt point by the customer. The point at which control transfers may differ from the point at which title to the product transfers.

In arrangements where the Company has concluded it is acting as the principal, the Company recognizes revenue on a gross basis. In arrangements where the Company has concluded it is acting as an agent or a broker, the Company recognizes revenue on a net basis, equal to the difference between the consideration received and the amount paid to third parties. This assessment of the Company’s role is performed for each revenue contract and may vary across the Company’s different revenue streams.

The Company also presents separately certain costs incurred that relate to the transportation of the Company’s production, including pipeline gathering, treating, processing and transportation costs. When control of the Company’s production has passed to the customer at the lease, these amounts are presented as a reduction of revenue because they directly reduce the Company’s realized price. When control of the Company’s production has not passed to the customer at the lease, these amounts are presented as “Transportation, processing and other operating” expense in the Consolidated Statement of Operations.

The Company’s contracts for the sale of oil, natural gas and NGLs have primarily market-based pricing, are typically one year or less in duration and provide for delivery of the specified commodity to a designated delivery point.

Transportation and Processing Revenue

The Company also provides gathering, transportation and processing services to third parties under contracts that generally provide for a stand-ready obligation to make a system available and transportation services for natural gas volumes supplied on a monthly basis. The Company recognizes revenue when the service is performed in an amount that reflects the consideration expected to be received in exchange for the service.

Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities

The Company may periodically enter into contracts to hedge a portion of its oil, natural gas and NGL sales to manage commodity price volatility. These contracts may include swaps, collars, puts, calls and other derivatives. The Company recognizes the fair value of derivative instruments on the Consolidated Balance Sheet and recognizes changes in fair value in the Consolidated Statement of Operations as they occur. The Company does not currently designate any derivative instruments for hedge accounting. The Company’s policy is to present derivative assets and liabilities net on the Consolidated Balance Sheet when legally enforceable master netting arrangements are in place with derivative counterparties.

Fair Value Measurements

The Company measures certain assets and liabilities at fair value on a recurring basis. The Company’s assessment of fair value is based on a hierarchy that prioritizes the inputs used in measuring fair value. This hierarchy gives the highest priority to quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities and the lowest priority to unobservable inputs. The three levels of the fair value hierarchy are:

• Level 1: Quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.

• Level 2: Observable inputs other than quoted prices included in Level 1, such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets or quoted prices for identical or similar assets or liabilities in markets that are not active.

• Level 3: Unobservable inputs supported by little or no market activity that are significant to the fair value of the assets or liabilities.

Management determines the appropriate level of the fair value hierarchy for each measurement based on the inputs used in the valuation techniques. Transfers between levels of the fair value hierarchy, if any, are recognized at the end of the reporting period.

Leases

The Company determines whether a contract contains a lease at the inception of the arrangement. A contract is or contains a lease if the contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration. Control is considered to exist if the Company has both the right to obtain substantially all of the economic benefits from use of the identified asset and the right to direct the use of the identified asset. The Company recognizes a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for each lease in which the Company is the lessee, except for leases with a term of 12 months or less, which are expensed on a straight-line basis over the lease term. The right-of-use asset and lease liability are measured at the present value of lease payments not yet paid. The Company discounts lease payments using its incremental borrowing rate at the lease commencement date based on the information available at the inception date to determine the present value of lease payments. The Company’s lease terms may include options to extend or terminate the lease when it is reasonably certain that the Company will exercise those options. The Company combines lease and nonlease components in the measurement of lease liabilities and right-of-use assets for its classes of underlying assets.

Lease payments include fixed payments, variable payments that depend on an index or rate, amounts probable of being owed under residual value guarantees, and the exercise price of a purchase option if the Company is reasonably certain to exercise that option. Lease payments do not include variable costs based on usage or performance of the asset. The Company’s operating leases primarily relate to office leases, certain midstream assets, vehicles and equipment. The Company’s financing leases primarily relate to certain equipment used in its operations. The Company presents right-of-use assets as “Other assets” and lease liabilities (current and non-current) in the Consolidated Balance Sheet.

The Company recognizes all derivatives on the Consolidated Balance Sheet at fair value. The accounting for changes in the fair value (i.e., gains or losses) of a derivative instrument depends on whether it is designated and qualifies as part of a hedging relationship and the type of hedging relationship. The Company does not currently designate any of its derivative instruments as hedges for accounting purposes. Accordingly, changes in the fair value of derivative instruments are recognized in earnings in the period of the change.

Concentration of Credit Risk

The Company is exposed to credit risk in the event of nonperformance by counterparties to derivative contracts. The Company manages credit risk by entering into transactions with high credit-quality counterparties, reviewing credit exposure and, when appropriate, requiring the counterparties to provide credit support. The Company’s derivative instruments are generally governed by master netting arrangements, which provide for right of setoff under certain circumstances. The Company offsets derivative assets and liabilities when it has both the legal right and the intention to offset.

Fair Value Measurements
The Company follows the authoritative guidance for fair value measurements, which defines fair value, establishes a framework for measuring fair value and establishes a fair value hierarchy that prioritizes the inputs to valuation techniques used to measure fair value. Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. The three levels of the fair value hierarchy are:

• Level 1 — Quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.

• Level 2 — Inputs other than quoted prices included within Level 1 that are observable for the asset or liability, either directly or indirectly, including quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets and inputs that are derived principally from or corroborated by observable market data by correlation or other means.

• Level 3 — Unobservable inputs that reflect the Company’s own assumptions about the assumptions market participants would use in pricing the asset or liability.

Valuation Techniques

The Company’s derivative instruments, consisting primarily of commodity price swaps, collars and basis swaps, are valued using industry-standard models that consider various assumptions, including quoted forward prices for commodities, time value, volatility factors and contractual terms. These valuations are corroborated by quotes obtained from counterparties or third-party valuation services, or a combination of the foregoing. The fair value of the Company’s outstanding debt is determined using a market approach based on quoted market prices, if available, or estimated using discounted cash flow analyses based on the Company’s current borrowing rates for similar types of borrowing arrangements. The Company’s outstanding debt is classified as Level 1 in the fair value hierarchy.

Credit Risk Adjustments

The Company’s valuation of derivative instruments includes adjustments to reflect nonperformance risk of both the Company and its counterparties. The Company uses a credit-risk-adjusted discount rate that is developed based on observable market credit spreads, taking into account the Company’s credit risk, the counterparty’s credit risk and the terms of the instruments.

Marketing Activities

Oil, Gas and NGL Marketing

The spot markets for oil, gas and NGLs are subject to volatility that can materially impact our realized prices and cash flows. We market our production using a combination of term and spot sales, as well as through transport arrangements to multiple end markets, including refineries, petrochemical plants, utilities, marketers and other purchasers. We sell oil, gas and NGLs under a variety of arrangements, including month-to-month agreements and short-term (less than one year) agreements at prices negotiated monthly or quarterly, and under longer-term contracts with formulas based on market indices adjusted for location and product quality differentials.

Oil is typically sold at or near the lease location or delivered to purchase points on gathering systems or pipelines with pricing based on regional differentials to published benchmarks. Natural gas production is sold at the wellhead, to gathering systems or processors that extract NGLs and return residue gas to the market, or transported on interstate pipelines. NGLs are generally sold to petrochemical, refining and other industrial customers at prices tied to Mont Belvieu or Conway benchmarks.

Our ability to obtain favorable pricing and secure adequate takeaway capacity is influenced by the availability of transportation infrastructure, including gathering systems, processing facilities, fractionation capacity, storage and pipelines in the regions where we operate. In certain areas, pipeline or processing capacity may be limited, and we may experience curtailments, increased basis differentials or the need to secure alternative transportation, including trucking or third-party arrangements, which may increase costs.

We also may enter into marketing or trading activities, including the purchase and resale of commodities, to optimize transportation capacity, fulfill contractual commitments and manage location and quality differentials. These activities can result in gains or losses depending on market conditions, price differentials and our ability to efficiently manage logistics. Our marketing activities are conducted in accordance with applicable regulations and risk management policies, and we monitor counterparty credit exposure and require appropriate credit support where necessary.

Delivery Commitments

We have various delivery commitments for oil, gas and NGLs under transportation, processing and sales contracts. These commitments are designed to provide reliable access to end markets and improve price realizations. Failure to deliver volumes under such agreements may subject us to deficiency payments or other contractual remedies. We regularly evaluate these commitments in light of our production forecasts, market conditions and available alternatives, and we may renegotiate, assign or terminate obligations where contract terms allow.

Midstream Infrastructure

We utilize a mix of owned and third-party midstream infrastructure to gather, process, transport and store our production. Our midstream strategy is intended to provide flexibility, reduce costs and ensure access to multiple end markets. We continue to evaluate opportunities to expand or optimize our midstream footprint to support our development plans and improve our price realizations.

Counterparty Credit and Risk Management

We have established credit policies and procedures to manage counterparty exposure in our marketing activities. These include ongoing credit evaluations, monitoring of receivables and, when appropriate, the use of credit support arrangements such as letters of credit. Our risk management program includes limits and controls designed to monitor and govern marketing activities and derivative positions.

Regulatory Considerations

Our marketing operations are subject to federal, state and local regulations, including those governing pipeline transportation, market transparency, trading practices and environmental protection. We monitor regulatory developments and adjust our marketing practices as needed to ensure compliance and to adapt to changes that could affect market dynamics, transportation availability or pricing mechanisms.

BLM and BIA leases contain restrictions, which, in certain circumstances, include acres limitations with respect to leases held by a party. Further, the federal government may include in new onshore leases provisions that increase the federal government’s royalty share by 2.5% where bids are equal or otherwise tied, include increased minimum acceptable bids or rental rates, adjust minimum acceptable bids or rental rates to inflation and/or include other terms or requirements that may make federal and Indian leases less competitive.

EOG is one of many companies that are involved in oil and natural gas exploration and production onshore in the United States on federal and Indian (Native American) lands. The United States government owns mineral rights in a significant portion of the United States, and the BLM is responsible for the onshore oil and gas program on federal and Indian lands. The BLM, pursuant to various laws and regulations, administers oil and gas leases for exploration and production, as well as other rights to use the land for purposes related to oil and gas exploration and production. Accordingly, EOG is subject to a number of additional regulations and reporting requirements for its operations conducted on federal and Indian lands.

On January 31, 2024, the BLM published in the Federal Register (89 Fed. Reg. 6306) a final rule addressing oil and gas leasing on federal lands (the BLM Final Rule), including provisions to increase minimum acceptable bids and rental rates for oil and gas leases, and to establish a new rule for “Diligent Exploration.” In addition, the BLM Final Rule allows certain new fees to be assessed by the BLM for oil and gas leasing and exploration activities on federal lands, including for expressions of interest in parcels to nominate for auction and new “Reclamation Fees” and “Inspection Fees.” The BLM Final Rule also makes other changes to the onshore leasing program; however, certain provisions of the BLM Final Rule do not apply to leases issued prior to its effective date. Several parties challenged the BLM Final Rule, and in May 2024, a North Dakota district court judge issued a preliminary injunction that prevents the BLM from applying the increased minimum acceptable bid and rental rate provisions to new lease sales in North Dakota, but allows the BLM to apply a new 18.75% royalty rate for onshore oil and gas leases nationwide.

Mineral royalty rates on onshore federal lands are set by the BLM. The BLM may adjust royalty rates, as well as rental rates, minimum bids and other terms and conditions applicable to federal oil and gas leases. The BLM also has the authority, under certain circumstances, to reduce royalty rates or reduce the minimum acreage requirement for a lease, upon the lessee’s request. Further, the BLM has authority under certain conditions to suspend leases, meaning that the lease term can be extended and payments tolled, thereby permitting a lessee additional time to exercise its rights under the lease. The BLM recently proposed a rule that adds new fees, such as for expressions of interest to nominate parcels for auction, and increases certain existing fees, including rental and minimum bids, which may increase costs for EOG’s operations on federal lands.

The Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) regulates oil and gas exploration and production operations on Indian lands. Leases on Indian lands are administered by the BIA and a tribal organization acting on behalf of the BIA. BIA and tribal approvals are required for oil and gas leases on Indian lands. As with federal lands, the BIA has the authority to require advanced approvals and to impose other restrictions on operations on Indian lands, which may increase costs or delay or inhibit operations. The terms and conditions of leases on Indian lands can vary, and it is possible that certain new rules impacting Indian leases will be finalized in the future.

In August 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (the IRA) was signed into law. The IRA includes a charge on methane emissions, reporting requirements for methane emissions and various incentives for renewable energy, among other provisions. In addition, the IRA provides that the BLM, with limited exceptions, cannot issue new rights-of-way for renewable energy projects on federal lands unless certain onshore oil and gas lease sales have occurred during the previous year. The IRA also increases the minimum royalty rate for onshore oil and gas leases to 16.67% (from 12.5%), subject to potential further adjustments by the BLM. The enactment and implementation of the IRA may impact EOG’s operations, including by increasing costs and/or by impacting access to federal lands.

The Natural Gas Policy Act of 1978 (NGPA) contains a regulatory scheme that applies to many aspects of natural gas operations. The NGPA provides the FERC with certain authority over the natural gas industry. With the passage of the NGPA and subsequent enactment of the Natural Gas Wellhead Decontrol Act of 1989, the pricing of natural gas was deregulated to a substantial extent. The NGPA contains provisions prohibiting manipulation and reporting of false information to federal entities regarding the price of natural gas, and also gives the FERC authority to promulgate rules for enhancing price transparency and order civil penalties for violations of the NGPA or any rules, regulations or orders of the FERC. The FERC actively exercises its authority to monitor the wholesale natural gas markets and to investigate possible transactions that fail to comply with statutory and regulatory requirements. The FERC has stated it intends to use its anti-market manipulation authority to the fullest extent possible and has established improved reporting requirements for regulated entities. However, the FERC’s Anti-Manipulation Rules, promulgated pursuant to the Energy Policy Act of 2005, apply to “any entity,” not just those entities that fall within the FERC’s jurisdiction.

The NGPA also regulates transportation and sale of natural gas in interstate commerce. The FERC has continued to adopt and implement various rules and orders intended to promote transparency in the natural gas industry and to reduce regulatory barriers to entry. The FERC has broad authority to review and approve new pipeline construction and to oversee environmental and other issues with respect to the interstate natural gas pipeline system. The Natural Gas Act (NGA) provides the FERC authority over natural gas companies and natural gas pipeline transportation in interstate commerce. The FERC also has authority to approve rates and charges for the transportation and sale of natural gas for resale in interstate commerce. In December 2023, the FERC issued Order No. 2023-A revising its standard large generator interconnection procedures and agreements, which may impact the timing and cost of interconnections, including for natural gas-fired generation facilities.

In December 2023, the FERC issued Order No. 2023-A, a final rule that addresses transmission interconnection queues; however, the final parameters implementing the new royalty rate were finalized in April 2024.

Fair value measurements are based on the assumptions that market participants would use in pricing the asset or liability, including assumptions about risk. The Company uses various valuation techniques appropriate under the circumstances and maximizes the use of observable inputs and minimizes the use of unobservable inputs. The fair value hierarchy gives the highest priority to Level 1 measurements and the lowest priority to Level 3 measurements. Depending on the inputs used in the valuation techniques, the Company classifies the fair value measurements in their entirety in the fair value hierarchy.

The three levels of the fair value hierarchy are as follows:

• Level 1 inputs are quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for identical assets or liabilities that the reporting entity can access at the measurement date.

• Level 2 inputs are inputs other than quoted prices included within Level 1 that are observable for the asset or liability, either directly or indirectly.

• Level 3 inputs are unobservable inputs for the asset or liability.

The Company’s assessment of the significance of a particular input to the fair value measurement requires judgment and may affect the classification of the fair value measurements within the fair value hierarchy. The Company recognizes transfers between levels of the fair value hierarchy at the end of the reporting period.

Assets and Liabilities Measured at Fair Value on a Recurring Basis

The Company’s assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis include derivative instruments and certain investments. These assets and liabilities are measured at fair value at each reporting date and are classified based on the lowest level of input that is significant to the fair value measurement in its entirety.

Assets and Liabilities Measured at Fair Value on a Nonrecurring Basis

The Company measures certain assets and liabilities at fair value on a nonrecurring basis, such as asset retirement obligations recognized in business combinations, the initial recognition of certain long-lived assets, and impairments of long-lived assets, including proved and unproved oil and gas properties, when events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts of these assets may not be recoverable. The fair value of asset retirement obligations is based on discounted cash flows using market participant assumptions about settlement amounts, inflation rates and credit-adjusted risk-free rates. The fair value of long-lived assets is determined based on expected future cash flows, market participant assumptions and observable market information, when available. These fair value measurements are classified within Level 3 of the fair value hierarchy due to the significant unobservable inputs utilized in the valuations.

Fair Value of Financial Instruments

The carrying amounts of cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, accounts payable and other current liabilities approximate fair value due to the short-term maturities of these instruments. The fair value of the Company’s outstanding debt is estimated using quoted market prices, if available, or discounted cash flow analyses based on the current market rates for debt of similar terms and maturities.

Nonrecurring Measurements and Disclosure

When events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts of long-lived assets may not be recoverable, the Company performs an assessment to determine if an impairment exists. If an impairment is indicated, the Company measures the impairment as the amount by which the carrying amount of the asset exceeds its fair value. The fair value of long-lived assets is determined using discounted cash flow models that include significant estimates and assumptions related to forecasted commodity prices, production volumes, operating costs, development timing and capital expenditures, and other factors. The Company revises these estimates and assumptions when necessary based on new information or changes in market conditions.

Additional fair value disclosures are included in Note X — Derivative Instruments and Fair Value Measurements.
