Postretirement Benefits

The Company provides health care benefits to certain former employees, including their spouses, eligible dependents and surviving spouses (retirees). These benefits are commonly called postretirement benefits. The health care plans are contributory, with participants’ contributions adjusted annually. Most employees that participate in the plan become eligible for these benefits when they meet certain age and service requirements at retirement.

At the end of 2024 and 2023, the Company provided postretirement benefits to 267and 290retirees and their dependents, respectively.

During 2022, the Company amended its postretirement plans to phase out all postretirement benefits and freeze future participation in the plan. Certain employees were grandfathered under the plan amendment and remain eligible for future participation in the pre-65 plan upon their retirement based on certain age and years of service criteria, while the post-65 benefit for all plan participants that reach the age of 65 after December 31, 2022, including current retirees participating in the pre-65 plan, was eliminated. Existing retirees participating in both the pre-65 and post-65 plans prior to December 31, 2022 will continue to receive benefits under the plan until the age of 65 in the case of the pre-65 participants, or voluntary termination of benefits or by death in the case of post-65 participants.

Retirement Savings Plan

The Company has a Retirement Savings Plan (“RSP”), which is a defined contribution plan. The Company matches a portion of employees’ contributions in cash. Participation in the RSP is voluntary and all employees of the Company are eligible to participate. The Company matches employee contributions dollar-for-dollar, up to the maximum Internal Revenue Service (“IRS”) limit, on the first sixpercent of an employee’s pre-tax earnings. The RSP also provides for discretionary contributions in an amount equal to 10percent of an eligible plan participant’s salary and bonus.

In connection with the merger with Cimarex Energy Co. (now known as Coterra Energy Operating Co, or “Cimarex”), the Company assumed the Cimarex Energy Co. 401(k) Plan (the “401(k) Plan”) with respect to Cimarex employees. The Company maintained this plan throughout the integration process and terminated this plan effective December 31, 2022, with all legacy Cimarex employees becoming eligible for the Company’s RSP effective January 1, 2023.

During the years ended December 31, 2024, 2023 and 2022, the Company made aggregate contributions to the RSP and 401(k) Plan of $ 19million, $ 19million and $ 12million, respectively, which are included in G&A expense in the Consolidated Statement of Operations. The Company’s common stock was an investment option within the RSP and the 401(k) Plan through December 31, 2022, at which time the Company eliminated this option.

Deferred Compensation Plans

The Company has deferred compensation plans which are available to officers and select employees and act as a supplement to the RSP. The Internal Revenue Code does not cap the amount of compensation that may be taken into account for purposes of determining contributions to the deferred compensation plans and does not impose limitations on the amount of contributions to the deferred compensation plans. At the present time, the Company anticipates making a contribution to the deferred compensation plans on behalf of a participant in the event that Internal Revenue Code limitations cause a participant to receive less than the Company contribution under the RSP.

The assets of the deferred compensation plans are held in a rabbi trust and are subject to additional risk of loss in the event of bankruptcy or insolvency of the Company.

Under the deferred compensation plans, the participants direct the deemed investment of amounts credited to their accounts. The trust assets are invested in mutual funds that cover the investment spectrum from equity to money market. The mutual funds are publicly traded and have market prices that are readily available. Settlement payments are made to participants in cash, either in a lump sum or in periodic installments.

The market value of the trust assets was $ 17million and $ 33million at December 31, 2024 and 2023, respectively, and is included in other assets in the Consolidated Balance Sheet. Related liabilities totaled $ 17million and $ 33million at December 31, 2024 and 2023, respectively, and are included in other liabilities in the Consolidated Balance Sheet. There is no impact on earnings or earnings per share from the changes in market value of the other deferred compensation plan assets because the changes in market value of the trust assets are offset completely by changes in the value of the liability, which represents trust assets belonging to plan participants.

The Company made contributions to the deferred compensation plans of $ 3million, $ 3million and $ 1million in 2024, 2023 and 2022, respectively, which are included in G&A expense in the Consolidated Statement of Operations.

Human Capital Resources
As of December 31, 2024, we had 981 employees, 749 of whom were located in our corporate headquarters in Houston, Texas and 232 of whom were located in our regional offices in Midland, Texas and Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania and field offices throughout the states of Texas, Pennsylvania, Oklahoma and Wyoming. As of this same date, approximately 8% of our workforce served in the military or are married to a military service member. Additionally, we have 42 employees that are employed by our wholly-owned subsidiaries Monarch Resource Partners LLC and EQT Adwin GP LLC, 3 of which were located in Pennsylvania. During 2024, approximately 15% of our workforce were new hires, with a turnover rate of approximately 13%. In addition to our employees, we engage both third party contractors and service companies to perform a significant portion of our field and administrative functions.

We believe our employees are key to our success and, as such, we devote significant resources to attract, develop and retain our employees.

Recruitment, Training and Development

We use a consistent, objectives-based selection framework to attract and hire qualified candidates for positions across our Company and use an interview framework that aligns the areas of the highest value based on the role and level. We also engage in campus recruitment programs to create strong relationships with students and offer internships throughout the organization as a key way to identify talent. We offer a program for recent college graduates who are new hires to help them develop relationships during the transition to the Company and into their careers. During 2024, we established talent profiles that outline competencies for desired behaviors that strengthen our culture and drive performance. These competencies are integrated into our interview process and a Manager Excellence program to help leaders assess team member performance and enable development dialogue. In addition to on-the job training, we provide new manager training programs, professional development courses, management development programs and leadership training to support and develop our managers and employees.

Compensation and Benefits

Our pay programs, in connection with other human resources practices, enable our efforts to hire, motivate and retain highly qualified and experienced personnel. We have a competitive compensation program designed to, among other things, attract the talent needed to achieve our business objectives, further a pay-for-performance philosophy by aligning executive compensation with the Company’s long-term strategic plan and financial objectives, establish a clear link between pay and performance and align our interests with those of our stockholders. Under our pay program, we provide competitive base salaries and incentives that reward individual and Company performance, such as short-term and long-term incentive programs. Our benefits and pay-for-performance programs are designed to incentivize our employees at all levels to contribute to our success and we believe they are critical to the achievement of our performance goals.

In addition, we support employee well-being by offering comprehensive medical plan options, dental and vision plans and income protection benefits, including short-term and long-term disability plans and life insurance plans, as well as solutions to support emotional well-being. Inclusion, Diversity and Equity

Our guiding principles are an integral part of who we are and what we stand for at Coterra. These principles include our commitment to respecting the quality of people and the diversity of ideas. We strive to have a corporate culture that reaches beyond diversity by promoting an environment that is inclusive and values the contributions of each individual employee and embraces the diversity of our work force across race, ethnicity, gender, religion, age, sexual orientation, disability and other diverse traits. We believe that having an inclusive and diverse workforce not only enriches our Company but also gives us a competitive advantage in the marketplace. We also have established various employee resource groups focused on expanding the knowledge of the inclusivity and diversity within the Company.

6. Fair Value Measurements
The accounting guidance for fair value measurements establishes a framework for measuring fair value and clarifies that fair value is an exit price, representing the amount that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. This guidance establishes a fair value hierarchy that prioritizes the inputs used to measure fair value as follows: Level 1 inputs are quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for identical assets or liabilities; Level 2 inputs are observable inputs other than quoted prices included within Level 1 for the asset or liability, either directly or indirectly, including inputs in markets that are not considered to be active by market participant inputs that are observable for substantially the full term of the asset or liability; and Level 3 inputs are unobservable inputs for the asset or liability and are typically based on the Company’s own assumptions, as there is little, if any, related market activity or information available.

Recurring Fair Value Measurements

The following tables present the Company’s assets and liabilities accounted for at fair value on a recurring basis as of March 31, 2025 and December 31, 2024 by level within the fair value hierarchy:

Commodity Derivatives

The Company records the fair value of commodity derivative instruments, which are categorized as Level 2 in the fair value hierarchy, using industry-standard models that consider various assumptions, including quoted forward prices for commodities, time value, volatility factors and current market and contractual prices for the underlying instruments. Investment Securities

The Company’s investment securities include funds held in connection with certain Company operations and are categorized as Level 1 in the fair value hierarchy. Investment securities consist primarily of highly liquid money market funds. The fair values of the funds are determined using quoted prices in active markets.

Other

The Company also holds other assets measured at fair value, which include certain insurance-related assets and marketable securities. These assets are categorized as Level 1 or Level 2 within the fair value hierarchy depending on the nature of the inputs used in the valuation.

Nonrecurring Fair Value Measurements

Certain assets are reported at fair value on a nonrecurring basis. These nonrecurring fair value measurements typically involve significant unobservable inputs and are categorized as Level 3 within the fair value hierarchy. Nonrecurring fair value measurements primarily relate to impairment of oil and gas properties, proved and unproved, goodwill, and other long-lived assets. When indicators of impairment are present, the Company estimates the fair value of the asset group using discounted cash flow models based on the Company’s estimates of future commodity prices, production, operating expenses, development costs, and a market participant weighted average cost of capital.

Counterparty Credit Risk

The Company is exposed to credit loss in the event of nonperformance by counterparties to its commodity derivative contracts. The Company actively monitors the creditworthiness of its counterparties. The Company enters into commodity derivative contracts with a number of counterparties, thereby mitigating the concentration of credit risk. The Company generally does not require collateral from its counterparties. The Company’s derivative contracts do not contain any credit-risk-related contingent features, including a requirement to post collateral.

Other Financial Instruments

The carrying amount of cash and cash equivalents, receivables, payables and other current maturities approximate fair value due to the short-term nature of these instruments. The fair value of the Company’s fixed-rate long-term debt is based on quoted market prices and is categorized as Level 1 in the fair value hierarchy. The carrying amount of the Company’s variable-rate debt approximates fair value as the interest rates on these instruments are comparable to current market rates for similar instruments with comparable maturities and credit profiles.

Retirement Plans
Defined Contribution Plans Devon sponsors defined contribution retirement savings plans. U.S. Legacy Plan. Employees who are at least 18 years old may participate in Devon’s U.S. legacy defined contribution plans, which provide for both employee tax-deferred contributions and Company contributions. Devon matches up to 6% of an eligible employee’s compensation and may provide an additional discretionary contribution based on the Company’s performance and other factors. U.S. Enhanced Plan. For certain eligible employees, Devon provides an enhanced match up to 8% of compensation and may provide an additional discretionary contribution. Canadian Plan. Devon also sponsors a defined contribution plan for its Canadian operations where employees can contribute a portion of their compensation with a corresponding employer match up to a specified limit. Vesting and Withdrawals. Employer contributions vest subject to the terms of the plans. Participants may make withdrawals as permitted under applicable law and plan provisions. Plan Administration. The plans are administered by a third-party service provider and are subject to ERISA and the applicable laws of the jurisdictions where they operate. Plan participants direct the investment of contributions among a variety of investment options.

Defined Benefit Pension Plans Devon sponsors certain defined benefit pension plans covering eligible employees, including qualified and non-qualified plans. These plans provide benefits based on years of service and final average compensation or other formulas specified in the plan documents. The defined benefit plans are funded through trusts, as required by applicable law and plan terms. The Company makes contributions to the pension plans as required and may make additional voluntary contributions. Pension plan assets are managed by external investment managers and are diversified across asset classes. The Company’s funding policy is to contribute amounts sufficient to meet regulatory minimums and to achieve the long-term funding objectives of the plans. Pension expense is recognized using actuarial valuations that include assumptions about discount rates, expected return on plan assets, mortality rates and other factors. Actuarial gains and losses are amortized over periods consistent with applicable accounting standards.

Postretirement Benefit Plans Devon provides certain postretirement health care and life insurance benefits to eligible retirees and their dependents under various plans. The Company may amend or terminate these benefits at any time, subject to applicable law. The postretirement benefit plans are not required to be funded, and the Company generally pays benefits as they come due. The cost of postretirement benefits is recognized using actuarial valuations and includes assumptions about health care cost trends, discount rates and other factors. The Company continues to evaluate these plans to manage costs and align with market practices.

Non-Qualified Deferred Compensation Plan Devon maintains a non-qualified deferred compensation plan that allows eligible employees to defer a portion of their compensation. Participant deferrals are credited to notional investment accounts based on investment options selected by the participant. The Company may, at its discretion, make contributions to the deferred compensation plan. Amounts deferred under the plan are unsecured obligations of the Company and are subject to the claims of general creditors. The deferred compensation plan is not intended to qualify under Section 401(a) of the Internal Revenue Code. The plan is designed to comply with Section 409A of the Internal Revenue Code and applicable regulations.

Plan Costs and Assumptions Devon recognizes the cost of these retirement and postretirement plans in accordance with applicable accounting guidance. Key assumptions used in measuring the benefit obligations and costs include discount rates, expected long-term rates of return on plan assets, compensation increase rates, health care cost trend rates and mortality assumptions. Changes in these assumptions, differences between actual and expected investment returns and other factors may cause volatility in the amounts recognized in earnings and other comprehensive income. The Company regularly reviews plan assumptions with its actuaries and monitors plan performance.

Regulatory and Compliance Matters The Company’s retirement and postretirement plans are subject to various laws and regulations, including ERISA, the Internal Revenue Code and similar laws in non-U.S. jurisdictions. The Company is committed to compliance with these requirements and maintains internal controls and procedures designed to ensure compliance. The Company may adjust plan features or contributions in response to changes in regulatory requirements or market conditions. For additional information regarding the Company’s retirement and postretirement plans, see the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements.

Human Capital Management
EOG believes that its employees are key to its success and is committed to attracting, developing and retaining a high-quality workforce. As of December 31, 2024, EOG had approximately 3,350 employees worldwide, of which approximately 3,200 were located in the United States. EOG’s employees are not represented by labor unions, and EOG believes that it has good relations with its employees.

EOG is committed to fostering a workplace environment that values inclusion and diversity, and EOG seeks to attract and retain employees with diverse backgrounds, skills and ideas. EOG provides equal employment opportunities to all employees and applicants without regard to race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability, veteran status, sexual orientation or gender identity. EOG also has policies in place to prevent harassment and discrimination and provides training to employees on these topics.

EOG focuses on employee development and offers training and development programs to help employees enhance their skills and advance their careers. EOG encourages employees to be innovative and provides opportunities for employees to develop leadership skills. EOG also offers competitive compensation and benefits to attract and retain employees. These benefits include health and welfare benefits, retirement plans and programs that support work-life balance.

EOG is committed to maintaining a safe and healthy work environment. EOG’s safety programs are designed to promote a culture of safety, with an emphasis on continuous improvement. EOG provides training and resources to employees to help them perform their jobs safely and effectively. EOG also monitors safety metrics and conducts regular audits and assessments to identify areas for improvement. EOG strives to minimize safety incidents and ensure that employees and contractors work in a safe environment.

EOG is also committed to community engagement and corporate responsibility. EOG supports community organizations and initiatives through charitable contributions and volunteer efforts. EOG seeks to operate in a manner that is environmentally responsible and works to reduce the environmental impact of its operations. EOG’s corporate responsibility initiatives include efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, manage water resources responsibly and minimize the footprint of its operations.

question: Information about preparation of reserve estimates?
answer: CTRAs proved reserves are estimated under strict SEC guidelines, using multiple engineering and economic methods and a structured internal review process that is independent from exploration and production functions. While the estimates rely on significant professional judgment and are subject to revision as new data emerges, they are reinforced by oversight from senior technical management and independent third-party validation by DeGolyer and MacNaughton. This layered approach aims to ensure that reported reserves represent the most reasonable and reliable assessment possible, despite the inherent uncertainties of oil and gas reservoir evaluation.

Preparation of Reserves Estimates
All of the Company’s reserves estimates are maintained by the Company’s internal Corporate Reservoir Engineering group, which is comprised of engineers and engineering analysts. The objectives and management of this group are separate from and independent of the exploration and production functions of the Company. The primary objective of the Company’s Corporate Reservoir Engineering group is to maintain accurate forecasts on all properties of the Company through ongoing monitoring and timely updates of operating and economic parameters (production forecasts, prices and regional differentials, operating expenses, ownership, etc.). In addition, the Corporate Reservoir Engineering group maintains a set of basic guidelines and procedures to ensure that critical checks and reviews of the reserves database are performed on a regular basis.

The Corporate Reservoir Engineering group is responsible for estimates of proved reserves. Corporate engineers interact with the exploration and production departments to ensure all appropriate available engineering and geologic data is taken into account prior to establishing or revising an estimate. The recommended revisions of the corporate engineers are reviewed with the Vice President - Corporate Reservoir Engineering and, after approval, entered into the reserves database by an engineering analyst. During the course of the year, the Corporate Reservoir Engineering group reviews their recommendations and updates with the Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer for additional oversight and approval. From time-to-time, the Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer also will confer with senior management, including the Chief Executive Officer, regarding reserves-related issues. Upon completion of the process, the estimated reserves are presented to senior management and the Board of Directors.

The Company’s Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer is the technical person primarily responsible for overseeing the Company’s internal reserves estimation process and the Company’s Corporate Reservoir Engineering group. This individual graduated from the University of Tulsa with a Bachelor of Science degree in Petroleum Engineering. He has held numerous engineering and management roles and has over 17 years of experience in oil and gas reservoir evaluation and is a member of the Society of Petroleum Engineers.

The Company utilizes various methods and technologies to estimate its proved reserves, including analysis of production performance, analogy, decline curve analysis, rate and pressure transient analysis, reservoir simulation, material balance calculations, volumetric calculations, and in some cases a combination of these methods.

Review of Estimates by Third-Party Engineers
The Company also engages independent petroleum engineering consulting firms as an additional confirmation of the reasonableness of its internal estimates.

During 2024, 2023 and 2022, estimates of net proved reserves representing greater than 90 percent of the total future net revenue discounted at 10 percent attributable to the Company’s proved reserves were subject to an independent evaluation performed by DeGolyer and MacNaughton.

In each of the respective periods, DeGolyer and MacNaughton indicated that, based on its investigations and subject to the limitations described in its reserves letters, they believe the Company’s estimates were, in the aggregate, reasonable. A copy of DeGolyer and MacNaughton’s letter regarding the 2024, 2023, and 2022 reserves estimates has been filed as an exhibit to this Annual Report on Form 10-K.

 Qualifications of Third-Party Engineers
DeGolyer and MacNaughton’s Executive Vice President is the technical person primarily responsible for the evaluation of the Company’s proved reserves. He is a Registered Professional Engineer in the State of Texas with over 14 years of experience in oil and gas reservoir studies and reserves evaluations and meets the requirements regarding qualifications, independence, objectivity, and confidentiality set forth in the Standards Pertaining to the Estimating and Auditing of Oil and Gas Reserves Information promulgated by the Society of Petroleum Engineers. DeGolyer and MacNaughton is an independent firm of petroleum engineers, geologists, geophysicists and petro-physicists; they do not own an interest in the Company’s properties and are not retained on a contingent fee basis.

Estimated Quantities of Proved Oil and Gas Reserves

Estimates of total proved reserves at December 31, 2024, 2023 and 2022 were computed using the trailing 12-month average index price for the respective commodity, calculated as the unweighted arithmetic average for the first day of the month price for each month during the respective year.

No major discovery or other favorable or unfavorable event after December 31, 2024, is believed to have caused a material change in the estimates of proved or proved developed reserves as of that date.

The Company’s reserves in the Marcellus Shale accounted for 55 percent of total proved reserves, the Permian Basin accounted for 35 percent, and the remaining 10 percent were in the Anadarko Basin.

During 2024, the Company added 189 MMBoe of proved reserves through extensions, discoveries, and other additions, which included 115 MMBoe in the Permian Basin, 28 MMBoe in the Marcellus Shale and 45 MMBoe in the Anadarko Basin. The Company had net positive revisions of prior estimates of 9 MMBoe, which included a 59 MMBoe negative revision due to price, offset by a 4 MMBoe positive revision in operating expenses and a positive 64 MMBoe performance revision.

During 2023, the Company added 228 MMBoe of proved reserves through extensions, discoveries, and other additions, which included 102 MMBoe in the Permian Basin, 87 MMBoe in the Marcellus Shale and 39 MMBoe in the Anadarko Basin. The Company had net negative revisions of prior estimates of 60 MMBoe, which included 83 MMBoe negative revision due to price, a 10 MMBoe negative revision due to increases in operating expenses, partially offset by a positive 33 MMBoe performance revision.

During 2022, the Company added 406 MMBoe of proved reserves through extensions, discoveries, and other additions, which included 193 MMBoe in the Permian Basin, 191 MMBoe in the Marcellus Shale and 22 MMBoe in the Anadarko Basin. The Company had net negative revisions of prior estimates of 667 MMBoe, which included 571 MMBoe in downward performance revisions related to updated forecast parameters in the Marcellus Shale to account for a different decline behavior

observed in bounded wells compared to unbounded wells. The net negative revisions also included 168MMBoe associated with the removal of PUD reserves in the Marcellus Shale whose development is expected to be delayed beyond five years of initial booking. These negative revisions in the Marcellus Shale were partially offset by 32 MMBoe in positive performance revisions in the Permian Basin, 39 MMBoe in positive revisions related to upward price revisions, and 1 MMBoe in positive revisions related to decreases in operating expenses.

 Proved Undeveloped Reserves

At December 31, 2024, the Company had PUD reserves of 407 MMBoe, a decrease of 75 MMBoe from 482 MMBoe at December 31, 2023. In 2024, the Company transferred 202 MMBoe of PUD reserves to proved developed as a result of development activities and additions of 15 MMBoe, primarily related to successful drilling activities. Revisions of 92 MMBoe in the Lower 48 were primarily related to downward revisions associated with lower commodity prices and higher royalty rates, partially offset by positive revisions related to decreases in operating expenses.

The Company’s total PUD reserves are comprised of 66% natural gas, 20% oil and 14% NGLs. The Company expects that substantially all of its PUD reserves will be developed within five years from the date they were initially recorded and that will require an estimated future development cost of approximately $4.0 billion. Future Development Costs. Estimated future development costs related to the development of PUD reserves at December 31, 2024 were approximately $4.0 billion, which equates to $9.83 per Boe. The Company expects to fund these costs primarily from cash flow from operations and, as necessary, borrowings under its Credit Facility or Commercial Paper Program, or access to capital markets.

Development Plan for PUD Reserves. The Company’s development plan for PUD reserves includes drilling and completing new wells in the Delaware Basin and Marcellus Shale, as well as the continued development of its other operating areas. The timing of the development of the Company’s PUD reserves is subject to change based on a number of factors including commodity prices, well performance, drilling and completion efficiencies, availability of services and equipment, and other operational considerations.

PUD Reserve Changes. Revisions of prior estimates of PUD reserves for the year ended December 31, 2024 were primarily related to downward performance revisions associated with lower commodity prices and higher royalty rates, partially offset by positive revisions related to decreases in operating expenses. Transfers to proved developed reserves were primarily the result of continued development activities and the conversion of PUD reserves to proved developed reserves. Additions were primarily related to successful drilling activities and optimization of development plans in the Company’s core operating areas.

Limitations and Uncertainties. PUD reserve estimates are inherently imprecise and subject to change as additional information becomes available. Changes in PUD reserves can occur for a variety of reasons, including changes in commodity prices, well performance, operating costs, development plans and other factors. The Company’s ability to develop its PUD reserves within the five-year period depends on a number of factors beyond its control, including the availability of capital, services and equipment, regulatory approvals and surface access, and commodity price volatility.

Environmental, Regulatory and Other Considerations. The development of PUD reserves is subject to various environmental and regulatory requirements, including permits for drilling and completion activities, air and water quality regulations, and land use restrictions. Compliance with these requirements may increase costs and affect the timing of development. Additionally, the Company considers surface use, community impacts and other stakeholder concerns in its development planning.

The Company believes that its development plans for PUD reserves are reasonable and that it has the financial and operational resources necessary to execute those plans. However, actual results may differ materially from those anticipated as a result of various factors, including those discussed in “Risk Factors” and elsewhere in this report.

The standardized measure is a common industry metric prescribed by the SEC and FASB. It relies on significant assumptions and estimates, including future production rates, the timing and amount of future development and production costs, and the application of statutory tax rates. Changes in commodity prices, development plans and operating costs can cause significant variability in the standardized measure from period to period.

Standardized Measure of Discounted Future Net Cash Flows Relating to Proved Oil and Gas Reserves

The future cash flows presented below are based on sales prices, costs and statutory tax rates in effect at the end of each period. Changes in oil, natural gas and NGL prices or costs, or in assumptions of reserve quantities and the timing of their development and production, may significantly affect the standardized measure. The standardized measure does not purport to represent, nor should it be viewed as representative of, the current value of EOG.

(1) Future cash inflows are computed by applying the unweighted arithmetic average of the first-day-of-the-month price for each month within the year to the estimated future production of year-end proved reserves. (2) Future development costs include estimates of capital expenditures to convert proved undeveloped reserves to proved developed reserves.

The standardized measure is not intended to represent fair value of EOG’s reserves. It is a prescribed measure that facilitates comparisons among companies. The determination of standardized measure requires the use of significant estimates and assumptions, including those related to proved reserve quantities, the timing and amount of future development and production costs, and statutory income tax rates. Accordingly, changes in such estimates and assumptions, as well as in commodity prices, can materially affect the standardized measure from period to period.

Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates
Our discussion and analysis of our financial condition and results of operations are based upon our consolidated financial statements, which have been prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States. The preparation of these financial statements requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses. Refer to our Form 10-K for further discussion of our critical accounting policies.

Purchase Accounting

From time-to-time, we may acquire assets and assume liabilities in transactions accounted for as business combinations. The purchase price is allocated to the assets acquired and liabilities assumed based on their estimated fair values as of the closing dates of the respective acquisition.

We made a number of assumptions in estimating the fair value of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed. Significant assumptions used in determining the fair value of proved and unproved oil and gas properties include, among others, estimates of future production volumes, future commodity prices and price differentials, expected development costs, lease operating costs, reserve risk adjustments and a discount rate that reflects the risk of the underlying cash flow estimates.

Estimated fair values assigned to assets acquired can have a significant effect on current and future results of operations due to the underlying accounting used to record depletion, depreciation and amortization expense and to measure future impairment charges, if any. As the fair values are finalized during the measurement period, if any estimates of the acquisitions change, the likelihood increases that certain costs may be determined to be unrecoverable.

In addition to the fair value of proved and unproved oil and gas properties, we also estimated the fair values of other assets acquired and liabilities assumed, including accounts receivable, inventory, other current assets, other property, plant and equipment, asset retirement obligations, and other liabilities, as of the closing date of the acquisitions. The fair value estimates were based on significant unobservable inputs (Level 3), such as historical information, derived forward price curves and other proprietary information used by market participants.

Depletion, Depreciation and Amortization (DD&A)

We follow the successful efforts method of accounting for oil and gas properties. Proved oil and gas properties are depreciated and amortized on a field-by-field basis using the unit-of-production method based on estimated proved reserves. The economic life of each producing property depends upon a number of factors, including geological and engineering estimates of recoverable reserves, which are subject to change. Changes in oil and natural gas prices will impact the level of proved developed reserves which, in turn, impacts DD&A expense. Higher prices generally have the effect of increasing reserve quantities and extending the economic life of a field, which generally reduces depletion expense. Conversely, lower prices generally have the effect of decreasing reserve quantities and shortening the economic life of a field, which generally increases depletion expense. The cost of replacing production also impacts our depletion expense. In addition, changes in reserve quantities or production volumes are reflected in DD&A expense in the period that the changes are known. Changes in our estimate of proved reserves will impact both the DD&A rate and the net book value of our oil and gas properties. Changes in future estimates of operating costs and development costs will also impact the DD&A rate.

Impairment of Oil and Gas Properties

We review oil and gas properties for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate that their carrying amounts may not be recoverable over their estimated remaining economic lives. If the undiscounted expected future cash flows from a property, using future price estimates and cost assumptions consistent with those that a market participant would use, are less than the carrying amount of the property, we recognize an impairment loss equal to the difference between the carrying amount and fair value. Fair value is estimated using expected future cash flows, which consider estimates of production volumes, commodity prices and price differentials, expected development and operating costs and a discount rate commensurate with the risks involved.

The estimates of reserves are used in the evaluation of the carrying value of oil and gas properties for impairment and in the calculation of DD&A. Changes in reserve estimates, production rates, commodity prices and costs can have a material effect on DD&A expense and impairment assessments.

question: CTRA commodity price indices used?
answer: CTRA bases its pricing on key commodity benchmarks, primarily NYMEX WTI for oil, Henry Hub for natural gas, and Mont Belvieu for NGLs, while also incorporating regional natural gas indices such as Transco Leidy Line and Transco Zone 6 Non-NY. These indices determine realized prices and drive revenue sensitivity to commodity markets. In essence, Coterra’s financial performance is closely tied to these benchmark price movements.

Year-end 2024 proved reserves decreased approximately two percent from year-end 2023 proved reserves to 2,271 MMBoe. The Company’s reserves in the Marcellus Shale accounted for 55 percent of total proved reserves, the Permian Basin accounted for 35 percent, and the remaining 10 percent were in the Anadarko Basin.

During 2024, the Company added 189 MMBoe of proved reserves through extensions, discoveries, and other additions, which included 115 MMBoe in the Permian Basin, 28 MMBoe in the Marcellus Shale and 45 MMBoe in the Anadarko Basin. The Company had net positive revisions of prior estimates of 9 MMBoe, which included a 59 MMBoe negative revision due to price, offset by a 4 MMBoe positive revision in operating expenses and a positive 64 MMBoe performance revision.

During 2023, the Company added 228 MMBoe of proved reserves through extensions, discoveries, and other additions, which included 102 MMBoe in the Permian Basin, 87 MMBoe in the Marcellus Shale and 39 MMBoe in the Anadarko Basin. The Company had net negative revisions of prior estimates of 60 MMBoe, which included 83 MMBoe negative revision due to price, a 10 MMBoe negative revision due to increases in operating expenses, partially offset by a positive 33 MMBoe performance revision.

During 2022, the Company added 406 MMBoe of proved reserves through extensions, discoveries, and other additions, which included 193 MMBoe in the Permian Basin, 191 MMBoe in the Marcellus Shale and 22 MMBoe in the Anadarko Basin. The Company had net negative revisions of prior estimates of 667 MMBoe, which included 571 MMBoe in downward performance revisions related to updated forecast parameters in the Marcellus Shale to account for a different decline behavior

observed in bounded wells compared to unbounded wells. The net negative revisions also included 168MMBoe associated with the removal of PUD reserves in the Marcellus Shale whose development is expected to be delayed beyond five years of initial booking. These negative revisions in the Marcellus Shale were partially offset by 32 MMBoe in positive performance revisions in the Permian Basin, 39 MMBoe in positive revisions related to upward price revisions, and 1 MMBoe in positive revisions related to decreases in operating expenses.

 Proved Undeveloped Reserves
At December 31, 2024, the Company had PUD reserves of 407 MMBoe, down 75 MMBoe, or 15 percent, from 482 MMBoe of PUD reserves at December 31, 2023. Future development plans are reflective of the current commodity price environment and have been established based on expected available cash flows from operations. By the end of 2025, the Company expects to complete substantially all the work necessary to convert its PUD reserves associated with wells that were drilled but uncompleted at December 31, 2024 to proved developed reserves. As of December 31, 2024 all PUD reserves are expected to be drilled and completed within five years of initial disclosure of these reserves. Commodity Price Risk
Our most significant market risk exposure is pricing applicable to our oil, natural gas and NGL production. Realized prices are mainly driven by the worldwide price for oil and spot market prices for North American natural gas and NGL production. As noted above, these prices have been volatile and unpredictable. To mitigate the volatility in commodity prices, we may enter into derivative instruments to hedge a portion of our production.

Derivative Instruments and Risk Management Activities

Our commodity price risk management strategy is designed to reduce the risk of commodity price volatility for our production in the oil and natural gas markets through the use of financial commodity derivatives. A committee that consists of members of senior management oversees our risk management activities. Our financial commodity derivatives generally cover a portion of our production and, while protecting us in the event of price declines, limit the benefit to us in the event of price increases. Further, if any of our counterparties defaulted, this protection might be limited as we might not receive the full benefit of our financial commodity derivatives. Please read the discussion below as well as Note 5 of the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements, “Derivative Instruments,” in Item 8 for a more detailed discussion of our derivatives.

Periodically, we enter into financial commodity derivatives, including collar, swap, and basis swap agreements, to protect against exposure to commodity price declines. All of our financial derivatives are used for risk management purposes and are not held for trading purposes. Under the collar agreements, if the index price rises above the ceiling price, we pay the counterparty. If the index price falls below the floor price, the counterparty pays us. Under the swap agreements, we receive a fixed price on a notional quantity of natural gas or oil in exchange for paying a variable price based on a market-based index.

However, the market risk exposure on these derivative contracts is generally offset by the gain or loss recognized upon the ultimate sale of the commodity. Although notional contract amounts are used to express the volume of oil and natural gas agreements, the amounts that can be subject to credit risk in the event of non-performance by third parties are substantially smaller. Our counterparties are primarily commercial banks and financial service institutions that our management believes present minimal credit risk and our derivative contracts are with multiple counterparties to minimize our exposure to any individual counterparty. We perform both quantitative and qualitative assessments of these counterparties based on their credit ratings and credit default swap rates where applicable. We have not incurred any losses related to non-performance risk of our counterparties and we do not anticipate any material impact on our financial results due to non-performance by third parties. However, we cannot be certain that we will not experience such losses in the future.

hard_negatives.text:
Market Conditions and Commodity Prices
Our financial results depend on many factors, particularly commodity prices and commodity price dynamics for oil, natural gas and NGLs. Commodity prices are affected by many factors outside of our control, including supply and demand factors, seasonal influences, political events and economic conditions. Price volatility may be expected to continue in the future as a result of near-term supply and demand imbalances, in addition to longer-term changes in the macroeconomic backdrop.

Oil

The oil markets continued to be dynamic in 2024. Fluctuations in commodity prices and regional differences in oil pricing were affected by global news events, changes in worldwide supply and demand and agreements among the Organization of Oil and Other-Producing Countries and allies that are party to production reduction agreements (collectively referred to as “OPEC+”), including production cuts that were announced in the first quarter of 2023 and subsequently extended multiple times through the fourth quarter of 2025.

Related to Non-U.S. issues, commodity prices reflect geopolitical risks and market concerns around production disruptions, new sanctions, weakness in the manufacturing sector for a variety of developed economies that include the United States, China and European nations, the potential for recessions in various countries during 2023 and international restrictions and supply chain disruptions. Some factors that affect oil prices include the session outlook for OPEC+ supply, oil and refined products inventory levels in the U.S. and abroad and the value of the U.S. dollar, as oil is priced in dollars.

United States oil benchmark prices increased moderately in 2024 compared to 2023, with 2024 prices ranging during the year from approximately $68 per barrel to $95 per barrel. As a result, overall oil price trends in 2024 indicated general price volatility in the short-term while lowering the overall trend of oil benchmark prices when compared to 2022.

Natural Gas

Natural gas prices continued to be lower in 2024 when compared to 2023. Due to global economic activity slowdown, changes in weather conditions compared to 2023, and other factors unrelated to our business (including production levels), natural gas pricing continued to be lower in 2024 than in 2023 in connection with these market events. During 2024, the benchmark Henry Hub natural gas price ranged from approximately $1.50 per MMBtu to $4.60 per MMBtu.

Liquified Natural Gas (LNG)

LNG exports continued to be a source of incremental demand and represent the fastest-growing source of demand for U.S. natural gas with various new LNG export terminals under development and approval by the U.S. Department of Energy. U.S. LNG exports are influenced by global price benchmarks for natural gas, transportation costs via LNG shipping vessels, and demand stemming from weather and production conditions. Developing international energy markets have placed an increased reliance on U.S. LNG as a key source of supply stabilization.

NGLs

NGL prices are associated with the prices of natural gas and crude oil and therefore share many price influences, including periods of oversupply in either crude oil or natural gas markets. NGL pricing is also influenced by the availability and capacity of natural gas processing infrastructure. Products with NGL components (like propane and butane) are often used in final products by petrochemical manufacturers and their seasonal demand can be influenced by cold weather that increases propane consumption rates for heating.

Price Variability and Basis Differentials

Commodity price variances and basis differentials fluctuate significantly by region. As a result, we might realize different prices for the same commodity in various regions. The specific prices realized depend on many factors, including local supply and demand conditions, the quality and energy content of the product, the availability and cost of transportation to different markets, and contractual arrangements. In addition, basis differentials may be influenced by market conditions, changes in infrastructure capacity and limitations and regional or local imbalances.

Outlook

We cannot predict future commodity prices and whether the prices that prevailed during 2024 will continue during 2025. However, factors that affect benchmark oil prices in 2025 and beyond include the pace of global economic growth, OPEC+ production decisions, geopolitical events and domestic and international energy policy changes. For natural gas and NGLs, the extent and timing of increased LNG export capacity in the U.S., changes in weather patterns and demand from industrial and power-generation sectors will continue to be significant drivers of price dynamics.

The following table presents historical information about our total production and reserve replacement trends for oil, natural gas and NGLs; average sales prices; and average production costs per oil equivalent:

Our realized prices are influenced by a number of factors including local market dynamics, quality and energy content of the products sold, and transportation arrangements. Realized prices for oil, natural gas and NGLs may differ significantly from benchmark prices due to basis differentials, market conditions, product quality, location and contractual terms.

Production costs per unit are affected by changes in service costs, labor, fuel and power, workover activities and the timing of maintenance and other operating activities. Costs also vary due to the timing of production start-ups, the maturity of operating areas and the mix of production across our asset portfolio.

Our ability to improve production efficiency and reduce costs is influenced by drilling and completion techniques, supply chain initiatives, economies of scale and technological advancements in horizontal drilling and multi-stage completions. These activities may reduce unit costs and improve recovery rates over time, but are subject to uncertainty and risk.

Future production and realized pricing are also impacted by commodity price volatility, changes in demand for oil, natural gas and NGLs, weather patterns and general economic conditions. Transportation capacity, availability of processing facilities and regulatory changes can also affect realized prices and margins.

We continue to monitor market conditions and focus on optimizing our development plans to maximize returns and cash flows under a range of pricing scenarios.

Market Conditions and Commodity Prices
Our results of operations and cash flows are highly dependent on commodity prices for oil, natural gas and NGLs. Commodity prices are influenced by many factors outside of our control, including changes in supply and demand, inventory levels, weather, geopolitical events, macroeconomic conditions, transportation and processing capacity, and government policies. Prices may also be affected by regional supply and demand balances and basis differentials.

Oil prices are influenced by global factors such as OPEC+ production decisions, geopolitical tensions, global economic growth and inventory levels. Price volatility may be expected to continue in the future as a result of these factors and changes in market expectations.

Natural gas prices can be affected by seasonal weather patterns, changes in storage levels, LNG exports, power generation demand and industrial activity. Regional basis differentials can have a significant impact on realized natural gas prices depending on local supply-demand conditions and transportation constraints.

NGL prices are affected by the prices of oil and natural gas, as well as the supply-demand balance for NGL products used in petrochemical and heating markets. Seasonal demand, changes in petrochemical feedstock preferences and export capacity can impact NGL prices.

Due to fluctuations in commodity prices and basis differentials, our realized prices can differ from benchmark prices. The magnitude of the difference depends on product quality, location, market conditions, transportation and processing costs and the terms of our sales contracts.

We cannot predict future commodity prices. Our capital allocation and development plans are designed to provide flexibility in response to commodity price volatility and to maintain a strong financial position across a range of price environments.

Item 7A.Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk

The primary objective of the following information is to provide forward-looking quantitative and qualitative information about our exposure to market risk. The term “market risk” refers to the risk of loss arising from adverse changes in market rates and prices. We are exposed to market risk primarily in the form of commodity price risk, interest rate risk, foreign currency exchange rate risk and equity price risk. The following information is not meant to be precise indicators of expected future losses but rather indicators of reasonably possible losses.

Commodity Price Risk

We are exposed to the risk of changing commodity prices due to the volatility in the prices for oil, natural gas and NGLs. To manage the risk of commodity price volatility, we may enter into various derivative financial instruments, such as swaps, options and collars. The extent of our commodity price risk management activities and the level of coverage we may elect to obtain will vary based on our views of the current and future market conditions, desired risk mitigation and other factors.

Interest Rate Risk

We are exposed to interest rate risk on our variable-rate debt. We manage interest rate risk through a combination of fixed- and variable-rate debt as well as the possible use of interest rate derivatives.

Foreign Currency Exchange Rate Risk

We are exposed to foreign currency exchange rate risk related to certain transactions denominated in currencies other than the U.S. dollar. We may enter into foreign currency exchange contracts to manage exposures arising from fluctuations in currency exchange rates.

Equity Price Risk

We are exposed to equity price risk related to certain investments that are measured at fair value with changes in fair value recognized in earnings.

We regularly evaluate our exposure to these risks and the effectiveness of our risk management strategies.

Marketing
In 2024, EOG continued its diversified approach to marketing crude oil, NGLs and natural gas through a combination of spot and term sales, direct sales and sales through intermediaries. EOG seeks to maximize realized prices and margins by optimizing destination markets, transportation options and sales timing within the constraints of operational and contractual requirements. EOG’s marketing strategy is designed to provide flexibility to respond to market conditions and to reduce exposure to localized price disruptions.

Crude oil marketing activities include sales at or near the wellhead, deliveries into gathering systems and pipelines and sales to refineries and other end users. EOG also pursues opportunities to sell crude oil at downstream hubs along the U.S. Gulf Coast, including Houston and Corpus Christi, and may use storage, term contracts and transportation arrangements to access additional markets and improve realizations. Realized prices for crude oil are affected by product quality, location differentials, transportation costs and market conditions at the time of sale.

Natural gas marketing activities include sales at the wellhead, into gathering systems, at processing plants and at downstream delivery points. EOG evaluates whether it acts as principal or agent in each arrangement based on control of the product before transfer to the customer and recognizes revenues accordingly. Realized natural gas prices are influenced by supply and demand dynamics, seasonal weather patterns, storage levels, LNG exports, transportation capacity and basis differentials between producing regions and consuming markets.

NGL marketing includes sales of raw mix and fractionated products such as ethane, propane, normal butane, isobutane and natural gasoline. EOG’s marketing activities for NGLs may include sales at processing plants, deliveries to fractionators and sales to petrochemical and other end-use customers. Realized NGL prices are affected by product specifications, feedstock substitution in the petrochemical industry, export capacity, seasonal demand and transportation and fractionation fees.

EOG enters into a variety of transportation and processing arrangements to support its marketing activities, including pipeline capacity agreements, gathering and processing contracts, and storage and terminal agreements. These arrangements can help ensure access to markets, reduce transportation constraints and provide optionality to capture regional price opportunities.

EOG manages credit exposure by monitoring the financial condition of customers and counterparties and by establishing and reviewing credit limits and requiring collateral where appropriate. EOG also evaluates opportunities to optimize transportation and market access through periodic renegotiation of agreements and the use of third-party services.

EOG’s marketing activities are conducted in accordance with applicable laws and regulations and are designed to support reliable deliveries, maintain strong customer relationships and enhance overall value from the Company’s production.

question: Risks CTRA identifies in relation to commodity price volatility, climate change regulation, and ongoing legal proceedings?
answer: CTRA faces three main risk areas: commodity price volatility, which remains its most significant financial exposure despite hedging strategies; climate change regulation, which could raise costs, delay projects, and increase competition from renewables; and ongoing legal proceedings, particularly environmental compliance matters that may result in fines and corrective costs. While management does not currently expect these issues to materially impact financial results, prolonged low prices, stricter regulation, or adverse legal outcomes could pressure operations and profitability.

Market Conditions and Commodity Prices
Our financial results depend on many factors, particularly commodity prices and our ability to find and develop oil and gas reserves and market our production on economically attractive terms. Commodity prices are affected by many factors outside of our control, including changes in market supply and demand, which can be impacted by pipeline capacity constraints, inventory storage levels, basis differentials, weather conditions, and geopolitical, economic and other factors.

While oil prices were relatively steady in 2024, prices have begun to decline in 2025, with the largest decline occurring in April 2025 in both spot and forward pricing. Global oil demand has been projected by some, including the International Energy Agency, to be adversely impacted by escalating trade tensions as a result of U.S. economic policy, including tariffs and retaliatory tariffs. However, these forecasts are subject to volatile market conditions, including as a result of changing U.S. and international trade policy. OPEC+ also recently announced both production cuts and increased production quotas. The impacts of these changes remain to be seen.

Natural gas prices increased in early 2025 but have subsequently begun to trend down, due in part to warmer temperatures and record high domestic production. Additionally, shifting U.S. and international trade policy and uncertainty related thereto, including potential retaliatory tariffs on U.S. exports of LNG, have created further uncertainty in natural gas pricing looking forward. Meanwhile, basis differentials have persisted in the U.S., with prices at the Waha Hub in the Permian Basin particularly depressed due to oversupply and turning negative in March 2025 before increasing again in April 2025. Despite these headwinds, we expect natural gas prices overall to be stronger in 2025 compared to 2024.

In recent months, the potential for increasing tariffs has emerged as a contributing factor to increased volatility in commodity markets and uncertainty in the general economic outlook. Higher tariffs could result in increased costs of materials used in our operations, less ready access to capital markets or less favorable general economic conditions. The uncertainty surrounding tariff policies has led to fluctuations in commodity prices which could impact our ability to forecast future results. We are continuing to monitor developments related to tariff policies.

Although the current outlook on oil and natural gas prices is generally favorable and our operations have not been significantly impacted in the short-term, in the event further disruptions occur or the current market volatility and U.S. and international economic policy uncertainty continues for an extended period of time, our operations could be adversely impacted, commodity prices could decline and our costs may increase. We expect commodity price volatility to continue, including as a result of U.S. and international economic policy (such as tariffs or retaliatory tariffs), actions of OPEC+ (including the ability of OPEC+ to successfully coordinate production quotas) and potentially swift near- and medium-term fluctuations in supply and demand, including potential changes to drilling and capital programs in the short term by U.S. producers. While we are unable to predict future commodity prices, at current oil, natural gas and NGL price levels, we do not believe that an impairment of our oil and gas properties is reasonably likely to occur in the near future. However, in the event that commodity prices significantly decline or costs significantly increase from current levels, our management would evaluate the recoverability of the carrying value of our oil and gas properties.

In addition, the issue of, and increasing political and social attention on, climate change has resulted in both existing and pending national, regional and local legislation and regulatory measures, such as mandates for renewable energy and emissions reductions. Changes in these laws or regulations may result in delays or restrictions in permitting and the development of projects, may result in increased costs and may impair our ability to move forward with our construction, completions, drilling, water management, waste handling, storage, transport and remediation activities, or may result in renewable energy alternatives that become more competitive with traditional oil and natural gas-derived products (including government subsidies and incentives for electric vehicles), any of which could have an adverse effect on our financial results.

For information about the impact of realized commodity prices on our revenues, refer to “Results of Operations” below.

Commodity Price Risk
Our most significant market risk exposure is pricing applicable to our oil, natural gas and NGL production. Realized prices are mainly driven by the worldwide price for oil and spot market prices for North American natural gas and NGL

production. As noted above, these prices have been volatile and unpredictable. To mitigate the volatility in commodity prices, we may enter into derivative instruments to hedge a portion of our production.

Derivative Instruments and Risk Management Activities

Our commodity price risk management strategy is designed to reduce the risk of commodity price volatility for our production in the oil and natural gas markets through the use of financial commodity derivatives. A committee that consists of members of senior management oversees these risk management activities. Our financial commodity derivatives generally cover a portion of our production and, while protecting us in the event of price declines, limit the benefit to us in the event of price increases. Further, if any of our counterparties defaulted, this protection might be limited as we might not receive the full benefit of our financial commodity derivatives. Please read the discussion below as well as Note 5 in this Form 10-Q and Note 5 of the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements in our Form 10-K for a more detailed discussion of our derivatives.

Periodically, we enter into financial commodity derivatives, including collar, swap and basis swap agreements, to protect against exposure to commodity price declines. All of our financial derivatives are used for risk management purposes and are not held for trading purposes. Under the collar agreements, if the index price rises above the ceiling price, we pay the counterparty. If the index price falls below the floor price, the counterparty pays us. Under the swap agreements, we receive a fixed price on a notional quantity of natural gas in exchange for paying a variable price based on a market-based index.
