Oil swaps covered 1.7 MMBbls, or 13 percent, of our oil production at a weighted-average price of $69.18 per Bbl. Oil basis swaps covered 6.3 MMBbls, or 50 percent, of our oil production at a weighted-average differential of $1.07 per Bbl.

During the three months ended March 31, 2025, natural gas collars with floor prices ranging from $2.75 to $3.40 per MMBtu and ceiling prices ranging from $3.40 to $7.00 per MMBtu covered 55.5 Mcf, or 20 percent of our natural gas production at a weighted-average price of $3.68 per MMBtu. Gas basis swaps covered 29.2 Bcf, or 11 percent of natural gas production at a weighted-average differential of $(0.58) per MMBtu.

We are exposed to market risk on financial commodity derivative instruments to the extent of changes in market prices of the related commodity. However, the market risk exposure on these derivative contracts is generally offset by the gain or loss recognized upon the ultimate sale of the commodity. Although notional contract amounts are used to express the volume of oil and natural gas agreements, the amounts that can be subject to credit risk in the event of non-performance by third parties are substantially smaller. Our counterparties are primarily commercial banks and financial service institutions that our management believes present minimal credit risk, and our derivative contracts are with multiple counterparties to minimize our exposure to any individual counterparty. We perform both quantitative and qualitative assessments of these counterparties based on their credit ratings and credit default swap rates where applicable. We have not incurred any losses related to non-performance risk of our counterparties, and we do not anticipate any material impact on our financial results due to non-performance by third parties. However, we cannot be certain that we will not experience such losses in the future.

Legal Matters
The information set forth under the heading “Legal Matters” in Note 8 of the Notes to Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements included in this Form 10-Q is incorporated by reference in response to this item.

 Governmental Proceedings
From time-to-time, we receive notices of violation from governmental and regulatory authorities, including notices relating to alleged violations of environmental statutes or the rules and regulations promulgated thereunder. While we cannot predict with certainty whether these notices of violation will result in fines, penalties or both, if fines or penalties are imposed, they may result in monetary sanctions, individually or in the aggregate, in excess of $300,000.

In June 2023, we received a Notice of Violation and Opportunity to Confer (“NOVOC”) from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) alleging violations of the Clean Air Act, the Texas State Implementation Plan, the New Mexico State Implementation Plan (“NMSIP”) and certain other state and federal regulations pertaining to Company facilities in Texas and New Mexico. Separately, in July 2023, we received a letter from the U.S. Department of Justice that the EPA has referred this NOVOC for civil enforcement proceedings. In August 2023, we received a second NOVOC from the EPA alleging violations of the Clean Air Act, the NMSIP, and certain other state and federal regulations pertaining to Company facilities in New Mexico. We have exchanged information with the EPA and continue to engage in discussions aimed at resolving the allegations. At this time we are unable to predict with certainty the financial impact of these NOVOCs or the timing of any resolution. However, any enforcement action related to these NOVOCs will likely result in fines or penalties, or both, and corrective actions, which may increase our development costs or operating costs. We believe that any fines, penalties, or corrective actions that may result from these matters will not have a material effect on our financial position, results of operations, or cash flows.

hard_negatives.text:
Our operations present hazards and risks that require significant and continuous oversight and management.

The scope and nature of our operations present a variety of significant hazards and risks, including injuries and loss of life, property damage, sudden subsurface failure or migration of hydrocarbons or well failure caused by natural disasters or operational systems failure, and release of hydrocarbons, production fluids or other hazardous materials, any of which could result in environmental or property damage and other harm.

We are subject to numerous possible disruptions from unexpected events and circumstances beyond our control, including natural disasters, extreme weather conditions, war, violent conflict, geopolitical events and local security concerns, public health crises such as outbreaks of pandemic or contagious diseases and misinformation related to these events. The occurrence of any of such events or issues, as well as a sustained disruption to the capital markets, could cause damage or reduce demand for our products or cause us to incur significant losses.

We are constantly pursuing new technologies and practices in order to minimize hazards and risks in our operations. Despite these efforts, unexpected events may occur that cause personal injury and widespread and significant property damage or other harm resulting in disturbance or cessation of our operations. Our insurance and indemnities may not be adequate or enforceable to cover all risks and liabilities we may sustain. For example, oil and gas properties are typically not fully insured against all risks, because of the economic limits of available coverage. The occurrence of an event not fully covered by insurance could have a material adverse effect on our operations and financial condition. In addition, insurance coverage may not be available in the future at current levels of cost or coverage, which could adversely affect our ability to maintain insurance coverage after liability for a catastrophic event.

Our proved reserves are estimates. Any material inaccuracies in those estimates or underlying assumptions will materially affect the quantities and present value of our reserves.

Reserves engineering is a subjective process of estimating underground accumulations of oil and natural gas that cannot be measured in an exact manner. The process relies on interpretations of available geologic, geophysical, engineering and production data. The extent, quality and reliability of this data can vary. The process also requires many assumptions relating to current and future economic and regulatory conditions and commodity prices. Any significant inaccuracy of these assumptions causes the relevant quantities and present value estimates of the reserves to be inaccurate.

You should not assume that the present value of future net cash flows referred to in this document is the current market value of our estimated proved oil and natural gas reserves. In accordance with SEC requirements, the standardized measure is generally limited to the present value of future net revenues derived from estimated quantities of proved reserves. It generally excludes the effects of changes in product prices and costs that may occur in the future and differs from the full-cost ceiling test, which is calculated on different assumptions. The timing of both production and development expenditures in the future will result in lower present values for future net cash flows since we are discounting future net cash flows based on expected timing of such production and expenditures. In addition, the use of a 10 percent discount factor may or may not be appropriate to calculate present value depending on interest rates and other factors.

We can provide no assurance that any additions to proved reserves will be made in the future. We can give no assurance that any of our undeveloped reserves will be developed within five years of initial booking or at all.

We may not be able to economically find, develop, or acquire additional reserves to replace our current and future production.

Unless we successfully develop our proved undeveloped reserves, find, develop or acquire additional reserves, our reserves and production will decline from their current levels as reserves are depleted. If we are unable to replace reserves in the future, our cash flows and the value of our common stock may be adversely affected.

We may not be able to obtain the capital required to maintain and grow our business on satisfactory terms or access the capital markets at all.

We rely in part on access to capital markets as a source of liquidity for capital requirements not satisfied by cash flows from operations. Our ability to access these markets may be affected by, among other things, oil and natural gas prices, interest rates, our credit ratings, a deterioration in general market conditions or market perceptions of the oil and natural gas industry, and concerns regarding environmental matters, including climate change, and our business. Disruptions in the capital markets, including as a result of general economic conditions or governmental policies, may also increase the cost of borrowing or adversely affect our ability to access one or more sources of capital. If we are unable to access capital at reasonable costs when needed, we may be forced to curtail our drilling and development programs, sell assets, reduce our capital expenditures and/or reduce or eliminate our dividend in order to continue meeting our capital requirements and to execute our business strategy. Any of the foregoing could adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.

We depend on certain key customers for sales of our oil and natural gas and on certain key vendors and suppliers for the delivery of necessary infrastructure, components and services.

We currently have multiple customers for the sale of our natural gas, oil and NGLs. However, a limited number of purchasers of natural gas, oil and NGLs control a significant portion of the market, and if we were unable to sell to one or more of these major customers, this could cause a significant reduction in our revenues and adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition. Additionally, if any of our customers were unable to meet their obligations, such as in the case of bankruptcy, we could incur losses.

We rely on, among others, midstream and downstream service providers and pipeline, storage, water and other infrastructure that we do not own or operate in connection with the gathering, processing, fractionation, transportation, storage and sale of our production, and the availability and capacity of these third-party services and infrastructure is essential for the timely marketing of our products. If transportation or processing capacity arrangements become unavailable or restricted, our ability to produce and sell our production may be limited. We also rely on contractors, suppliers and service providers in our operations. The loss of any significant service provider, delays in deliveries, capacity constraints, labor availability or quality issues could negatively impact our operations and the timing of our projects. If any of these parties fail to meet their obligations to us, experience disruptions, quality or safety issues, delays or capacity constraints, we may incur costs or be forced to curtail or shut-in production. Any of these risks could have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations and financial condition.

We are dependent on information systems and other technology, and disruptions or failures of our information systems, including as a result of cyberattacks, could adversely affect our business and operations.

We rely on information technology to support our operations, including field operations, business processes and financial reporting. We also rely on certain third-parties for information systems and other technology services, such as cloud-based applications. Our information systems are subject to damage or interruption from power outages, telecommunications failures, computer viruses, cyberattacks, security breaches, data corruption, human error and natural disasters. Significant disruption of, or significant security breaches in, our computer systems or the failure to timely identify or appropriately respond to or mitigate such disruptions could adversely affect our ability to operate effectively, including our ability to manage our operations and financial reporting, business planning and communications. In addition, cyberattacks could result in the theft, destruction, loss, misappropriation or release of sensitive, confidential or valuable information, or otherwise compromise our proprietary information and technology, any of which could have a material adverse effect on our business and operations.

We have established processes and security measures to protect against cyber risks and to ensure that the effective operation of our information systems is not disrupted. However, there can be no assurance that those efforts will be successful in preventing interruptions in our operations or in preventing or mitigating the impact of cyberattacks. We remain susceptible to potentially significant costs and disruptions of our operations in the event of a cyber incident. We could incur significant costs in the event of a security breach, including costs to respond to, investigate and remedy the incident, as well as take remedial steps to address the breach and costs to comply with applicable data breach notification laws. Moreover, security breaches could result in possible claims against us and/or require us to locate or contract with additional resources or to engage third-party service providers, and could damage our reputation and cause us to lose customers and revenues.

We may be adversely affected by inflation, changes in interest rates, volatility in foreign currency exchange rates and commodity prices, and other macroeconomic factors, which may increase our costs or limit our access to capital.

Inflation may increase the costs of materials, services, labor and other items required for our operations and may also increase our costs associated with interest and debt.

We depend upon the availability of water sourcing, treatment and disposal; our operations could be adversely impacted if we are unable to obtain water or dispose of water affordably and in an environmentally responsible manner.

Our operations require large volumes of water to drill and complete wells. The supply of water is dependent upon a variety of factors, including local and regional drought conditions, governmental requirements and other users in the region. Inability to obtain sufficient quantities of water could delay or increase the costs associated with our drilling and completion operations. Conversely, our operations also generate significant volumes of water that must be properly handled and disposed. Limitations on the availability of disposal wells, regulatory restrictions, seismicity concerns and increased costs associated with disposal could adversely impact our operations. We continue to evaluate and implement water recycling and reuse practices where feasible to reduce reliance on freshwater sources and disposal needs; however, these efforts may not be sufficient to offset all constraints. Any of these issues could adversely affect our operations and financial condition.

ITEM 3. LEGAL PROCEEDINGS

 Legal Matters
We are involved in various legal proceedings incidental to our business. These proceedings include claims related to personal injury and property damage, royalty and contract disputes, land and lease title claims, resurveyed boundaries, alleged environmental contamination, disputes regarding access to or use of water, as well as other matters arising in the ordinary course of business. The results of litigation cannot be predicted with certainty and, because litigation is inherently subject to many uncertainties, there can be no assurance that our defense of these cases will be successful. Therefore, it is possible that our business, financial condition, results of operations or liquidity could be materially adversely affected in any particular period by unfavorable developments in pending matters. We establish provisions for losses in cases where we believe that the outcome is probable and reasonably estimable. For additional information, see Note 17 to the consolidated financial statements.

The information set forth under the heading “Legal Matters” in Note 17 to our consolidated financial statements included in this Form 10-K is incorporated by reference in response to this item.

 Governmental Proceedings
From time to time we receive notices of violation from governmental agencies or notices of citizen suits filed or threatened under various environmental statutes. We are not currently aware of any proceedings, or such known to be contemplated by governmental authorities, that we reasonably believe will result in monetary sanctions, individually or in the aggregate, in excess of $300,000.

In June 2023, we received a Notice of Violation and Opportunity for Hearing (“NOV”) from the U.S. EPA alleging violations of the Clean Air Act, the Texas State Implementation Plan, the New Mexico State Implementation Plan and Titles V and VI of the Clean Air Act. The NOV is for alleged violations at locations that we acquired during the Cimarex merger. We are continuing conversations with the EPA to resolve these alleged violations and are unable to estimate the potential penalties at this time. Separately, in 2023, we received a second NOV from the EPA related to the Clean Air Act’s Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program. We are addressing the matter with the EPA and will continue discussions to resolve the issue. We cannot predict the ultimate outcome of these or any other governmental proceedings or notices of violation received from time to time, nor can we reasonably estimate the range of possible loss, if any, at this time.

Regulation
General. New or revised rules, regulations and policies may be issued, and new legislation may be enacted, that could materially affect the oil and gas exploration and production industry. Such changes could affect, among other things, our production levels, the way we operate, our environmental and safety practices, the costs of compliance, and our financial performance.

Federal, State and Local Regulation. Our operations are subject to extensive regulation by federal, state and local authorities. These regulations cover a broad range of matters including, but not limited to, drilling and completion practices, well construction, groundwater protection, air emissions, waste disposal, and surface land usage. The requirements can vary significantly between jurisdictions, and we must obtain and maintain numerous permits and approvals to conduct our activities. Failure to comply with these regulations could result in fines, penalties, or restrictions on operations.

Environmental and Safety Standards. We are subject to environmental laws and regulations that aim to protect air and water quality, manage waste, and ensure safe operations. Compliance with these standards may require significant expenditures for monitoring, reporting, equipment upgrades, and facility modifications. We continuously review and adapt our practices to meet evolving requirements and to support responsible development.

Hydraulic Fracturing. Our completion operations commonly utilize hydraulic fracturing. Regulators at various levels of government continue to evaluate and, in some cases, implement more stringent requirements related to well construction, chemical disclosure, water sourcing and disposal, and induced seismicity. We expect ongoing scrutiny and potential changes to the regulatory framework applicable to hydraulic fracturing. Additional restrictions or requirements could increase costs, limit the availability of services, or affect the timing of our projects.

Air Emissions and Methane. We are subject to regulations governing emissions of greenhouse gases, volatile organic compounds, and other air pollutants. Recent and pending rulemakings may result in additional monitoring, control technologies, and reporting obligations. We evaluate the applicability of these rules to our assets and implement measures designed to comply with current requirements and to prepare for potential future changes.

Water Management. Our operations require the sourcing, handling, storage, and disposal of water. We manage water through a combination of supply planning, transportation and storage infrastructure, treatment, and disposal methods. Regulatory requirements related to water use, discharge, and disposal wells can affect our costs and operational flexibility.

Waste and Spill Prevention. We maintain programs and procedures aimed at preventing spills and managing waste generated during drilling and production activities. Applicable regulations may require secondary containment, spill response planning, and the use of approved disposal methods for certain materials. We regularly review these programs to maintain compliance and to address any changes in regulatory expectations.

Liquidity and Capital Resources
We strive to maintain an adequate liquidity level to address commodity price volatility and risk. Our liquidity requirements consist primarily of our planned capital expenditures (including acquisitions), payment of contractual obligations (including debt maturities and interest payments), working capital requirements, dividend payments and share repurchases. Although we have no obligation to do so, we may also from time-to-time refinance or retire our outstanding debt through privately negotiated transactions, open market repurchases, redemptions, exchanges, tender offers or otherwise.

Our primary sources of liquidity are cash on hand, net cash provided by operating activities and available borrowing capacity under our revolving credit agreement. Our liquidity requirements are generally funded with cash flows provided by operating activities, together with cash on hand. However, from time-to-time, our investments may be funded by bank borrowings (including draws on our revolving credit agreement), sales of assets, and private or public financing based on our monitoring of capital markets and our balance sheet. While there are no “rating triggers” in any of our debt agreements that would accelerate the scheduled maturities should our debt rating falls below a certain level, a change in our debt rating could adversely impact our interest rate on any borrowings under our revolving credit agreement and our ability to economically access debt markets and could trigger the requirement to post credit support under various agreements, which could reduce the borrowing capacity under our revolving credit agreement. As of the date hereof, our debt is currently rated as investment grade by the three leading ratings agencies. For more on the impact of credit ratings on our interest rates and fees for unused commitments under our revolving credit agreement, see Note 4 of the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements in our Form 10-K. We believe that, with operating cash flow, cash on hand and availability under our revolving credit agreement, we have the ability to finance our spending plans over the next 12 months and, based on current expectations, for the longer term.

Our working capital is substantially influenced by the variables discussed above and fluctuates based on the timing and amount of borrowings and repayments under our revolving credit agreement, borrowings and repayments of debt, the timing of cash collections and payments on our trade accounts receivable and payable, respectively, payment of dividends, repurchases of our securities and changes in the fair value of our commodity derivative activity. From time-to-time, our working capital will reflect a deficit, while at other times it will reflect a surplus. This fluctuation is not unusual. As of March 31, 2025, we had a working capital deficit of $162 million, primarily due to a lower cash position compared to prior periods as a result of funding the purchase price of the FME and Avant acquisitions that closed in January 2025. As of December 31, 2024, we had a working capital surplus of $2.2 billion. We believe we have adequate liquidity and availability under our revolving credit agreement as outlined above to meet our working capital requirements over the next 12 months.

As of March 31, 2025, we had no borrowings outstanding under our revolving credit agreement, our unused commitments were $2.0 billion, and we had unrestricted cash on hand of $186 million.

Our revolving credit agreement and term loan include a covenant potentially limiting our borrowing capacity as determined by our leverage ratio. As of March 31, 2025, we were in compliance with all financial covenants applicable to our revolving credit agreement, term loan and private placement senior notes.  FINANCIAL CONDITION

 Liquidity and Capital Resources
We strive to maintain an adequate liquidity level to address commitments associated with our business operations, including exploration, development and production activities; the repayment of debt and interest; working capital requirements; and to return capital to stockholders through dividend payments and share repurchases. Although we have no obligation to do so, our Board of Directors has authorized us to repurchase shares of our common stock through open market purchases and other transactions. The timing and amount of any repurchases are determined by several factors, including commodity prices, cash flow and market conditions.

Our primary sources of liquidity are cash on hand, net cash provided by operating activities and available borrowing capacity under our revolving credit agreement. Our liquidity may also be supplemented by proceeds from sales of non-strategic assets or issuances of debt or equity securities in public or private transactions. We may also access the commercial paper market from time to time to support short-term liquidity needs. We believe our sources of liquidity are sufficient to fund our planned capital expenditures, debt service obligations, dividend payments and share repurchases, if any, for the next 12 months and, based on current expectations, for the longer term.

Our working capital is substantially influenced by the variables that impact our cash flows from operating activities, primarily realized commodity prices, sales volumes, operating expenses and other costs. Changes in these variables, as well as timing of cash receipts and disbursements, may cause our working capital to vary significantly from period to period. We expect to fund our working capital requirements primarily from cash on hand and cash provided by operating activities, supplemented by our revolving credit agreement, if necessary.

As of December 31, 2024, we had no borrowings outstanding under our revolving credit agreement and had $3.0 billion of borrowing capacity available. In January 2025, we borrowed $1.0 billion under the term loan to fund a portion of the cash consideration for the acquisition of PDC Energy, Inc. We subsequently repaid the $1.0 billion term loan in full in February 2025. See Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements under the captions “Acquisitions” and “Long-Term Debt and Credit Agreements” for additional information.

We regularly review our capital structure and consider the costs and benefits of various financing alternatives, including the issuance or repurchase of equity or debt securities, amendments to our credit facilities, or other transactions to optimize our capital structure. Future transactions could include debt refinancing, additional borrowing capacity, extension of maturities or changes in covenants, depending on market conditions and our operational needs.

Our revolving credit agreement and term loan include a covenant that requires us to maintain a minimum current ratio of 1.0 to 1.0, as defined in the agreements. We were in compliance with this covenant as of December 31, 2024 and March 31, 2025. Failure to comply with this covenant or other covenants contained in our credit agreements could result in an event of default, which, if not cured or waived, could accelerate the repayment of our outstanding indebtedness under the agreements and may adversely affect our financial condition.

We may from time to time seek to retire or purchase our outstanding debt through cash purchases, open market repurchases, redemptions, exchanges, tender offers or otherwise.

Our primary sources of liquidity are cash on hand, net cash provided by operating activities and available borrowing capacity under our revolving credit agreement. Our liquidity may be supplemented by proceeds from sales of non-strategic assets or issuances of debt or equity securities in public or private transactions. Our ability to access capital markets on favorable terms, or at all, may be limited by factors beyond our control, including general market conditions, economic conditions, competition, regulatory changes and other factors.

Our working capital is substantially influenced by the variables that impact our cash flows from operating activities. We expect to fund our working capital requirements primarily from cash on hand and cash provided by operating activities, supplemented by our revolving credit agreement, if necessary. We believe our sources of liquidity are sufficient to fund our planned capital expenditures, debt service obligations, dividend payments and share repurchases, if any, over the next 12 months and, based on current expectations, for the longer term.

Capital and Exploration Expenditures

Our capital program is designed to be flexible and is adjusted based on commodity price expectations, drilling results and other factors. We allocate capital among our operating areas based on expected returns, capital efficiency, infrastructure availability and other considerations. For 2025, our capital expenditures are expected to be focused primarily on development activities in the Permian Basin, Marcellus Shale and Anadarko Basin, with a smaller allocation for exploration and other activities. We expect to fund our 2025 capital program with cash on hand and cash provided by operating activities. We believe our capital program will enable us to efficiently develop our resource base, maintain operational flexibility and deliver long-term value to our stockholders.

We continue to monitor market conditions and may adjust our capital program based on changes in commodity prices, service costs, supply chain dynamics and other factors. Additionally, we may pursue acquisitions or divestitures of assets to optimize our portfolio, enhance capital efficiency and improve returns. We consider a variety of factors when evaluating potential acquisitions and divestitures, including strategic fit, expected returns, impact on our balance sheet and alignment with our long-term strategy.

We also allocate a portion of our capital to infrastructure and other projects that support our operations, including gathering systems, compression, water handling and disposal facilities. These investments are intended to increase operational efficiency, reduce costs and improve reliability. We continue to evaluate opportunities to deploy capital in a manner that enhances our operational performance and aligns with our sustainability objectives.

We may also consider returning additional capital to stockholders through dividends and share repurchases, subject to market conditions, cash flow and other considerations. The declaration, payment and amounts of future dividends, and the authorization and amounts of any share repurchases, are at the discretion of our Board of Directors and depend on a number of factors, including our financial condition, results of operations, cash requirements, restrictions under our debt agreements, business prospects and other factors that our Board of Directors may deem relevant.

We believe our liquidity position, together with our expected cash flows from operations and available borrowing capacity under our revolving credit agreement, provide us with sufficient financial resources to execute our business strategy, meet our obligations as they come due and return capital to our stockholders, while maintaining financial flexibility to respond to changing market conditions.

 Capital Program Outlook

We expect to deploy capital to projects that are expected to generate attractive returns at current commodity prices. Our business strategy is focused on delivering a consistently competitive shareholder return through a combination of disciplined capital allocation, innovation, and a continued focus on safety and environmental stewardship. Market Conditions and Commodity Prices
Our financial results depend on many factors, particularly commodity prices and our ability to find, develop and market our production on economically attractive terms. Commodity prices are affected by many factors outside of our control,

including changes in market supply and demand, which can be impacted by pipeline capacity constraints, inventory storage levels, basis differentials, weather conditions, and geopolitical, economic and other factors.

Oil prices were relatively steady in 2024 compared to 2023 as demand has continued for oil supply. Following global conflict and supply chain disruptions that drove high oil prices in 2022, OPEC+ reacted with supply reductions which helped to stabilize oil price levels in 2023. U.S. oil production was relatively flat from 2023 to 2024, which, when combined with OPEC+’s reductions, contributed to relatively steadier oil prices in 2023 and 2024. Additionally, while OPEC+ previously announced gradually increasing oil production over the course of 2025, several key members of OPEC+ have indicated their intent to delay such increases until the second half of 2025 and into 2026.

Natural gas prices trended down in 2024 compared to 2023 as strong production and relatively weak demand drove inventory levels above the five-year average. While natural gas prices have recovered from their lows in early 2024, natural gas prices in 2024 still trended lower overall compared to 2023. In response to the weakness of natural gas prices, we reduced our capital expenditures in the Marcellus Shale and also strategically curtailed our natural gas production in the basin from August 2024 through November 2024, resulting in an estimated curtailment of 232 MMcf per day of net production during that period. Natural gas prices increased slightly during the last quarter of 2024 and so far have continued to increase into early 2025 due to, among other factors, colder temperatures resulting in increased seasonal demand. Meanwhile, basis differentials became more divergent in 2024, in part due to constrained pipeline capacity and oversupply in certain geographic areas, and at times have resulted in negative spot market pricing for natural gas during 2024, such as the Waha Hub in the Permian Basin. While such issues have abated so far in 2025 in part due to the opening of the Matterhorn Express Pipeline in the fourth quarter of 2024, basis differentials may increase in magnitude again in 2025 due to a variety of factors we cannot predict. Looking to 2025, forward pricing indicates the recent increase in natural gas prices overall is expected to continue through the remainder of 2025, partially as a result of, among other factors, an expected increase in demand driven by LNG exports. However, LNG exports may be impacted by retaliatory tariffs (including China’s recently announced LNG tariffs), which could reduce the expected demand for LNG in 2025. Nevertheless, we expect natural gas prices overall to be stronger in 2025 compared to 2024.

Although the current outlook on oil and natural gas prices is generally favorable and our operations have not been significantly impacted in the short-term, in the event further disruptions occur and continue for an extended period of time, our operations could be adversely impacted, commodity prices could decline, and our costs may increase. We expect commodity price volatility to continue, including as a result of conflicts in the Middle East, actions of OPEC+ (including the ability of OPEC+ to successfully coordinate production quotas), and potentially swift near- and medium-term fluctuations in supply and demand. While we are unable to predict future commodity prices, at current oil, natural gas and NGL price levels, we do not believe that an impairment of our oil and gas properties is reasonably likely to occur in the near future. However, in the event that commodity prices significantly decline or costs significantly increase from current levels, our management would evaluate the recoverability of the carrying value of our oil and gas properties.

In addition, the issue of, and increasing political and social attention on, climate change has resulted in both existing and pending national, regional and local legislation and regulatory measures, such as mandates for renewable energy and emissions reductions. Changes in these laws or regulations may result in delays or restrictions in permitting and the development of projects, may result in increased costs and may impair our ability to move forward with our construction, completions, drilling, water management, waste handling, storage, transport and remediation activities, or may result in renewable energy alternatives that become more competitive with traditional oil and natural gas-derived products (including government subsidies and incentives for electric vehicles), any of which could have an adverse effect on our financial results.

question: BS impact if FCM used instead of SEM?
answer: If CTRA had applied the Full Cost Method (FCM) instead of the Successful Efforts Method (SEM), its balance sheet would likely show higher PP&E, retained earnings, and stockholders’ equity, along with a larger deferred tax liability. The key driver is that under FCM all exploration costs (including unsuccessful wells) are capitalized, whereas under SEM they are expensed. In short, FCM makes the balance sheet look stronger, but the difference is largely a matter of accounting presentation rather than underlying cash flow or economic value.

Depletion of our producing properties is computed on a field basis using the units-of-production method based on estimated proved developed reserves. The economic life of each producing property depends upon the extent to which reserves can be economically produced and is determined by the reserve engineers in accordance with SEC rules and regulations. Our depletion rate is highly dependent upon the estimate of proved reserves and proved developed reserves, which can change based on revisions to those estimates. We follow the successful efforts method of accounting. The economic life of each producing property depends upon the extent to which reserves can be economically produced and is determined by the reserve engineers in accordance with SEC rules and regulations. As such, the level of oil and natural gas prices impacts the anticipated production of reserves and can impact the economic life of each producing property. Higher prices generally have the effect of extending the economic lives of the properties and increasing proved reserves, which reduces depletion expense. Conversely, lower prices generally have the effect of shortening the economic lives of the properties and decreasing proved reserves, which increases depletion expense.

The successful efforts method includes expensing geological and geophysical costs as incurred and expensing costs of unsuccessful exploratory wells. Exploratory well costs are capitalized pending determination of whether the well has found proved reserves. If proved reserves are not found, the exploratory well costs are expensed. Costs to acquire proved and unproved properties are capitalized when incurred. The costs of development wells, including the costs to drill and equip development wells and the costs to install production facilities, are capitalized. Gains or losses on sales of properties are included in earnings.

Impairment of long-lived assets is evaluated when events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the asset may not be recoverable. For proved oil and gas properties, impairment is assessed on a field-by-field basis by comparing the carrying amount of the asset group to the undiscounted future net cash flows expected to be generated by the asset group. If the carrying amount exceeds the sum of the undiscounted future net cash flows, an impairment loss is recognized for the amount by which the carrying amount exceeds the fair value of the asset group. Fair value is estimated using assumptions that market participants would use in pricing the asset, including commodity prices, reserves quantities, expected production, operating costs and discount rates. For unproved properties, impairment is assessed periodically based on the Company’s plans for the properties, the results of exploration activities, the terms of the leases and other relevant factors. Unproved properties that are individually significant are assessed individually for impairment, while the remainder are assessed in the aggregate.

Oil and Gas Properties

The Company uses the successful efforts method of accounting for its oil and gas producing activities. Under this method, acquisition costs for proved and unproved properties, costs of successful exploration wells and development wells, and equipment and facilities costs are capitalized. Geological and geophysical costs, including seismic costs, and the costs of unsuccessful exploration wells are expensed as incurred. The costs of carrying and retaining unproved properties are also expensed as incurred. Costs of exploratory wells are capitalized pending the determination of whether proved reserves have been found. If proved reserves are not found, exploratory well costs are expensed. If an exploratory well is determined to be successful, the costs of drilling the exploratory well are reclassified to proved properties.

Exploratory drilling costs are capitalized when incurred pending determination of whether the well has found proved reserves. The determination is based on information obtained during the drilling process and upon completion of sufficient testing and evaluation, including, where applicable, the drilling of additional exploratory wells. The Company relies on interpretations of available geologic, geophysical and engineering data. If a well is determined to be successful, the costs are reclassified to proved properties and depleted on a units-of-production basis. If an exploratory well finds reserves that cannot be classified as proved at the end of the reporting period, the well is considered to be suspended and the related costs continue to be capitalized if certain criteria are met, including whether there is sufficient progress assessing the reserves and if additional exploratory drilling is planned. If the Company cannot justify the continued capitalization of suspended exploratory well costs, the costs are expensed.

Development costs include the costs to drill and equip development wells, including those to access proved reserves and to provide facilities for the extraction, treatment, gathering and storage of oil and gas, and are capitalized. Depreciation, depletion and amortization of capitalized costs of proved oil and gas properties are calculated using the units-of-production method based on the ratio of current period production to estimated total proved reserves. Successful Efforts Method of Accounting and Classification

We utilize the successful efforts method of accounting for our oil and gas exploration and development activities. Under this method, acquisition costs for proved and unproved properties, costs of successful exploration wells and development wells, and equipment and facilities costs are capitalized. Geological and geophysical costs and costs of unsuccessful exploration wells are expensed as incurred. Exploratory well costs are initially capitalized but are charged to expense if the well is determined to be unsuccessful. If an exploratory well finds reserves that cannot be classified as proved at the end of the reporting period, the costs may continue to be capitalized as long as certain criteria are met, including the intent to continue exploration or evaluation of the discovery and the availability of sufficient evidence that the reserves are likely to be proved in the future.

Property acquisition costs include costs to purchase or lease mineral rights. Costs to acquire proved properties are amortized on a unit-of-production basis over the life of the proved reserves of the properties. Costs to acquire unproved properties are assessed periodically to determine whether they have been impaired or have reached the end of their useful lives. When unproved properties are determined to be impaired, the costs are charged to expense. If the properties are subsequently developed and reserves are proved, the costs are reclassified to proved properties and amortized accordingly.

Development costs include the costs of development wells and related equipment and facilities, including costs to access proved reserves and to provide facilities for the extraction, treatment, gathering and storage of oil and gas. Development costs are capitalized and amortized on a unit-of-production basis over the life of the proved developed reserves.

Depreciation, depletion and amortization (DD&A) of capitalized costs of proved properties are calculated using the unit-of-production method based on the ratio of current period production to estimated total proved reserves. The estimates of proved reserves are revised periodically as additional information becomes available as a result of continued exploration and development activities and production history. Changes in proved reserves estimates may result in significant changes to DD&A expense.

Impairment of oil and gas properties is evaluated when events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts of the properties may not be recoverable. For proved properties, impairment is assessed on a field-by-field basis by comparing the carrying amount of the asset group to the undiscounted future net cash flows expected to be generated by the asset group. If the carrying amount exceeds the sum of the undiscounted future net cash flows, an impairment loss is recognized for the amount by which the carrying amount exceeds the fair value of the asset group. Fair value is estimated based on assumptions that market participants would use in pricing the asset, such as commodity prices, reserves quantities, expected production, operating costs and discount rates.

For unproved properties, impairment is assessed periodically based on the Company’s plans for the properties, the results of exploration activities, the terms of the leases and other relevant factors. Unproved properties that are individually significant are assessed individually for impairment, while the remainder are assessed in the aggregate.

Oil and Gas Operations. EOG accounts for its crude oil and natural gas exploration and production activities under the successful efforts method of accounting. Acquisition costs for proved and unproved properties, costs of successful exploratory wells and development wells and the costs of acquiring support equipment and facilities are capitalized. Geological and geophysical costs, including seismic costs, and the costs of unsuccessful exploratory wells are expensed as incurred. Depreciation, depletion and amortization (DD&A) of capitalized costs of proved properties are computed using the units-of-production method based on estimated proved reserves. EOG evaluates its oil and gas properties for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts may not be recoverable. If the carrying amount exceeds the sum of the undiscounted future net cash flows expected to be generated by the properties, an impairment loss is recognized for the amount by which the carrying amount exceeds the fair value of the properties. If an exploratory well finds reserves that cannot be classified as proved at the end of the reporting period, the well is considered to be suspended and related costs continue to be capitalized as long as certain criteria are met, including whether there is sufficient progress assessing the reserves.

Oil and gas lease acquisition costs are capitalized when incurred and are amortized over the expected economic life or reclassified to proved properties when proved reserves are discovered. Unproved leasehold costs with individually significant acquisition costs are assessed individually for impairment and those with not individually significant acquisition costs are assessed on an aggregate basis by major geographical cost centers. When EOG determines that unproved properties are impaired or the leases have expired, the related costs are charged to expense. When proved reserves are discovered, the related costs are transferred to proved oil and gas properties.

EOG capitalizes interest on expenditures for significant investments in unproved properties and on the construction of facilities. Capitalized interest is included in the carrying amount of the related assets and is amortized over the assets’ useful lives. EOG also capitalizes certain internal costs that are directly related to acquisition, exploration and development activities. Maintenance and repairs are charged to expense as incurred, while renewals and betterments that extend the useful lives of assets are capitalized.

Item 1 C. Cybersecurity We maintain a corporate information security program (the “Program”) designed to identify, assess, manage, and mitigate material risks resulting from cybersecurity threats. The Program is a component of our overall enterprise risk management framework and is reasonably designed, based on our business operations, to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of our key systems and data. The Program incorporates measures and processes designed to address prevention, detection, mitigation and remediation of cybersecurity incidents and threats and to facilitate the prompt diagnosis, triage and response to any suspected or confirmed cybersecurity incident. We have implemented administrative, technical, and physical safeguards designed to protect against and detect cybersecurity threats and vulnerabilities, including multi-factor authentication, periodic access reviews and controls targeted to protect our networks and information systems. We also provide periodic employee and contractor cybersecurity training and awareness programs to help ensure understanding and to reduce risks related to cybersecurity, including phishing simulations. We have made efforts to align the Program with industry standards and best practices and it is designed to scale to address emerging requirements across the Company’s business as needed. The Program is administered by our Digital Security Office (“DSO”). The team that supports the Program is composed of personnel with a mix of professional certifications and industry experience. We periodically engage third-party cybersecurity assessment and testing specialists to assess our overall capabilities and to perform and report results of testing of our cybersecurity controls, including periodic testing of our incident response.

Cybersecurity Risk Management and Strategy Our cybersecurity risk management and strategy processes have been developed based on industry standards and best practices within our industry and are designed to identify, assess, manage, and mitigate material risks from cybersecurity threats. The processes are intended to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of our information systems and the data residing on those systems. Our information technology (“IT”) systems are comprised of a mixture of Company-hosted applications and third-party cloud services. The Program includes processes designed to identify and assess threats from external influencers, and from potential internal impacts relating to user misuse or technology failure. These processes are designed to rapidly detect and triage cybersecurity incidents, evaluate the severity of threats, assess potential system impacts, and escalate potential issues as appropriate. The Program includes periodic testing of preventative and detective security controls and we regularly conduct tabletop exercises. We supplement these internal efforts by periodically engaging third-party specialist firms to conduct independent cybersecurity controls assessments, security penetration testing and to assist in our ongoing monitoring, detection and remediation efforts. Our security team maintains and periodically reviews the asset inventory of critical information systems and evaluates risks presented by third-party suppliers, vendors and other entities in our supply chains.

Cybersecurity Governance Our Board of Directors has oversight responsibility for Company risk management, with the Audit Committee having primary responsibility for risk management oversight generally, including cybersecurity. Our Audit Committee receives periodic updates from the Company’s Digital Security Office regarding policies, activities and incident monitoring and response. The DSO organization is led by a member of our management team, the Head of Digital Security, who reports to our Chief Information Officer. The Head of Digital Security is supported by our DSO’s management team, which includes individuals with deep experience in IT and cybersecurity from prior and current roles and the team has a variety of relevant professional certifications. On at least an annual basis, our Board receives a presentation from the DSO summarizing enterprise risk management, compliance with Company policies, cyber risk trends, evolving cybersecurity threats and vulnerability monitoring and response activities. The DSO has established processes for prompt reporting and escalation to management of material cybersecurity threats and incidents and, to our Board when appropriate. We maintain cybersecurity insurance covering costs and liabilities associated with cybersecurity events; however, this insurance may not be adequate to cover all costs, expenses or losses from such events.

24

The Program also includes documenting and communicating to all personnel the procedures for reporting an actual or suspected cybersecurity incident. We proactively monitor against the threat of ransomware and maintain process controls designed to mitigate threats. We recognize that cyber and technology security risks are constantly evolving and seek to update the Program to address new and emerging threats and to minimize potential exposure. 

25

In the normal course of business, we transmit and receive information by electronic means and rely on third-party service providers to help manage and improve our access to networks, systems and cloud-based platforms along with the applications that support the organization with critical business operations. Such service providers could be the subject of a cyberattack, which may affect our information security. The Company has designed processes and procedures to maintain and update awareness relating to third-party service providers and to evaluate known or suspected security incidents at a third party and any impact upon the Company. Maintaining cybersecurity and safeguarding IT systems requires constant vigilance by the Company and its service providers. When we are affected by known or suspected cybersecurity incidents, we follow a consistent reporting and escalation process to our DSO in accordance with our IRP.

Critical Audit Matters
The critical audit matter communicated below is a matter arising from the current period audit of the consolidated financial statements that was communicated or required to be communicated to the audit committee and that (i) relates to accounts or disclosures that are material to the consolidated financial statements and (ii) involved our especially challenging, subjective, or complex judgments. The communication of critical audit matters does not alter in any way our opinion on the consolidated financial statements, taken as a whole, and we are not, by communicating the critical audit matter below, providing a separate opinion on the critical audit matter or on the accounts or disclosures to which it relates.

The Impact of Proved Developed Oil and Natural Gas Reserves on Proved Oil and Gas Properties, Net

As described in Notes 1 and 3 to the consolidated financial statements, a significant portion of the Company’s properties and equipment, net balance of $17,890 million as of December 31, 2024 and depreciation, depletion and amortization (DD&A) expense of $1,840 million for the year ended December 31, 2024 relate to proved oil and gas properties. The Company uses the successful efforts method of accounting for its oil and gas producing activities. As disclosed by management, the Company’s rate of recording DD&A expense is dependent upon the estimate of proved reserves and proved developed reserves, which are utilized in the unit-of-production calculation. In estimating proved oil and natural gas reserves, management relies on interpretations and judgment of available geological, geophysical, engineering and production data, as well as the use of certain economic assumptions such as commodity prices. Additional assumptions include drilling and operating expenses, capital expenditures, taxes and availability of funds. The estimates of proved oil and natural gas reserves have been developed by specialists, specifically petroleum engineers.

The principal considerations for our determination that performing procedures relating to the impact of proved developed oil and natural gas reserves on proved oil and gas properties, net is a critical audit matter are (i) the significant judgment by management, including the use of specialists, when developing the estimates of proved developed oil and natural gas reserves, which in turn led to (ii) a high degree of auditor judgment, subjectivity, and effort in performing procedures and evaluating audit evidence related to data, methods, and assumptions used by management and its specialists in developing the estimates of proved developed oil and natural gas reserves.

Addressing the matter involved performing procedures and evaluating audit evidence in connection with forming our overall opinion on the consolidated financial statements. These procedures included testing the effectiveness of controls relating to management’s estimates of proved developed oil and natural gas reserves. The work of management’s specialists was used in performing the procedures to evaluate the reasonableness of the proved developed oil and natural gas reserves. As a basis for using this work, the specialists’ qualifications were understood and the Company’s relationship with the specialists was assessed. The procedures performed also included evaluating the methods and assumptions used by the specialists, testing the completeness and accuracy of data used by the specialists, and evaluating the specialists’ findings.

/s/ PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP

Houston, Texas

February 25, 2025

We have served as the Company’s auditor since 1989.

Critical Accounting Estimates
The preparation of financial statements in conformity with GAAP requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities, the reported amounts of revenues and expenses, and certain disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities. The estimates and assumptions are based on historical experience, the best available information at the time and other factors, which management believes are reasonable under the circumstances. We evaluate these estimates and assumptions on an ongoing basis and may retain outside consultants, including engineers, to assist in our evaluation. However, future events and their effects cannot be determined with certainty. Therefore, actual results could differ materially from these estimates. We have identified the following as our most critical estimates that involve judgement of management.

Successful Efforts Method of Accounting

We follow the successful efforts method of accounting for our oil and gas operations. Under this method, all property acquisition costs and costs of exploratory and development wells are capitalized until a determination is made that the well has either discovered proved reserves or proved reserves cannot be obtained that justify completion as a producing well. If an exploratory well is determined to be unsuccessful, the well costs are expensed as exploration expense and all other costs are capitalized as oil and gas properties. Costs incurred in connection with development drilling are capitalized and are included in the amortization base.

Costs of internally developed software for information technology systems that provide a competitive advantage or substantial efficiency gains are capitalized during the application development stage and amortized over the expected useful life of the software. Costs incurred in the preliminary project and post-implementation/operation stages of an IT project are expensed as incurred.

Oil and Gas Reserves

Proved oil and gas reserves are the estimated quantities of oil and gas that geologic and engineering data demonstrates with reasonable certainty to be recoverable in future years from known reservoirs under existing economic and operating conditions. Proved reserve estimates are critical to the determination of depletion and impairment of oil and gas properties. Proved reserve estimates are prepared by our internal and/or independent petroleum engineers and are based on various assumptions and estimates including, but not limited to, geological and engineering data, projected future rates of production, the timing and amount of future capital expenditures, the economic life of the properties, the expected prices and costs to produce and expected operational efficiencies. The estimation of proved reserves is sensitive to the inputs used in the reserve estimation process. Accordingly, the determination of these reserves requires significant estimates that may be revised in the future as additional information becomes available.

Depletion and Depreciation

The provision for depletion and depreciation of oil and gas properties is determined on the basis of estimates of proved developed oil and gas reserves. In addition, costs associated with proved undeveloped reserves are depleted on the basis of total proved reserves. Equipment and facilities are depreciated on the straight-line method over their estimated useful lives. Determination of capitalization, useful lives and salvage values are based on estimates of the period that assets will be utilized in operations. Changes in useful lives or salvage values could have a material effect on our depletion and depreciation expense.

Impairment of Long-Lived Assets

We review our oil and gas properties for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of such properties may not be recoverable. A long-lived asset is considered impaired when the carrying amount of the asset exceeds the sum of the undiscounted expected future cash flows, based on our estimates and assumptions. The amount of impairment recognized is measured as the excess of the carrying amount over the fair value of the asset. Fair value is estimated using discounted future cash flows or recent comparable transactions. The estimates and assumptions used to determine whether impairment has occurred and to calculate the amount of impairment include, but are not limited to, estimates of future commodity prices and costs, timing and amount of future production, assumed production decline curves, discount rates and the probability that any one scenario may occur. Because these variables are derived from, or tied to, estimates of future performance and economic conditions, an impairment determination is subject to a high degree of uncertainty and variability. We did not record any impairment of our proved oil and gas properties during the periods presented; however, changes in the factors used to assess impairment in the future could result in impairment charges.

Asset Retirement Obligations

We record the fair value of asset retirement obligations associated with tangible long-lived assets, such as oil and gas wells, in the period in which the obligations are incurred. The fair value of the obligation is measured using expected future cash outflows, discounted at our credit-adjusted risk-free rate. The associated asset retirement cost is capitalized as part of the carrying amount of the related long-lived asset and is depreciated over the asset’s useful life. The asset retirement obligation is accreted to its then-present value each period, and the associated accretion expense is recognized in the Consolidated Statements of Operations. Estimating the future asset retirement obligations requires significant judgment, including the timing of retirement activities, estimated costs to perform the activities and the credit-adjusted risk-free rate. Changes in estimates regarding our future asset retirement obligations could have a material impact on the amounts recorded for asset retirement obligations and related assets.

Income Taxes

We account for income taxes using the asset and liability method. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are recognized for temporary differences between the financial statement and tax bases of assets and liabilities using enacted tax rates expected to apply to taxable income in the years in which the temporary differences are expected to reverse. Valuation allowances are recorded to reduce deferred tax assets to the amount that will more likely than not be realized. The amount of valuation allowance required is based on our estimates regarding our future taxable income and the timing and character of future sources of taxable income. Changes in our estimates may require increases or decreases to our valuation allowance, which could have a material impact on our results of operations and financial position.

Revenue Recognition

We recognize revenue from the sale of oil, natural gas and NGLs when control of the product passes to the customer, which is typically at the delivery point specified in the contract and when collectability is reasonably assured. We allocate the transaction price to each performance obligation in the contract based on the relative standalone selling price of each performance obligation. Variable consideration, such as price differentials, quality adjustments and transportation costs, is estimated and included in the transaction price to the extent that it is probable that a significant reversal of cumulative revenue recognized will not occur when the uncertainty is resolved. Estimating variable consideration requires judgment and consideration of current and historical facts and circumstances. We routinely review contracts and estimates of variable consideration and adjust revenue accordingly.

Hedging Activities

We may use derivative financial instruments to manage our exposure to commodity price risk. We recognize all derivatives on the balance sheet at fair value. Changes in the fair value of derivatives that are not designated as accounting hedges are recognized in earnings. The fair value of derivatives is based on quoted market prices, where available, or on other valuation techniques that are subject to assumptions and estimates. The use of different assumptions and estimates could have a material effect on the reported fair values of derivatives and related gains and losses recognized in earnings.

2. Acquisitions
Franklin Mountain Energy (“FME”) Acquisition

On January 27, 2025, the Company closed on its acquisition of all of the issued and outstanding membership interests of certain subsidiaries of FME (the “FME Acquisition”). Pursuant to the Membership Interest Purchase Agreement, dated November 2, 2024, by and among Coterra and certain members of FME (the “FME Sellers”), Coterra acquired certain oil and gas properties and related assets located in the Delaware Basin in New Mexico and Texas from the FME Sellers, for total consideration consisting of $1.85 billion in cash and the issuance of 28,190,682 shares of our common stock. The cash consideration of $1.85 billion was funded through a combination of cash on hand and borrowings under the Company’s revolving credit facility.

Avant Acquisition

In January 2025, we closed on the acquisition of certain interests in oil and gas properties and related assets from Avant Operating, LLC (“Avant”), for total consideration consisting of $1.5 billion, subject to certain post-closing adjustments. The Avant acquisition included proved and unproved properties in the Permian Basin and related midstream assets.

Cimarex Merger

On October 1, 2021, we completed a merger transaction (the “Merger”) with Cimarex Energy Co. (“Cimarex”), pursuant to the Agreement and Plan of Merger, dated as of May 23, 2021, by and among Cabot Oil & Gas Corporation (“Cabot”), Double C Merger Sub, Inc., a wholly owned subsidiary of Cabot, and Cimarex. At the effective time of the Merger, each share of Cimarex common stock was converted into the right to receive 4.0146 shares of Cabot common stock. Following the Merger, Cabot changed its name to Coterra Energy Inc. The Merger was accounted for as a reverse acquisition under ASC 805, with Cimarex being treated as the acquirer for accounting purposes. The Merger resulted in a step-up in basis of the acquired assets and liabilities to their estimated fair values as of the acquisition date.

Preliminary Purchase Price Allocation

The transaction was accounted for using the acquisition method of accounting. The preliminary allocation of the purchase price for the FME Acquisition is based on provisional estimates and assumptions that are subject to change as we finalize the valuation of assets acquired and liabilities assumed. The fair values assigned to the assets acquired and liabilities assumed were based on estimates and assumptions based on information available as of the acquisition date. We expect to finalize the allocation of the purchase price as soon as practicable but no later than one year from the acquisition date.

The valuation of certain tangible assets was based on replacement cost and market comparables. The fair value measurements were based on significant inputs that are not observable in the market and thus represent Level 3 measurements under ASC 820.

Transaction Costs

We incurred transaction costs, including advisory, legal, accounting and other professional fees, related to the FME Acquisition and the Avant acquisition, which are included in “general and administrative expense” in our Consolidated Statements of Operations for the three months ended March 31, 2025. Critical Audit Matter
Proved Oil and Gas Properties and Depletion — Crude Oil, NGL and Natural Gas Reserves — Refer to Note 1 to the Financial Statements

Critical Audit Matter Description

The Company’s proved oil and gas properties are depleted using the units-of-production method based on estimates of proved developed reserves for most wells and field level reserves for other assets. The Company’s crude oil, NGL and natural gas reserves are estimated by Company engineers. The estimation of reserves requires management to make significant assumptions and judgments related to forecasted production volumes and costs, forecasted commodity prices, timing and amount of future development activity, and the interpretation of geological and engineering data. Changes in proved reserves can have a significant impact on depletion expense and the carrying value of proved properties. Given the significant judgments made by management to estimate reserves and the potential for changes in reserves to have a significant effect on the financial statements, auditing estimates of reserves involved a high degree of auditor judgment and an increased extent of effort, including the involvement of our specialists.

How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit

Our audit procedures related to the estimation of the Company’s proved reserves and the impact of those estimates on depletion expense included the following, among others:

• We evaluated the effectiveness of controls over the Company’s process to estimate reserves, including management’s controls over the completeness and accuracy of the underlying data and the review of significant assumptions.

• With the assistance of our internal engineering specialists, we evaluated the Company’s proved reserve estimates and the significant assumptions used by management by:

— Testing the completeness and accuracy of data inputs used in reserve estimates, including historical production volumes and realized prices.

— Comparing the Company’s historical estimates of proved reserves to actual production results to assess the historical accuracy of the Company’s reserve estimates.

— Evaluating the reasonableness of forecasted commodity prices by comparing them to independent market data.

— Evaluating the reasonableness of forecasted development and operating costs by comparing them to historical costs and budgets.

— Assessing the reasonableness of the Company’s future development plans by comparing them to historical development activities and capital budgets.

• We tested the mathematical accuracy of the Company’s depletion calculations, including the units-of-production rates, and assessed the consistency of the methods and assumptions used in the calculations.

• We evaluated the adequacy of the Company’s disclosures related to proved reserves and depletion in the financial statements.

Standardized Measure of Discounted Future Net Cash Flows Relating to Proved Oil and Gas Reserves

The following information has been developed based on oil and natural gas reserve and production volumes estimated by independent petroleum engineers and is presented in accordance with the requirements of the Financial Accounting Standards Board and the SEC. The Standardized Measure does not purport to present the fair value of the Company’s oil and gas reserves. An estimate of fair value would also consider, among other things, the recovery of reserves in future years at prices other than those required by the SEC, as well as the timing and quantity of future production, the effect of future changes in commodity prices, the effect of future costs, changes in tax rates, and the risk that future development may differ from the proved properties disclosed herein. As such, the Standardized Measure should not be viewed as representative of the current value of the Company.

The Company believes that the following factors should be taken into account when reviewing the following information:

• Future costs and selling prices will differ from those required to be used in these calculations.

• Due to future market conditions and governmental regulations, there may be increases or decreases in currently established prices that could significantly affect the estimates based on current conditions.

• The rates of production may vary significantly from the rate of production assumed in the calculations.

• Selection of a 10 percent discount rate is arbitrary and may not be indicative of the risks that are part of realizing future net oil and gas revenues.

• Future net revenues may be subject to different rates of income taxation.

Under the Standardized Measure, future cash inflows were estimated by applying the trailing 12-month average index price for the respective products (determined as an unweighted arithmetic average of the first-day-of-the-month price for each month within the 12-month period prior to the end of the reporting period) to the year-end quantities of estimated proved reserves. Future development and production costs, including transportation and marketing costs, were estimated based on the Company’s internal estimates and historical experience and were assumed to be constant in today’s dollars. Estimated future income taxes were computed by applying the appropriate year-end statutory tax rates, with consideration for the effects of tax credits and allowances. The future net cash flows after income taxes were then discounted at 10 percent per annum to arrive at the Standardized Measure.

The following table sets forth the changes in the Standardized Measure of discounted future net cash flows relating to proved oil and natural gas reserves for the years indicated (in millions):

| Changes in Standardized Measure | | 2024 | | 2023 | |
|:--------------------------------|:----|-----:|:--|-----:|:--|
| Sales of oil and gas produced, net of production costs | | | | | |
| Net changes in prices and production costs | | | | | |
| Extensions, discoveries and improved recovery | | | | | |
| Revisions of previous quantity estimates | | | | | |
| Purchases and sales of minerals in place | | | | | |
| Accretion of discount | | | | | |
| Changes in future development costs | | | | | |
| Net change in income taxes | | | | | |
| Net change | | | | | |

Management cautions that the Standardized Measure is not a realistic assessment of the value of the Company’s proved reserves. It is based on assumptions that are prescribed by the FASB and the SEC that do not reflect the risks inherent in reserve estimates or the expected cash flows from future production. The Standardized Measure should be considered in conjunction with information contained in the financial statements and related notes, including the disclosures regarding proved reserves, changes in proved reserves and the Company’s policies for estimating reserves.
