Allowance for Credit Losses

The Company records an allowance for credit losses based on the Company’s estimate of future expected credit losses on outstanding receivables.

Inventories

Inventories are primarily comprised of tubular goods and well equipment and commodity inventory, including pipeline imbalances.

Tubular goods and well equipment are carried at average cost and are assessed periodically for obsolescence. Commodity inventories are recorded at actual purchase prices and are adjusted monthly to market prices. Commodity inventories generally turn monthly.

Short-term Investments

The Company’s short-term investments include certificates of deposit with maturities between three months and one year. Certificates of deposit are recorded at cost.

Properties and Equipment

Oil and Gas Properties

The Company uses the successful efforts method of accounting for oil and gas producing activities. Under this method, acquisition costs for proved and unproved properties are capitalized when incurred. Exploration costs, including geological and geophysical costs, the costs of carrying and retaining unproved properties and exploratory dry hole drilling costs, are expensed. Development costs, including the costs to drill and equip development wells and successful exploratory drilling costs to locate proved reserves are capitalized.

Exploratory drilling costs are capitalized when incurred pending the determination of whether a well has found proved reserves. The determination is based on a process which relies on interpretations of available geologic, geophysical and engineering data. If a well is determined to be successful, the capitalized drilling costs will be reclassified as part of the cost of the well. If a well is determined to be unsuccessful, the capitalized drilling costs will be charged to exploration expense in the Consolidated Statement of Operations in the period the determination is made. If an exploratory well requires a major capital expenditure before production can begin, the cost of drilling the exploratory well will continue to be carried as an asset pending determination of whether reserves have been found only as long as: (1) the well has found a sufficient quantity of reserves to justify its completion as a producing well if the required capital expenditure is made and (2) drilling of an additional exploratory well is under way or firmly planned for the near future. If drilling in the area is not under way or firmly planned or if the well has not found a commercially producible quantity of reserves, the exploratory well is assumed to be impaired and its costs are charged to exploration expense.

Development costs of proved oil and gas properties, including estimated dismantlement, restoration and abandonment costs and acquisition costs, are depreciated and depleted on a field basis by the unit-of-production method using both proved developed and proved reserves.

Costs of sold or abandoned properties that make up a part of an amortization base (partial field) remain in the amortization base if the unit-of-production rate is not significantly affected. If significant, a gain or loss, if any, is recognized and the sold or abandoned properties are retired. A gain or loss, if any, is also recognized when a group of proved properties (entire field) that make up the amortization base has been retired, abandoned or sold.

The Company evaluates its proved oil and gas properties for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate an asset’s carrying amount may not be recoverable. The Company compares expected undiscounted future cash flows to the net book value of the asset. If the future undiscounted expected cash flows, based on estimates of future commodity prices, operating costs and anticipated production from proved reserves and risk-adjusted probable and possible reserves, are lower than the net book value of the asset, the capitalized cost is reduced to fair value. Commodity pricing is estimated by using a combination of assumptions management uses in its budgeting and forecasting process as well as historical and current prices adjusted for geographical location and quality differentials, as well as other factors that management believes will impact realizable prices. Fair value is calculated by discounting the future cash flows. The discount factor used is based on rates utilized by market participants that are commensurate with the risks inherent in the development and production of the underlying oil and natural gas.

Unproved oil and gas properties are assessed periodically for impairment on an aggregate basis through periodic updates to the Company’s unproved acreage amortization based on past drilling and exploration experience, the Company’s expectation of converting leases to held by production and average property lives. Average property lives are determined on a geographical basis and based on the estimated life of unproved property leasehold rights.

Fixed Assets

Fixed assets consist primarily of gas gathering systems, water infrastructure, buildings, vehicles, aircraft, furniture and fixtures, and computer equipment and software. These items are recorded at cost and are depreciated on the straight-line method based on expected lives of the individual assets, which range from threeto 30years.

Asset Retirement Obligations

The Company records the fair value of a liability for an asset retirement obligation in the period in which it is incurred if a reasonable estimate of fair value can be made. The associated asset retirement cost is capitalized as part of the carrying amount of the long-lived asset. Asset retirement costs for oil and gas properties are depreciated using the unit-of-production method, while asset retirement costs for other assets are depreciated using the straight-line method over estimated useful lives.

Additional retirement obligations increase the liability associated with new oil and gas wells and other facilities as these obligations are incurred. Accretion expense is included in DD&A expense in the Consolidated Statement of Operations.

Derivative Instruments

The Company enters into financial derivative contracts, primarily collars, swaps and basis swaps, to manage its exposure to price fluctuations on a portion of its anticipated future production volumes. All of the Company’s derivatives are used for risk management purposes and are not held for trading purposes. The Company has elected not to designate its financial derivative instruments as accounting hedges under the accounting guidance.

The Company evaluates all of its physical purchase and sale contracts to determine if they meet the definition of a derivative. For contracts that meet the definition of a derivative, the Company may elect the normal purchase normal sale (“NPNS”) exception provided under the applicable accounting guidance and account for the contract using the accrual method

As used in this calculation, total capitalization represents the sum of total current and long-term debt and total stockholders' equity.

At December 31, 2024, EOG maintained a strong financial and liquidity position, including $7.1 billion of cash and cash equivalents on hand and $1.9 billion of availability under its senior unsecured revolving credit facility (discussed below).

On November 21, 2024, EOG closed on its offering of $1.0 billion aggregate principal amount of its 5.650% Senior Notes due 2054 (the Notes). EOG received net proceeds of $985 million from the issuance of the Notes, which will be used for general corporate purposes, including (i) the repayment of the $500 million aggregate principal amount of 3.15% Senior Notes due 2025 and (ii) the funding of future capital expenditures.

The Internal Revenue Service previously announced tax relief related to 2024 severe weather events occurring in various Texas counties, including Harris County, where EOG's corporate offices are located. The tax relief permitted eligible taxpayers to postpone certain tax filings and payments. In February 2025, EOG paid approximately $700 million of such federal tax payments related to the 2024 tax year.

During 2024, EOG funded $6.7 billion ($109 million of which was non-cash) in exploration and development and other property, plant and equipment expenditures (excluding asset retirement obligations), paid $2.1 billion in dividends to common stockholders and paid $3.2 billion to repurchase shares of common stock, primarily by utilizing net cash provided by its operating activities and cash on hand.

Total anticipated 2025 capital expenditures are estimated to range from approximately $6.0 billion to $6.4 billion, including exploration and development drilling, facilities, leasehold acquisitions, capitalized interest, dry hole costs and other property, plant and equipment and excluding property acquisitions, asset retirement costs, non-cash exchanges and transactions and exploration costs incurred as operating expenses. The majority of 2025 expenditures will be focused on United States crude oil drilling activities. EOG has significant flexibility with respect to financing alternatives, including borrowings under its commercial paper program, bank borrowings, borrowings under its senior unsecured revolving credit facility, joint development agreements and similar agreements and equity and debt offerings.

Management continues to believe EOG has one of the strongest prospect inventories in EOG's history. When it fits EOG's strategy, EOG will make acquisitions that bolster existing drilling programs or offer incremental exploration and/or production opportunities.

Cash Return Framework. In November 2023, EOG announced an increase in its cash return commitment - specifically, a commitment, effective beginning with fiscal year 2024, to return a minimum of 70% of annual net cash provided by operating activities before certain balance sheet-related changes, less total capital expenditures, to stockholders through a combination of quarterly dividends, special dividends and share repurchases. For discussion regarding EOG's payment of dividends and share repurchases, see ITEM 1A, Risk Factors, and ITEM 5, Market for Registrant's Common Equity, Related Stockholder Matters and Issuer Purchases of Equity Securities.

At December 31, 2024, the Company had PUD reserves of 407 MMBoe, down 75 MMBoe, or 15 percent, from 482 MMBoe of PUD reserves at December 31, 2023. Future development plans are reflective of the current commodity price environment and have been established based on expected available cash flows from operations. By the end of 2025, the Company expects to complete substantially all the work necessary to convert its PUD reserves associated with wells that were drilled but uncompleted at December 31, 2024 to proved developed reserves. As of December 31, 2024 all PUD reserves are expected to be drilled and completed within five years of initial disclosure of these reserves. During 2023, the Company invested $1.3 billion to develop and convert 33 percent of its 2022 PUD reserves to proved developed reserves. During 2022, the Company invested $945 million to develop and convert 37 percent of its 2021 PUD reserves to proved developed reserves.

During 2024, the Company’s 155 MMBoe of PUD reserves additions consisted of 90 MMBoe added in the Permian Basin, 37 MMBoe added in the Anadarko Basin and 28 MMBoe added in the Marcellus Shale. At December 31, 2024, 52 percent were in the Permian Basin, 35 percent were in the Marcellus Shale, and the remaining 13 percent were in the Anadarko Basin.

During 2024, the Company had a net negative PUD reserves revision of 28 MMBoe, of which, 33 MMBoe is due to the removal of PUD reserves in the Marcellus Shale whose development is expected to be delayed beyond five years from the initial date of booking due to the Company’s updated development plans, which resulted in changes to the timing of capital investments. This negative revision was partially offset by a 5 MMBoe positive revision to PUD forecasts in the Marcellus Shale and Permian Basin due to better than expected well performance compared to previous proved reserves estimates.

INFORMATION ABOUT OUR EXECUTIVE OFFICERS
The following table shows certain information as of February 25, 2025 about our executive officers, as such term is defined in Rule 3b-7 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. All officers are elected annually by our Board of Directors.

Mr. Jorden was appointed Chief Executive Officer and President of Coterra following the Merger in October 2021 and Chairman of the Board of Coterra in November 2022. Mr. Jorden previously served as the Chief Executive Officer and President of Cimarex beginning September 2011 and as Chairman of the Board of Directors of Cimarex beginning August 2012. At Cimarex, he began serving as Executive Vice President of Exploration when the company formed in 2002. Prior to the formation of Cimarex, Mr. Jorden held multiple leadership roles at Key Production Company, Inc. (“Key”), which was acquired by Cimarex in 2002. He joined Key in 1993 as Chief Geophysicist and subsequently became Executive Vice President of Exploration. Before joining Key, Mr. Jorden served at Union Pacific Resources and Superior Oil Company.

Mr. Young was appointed Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer in July 2023. From 2019 to 2023, Mr. Young served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of Talos Energy Inc. Prior to joining Talos Energy Inc., Mr. Young served in similar positions with Sheridan Production Company, LLC, Cobalt International Energy, Inc. and Talos Energy LLC. Mr. Young served as a Managing Director for the Global Energy Group at Goldman, Sachs & Co. from 2010 to 2014 and was an investment banker at Morgan Stanley from 1998 to 2010.

Mr. Bell was appointed Executive Vice President of Business Development following the Merger in October 2021. At Cimarex, Mr. Bell was appointed Senior Vice President of Business Development and Land in September 2002 and was named Executive Vice President of Business Development in September 2012. Mr. Bell served at Key prior to its acquisition by Cimarex. He joined Key in 1994 as Vice President of Land and was appointed Senior Vice President of Business Development and Land in 1999.

Ms. Alexander was appointed Senior Vice President and Chief Human Resources Officer in July 2023. Ms. Alexander served as Chief People Officer at Rent the Runway from June 2021 to July 2023. Ms. Alexander served in various roles of increasing responsibility, including Associate Partner and Professional Development Manager, at McKinsey & Company, a management consulting company, from 2009 to 2021.

Mr. DeShazer was appointed Senior Vice President of Business Units in May 2024. Mr. DeShazer previously served as Vice President of Business Units following the Merger in October 2021. Mr. DeShazer joined Cimarex in 2007, serving in various engineering and reservoir manager positions, as well as multiple leadership roles, including Technology Group Manager from 2016 to 2018, Asset Evaluation Team Manager from 2018 to 2019 and Vice President of the Permian Business Unit in 2019.

Mr. Sirgo was appointed Senior Vice President of Operations in October 2022. Mr. Sirgo previously served as Vice President of Operations at Coterra from October 1, 2021 to October 1, 2022. Prior to the Merger in October 2021, Mr. Sirgo served in a number of technical and leadership roles since joining Cimarex in 2008, including Vice President of Operations from February 2020 to October 2021, Vice President of Operation Resources from November 2018 to February 2020, Permian Division Production Manager from June 2016 to November 2018, and in various engineering and production manager positions. Before joining Cimarex, Mr. Sirgo worked at Occidental Petroleum.

Changes in Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

There was no change in the Company’s internal control over financial reporting during the three months ended March 31, 2025 that has materially affected, or is reasonably likely to materially affect, the Company’s internal control over financial reporting.

Limitations on the Effectiveness of Controls

The Company does not expect that our disclosure controls and procedures or internal control over financial reporting will prevent all errors and all fraud. The design of a control system must reflect the fact that there are resource constraints, and the benefits of controls must be considered relative to their costs. Because of the inherent limitations in all control systems, no control system can provide absolute assurance that all control issues and instances of fraud, if any, within the Company have been detected. These inherent limitations include the realities that judgments in decision-making can be faulty and that breakdowns can occur because of simple error or mistake. Additionally, controls can be circumvented by the individual acts of some persons, by the collusion of two or more persons or by management override of the controls. The design of any system of controls is based in part upon certain assumptions about the likelihood of future events, and there can be no assurance that any design will be successful in achieving its stated goals under all potential future conditions. Projections of any evaluation of effectiveness to future periods are subject to risks, and changes in circumstances and technology may cause control effectiveness to vary.

CEO and CFO Certifications

The Company’s Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer are responsible for establishing and maintaining disclosure controls and procedures as defined in Rules 13a-15(e) and 15d-15(e) under the Exchange Act and internal control over financial reporting as defined in Rules 13a-15(f) and 15d-15(f) under the Exchange Act. Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

The Company’s management is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) for the Company. ICFR is a process designed by, or under the supervision of, the Company’s Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer and effected by the Company’s Board of Directors, management and other personnel to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America. Executive Overview

We are a leading independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company whose operations are primarily located onshore in the United States. Our operations are currently focused onshore in the U.S. and Canada. Our U.S. operations are focused on oil and liquids-rich plays, including the Delaware Basin in southeastern New Mexico and West Texas, the Anadarko Basin in western Oklahoma and the Williston Basin in North Dakota and Montana. Our Canadian operations are focused on liquids-rich natural gas plays in the Horn River and Montney formations in northeastern British Columbia. We also operate a midstream business that supports and enhances our exploration and production operations by providing natural gas gathering, treatment and processing and crude oil gathering, transportation and storage services. Our portfolio is focused on high-return projects that consistently generate free cash flow under a wide range of commodity price scenarios. We believe that our scale, operational capabilities, high-quality asset base and financial strength provide a strong foundation for long-term success.

Our strategy emphasizes disciplined capital allocation and returns to shareholders. We plan to allocate capital to our highest-return projects to maximize operating margins and free cash flow generation. Operationally, our priorities include executing on our development programs, improving efficiencies, reducing controllable costs and optimizing our well designs to enhance returns and resource recovery. We also plan to continue to invest in infrastructure and technologies that support our operations and sustainability initiatives.

During 2024, we continued to optimize our portfolio and advance our development activities. On September 27, 2024, we acquired the Williston Basin business from Grayson Mill Energy for total consideration of approximately $5.0 billion, consisting of cash and stock, which added approximately 307,000 net acres in the Williston Basin and approximately 100,000 Boe per day of net production at the time of closing. This acquisition expanded our exposure to oil-weighted assets and provided additional scale in the Williston Basin, which we believe enhances our long-term growth potential and creates significant synergies with our existing operations in the basin. We plan to integrate these assets into our development program and expect to realize operational and cost efficiencies through our scale and expertise.

Capital expenditures for 2025 are expected to be funded through cash flow from operations and available liquidity. Our capital allocation framework provides flexibility to adjust our spending based on commodity prices, service costs and operational performance. We plan to continue to prioritize projects with high returns and short payback periods while maintaining optionality to pursue value-enhancing opportunities.

We continue to evaluate opportunities to optimize our portfolio through acquisitions and divestitures. We remain focused on improving our cost structure and capital efficiency through improved well productivity, cycle times and cost control. We also remain committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet and liquidity profile to support our operational and strategic objectives.

Commodity prices are a significant driver of our results. Changes in commodity prices can impact our revenues, operating cash flow, capital program and the value of our reserves. We manage price volatility through a combination of financial hedging instruments, operational flexibility and disciplined capital allocation. We also seek to improve our realized prices through marketing arrangements and infrastructure investments.

We believe our diversified portfolio and operational execution will support our ability to deliver sustainable free cash flow, returns to shareholders and long-term value creation. Our strong financial position, liquidity and access to capital provide us with the flexibility to navigate commodity price cycles and pursue attractive opportunities as they arise.

We are committed to operating safely, responsibly and sustainably. Our environmental, social and governance (ESG) initiatives are focused on reducing emissions, improving energy efficiency, strengthening our communities and upholding strong governance practices. We believe these efforts support our long-term business objectives and risk management practices and are aligned with the interests of our stakeholders.

Overview
EOG Resources, Inc., together with its subsidiaries (collectively, EOG), is one of the largest independent (non-integrated) crude oil and natural gas companies in the United States of America (U.S.), with crude oil and natural gas reserves primarily in the U.S. and, to a lesser extent, in the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago (Trinidad). EOG operates under several different operating and reporting segments, primarily organized based on the geographic areas in which EOG's crude oil and natural gas properties are located. EOG's primary operating areas include the U.S. and Trinidad (the "International" segment). EOG also has exploration and production activities in other international locations, including in the Gulf of Mexico and other foreign jurisdictions. EOG's principal areas of operation in the U.S. include the Delaware Basin in West Texas and southeastern New Mexico, the Eagle Ford play in South Texas, the Denver-Julesburg Basin (DJ Basin) in Colorado, the Powder River Basin in Wyoming and the Anadarko Basin in western Oklahoma and the Texas Panhandle. EOG also has operations in the Williston Basin in North Dakota and Montana and in other areas of the U.S.

EOG's business strategy focuses on high-return capital allocation and sustainable free cash flow generation. EOG's disciplined capital allocation framework prioritizes investments in its highest-return projects, maintaining a strong balance sheet and returning cash to stockholders through dividends and share repurchases. EOG seeks to maximize returns on invested capital by focusing on continuous improvement in operating efficiency, well productivity and cost management. EOG's strategy is supported by a robust inventory of premium drilling locations across multiple basins, which provides long-term optionality and flexibility to allocate capital based on market conditions and relative returns.

EOG's financial performance is impacted by commodity prices, production volumes and operating costs. Crude oil and natural gas prices are volatile and can be influenced by global economic conditions, geopolitical events, supply and demand dynamics and regulatory developments. EOG's realized prices are also affected by transportation, processing and differentials in the markets in which EOG sells its production. EOG uses financial hedging instruments to manage a portion of its commodity price exposure, which can impact its realized prices and cash flows.

EOG's operating strategy emphasizes operational excellence, innovation and sustainability. EOG invests in technology and data analytics to improve drilling and completion techniques, enhance reservoir understanding and optimize production. EOG is also focused on reducing its environmental footprint by implementing emissions reduction initiatives, improving energy efficiency and minimizing flaring and venting. EOG's safety culture is a core value, and the company prioritizes safety in all aspects of its operations.

EOG's liquidity and capital resources are managed to support its operations, capital program and returns to stockholders. EOG maintains a strong balance sheet with low leverage and significant liquidity through cash on hand and an undrawn revolving credit facility. EOG's capital program is designed to be flexible and to be adjusted based on market conditions, commodity prices and operating performance. EOG also evaluates opportunities to optimize its portfolio through acquisitions and divestitures.

EOG's Board of Directors and management team are committed to long-term value creation and the prudent management of risks. EOG's governance framework includes robust risk management practices, internal controls and a focus on ethical conduct and compliance with laws and regulations. EOG engages with its stakeholders, including stockholders, employees, communities and regulators, to align its strategy with stakeholder interests and to support sustainable business practices.

EOG's dividend and share repurchase program is designed to return cash to stockholders while maintaining financial flexibility. EOG has a track record of paying regular dividends and, from time to time, paying special dividends and repurchasing shares. The level of dividends and share repurchases depends on EOG's financial condition, cash flows, capital requirements, market conditions and other factors.

EOG's 2025 capital program is expected to focus on high-return development projects and infrastructure investments in its core operating areas. EOG plans to continue to allocate capital to its highest-return opportunities while maintaining financial discipline. EOG believes that its high-quality asset base, operational capabilities and financial strength position it well to deliver long-term value to its stockholders.

On February 16, 2024, EOG entered into a new $1.25 billion unsecured revolving credit facility that matures on February 16, 2029. This credit facility replaced EOG's previous $2.0 billion unsecured revolving credit facility that was scheduled to mature on April 10, 2027. The new credit facility contains customary covenants and restrictions.

On March 1, 2025, EOG announced that its Board of Directors approved an increase to the quarterly cash dividend on its common stock from $0.91 per share to $0.98 per share, effective with the dividend payable on April 30, 2025, to stockholders of record as of April 16, 2025.

On April 15, 2025, EOG completed the acquisition of certain assets in the Delaware Basin for total consideration of approximately $1.2 billion, consisting of cash and the assumption of certain liabilities. These assets include approximately 60,000 net acres and associated production of approximately 25,000 Boe per day. EOG expects to integrate these assets into its development program and realize operational synergies and cost efficiencies.

On January 17, 2025, EOG issued $1.0 billion aggregate principal amount of 4.50% senior notes due January 17, 2035. The net proceeds of the offering were used for general corporate purposes, including the repayment of outstanding borrowings under EOG's revolving credit facility and the funding of capital expenditures. The notes are unsecured and rank equally with EOG's other unsecured obligations.

On February 27, 2025, the Board declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.98 per share, payable on April 30, 2025, to stockholders of record as of April 16, 2025.

Future cash inflows, development costs and production costs were computed using the same assumptions for prices and costs that were used to estimate proved reserves. Future cash inflows were estimated by applying year-end prices, adjusted for location and quality differentials, to the estimated future production of year-end proved reserves. Future income tax expense was computed using current statutory tax rates. The standardized measure is not intended to represent fair value, and estimates of reserves are imprecise and change as additional information becomes available.

Proved Reserves

Proved oil and gas reserves are those quantities of oil, gas and NGLs which, by analysis of geoscience and engineering data, can be estimated with reasonable certainty to be economically producible—from a given date forward, from known reservoirs, and under existing economic conditions, operating methods and government regulations—prior to the time at which contracts providing the right to operate expire, unless evidence indicates that renewal is reasonably certain. The project to extract the hydrocarbons must have commenced or the operator must be reasonably certain that it will commence the project within a reasonable time. The term economically producible, as used in the definition of proved reserves, means a resource which generates revenue that exceeds, or is reasonably expected to exceed, the costs of the operation. Proved developed reserves are reserves that can be expected to be recovered through existing wells with existing equipment and operating methods. Proved undeveloped reserves are proved reserves that are expected to be recovered from new wells on undrilled acreage, or from existing wells where a relatively major expenditure is required for recompletion. Additional information regarding our reserves is provided under “Supplemental Information to the Consolidated Financial Statements.” Our reserve estimates are prepared by our internal engineers and audited by independent petroleum engineering firms. These estimates are inherently imprecise and may change as additional information becomes available. The value of our reserves is highly dependent on commodity prices and operating costs, which have been volatile and may continue to be volatile. Changes in commodity prices, operating costs, development plans, production performance, and other factors could result in material revisions to proved reserve estimates, which could affect our depletion expense and the standardized measure of discounted future net cash flows.

Summary of Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates

EOG prepares its financial statements and the accompanying notes in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States (GAAP). The preparation of financial statements in conformity with GAAP requires EOG to make estimates and judgments that affect the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses, and related disclosures of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial statements. EOG identifies certain accounting policies and estimates as critical based on, among other things, their impact on EOG's financial condition, results of operations or cash flows. The following is a discussion of EOG's most critical accounting policies and estimates:

Proved Oil and Gas Reserves

EOG's engineers estimate proved oil and gas reserves in accordance with guidelines established by the SEC. Proved oil and gas reserves are the estimated quantities of crude oil, natural gas and NGLs which, by analysis of geoscience and engineering data, can be estimated with reasonable certainty to be economically producible—from a given date forward, from known reservoirs and under existing economic and operating conditions. The process of estimating quantities of proved oil and gas reserves is complex and requires significant decisions in the evaluation of all available geological, geophysical, engineering and economic data for each reservoir. Estimation of proved oil and gas reserves is also critical to certain accounting estimates because it requires significant judgment in the evaluation of engineering and geological data. Reserve estimates are key to calculation of DD&A and impairment assessments for proved properties. Reserve estimates may change as additional information becomes available or as a result of changes in economic conditions, including commodity prices and operating costs.

Depreciation, Depletion and Amortization for Oil and Gas Properties

The quantities of estimated proved oil and gas reserves are a significant component of EOG’s calculation of DD&A. Revisions to reserve estimates may result from economic changes, such as changes in commodity prices, operating costs and capital costs, as well as from actual operating results. Changes in the quantities of proved reserves will cause the per unit depletion rate to change prospectively. Holding all other factors constant, a reduction in proved reserves will increase the per unit DD&A rate, and an increase in proved reserves will decrease the per unit DD&A rate. EOG’s management reviews the reasonableness of reserve estimates and the associated DD&A on a regular basis and, where necessary, adjusts its estimates to reflect the best available information.

Oil and Gas Properties

The Company uses the successful efforts method of accounting for oil and gas properties. Under this method, all costs to acquire mineral interests in oil and gas properties, to drill and equip development wells and successful exploratory wells, and to construct and install production facilities are capitalized when incurred. Exploration costs, including geological and geophysical costs and the costs of carrying and retaining unproved properties and exploratory dry hole drilling costs, are expensed. Development costs, including the costs of drilling and equipping development wells, are capitalized. The Company capitalizes costs for exploratory wells if the well has found a sufficient quantity of reserves to justify its completion as a producing well and the Company is making sufficient progress assessing the reserves and the economic and operating viability of the project. For wells in areas requiring major capital expenditures before production could begin, such as offshore drilling or exploration activities, the Company may carry as an asset the costs of exploratory wells in large field areas if the well has found a sufficient quantity of reserves to justify its completion as a producing well and sufficient progress is being made in an assessment of the reserves and the project’s economic and operational viability. Exploratory drilling costs continue to be carried as an asset pending determination of whether reserves have been found only as long as: (1) the well has found a sufficient quantity of reserves to justify its completion as a producing well and (2) the Company is making sufficient progress assessing the reserves and the economic and operating viability of the project. If either condition ceases to be met, the well is considered to be impaired and its costs are charged to exploration expense.

Development costs of proved oil and gas properties, including estimated dismantlement, restoration and abandonment costs and acquisition costs of proved properties, are capitalized. Depreciation, depletion and amortization (“DD&A”) of the capitalized costs of proved oil and gas properties are provided on the unit-of-production method using both proved developed and proved reserves. Costs are depleted on a field-by-field basis based on the production for the period as a percentage of the total of estimated proved developed or proved reserves, as applicable.

The Company reviews its oil and gas properties for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the asset may not be recoverable. The Company compares expected undiscounted future net cash flows at a producing field level to the carrying amount of the asset. If the carrying amount exceeds the expected undiscounted future net cash flows, the Company reduces the carrying amount of the asset to its fair value. Fair value is estimated based on discounted cash flows using market-based inputs, when available, or management’s best estimate of the future cash flows of the asset group.

The Company evaluates unproved oil and gas properties periodically for impairment by considering various factors, including the expiration term of the leases, surrender of leases, drilling results on the Company’s leases and/or on adjacent leases, market conditions and commodity price outlooks, and the Company’s future drilling plans. Impairment of unproved properties is recorded as a component of exploration expense. The Company performs this evaluation at least annually and may impair unproved properties at any time management deems them to be impaired based on the above factors.

The Company records asset retirement obligations (“ARO”) for legal obligations associated with the retirement of tangible long-lived assets that result from the acquisition, construction, development or normal operation of such assets. The fair value of the liability is recognized in the period in which it is incurred if a reasonable estimate of fair value can be made. The associated asset retirement costs are capitalized as part of the carrying amount of the long-lived asset and subsequently depreciated over the asset’s useful life. The ARO liability is accreted to its present value each period, and the capitalized costs are depreciated over the useful lives of the related assets.

The Company capitalizes interest on expenditures made in connection with significant capital projects that require a period of time to be ready for their intended use. Capitalized interest is included in properties and equipment and is amortized over the useful lives of the related assets.

Midstream Assets

Midstream assets are recorded at historical cost. Depreciation is provided using the straight-line method based on expected lives of the individual assets, which range from five to 40 years. Expenditures for maintenance and repairs are expensed as incurred, while expenditures that extend the useful life of an asset are capitalized. Gains or losses on the sale or retirement of assets are recognized in the period of disposition.

Fixed Assets

Fixed assets consist primarily of buildings, leasehold improvements, computer equipment, furniture and fixtures, vehicles and other equipment. Our Operations Are Uncertain and Involve Substantial Costs and Risks

Our operating activities are subject to numerous costs and risks inherent in the oil and gas industry. There is no assurance that our exploration and development activities will be successful. Exploration and development drilling and production may be unprofitable, not only from dry holes, but from productive wells that do not return a profit because of high operating costs or other factors. In addition, drilling hazards or environmental damage could cause substantial losses. To the extent that we engage in exploration activities, our drilling involves greater risks of dry holes or failure to find commercial quantities of hydrocarbons. Our risks are increased because we sometimes drill in new or emerging plays.

Our future oil, gas and NGL production and, therefore, our cash flows and results of operations are highly dependent on the success of our development and exploration activities. If we are unable to replace reserves, we may not be able to sustain our production. We cannot assure that we will be able to find, develop or acquire additional reserves at an acceptable cost.

Our operations are subject to various hazards and risks associated with drilling for and producing oil, gas and NGLs, including encountering unexpected formations or pressures, premature declines of reservoirs, blowouts, loss of well control, fires, explosions, craterings, pollution, releases of toxic gas, spills, migration of harmful substances, hurricanes, tornadoes, severe storms, earthquakes and other natural disasters. Any of these risks could result in personal injury or loss of life, damage to or destruction of property, environmental damage, loss of wells, and suspension of operations. In addition, our operations are subject to risks associated with the availability of drilling rigs and other necessary equipment, and risks of shortages or increased costs of drilling and other oilfield services and equipment.

We maintain insurance against various losses and liabilities arising from our operations; however, our insurance may not be adequate to cover all losses or liabilities. In addition, our insurance is subject to deductibles and coverage limitations. The cost of insurance has risen in recent years and may continue to increase. We cannot assure that insurance will continue to be available to us at a reasonable cost or that the levels of insurance we carry will remain adequate to cover any losses we might sustain.

Because of these and other uncertainties, the costs associated with our exploration, development and production activities are difficult to predict with precision, and we may not be able to obtain capital on terms we find acceptable. As a result, our ability to pursue exploration and development opportunities and to grow our reserves and production could be adversely affected.

Our estimates of proved reserves are prepared in accordance with the rules and regulations of the SEC. Proved reserves are those estimated quantities of oil, natural gas and NGLs that geological and engineering data demonstrate with reasonable certainty to be recoverable in future years from known reservoirs under existing economic and operating conditions (i.e., prices and costs as of the date the estimate is made). The process of estimating quantities of proved reserves is very complex and requires significant subjective decisions in the evaluation of all available geological, engineering and economic data. The data for a given field may also change substantially over time as a result of numerous factors including, but not limited to, additional development activity, evolving production history and continual reassessment of the viability of production under varying economic conditions. Consequently, material revisions (upward or downward) to existing reserve estimates may occur from time to time. Also, the actual quantities of oil, natural gas and NGLs ultimately recovered from our properties may differ substantially from the quantities initially estimated.

Proved reserves are estimates based on many variables and assumptions. The accuracy of any reserve estimate depends on the quality of the available data as well as on the engineering and geological interpretation and judgment. In addition, reserve estimates are affected by economic factors such as the price we receive for oil, natural gas and NGLs and the associated costs of development and production. The SEC’s current rules require that reserve estimates be based on the unweighted arithmetic average of the first-day-of-the-month commodity prices for the preceding twelve months (the “SEC pricing”). Our reserve estimates are also constrained by our plans to develop our reserves. Accordingly, we may not be able to recover the estimated proved reserves if we revise our development plans, experiences in production differ from our expectations, or if commodity prices decline for extended periods.

We have numerous uncertainties inherent in estimating quantities of proved reserves, projecting future rates of production and the timing of development expenditures. The estimates of reserves are based on various factors, including drilling results, production decline analysis, geologic and seismic interpretation, and projected operating and commodity price assumptions. Our proved reserves estimates are prepared by our internal engineering staff and are audited by independent petroleum engineering consultants in accordance with generally accepted petroleum engineering and evaluation principles.

Property Dispositions and Asset Retirement Obligations

We may periodically dispose of certain non-core properties, which can impact our capitalized costs and related DD&A in future periods. Asset retirement obligations associated with our oil and gas properties are recorded in accordance with ASC 410, Asset Retirement and Environmental Obligations, and are accreted over time until settlement.

Full Cost Accounting Method and DD&A

We follow the successful efforts method of accounting for our oil and gas properties, which requires that certain costs of acquiring, exploring and developing oil and gas properties be capitalized and subsequently depleted or depreciated using the unit-of-production method. Depletion of capitalized costs is based on the relationship of current production to total proved reserves. The unit-of-production method requires significant estimates of proved reserves that can change significantly from period to period based on drilling results, commodity prices and other factors. If estimates of proved reserves decline, DD&A expense generally increases in future periods. Conversely, if proved reserves increase due to successful drilling or improved commodity prices, DD&A expense generally decreases in future periods.

Impairment and Ceiling Test Considerations

We assess our oil and gas properties for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts may not be recoverable. Under the successful efforts method, capitalized costs are assessed at the field level. Impairment is recognized when the net capitalized costs exceeds the expected undiscounted future net cash flows from the field. Our estimates of future net cash flows depend on many assumptions, including future commodity prices, operating costs, production profiles and development plans. Changes in these assumptions could result in impairment charges or recoveries in future periods.

Proved reserves are the estimated quantities of crude oil, natural gas and NGLs which geological and engineering data demonstrate with reasonable certainty are recoverable in future years from known reservoirs under existing economic conditions, operating methods and government regulations. Proved developed oil and gas reserves are reserves that can be expected to be recovered from existing wells with existing equipment and operating methods. Proved undeveloped reserves are reserves that are expected to be recovered from new wells on undrilled acreage, or from existing wells where a relatively major expenditure is required to re-complete the well. The accuracy of our proved reserve estimates is a function of the quality and quantity of available data and of engineering interpretation and judgment. As a result, the estimates of reported proved reserves and future production rates are often different from the quantities of oil, natural gas and NGLs that are ultimately recovered. A change in the estimated recoverable reserves for a given field also results in an increase or decrease in the rate of DD&A for that field, which is computed on a unit-of-production basis, as discussed below. Therefore, changes in proved reserves estimates affect the timing of our recognition of DD&A expense but not the actual total amount of DD&A expense over the life of a field.

Depletion of our producing properties is computed on a field basis using the unit-of-production method under the successful efforts method of accounting. Under this methodology, DD&A expense is recognized in proportion to the current period production as related to the estimated recoverable reserves from the field. Consequently, as proved reserves are revised, the rates of DD&A change. Such estimates require significant judgment with respect to forward commodity prices, expected production decline rates, estimates of operating costs and future development capital requirements. Accordingly, actual results may differ from our estimates and revisions to estimates of reserves could be material to our results of operations in future periods.

Impairment of oil and gas properties is recognized when the carrying value of an asset group is not recoverable from expected future undiscounted cash flows. If the expected undiscounted cash flows from an asset group are less than the carrying value, an impairment is recognized to the extent the carrying value exceeds the fair value of the asset group. Fair values are measured using various valuation techniques including, but not limited to, discounted cash flow models. These models require estimates of future production, commodity prices, operating costs, future capital expenditures, and risk-adjusted discount rates. Changes in these assumptions could have a significant impact on the amount of impairment recognized.

We capitalize certain costs incurred in connection with our oil and gas exploration and development activities, including leasehold acquisition costs, drilling and completion costs, and certain overhead costs directly associated with exploration and development activities. These costs are depleted on a unit-of-production basis over the life of the associated proved reserves. Exploration costs such as geological and geophysical costs, delay rentals and dry hole costs are expensed as incurred. Development costs for proved reserves are capitalized when incurred. The successful efforts method of accounting may result in greater volatility in our reported earnings compared to the full cost method because exploration costs are expensed as incurred while development costs are capitalized and depleted over time.

standardized measure of discounted future net cash flows from proved reserves

The standardized measure of discounted future net cash flows from proved reserves is a forward-looking estimate that should be read in conjunction with information included under the captions “Risk Factors,” “Forward-Looking Statements,” “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations,” and “Financial Statements and Supplementary Data.” Future net cash flows are the result of a complex series of assumptions including estimates of the quantities of our proved reserves, future production and timing thereof; the revenue we receive from the future sale of those volumes; and the future expenditures to develop and produce the proved reserves. In addition, GAAP requires a standardized measure calculation which uses the arithmetic average of the first-day-of-the-month oil and natural gas prices, unadjusted for basis differentials, during the 12-month period before the ending date of the period covered by the report. Proved oil and gas reserves are those quantities of oil, gas and NGLs which, by analysis of geoscience and engineering data, can be estimated with reasonable certainty to be economically producible – from a given date forward, from known reservoirs and under existing economic conditions, operating methods and government regulations – prior to the time at which contracts providing the right to operate expire, unless evidence indicates that renewal is reasonably certain regardless of whether deterministic or probabilistic methods are used for the estimation. The project to extract the hydrocarbons must have commenced, or the operator must be reasonably certain that it will commence the project, within a reasonable time.

Deterministic methods of estimation are those in which a single value for each parameter (from the geoscience, engineering or economic data) in the reserves calculation is used in the model deterministically. The estimate made is the best estimate based on known geological, engineering and economic data. Probabilistic methods of estimation are those in which the known geological, engineering or economic data are used to generate a range of estimates and their associated probabilities. In general, probabilistic methods are to be preferred and, where conditions allow, should be used for these assessments. In conventional reservoirs, the method employed involves combining historical production data with geological information to establish a measure of geological uncertainty and in evaluating continuous accumulation reservoirs, analytical and numerical simulation techniques are used together with a range of reservoir parameters which reflect the level of uncertainty appropriate to the project and consistent with available data.

The process of estimating oil, gas and NGL reserves is complex and requires significant judgment, as discussed in “Item 1A. Risk Factors” and “Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data” of this report.

Critical Audit Matter
The critical audit matter communicated below is a matter arising from the current period audit of the financial statements that was communicated or required to be communicated to the audit committee and that (1) relates to accounts or disclosures that are material to the financial statements and (2) involved especially challenging, subjective, or complex judgments. The communication of critical audit matters does not alter in any way our opinion on the financial statements, taken as a whole, and we are not, by communicating the critical audit matters below, providing a separate opinion on the critical audit matter or on the accounts or disclosures to which it relates.

Proved Oil and Gas Properties and Depletion — Crude Oil, NGL and Natural Gas Reserves — Refer to Note 1 to the Financial Statements

Critical Audit Matter Description

The Company’s proved oil and gas properties are depleted using the units-of-production method based on estimates of proved developed reserves for most wells and field level reserves for other assets. The Company’s crude oil, NGL and natural gas reserves are estimated by Company engineers. The estimation of reserves requires management to make significant assumptions and judgments related to forecasted production volumes and costs, forecasted commodity prices, timing and amount of future development activity, and the interpretation of geological and engineering data. Changes in proved reserves can have a significant impact on depletion expense and the carrying value of proved properties. Given the significant judgments made by management to estimate reserves and the potential for changes in reserves to have a significant effect on the financial statements, auditing estimates of reserves involved a high degree of auditor judgment and an increased extent of effort, including the involvement of our specialists.

How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit

Our audit procedures related to the estimation of the Company’s proved reserves and the impact of those estimates on depletion expense included the following, among others:

• We evaluated the effectiveness of controls over the Company’s process to estimate reserves, including management’s controls over the completeness and accuracy of the underlying data and the review of significant assumptions.

• With the assistance of our internal engineering specialists, we evaluated the Company’s proved reserve estimates and the significant assumptions used by management by:

— Testing the completeness and accuracy of data inputs used in reserve estimates, including historical production volumes and realized prices.

— Comparing the Company’s historical estimates of proved reserves to actual production results to assess the historical accuracy of the Company’s reserve estimates.

— Evaluating the reasonableness of forecasted commodity prices by comparing them to independent market data.

— Evaluating the reasonableness of forecasted development and operating costs by comparing them to historical costs and budgets.

— Assessing the reasonableness of the Company’s future development plans by comparing them to historical development activities and capital budgets.

• We tested the mathematical accuracy of the Company’s depletion calculations, including the units-of-production rates, and assessed the consistency of the methods and assumptions used in the calculations.

• We evaluated the adequacy of the Company’s disclosures related to proved reserves and depletion in the financial statements.

The Company determines if an arrangement is, or contains, a lease at inception based on whether that contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset in exchange for consideration for a period of time. Operating leases are included in right-of-use assets (“ROU assets”) and lease liabilities (current and non-current) in the Consolidated Balance Sheet. Financing leases are included in properties and equipment, net and lease liabilities (current and non-current) in the Consolidated Balance Sheet. Short-term leases (a lease that, at commencement, has a lease term of one year or less and does not contain a purchase option that the Company is reasonably certain to exercise) are not recognized in ROU assets and lease liabilities. For all operating leases, lease and non-lease components are accounted for as a single lease component.

ROU assets represent the Company’s right to use an underlying asset for the lease term and lease liabilities represent the Company’s obligation to make lease payments arising from the leases. ROU assets and lease liabilities are recognized at the lease commencement date based on the present value of minimum lease payments over the lease term. Most leases do not provide an implicit interest rate; therefore, the Company uses its incremental borrowing rate based on the information available at the inception date to determine the present value of the lease payments. Lease terms include options to extend the lease when it is reasonably certain that the Company will exercise that option. Lease cost for lease payments is recognized on a straight-line basis over the lease term. Certain leases have payment terms that vary based on the usage of the underlying assets. Variable lease payments are not included in ROU assets and lease liabilities.

Fair Value of Assets and Liabilities

The Company follows the authoritative accounting guidance for measuring fair value of assets and liabilities in its financial statements. Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly

63

transaction between market participants at the measurement date (exit price). The Company utilizes market data or assumptions that market participants who are independent, knowledgeable and willing and able to transact would use in pricing the asset or liability, including assumptions about risk and the risks inherent in the inputs to the valuation technique. The Company is able to classify fair value balances based on the observability of these inputs. The authoritative guidance for fair value measurements establishes three levels of the fair value hierarchy, defined as follows:

• Level 1: Unadjusted, quoted prices for identical assets or liabilities in active markets.

• Level 2: Quoted prices in markets that are not considered to be active or financial instruments for which all significant inputs are observable, either directly or indirectly for substantially the full term of the asset or liability.

• Level 3: Significant, unobservable inputs for use when little or no market data exists, requiring a significant degree of judgment.

The hierarchy gives the highest priority to Level 1 measurements and the lowest priority to Level 3 measurements. Depending on the particular asset or liability, input availability can vary depending on factors such as product type, longevity of a product in the market and other particular transaction conditions. In some cases, certain inputs used to measure fair value may be categorized into different levels of the fair value hierarchy. For disclosure purposes under the accounting guidance, the lowest level that contains significant inputs used in the valuation should be chosen.

Securities Litigation

In October 2020, a stockholder derivative action styled Ezell v. Dinges, et. al. (U.S. District Court, Middle District of Pennsylvania) was filed against Messrs. Dinges and Schroeder and the Board of Directors of the Company serving at that time. Several additional derivative complaints were also filed and have been consolidated with the Ezell lawsuit, which was later transferred to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas. The most recent consolidated amended derivative complaint asserted claims for alleged securities violations under Section 10(b) and Section 21D of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended, as well as claims based on alleged breaches of fiduciary duty and statutory contribution theories. In January 2024, the court issued an order and final judgment granting the Company’s and defendants’ motion to dismiss and dismissing the consolidated derivative case in its entirety with prejudice. The derivative plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal regarding the final judgment in February 2024, with oral arguments heard by the Fifth Court of Appeals on February 3, 2025. The Company intends to vigorously defend any further proceedings in the derivative lawsuit.

In March 2024, one of the plaintiffs in the above consolidated derivative action served a demand letter on the Company’s current Board of Directors. The letter demanded that the Board of Directors pursue legal claims against various current and former officers and directors of the Company based on similar factual allegations as contained in the corresponding securities class action (that was settled in late 2024) and consolidated stockholder derivative action described above. In June 2024, the individual who made the demand filed a stockholder derivative lawsuit styled Fischer v. Dinges et. al. (U.S. District Court, Southern District of Texas). The Board of Directors formed a committee to advise it in addressing each of the demands and the lawsuit. In April 2025, the committee advised counsel for the stockholders, who served the demand letters, that it had concluded its investigation, that it had determined that pursuing the claims asserted in the demands would not serve the Company’s interests, and that the committee was therefore rejecting the demands. The Company intends to move for dismissal of the Fischer action based on the committee’s determination.

Business and Industry Outlook

In 2024, Devon marked its 53rd anniversary in the oil and gas business. Since our founding in 1971, our Company has relentlessly pursued premier resources and people. Our pursuit of excellence in all facets of the business – talented people, tier-one assets and leading-edge technologies – has shaped our strategy for, and response to, opportunities and challenges through economic cycles. In 2024, we returned approximately $2.0 billion of cash flow to shareholders through our fixed-plus-variable dividend framework and share repurchases. We believe this combination of returning cash to shareholders while reinvesting in high-return projects strengthens our long-term outlook. We intend to continue to prioritize this shareholder return strategy in 2025.

In 2024, WTI oil prices averaged $75.79 per Bbl versus $77.62 per Bbl in 2023. For 2025, we expect oil demand to increase compared with 2024 prices due to increased demand, driven by global growth and ongoing supply discipline among major oil-producing countries. Despite this expected improvement, volatility can still influence our ability to forecast. We manage price risk through prudent hedging strategies. As of December 31, 2024, we had approximately 30% of our anticipated 2025 oil and gas production hedged.

Devon’s portfolio is focused on high-return, oil-weighted assets with significant inventory. Our operations are primarily concentrated in the Delaware Basin, the Williston Basin and the Anadarko Basin. In particular, we are increasingly focused on efficiency gains, cost reductions and optimizing well performance through improved completions and drilling techniques. We plan to allocate capital to our highest-return projects in 2025 while maintaining liquidity and financial flexibility.

We intend to continue share repurchases in 2025 under our existing authorization, subject to market conditions, capital requirements and other considerations. Additionally, we may pursue acquisition and divestiture opportunities to optimize our portfolio. In September 2024, Devon closed the acquisition of the Williston Basin business from Grayson Mill Energy for approximately $5.0 billion in a cash and stock transaction. This transaction expanded our Williston Basin footprint and provided additional scale and efficiency gains. We expect to recognize synergies and operational improvements over time as we integrate these assets.

We remain committed to safety, environmental stewardship and responsible operations. We continue to implement emissions reduction initiatives and evaluate opportunities to reduce our overall environmental footprint. We believe our technology investments and operational excellence position us to deliver sustainable value to our shareholders over the long term.

Capital Structure

One of management's key strategies is to maintain a strong balance sheet and financial flexibility, which we measure by a conservative leverage ratio (as measured by the ratio of total debt to total capitalization, where total capitalization is defined as the sum of total current and long-term debt and total stockholders' equity. At December 31, 2024, EOG maintained a strong financial and liquidity position with $5.4 billion of cash and cash equivalents and $1.25 billion of borrowing capacity under its senior unsecured revolving credit facility (discussed below).

On November 21, 2024, EOG closed on its offering of $1.0 billion aggregate principal amount of 5.10% Senior Notes due 2035. EOG expects to use the net proceeds from the offering for (i) the repayment of its 3.15% Senior Notes due 2025 and (ii) the funding of future capital expenditures.

The Internal Revenue Service previously announced tax relief related to the timing of certain federal tax payments related to 2024 owed by corporations, including EOG, in certain states that had been affected by weather-related disasters. As a result, EOG expects to make approximately $0.7 billion of such federal tax payments related to the 2024 tax year.

During 2024, EOG funded $6.7 billion ($109 million of which was capitalized) in exploration and development expenditures and $0.5 billion in property acquisitions, lease acquisitions and other property, plant and equipment, primarily from net cash provided by its operating activities and cash on hand.

Total anticipated 2025 capital expenditures are estimated to range from $6.0 to $6.4 billion, including exploration and development drilling, facilities, gathering and other infrastructure projects to support the expected production growth. EOG plans to continue to return cash to stockholders through regular dividends and opportunistic share repurchases subject to market conditions, while maintaining financial flexibility to pursue attractive investment opportunities.

ACQUISITIONS
On October 1, 2021, we completed a merger transaction (the “Merger”) with Cimarex Energy Co. (“Cimarex”) pursuant to the terms and subject to the conditions set forth in the Agreement and Plan of Merger, dated as of May 23, 2021 (the “Merger Agreement”). Under the terms of the Merger Agreement, each share of common stock, par value $0.10 per share, of Cimarex (the “Cimarex Common Stock”) issued and outstanding immediately prior to the effective time of the Merger (the “Effective Time”) was converted into the right to receive 4.0146 shares of our common stock at closing. Additionally, on October 1, 2021, we changed our name to Coterra Energy Inc. and our ticker symbol on the New York Stock Exchange to “CTRA”.

The Merger was accounted for as a “reverse acquisition” in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (“GAAP”), with Cimarex treated as the accounting acquirer and Cabot Oil & Gas Corporation (“Cabot”) treated as the accounting acquiree. As a result, the historical financial statements presented for periods prior to the Merger are those of Cimarex and do not include the historical financial statements of Cabot. The Merger has been reflected in the financial statements for periods after the Effective Time. The assets acquired and liabilities assumed from Cabot were recorded at their respective fair values as of the Effective Time. The excess of the consideration transferred over the fair value of the net identifiable assets acquired was recorded as goodwill.

The determination of the fair values of assets acquired and liabilities assumed required management to make significant estimates and assumptions, especially with respect to oil and gas reserves, future commodity prices, future development and operating costs, and discount rates. Management’s estimates and assumptions are inherently subjective and subject to change, and any changes to these estimates and assumptions could significantly impact the fair values assigned to the assets acquired and liabilities assumed and the resultant goodwill.

The fair values assigned to oil and gas properties were based on estimates of proved reserves and risk-adjusted probable and possible reserves, discounted using a market-participant weighted average cost of capital. The fair value of midstream assets was based on a discounted cash flow analysis using forecasted throughput volumes, rates, operating costs and an appropriate discount rate. The fair value of other property, plant and equipment was based on either a cost approach or an income approach, depending on the nature of the asset. The fair value of asset retirement obligations was determined using a discounted cash flow methodology that considered the expected timing of abandonment activities and an appropriate discount rate that reflects a market participant’s view of the risk associated with the obligation.

Transaction costs related to the Merger, which consisted primarily of financial advisory, legal, accounting and other professional fees, were expensed as incurred and are included in other operating expenses in the Consolidated Statement of Operations for the year ended December 31, 2021. Integration costs incurred subsequent to the Merger are also included in other operating expenses and primarily consist of consulting and professional fees, severance and employee-related costs, and other costs to integrate systems and processes. We expect to continue to incur integration costs in future periods as we complete our integration activities.

Pro forma financial information has been presented to illustrate the effects of the Merger as if it had occurred at the beginning of the earliest period presented. The pro forma information is not necessarily indicative of the results of operations that would have been achieved had the Merger been consummated on that date, nor is it indicative of future results. The pro forma financial information includes adjustments for depreciation, depletion and amortization based on the fair values assigned to the assets acquired, interest expense on additional borrowings, and the related income tax effects of the adjustments.

Following the Merger, we implemented various restructuring and optimization initiatives to integrate operations, align organizational structures and realize cost synergies. These initiatives included consolidation of overlapping functions, optimization of drilling and completion operations, and rationalization of the combined asset portfolio. We continue to evaluate our operations to identify additional opportunities to improve efficiencies and reduce costs.

In connection with the Merger, certain equity awards held by Cimarex employees were converted into equity awards of Coterra based on the exchange ratio set forth in the Merger Agreement. The fair value of the replacement awards was measured at the Effective Time, and the portion of the fair value attributable to pre-Merger service was included in the consideration transferred, while the portion attributable to post-Merger service will be recognized as compensation expense over the remaining service period. Certain change-in-control benefits were also triggered as a result of the Merger.

The results of operations of Cabot have been included in our Consolidated Statement of Operations from October 1, 2021. Revenues and earnings contributed by the acquired Cabot business since the Merger date are not presented separately, as it is impracticable to do so due to the integration of operations and the combined nature of the business post-Merger. The Merger has had a significant impact on our financial position and results of operations, including increased scale, a more diversified asset base and enhanced operational flexibility.

Property Profiles

Key summary data from each of our areas of operation as of and for the year ended December 31, 2024 are detailed in the map below.

Delaware Basin– The Delaware Basin is our largest and most active asset and is located in southeast New Mexico and west Texas. Over the past several years, we have built an industry-leading position in the Delaware Basin through multiple acquisitions and trades and by optimizing our existing asset base. In 2024, we executed a disciplined development program focused on optimizing returns and capital efficiency across our acreage.

Rockies– Our Rockies development consists of our Williston Basin assets located primarily in North Dakota and Montana. The Williston Basin is an established oil-weighted basin with multiple productive formations, including the Bakken, Three Forks, Mission Canyon, Ratcliffe, and other conventional reservoirs. The Williston Basin provides us with a deep inventory of high-margin opportunities. On September 27, 2024, we completed our acquisition of the Williston assets of Grayson Mill Energy for total consideration consisting of cash and stock. As of December 31, 2024, we had three operated rigs developing the Williston Basin.

Our Powder River asset is focused on emerging oil opportunities in Wyoming's Powder River Basin. The Powder River Basin is a liquids-rich play with multiple stacked-pay zones, including the Turner, Parkman, Teapot and Niobrara formations. Recent drilling successes and optimization of completion designs have improved well performance and capital efficiency. In 2024, we had one operated rig developing the Powder River Basin asset.

Eagle Ford– Our Eagle Ford operations are located in Texas' DeWitt, Karnes and surrounding counties. The Eagle Ford is a mature, oil-weighted play where we continue to optimize development spacing and completion intensity to enhance returns. In 2024, we had one operated and one non-operated rig developing this asset.

Anadarko Basin– Our Anadarko Basin development, located in western Oklahoma, is under a carried interest joint venture. The Anadarko Basin provides a balance of liquids and gas exposure, and our development plan is focused on high-return drilling opportunities. In 2024, we had a two rig program associated with this joint venture.

Purchase price allocation consists of the preliminary fair values assigned to the assets acquired and liabilities assumed in the acquisition of the Williston Basin assets from Grayson Mill Energy, consisting of $ 3.5 billion of cash and approximately 37.3 million shares of Devon common stock issued to the sellers. The allocation of the purchase price to the fair values of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed was based on management’s estimates and assumptions, which are subject to change as additional information becomes available during the measurement period. The measurement period will not exceed one year from the closing date of the acquisition. The preliminary fair value estimates were based upon, among other things, expected reserves and production volumes, future commodity prices, future development and operating costs, discount rates and other relevant factors.

The determination of the fair values of oil and gas properties acquired required the use of significant estimates and assumptions, including estimates of reserves and future net cash flows associated with those reserves. The fair values were estimated using a discounted cash flow model and reflect the amount a market participant would pay to acquire the assets. The fair value of asset retirement obligations was determined using the expected present value technique, which involves the use of assumptions and judgments regarding the expected timing of settlement and the discount rate used to calculate present value. The fair value of other assets and liabilities, including working capital items, was determined using either a cost or market approach as appropriate.

The Company expects to finalize the purchase price allocation within the measurement period as additional information becomes available. Adjustments to the preliminary allocation may result from changes in the fair values of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed as of the acquisition date and could be material. Any such adjustments will be recognized in the period in which the adjustments are determined. The Company will also record depreciation, depletion and amortization expense based on the final fair values assigned to the acquired properties, which may differ from the amounts recorded based on the preliminary allocation.
