Item 7A.Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk

The primary objective of the following information is to provide forward-looking quantitative and qualitative information about our potential exposure to market risks. The term “market risk” refers to our risk of loss arising from adverse changes in oil, gas and NGL prices, interest rates and foreign currency exchange rates. The following disclosures are not meant to be precise indicators of expected future losses but rather indicators of reasonably possible losses. This forward-looking information provides indicators of how we view and manage our ongoing market risk exposures. All of our market risk sensitive instruments were entered into for purposes other than speculative trading.

Commodity Price Risk

Our major market risk exposure is the pricing applicable to our oil, gas and NGL production. Realized pricing is primarily driven by the prevailing worldwide price for crude oil and spot market prices applicable to our gas and NGL production. Pricing for oil and gas production has been volatile and unpredictable as discussed in “Item 1A. Risk Factors” of this report. Consequently, we systematically hedge a portion of our production through various financial transactions. The key terms to our oil and gas derivative financial instruments as of December 31, 2024 are presented inNote 3in “Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data” of this report.

The fair values of our commodity derivatives are largely determined by estimates of the forward curves of the relevant price indices. At December 31, 2024, a 10% change in the forward curves associated with our commodity derivative instruments would have changed our net positions by approximately $300 million.

Interest Rate Risk

At December 31, 2024, we had total debt of $8.9 billion. $7.9 billion of this debt was comprised of debentures and notes that have fixed interest rates which average 5.7%. ITEM 1A. Risk Factors

Our cash flows, results of operations and financial condition are significantly affected by the prices we receive for oil, natural gas and NGLs. Prices are determined by supply and demand fundamentals, geopolitical events, OPEC+ decisions, U.S. and global economic conditions, weather patterns and other factors beyond our control. Prolonged periods of low prices can adversely impact revenues, earnings, liquidity and the ability to fund capital programs, including dividends and share repurchases. Conversely, higher commodity prices generally result in increased revenues and cash flows, though they may also increase service costs and governmental scrutiny.

We attempt to mitigate commodity price volatility through hedging programs; however, these activities have limitations and may not fully protect cash flows. Our shareholders should recognize that fluctuations in commodity prices can materially influence our stock price, credit profile and ability to return capital. Additionally, sustained downturns may result in impairments, reduced borrowing capacity and diminished access to capital markets.

Shareholder activism and ESG-related pressures may also affect our approach to capital allocation. Expectations regarding dividends, repurchases and sustainability initiatives may not always align with commodity-driven cash flows or long-term value creation. These risks could impact the timing and scale of share repurchase programs, particularly in periods of declining market capitalization.

Capital Resources, Uses and Liquidity

Our sources of liquidity include cash flow from operations, cash on hand and our $3.0 billion revolving credit facility, which matures in 2028. We regularly assess our capital allocation priorities in light of commodity prices, market conditions, and financial strategy. Debt financing is used selectively to preserve flexibility and maintain investment grade credit ratings.

The level of capital returned to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases depends on free cash flow, balance sheet considerations and commodity price realizations. While we have authorization to repurchase shares, execution of repurchases is subject to market conditions and management discretion. We believe disciplined allocation of capital across development activity, balance sheet management and shareholder returns is essential to sustaining value creation. Future repurchases will be assessed alongside other uses of cash, including reinvestment in operations and debt reduction.

We remain focused on maintaining a conservative financial position while delivering competitive shareholder returns. Our strategy is to align capital returns with underlying cash flow generation rather than short-term fluctuations in market capitalization or commodity prices.

Note 16 – Stockholders’ Equity

We have an authorized share repurchase program approved by our Board of Directors. Repurchases are executed in the open market or through negotiated transactions, and are subject to market conditions, applicable law and other factors. During the three months ended March 31, 2025, we did not repurchase any shares under the program. As of March 31, 2025, approximately $1.1 billion remained available under the authorization.

The program is intended to provide flexibility in returning capital to stockholders alongside dividends. Management evaluates repurchase activity in the context of liquidity, commodity price environment, cash flow generation and alternative investment opportunities. The timing and amount of repurchases may fluctuate materially from period to period depending on these factors. There can be no assurance that we will continue to repurchase shares at historical levels or at all in the future.

We also declared and paid quarterly dividends of $0.28 per share in the first quarter of 2025. Future dividends will be determined by the Board of Directors based on results of operations, liquidity and other relevant factors. Shareholder returns remain a key component of our capital allocation strategy, though subject to variability driven by commodity markets and financial performance.

Stockholder Returns. We remain committed to returning meaningful capital to our stockholders through dividends and our share repurchase program, consistent with our free cash flow and long-term outlook. We regularly evaluate the appropriate level and mix of stockholder returns based on market conditions, investment opportunities and our financial priorities. During the year, we increased the annualized base dividend on our common stock to $0.84 per share and have returned over $3.0 billion to stockholders since our merger, primarily through dividends and share repurchases. Future levels of dividends and the timing and amount of share repurchases will continue to be assessed by our Board of Directors and management, and will depend on a variety of factors, including commodity prices, cash flow generation, investment opportunities, balance sheet considerations and other market conditions. There can be no assurance that we will continue to pay dividends at current levels or repurchase shares at historical levels.

Capital Allocation. Our capital allocation framework prioritizes investments that enhance capital efficiency, improve returns on invested capital and support long-term value creation. We intend to deploy capital across our portfolio with a focus on projects that meet our return thresholds and align with our strategic objectives. We believe that maintaining a disciplined approach to capital allocation, including the potential for opportunistic acquisitions or divestitures, positions us to create value for stockholders through commodity price cycles.

Liquidity and Financial Flexibility. We maintain access to diverse sources of liquidity, including cash on hand, operating cash flow and our revolving credit facility. We believe our liquidity position, combined with our cost structure and portfolio depth, provides flexibility to execute our business plans and return capital to stockholders while maintaining financial strength.

We continue to evaluate our dividend framework in light of our cash flow profile, capital program and market environment. The level and timing of dividends will be determined by our Board of Directors based on, among other things, our financial results, liquidity, outlook for commodity prices, investment opportunities and legal requirements. Future dividends are not assured and will depend on our ability to generate sufficient cash from operations and maintain appropriate liquidity and leverage levels. Similarly, we may repurchase shares of our common stock under the share repurchase authorization approved by our Board of Directors from time to time. The timing and amounts of any such repurchases will depend on various factors, including market conditions, available liquidity, the trading price of our common stock, alternative investment opportunities, accounting and tax considerations, and other factors deemed relevant by management.

We believe maintaining a strong balance sheet and low-cost operations are key to delivering sustainable shareholder returns. Our emphasis on capital efficiency, cost control and operational excellence is intended to enhance free cash flow generation and support the consistent return of capital to stockholders through commodity cycles. We also remain focused on managing risks associated with our operations, including commodity price risk, regulatory risk, operational risk and other factors that could impact our financial performance and ability to return capital.

In addition to dividends and share repurchases, we may consider other methods of returning capital to stockholders, such as special dividends or strategic transactions, depending on market conditions and our long-term strategic objectives. There can be no assurance that we will continue to pay dividends or make share repurchases in any particular amounts or at any particular times, and any such actions may be modified, suspended or discontinued at any time at the discretion of our Board of Directors and management.

Commodity Price Risk
Our most significant market risk exposure is pricing applicable to our oil, natural gas and NGL production. Realized prices are mainly driven by the supply and demand for commodities and published market prices, after differentials and the impact of derivative activities. We enter into derivative instruments to hedge a portion of our production.

Derivative Instruments and Risk Management Activities

Our commodity price risk management strategy is designed to reduce the risk of commodity price volatility for our anticipated oil, natural gas and NGL production and to protect our cash flows, capital program and balance sheet. We have a Risk Management Committee that oversees our risk management activities, including our derivative strategy, and provides guidance in line with our overall business objectives. Our risk management activities are governed by a Corporate Risk Management Policy which is approved by the Board of Directors.

The primary purpose of our commodity derivatives is to reduce the effect of price volatility on a portion of our forecasted sales volumes and thereby protect a portion of our future cash flows. We may also use interest rate derivatives from time to time as part of our overall risk management strategy.

The commodity derivative instruments in which we may participate include swaps, collars and basis swaps. A commodity swap is an agreement whereby we pay a variable price based on a market-based index in exchange for a fixed price; a collar is an agreement that establishes a floor and a ceiling price for the volumes under contract; and a basis swap is an agreement whereby we swap pricing for production at one pricing point for another pricing point. While our derivative instruments reduce the volatility of commodity price changes, these instruments also limit the benefit of increases in commodity prices. Our Board of Directors has prudently set limits on the notional amount of future production that can be hedged.

Critical Accounting Estimates

The preparation of financial statements in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the U.S. requires us to make estimates, judgments and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial statements and the reported amounts of revenues and expenses during the reporting period. Actual amounts could differ from these estimates, and changes in these estimates are recorded when known. We consider the following to be our most critical accounting estimates that involve judgment and have reviewed these critical accounting estimates with the Audit Committee of our Board of Directors.

Purchase Accounting

Periodically, we acquire assets and assume liabilities in transactions accounted for as business combinations, such as the acquisition of the Williston Basin business of Grayson Mill. In connection with the acquisition, we allocated the $5.0 billion of purchase price consideration to the assets acquired and liabilities assumed based on estimated fair values as of the date of the acquisition. The preliminary purchase price assessment remains an ongoing process and is subject to change for up to one year subsequent to the closing date of the acquisition.

We made a number of assumptions in estimating the fair value of assets acquired and liabilities assumed in the acquisition. The most significant assumptions relate to the estimated fair values of proved and unproved oil and gas properties. Since sufficient market data was not available regarding the fair values of proved and unproved oil and gas properties, we prepared estimates and engaged third-party valuation experts. Significant judgments and assumptions are inherent in these estimates and include, among other things, estimates of reserve quantities, estimates of future commodity prices, drilling plans, expected development costs, lease operating costs, reserve risk adjustment factors and an estimate of an applicable market participant discount rate that reflects the risk of the underlying cash flow estimates.

Estimated fair values ascribed to assets acquired can have a significant impact on future results of operations presented in our financial statements. A higher fair value ascribed to a property results in higher DD&A expense, which results in lower net earnings. Fair values are based on estimates of future commodity prices, reserve quantities, development costs and operating costs. In the event that future commodity prices or reserve quantities are lower than those used as inputs to determine estimates of acquisition date fair values, the likelihood increases that certain costs may be determined to not be recoverable.

Oil and Gas Assets Accounting, Classification, Reserves & Valuation

Successful Efforts Method of Accounting and Classification

We utilize the successful efforts method of accounting for our oil and natural gas exploration and development activities which requires management’s assessment of the proper designation of wells and associated costs as developmental or exploratory. This classification assessment is dependent on the determination and existence of proved reserves, which is a critical estimate discussed in the section below. The classification of developmental and exploratory costs has a direct impact on the amount of costs we initially recognize as exploration expense or capitalize, then subject to DD&A calculations and impairment assessments and valuations.

Once a well is drilled, the determination that proved reserves have been discovered may take considerable time and requires both judgment and application of industry experience. Development wells are always capitalized. Costs associated with drilling an exploratory well are initially capitalized, or suspended, pending a determination as to whether proved reserves have been found. At the end of each quarter, management reviews the status of all suspended exploratory drilling costs to determine whether the costs should continue to remain capitalized or shall be expensed. When making this determination, management considers current activities,

40

near-term plans for additional exploratory or appraisal drilling and the likelihood of reaching a development program. If management determines future development activities and the determination of proved reserves are unlikely to occur, the associated suspended exploratory well costs are recorded as dry hole expense and reported in exploration expense in the consolidated statements of comprehensive earnings. Oil sales

Devon’s oil sales contracts are generally structured in one of two ways. First, production is sold at the wellhead at an agreed-upon index price, net of pricing differentials. In this scenario, revenue is recognized when control transfers to the purchaser at the wellhead at the net price received. Alternatively, production is delivered to the purchaser at a contractually agreed-upon delivery point where the purchaser takes custody, title and risk of loss of the product. Under this arrangement, a third party is paid to transport the product and Devon receives a specified index price from the purchaser with no transportation deduction. In this scenario, revenue is recognized when control transfers to the purchaser at the delivery point based on the price received from the purchaser. The third-party costs are recorded as gathering, processing and transportation expense as a component of production expenses in the consolidated statements of comprehensive earnings.

Natural gas and NGL sales

Under Devon’s natural gas processing contracts, natural gas is delivered to a midstream processing entity at the wellhead or the inlet of the midstream processing entity’s system. The midstream processing entity gathers and processes the natural gas and remits proceeds for the resulting sales of NGLs and residue gas. In these scenarios, Devon evaluates whether it is the principal or the agent in the transaction. Devon has concluded it is the principal under these contracts and the ultimate third party is the customer. Revenue is recognized on a gross basis, with gathering, processing and transportation fees presented as a component of production expenses in the consolidated statements of comprehensive earnings.

In certain natural gas processing agreements, Devon may elect to take residue gas and/or NGLs in-kind at the tailgate of the midstream entity’s processing plant and subsequently market the product. Through the marketing process, the product is delivered to the ultimate third-party purchaser at a contractually agreed-upon delivery point, and Devon receives a specified index price from the purchaser. In this scenario, revenue is recognized when control transfers to the purchaser at the delivery point based on the index price received from the purchaser. The gathering, processing and compression fees attributable to the gas processing contract, as well as any transportation fees incurred to deliver the product to the purchaser, are presented as gathering, processing and transportation expense as a component of production expenses in the consolidated statements of comprehensive earnings.

 Market Conditions and Commodity Prices
Our financial results depend on many factors, particularly commodity prices and our ability to find, develop and market our production on economically attractive terms. Commodity prices are affected by many factors outside of our control,

including changes in market supply and demand, which can be impacted by pipeline capacity constraints, inventory storage levels, basis differentials, weather conditions, and geopolitical, economic and other factors.

Oil prices were relatively steady in 2024 compared to 2023 as demand has continued for oil supply. Following global conflict and supply chain disruptions that drove high oil prices in 2022, OPEC+ reacted with supply reductions which helped to stabilize oil price levels in 2023. U.S. oil production was relatively flat from 2023 to 2024, which, when combined with OPEC+’s reductions, contributed to relatively steadier oil prices in 2023 and 2024. Additionally, while OPEC+ previously announced gradually increasing oil production over the course of 2025, several key members of OPEC+ have indicated their intent to delay such increases until the second half of 2025 and into 2026.

Natural gas prices trended down in 2024 compared to 2023 as strong production and relatively weak demand drove inventory levels above the five-year average. While natural gas prices have recovered from their lows in early 2024, natural gas prices in 2024 still trended lower overall compared to 2023. In response to the weakness of natural gas prices, we reduced our capital expenditures in the Marcellus Shale and also strategically curtailed our natural gas production in the basin from August 2024 through November 2024, resulting in an estimated curtailment of 232 MMcf per day of net production during that period. Natural gas prices increased slightly during the last quarter of 2024 and so far have continued to increase into early 2025 due to, among other factors, colder temperatures resulting in increased seasonal demand.

Defined Contribution Plans Devon sponsors defined contribution plans covering its employees. Such plans include its 401(k) plan and enhanced contribution plan. Devon makes matching contributions and additional retirement contributions, with the matching contributions being primarily based upon percentages of annual compensation and years of service. In addition, each plan is subject to regulatory limitations by the U.S. government. Devon contributed $ 44 million, $ 38 million and $ 37 million to these plans in 2024, 2023 and 2022, respectively. Defined Benefit Plans Devon has various non-contributory defined benefit pension plans, including qualified plans and nonqualified plans covering eligible employees and former employees meeting certain age and service requirements. Benefits under the defined benefit plans have

been closed to new employees and effective, as of December 31, 2020, Devon’s benefits committee approved a freeze of all future benefit accruals under the plans. Benefits are primarily funded from assets held in the plans’ trusts. Devon’s investment objective for its plans’ assets is to achieve stability of the funded status while providing long-term growth of invested capital and income to ensure benefit payments can be funded when required. Devon has established certain investment strategies, including target allocation percentages and permitted and prohibited investments, designed to mitigate risks inherent with investing. Devon’s target allocations for its plan assets are 70 % fixed income and 30 % equity. See the following discussion for Devon’s pension assets by asset class. Fixed-income – Devon’s fixed-income securities consist of U.S. Treasury obligations, bonds issued by investment-grade companies from diverse industries and asset-backed securities. These fixed-income securities do not consistently trade actively in an established market. The fair values of these Level 2 securities are estimated based upon rates available for securities with similar terms and maturity when active trading is not available and were $ 286 million and $ 418 million at December 31, 2024 and 2023, respectively. Equity – Devon’s equity securities include commingled global equity funds that invest in large, mid and small capitalization stocks across the world’s developed and emerging markets and international large cap equity securities. These equity securities can be sold on demand but are not actively traded. The fair values of these securities are based upon the net asset values provided by the investment managers and were $ 97 million and $ 44 million at December 31, 2024 and 2023, respectively. Other – Devon’s other securities include short-term investment funds that invest both long and short term using a variety of investment strategies. The fair value of these securities is based upon the net asset values provided by investment managers and were $ 64 million and $ 14 million at December 31, 2024 and 2023, respectively. Defined Postretirement Plans Devon also has defined benefit postretirement plans that provide benefits for substantially all qualifying retirees. Benefit obligations for such plans are estimated based on Devon’s future cost-sharing intentions. Devon’s funding policy for the plans is to fund the benefits as they become payable with available cash and cash equivalents.

11. Employee Benefit Plans
Postretirement Benefits

The Company provides health care benefits to certain former employees, including their spouses, eligible dependents and surviving spouses (retirees). These benefits are commonly called postretirement benefits. The health care plans are contributory, with participants’ contributions adjusted annually. Most employees that participate in the plan become eligible for these benefits when they meet certain age and service requirements at retirement.

At the end of 2024 and 2023, the Company provided postretirement benefits to 267and 290retirees and their dependents, respectively.

During 2022, the Company amended its postretirement plans to phase out all postretirement benefits and freeze future participation in the plan. Certain employees were grandfathered under the plan amendment and remain eligible for future participation in the pre-65 plan upon their retirement based on certain age and years of service criteria, while the post-65 benefit for all plan participants that reach the age of 65 after December 31, 2022, including current retirees participating in the pre-65 plan, was eliminated. Existing retirees participating in both the pre-65 and post-65 plans prior to December 31, 2022 will continue to receive benefits under the plan until the age of 65 in the case of the pre-65 participants, or voluntary termination of benefits or by death in the case of post-65 participants.

Retirement Savings Plan

The Company has a Retirement Savings Plan (“RSP”), which is a defined contribution plan. The Company matches a portion of employees’ contributions in cash. Participation in the RSP is voluntary and all employees of the Company are eligible to participate. The Company matches employee contributions dollar-for-dollar, up to the maximum Internal Revenue Service (“IRS”) limit, on the first sixpercent of an employee’s pre-tax earnings. The RSP also provides for discretionary contributions in an amount equal to 10percent of an eligible plan participant’s salary and bonus.

In connection with the merger with Cimarex Energy Co. (now known as Coterra Energy Operating Co, or “Cimarex”), the Company assumed the Cimarex Energy Co. 401(k) Plan (the “401(k) Plan”) with respect to Cimarex employees. The Company maintained this plan throughout the integration process and terminated this plan effective December 31, 2022, with all legacy Cimarex employees becoming eligible for the Company’s RSP effective January 1, 2023.

During the years ended December 31, 2024, 2023 and 2022, the Company made aggregate contributions to the RSP and 401(k) Plan of $ 19million, $ 19million and $ 12million, respectively, which are included in G&A expense in the Consolidated Statement of Operations. The Company’s common stock was an investment option within the RSP and the 401(k) Plan through December 31, 2022, at which time the Company eliminated this option.

81

Deferred Compensation Plans

The Company has deferred compensation plans which are available to officers and select employees and act as a supplement to the RSP. The Internal Revenue Code does not cap the amount of compensation that may be taken into account for purposes of determining contributions to the deferred compensation plans and does not impose limitations on the amount of contributions to the deferred compensation plans. At the present time, the Company anticipates making a contribution to the deferred compensation plans on behalf of a participant in the event that Internal Revenue Code limitations cause a participant to receive less than the Company contribution under the RSP.

The assets of the deferred compensation plans are held in a rabbi trust and are subject to additional risk of loss in the event of bankruptcy or insolvency of the Company.

Under the deferred compensation plans, the participants direct the deemed investment of amounts credited to their accounts. The trust assets are invested in mutual funds that cover the investment spectrum from equity to money market. The mutual funds are publicly traded and have market prices that are readily available. Settlement payments are made to participants in cash, either in a lump sum or in periodic installments.

Stock-Based Compensation

During 2024, EOG maintained various stock-based compensation plans as discussed below. Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP). Stock-based compensation expense is calculated based upon the grant date estimated fair value of the awards, net of forfeitures, based upon EOG's historical employee turnover rate. Compensation expense is amortized over the shorter of the vesting period or the period from the grant date to the date the employee becomes eligible for retirement without requiring company approval, with a minimum amortization period of one year.

Stock-based compensation expense is included on the Consolidated Statements of Income and Comprehensive Income based upon the job functions of the employees receiving the grants. Acquisitions and Divestitures

Grayson Mill Acquisition On September 27, 2024, Devon completed its acquisition of the Williston Basin business of Grayson Mill for total consideration of approximately $ 5.0 billion, consisting of $ 3.5 billion of cash and approximately 37.3 million shares of Devon common stock, including purchase price adjustments. Devon funded the cash portion of the purchase price through cash on hand and debt financing. For additional information regarding the debt financing, see Note 13 . Purchase Price Allocation This transaction has been accounted for using the acquisition method of accounting. Under the acquisition method of accounting, the assets and liabilities of Grayson Mill and its subsidiaries have been recorded at their respective fair values as of the date of completion of the acquisition and added to Devon’s. The preliminary purchase price assessment remains an ongoing process and is subject to change for up to one year subsequent to the closing date of the acquisition. Determining the fair value of the assets and liabilities of Grayson Mill requires judgment and certain assumptions to be made, the most significant of these being related to the valuation of Grayson Mill’s oil and gas properties. The inputs and assumptions related to the oil and gas properties are categorized as level 3 in the fair value hierarchy.

Cash Flow

Executive Overview

 On September 27, 2024, we acquired the Williston Basin business of Grayson Mill for total consideration of approximately $5.0 billion, consisting of $3.5 billion of cash and approximately 37.3 million shares of Devon common stock, including purchase price adjustments. We funded the cash portion of the purchase price through cash on hand and debt financing. On April 1, 2025, we completed an asset exchange transaction with an industry counterparty in which we exchanged certain non-core assets located in the Delaware and Williston basins for core assets located in the Delaware Basin. These transactions complement our existing asset portfolio and are consistent with our disciplined capital allocation framework and our strategy to build long-term value through high-return development projects in the core of our basins.

 As evidenced by this acquisition, we remain focused on building economic value by executing on our strategic priorities of moderating production growth, emphasizing capital and operational efficiencies, optimizing reinvestment rates to maximize free cash flow, maintaining low leverage, delivering cash returns to our shareholders and pursuing operational excellence. Our recent performance highlights for the first quarter of 2025 include the following items for the first quarter of 2025:

 •Oil production totaled 388 MBbls/d, exceeding our plan by 1%.

 •As of March 31, 2025, completed approximately 73% of our authorized $5.0 billion share repurchase program, with approximately 75 million of our common shares purchased for approximately $3.6 billion, or $48.25 per share, since inception of the plan.

 •In May 2025, announced a cash dividend in the amount of $0.22 per share payable on June 28, 2025 to shareholders of record at the close of business on June 14, 2025. The dividend declared for the second quarter of 2025 includes only a fixed dividend component of $0.22 per share and will total approximately $154 million.

 •We continued to maintain a strong balance sheet and liquidity profile. As of March 31, 2025, we had $0.8 billion of cash and $3.0 billion of available borrowing capacity under our Senior Credit Facility.

 •We are focused on executing our development programs safely and efficiently, while continuing to advance our environmental, social and governance initiatives.

 Capital Resources, Uses and Liquidity

 Our primary source of capital is cash flows from operations and our primary uses of capital are capital expenditures, share repurchases, dividends, debt service and acquisitions. We also have access to a Senior Credit Facility and the capital markets to supplement cash flows from operations as needed. Our capital program remains flexible and is designed to be responsive to changes in commodity prices and service costs. We will continue to evaluate our capital allocation to maximize free cash flow and create value for shareholders, while maintaining a strong balance sheet and liquidity profile.

 Outlook

 Our 2025 development program will remain focused in our highest-return asset areas. We will continue to monitor market conditions and adjust activity levels as needed to optimize returns and free cash flow. The declaration and payment of any future dividend, whether fixed or variable, will remain at the discretion of our Board of Directors and will depend on our financial results, cash requirements, future prospects and other factors deemed relevant by the Board.

Introduction

We are a leading independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company whose operations are focused onshore in the United States. Our operations are currently focused in five core areas: the Delaware Basin, Eagle Ford, Anadarko Basin, Williston Basin and Powder River Basin. Our asset base is underpinned by premium acreage in the economic core of the Delaware Basin and our diverse, top-tier resource plays provide a deep inventory of opportunities for years to come. In the third quarter of 2022, we acquired additional producing properties and leasehold interests in both the Williston Basin and Eagle Ford that were complementary to our existing acreage, offered operational synergies and added additional high-quality inventory to our portfolio. Moving forward into 2024, we plan to refine our capital allocation by further concentrating investment in the Delaware Basin. By shifting more capital to the core of this world-class basin and high-grading activity across the rest of our diversified portfolio, we anticipate delivering meaningful improvements to our capital efficiency which will position us to generate growth in free cash flow which can be returned to shareholders.

We remain focused on building economic value by executing on our strategic priorities of moderating production growth, emphasizing capital and operational efficiencies, optimizing reinvestment rates to maximize free cash flow, maintaining low leverage, delivering cash returns to our shareholders and pursuing ESG excellence. Common Stock and Dividends

We have paid a quarterly fixed dividend since May 30, 1993 and since 2021 have also paid variable dividends.

On February7, 2024, our Board of Directors (our “Board”) approved a plan to increase the fixed portion of our dividend in 2024. In February, March, May and August of 2024, respectively, our Board declared fixed-plus-variable per share dividends of $0.44, $0.49, $0.44 and $0.57, which were paid in March, June, September and December 2024. In February 2025, our Board declared a fixed-plus-variable dividend of $0.35 per share that will be paid in March 2025. Our Board’s determination of the amount of quarterly dividends is based on a number of factors, including the then-current and projected level of free cash flow available for dividends, our liquidity position and other considerations.

In May 2023, our Board approved a new share repurchase program that authorizes the repurchase of up to $3.0billion of our common stock through December 31, 2025. As of December31, 2024, we had repurchased a total of 64.2million shares for $3.0billion, or $46.78 per share, since the start of our repurchase programs in 2021. The Company does not enter into derivatives for trading or speculative purposes. The effectiveness of these strategies can vary based on market conditions.

The Company expects to continue paying regular quarterly dividends and opportunistically repurchasing shares, subject to Board approval and market conditions. EOG’s ability to execute its capital program and return capital to stockholders will depend on operating performance, commodity prices, access to services and materials, and other factors outside its control.

Gathering, Processing and Transportation

Gathering, processing and transportation costs principally consist of expenditures to prepare and transport production downstream from the wellhead, including gathering, fuel, and compression, along with processing costs, which are incurred to extract NGLs from the raw natural gas stream. Gathering costs also include costs associated with operating our gas gathering infrastructure, including operating and maintenance expenses. Costs vary by operating area and will fluctuate with increases or decreases in production volumes, contractual fees, and changes in fuel and compression costs.

Gathering, processing and transportation increased $1 million primarily due to higher gathering and transportation costs in the Permian Basin related to higher production and higher transportation rates, partially offset by lower gathering charges in the Marcellus Shale related to lower production.

Taxes Other Than Income

Taxes other than income consist of production (or severance) taxes, drilling impact fees, ad valorem taxes and other taxes. State and local taxing authorities assess these taxes, with production taxes being based on the volume or value of production, drilling impact fees being based on drilling activities and prevailing natural gas prices and ad valorem taxes being based on the value of properties.

6

 2025 OUTLOOK
Our 2025 full year capital program is expected to be in the range of approximately $2.1 to $2.3 billion. This estimate includes exploration, development and other capital expenditures and excludes acquisitions. Projected spending includes drilling and completion activities, leasing activity, infrastructure, and other capital spending. Additionally, we expect to incur approximately $100 million to $150 million for gathering systems infrastructure, saltwater disposal and other spend.

In 2025, we expect to average approximately 11 drilling rigs and four completion crews operating in the Permian Basin, two drilling rigs and one completion crew operating in the Marcellus Shale, and one drilling rig and one half of a completion crew operating in the Anadarko Basin.

In the normal course of our business, we will continue to assess our capital program and allocation of capital to our assets. We expect to be disciplined and flexible in our capital allocation to optimize returns and free cash flow, considering the prevailing commodity price environment and other economic factors. We will also evaluate opportunities to enhance our asset base through acquisitions and divestitures, as we have done historically, to further strengthen our portfolio and balance sheet. We intend to maintain a strong focus on operational efficiency and cost management as we execute our capital program. Our capital allocation framework is designed to balance reinvestment in our business with returning cash to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases as appropriate in different commodity price environments.

Capital. EOG plans to continue to focus a substantial portion of its 2025 capital program on high-return drilling and completion activities in its major producing areas in the United States. In particular, EOG will be focused on United States drilling activity in the Delaware Basin play, Eagle Ford play, Powder River Basin play and South Texas Dorado play, where EOG has made significant investments in production facilities and gathering systems for crude oil, NGLs and natural gas. EOG will also continue its exploration, exploitation and development activities in other plays in the United States. EOG plans to allocate its 2025 capital program to optimize the development of its assets in the highest return drilling locations in these plays. This planned activity is expected to help EOG continue to generate high rates-of-return. To further enhance the economics of these plays, EOG expects to continue to improve well performance and mitigate cost inflation through continued efficiency gains and by locking in certain service costs for drilling and completion activities. In addition, EOG expects to spend capital on international exploration, acreage, evaluating new prospects, gathering and processing infrastructure, transportation infrastructure and environmental projects.

The total anticipated 2025 capital expenditures of approximately $6.2 billion to $6.4 billion, including exploration and development drilling, facilities, leasehold acquisitions, capitalized interest and other property, plant and equipment, are expected to be funded through internally generated cash flow. EOG believes this level of capital expenditures is sufficient to support its current operations and growth plans, subject to commodity price fluctuations and other market conditions.

Marketing Activities

Oil, Gas and NGL Marketing

The spot markets for oil, gas and NGLs are subject to volatility as supply and demand factors fluctuate. As detailed below, we sell our production under both long-term (one year or more) and short-term (less than one year) agreements at prices negotiated with third parties. Regardless of the term of the contract, the vast majority of our production is sold at variable, or market-sensitive, prices.

Additionally, we may enter into financial hedging arrangements or fixed-price contracts associated with a portion of our oil, gas and NGL production. These activities are intended to support targeted price levels and to manage our exposure to price fluctuations. SeeNote 3in “Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data” of this report for further information.

Contract Assets and Liabilities

We recognize a receivable when our right to consideration becomes unconditional, typically upon delivery to the purchaser. Contract assets and liabilities are recorded when either party to the contract has performed. As of March 31, 2025, we had no significant contract assets or liabilities related to our revenue contracts.

Revenue Recognition

We recognize revenue at a point in time when control of the product transfers to the customer, typically at the wellhead or a designated delivery point. Revenue is measured as the amount of consideration we expect to receive in exchange for transferring goods or providing services, net of allowances and price adjustments. Our contracts contain customary quality and volume adjustments.

Marketing, Gathering and Transportation

Federal legislation and regulatory controls have historically affected the natural gas industry and the transportation of natural gas through interstate pipelines. In the past, the Federal Power Commission (“FPC”) and, subsequently, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) regulated the field prices for natural gas, and the FERC regulates the interstate transportation and sale for resale of natural gas for ultimate consumption. Regulation of production of natural gas and its gathering and processing may also be performed by state agencies. In 1978, Congress enacted the Natural Gas Policy Act (“NGPA”) which removed price controls from certain categories of gas. The NGPA also provided for a phased deregulation of wellhead prices for “new” natural gas while subjecting most producers to the jurisdiction of the FERC in other respects. In 1989, Congress enacted the Natural Gas Wellhead Decontrol Act that removed all remaining NGPA price controls on wellhead sales of natural gas as of January 1, 1993. Sales of natural gas, oil and NGLs by producers can be made at freely negotiated prices but are affected by, among other things, the availability, terms, cost and capacity of gathering and transportation services and by the Interstate Natural Gas Transportation market, and, for oil, the availability, terms, cost and capacity of transportation by pipeline, rail, truck and barge.

Gathering systems, pipelines and processing facilities are subject to complex federal, state and local laws and regulations that can affect a producer’s operations. State public utility commissions regulate local distribution companies and intrastate pipelines that transport and distribute natural gas. The rates charged by local distribution companies, such as utilities, are generally subject to regulation by state public utility commissions. In addition, the FERC regulates the sale for resale of natural gas in interstate commerce under the Natural Gas Act of 1938. The intrastate transportation of natural gas and NGLs can also be subject to state regulation. Changes in regulations or the imposition of additional requirements could increase costs and affect the economics of marketing, gathering and transportation activities.

Marketing
In 2024, EOG continued its diversified approach to marketing its production to a wide variety of purchasers, including refiners, marketers, integrated major oil companies and industrial users. EOG sells production at market-responsive prices under both short-term and long-term contracts. The terms of these contracts vary by commodity and region and may include delivery obligations, take-or-pay provisions and index-based pricing mechanisms. EOG’s marketing strategy seeks to maximize netbacks and minimize basis risk by leveraging access to multiple pipelines, gathering systems, terminals and storage facilities.

EOG markets its United States crude oil production from its major operating areas, including the Delaware Basin, South Texas and the Rocky Mountain area, through a combination of pipeline transport and, where necessary, trucking arrangements. EOG’s natural gas production is marketed to a range of purchasers, with sales points at or near the wellhead, regional hubs and downstream markets. EOG also markets NGLs extracted at processing plants under agreements with midstream providers and purchasers. The company utilizes a portfolio of contracts that include both fixed and floating pricing components and evaluates opportunities to enhance price realizations through basis hedges and other risk management tools.

EOG endeavors to maintain flexibility in its marketing operations to respond to changing market conditions, infrastructure constraints and regional pricing differentials. The company’s marketing activities are supported by internal commercial teams with expertise in logistics, scheduling and market analytics. EOG’s marketing arrangements generally do not obligate it to deliver fixed quantities of commodities beyond its expected production, and any such obligations are expected to be sourced from future production of available reserves.

In 2024, EOG processed certain of its United States natural gas volumes at third-party processing facilities, extracting NGLs. NGLs were sold at prevailing market prices, and natural gas residue was sold under a combination of indexed and negotiated pricing.

Executive Overview

Devon is a leading independent energy company with a large and geographically diverse portfolio of crude oil, natural gas and NGLs assets. Our core operations are located in four North American resource plays: the Delaware Basin, the Anadarko Basin, the Williston Basin and the Eagle Ford. Through focused execution, operational excellence and disciplined capital allocation, we strive to efficiently develop reserves and grow production over time while maintaining a strong balance sheet and returning capital to shareholders.

We remain focused on building economic value by executing on our strategic priorities of moderating production growth, emphasizing capital and operational efficiencies, optimizing reinvestment rates to maximize free cash flow, maintaining low leverage, delivering cash returns to our shareholders and pursuing operational excellence. Our first-quarter 2025 performance highlights for these priorities include the following items:

• Oil production averaged 348 MBbls/d, an increase from the prior-year quarter, benefiting from strong well productivity and improved cycle times.

• We completed approximately 73% of our authorized $5.0 billion share repurchase program, with approximately 77 million of our common shares repurchased for approximately $3.6 billion since inception of the plan.

• We exited the quarter with $3.9 billion of liquidity, including $1.2 billion of cash, and we retained investment-grade credit ratings.

• We generated operating cash flow that exceeded capital expenditures, supporting continued shareholder returns and balance sheet strength.

• We paid dividends of $163 million during the quarter.

• We continued to advance integration of the Williston Basin assets acquired in late 2024, progressing development plans and capturing operational synergies.

Capital Resources, Uses and Liquidity

We believe our strong financial position and operational flexibility provide us with the capacity to fund our capital program, meet existing commitments and continue returning capital to shareholders. Our sources of liquidity include cash on hand, cash generated from operations and, as needed, our commercial paper program supported by our revolving credit facility. In addition, we may access the debt and equity capital markets from time to time, subject to market conditions. We monitor commodity prices, service costs and other market factors and may adjust our activity and capital allocation accordingly.

We prioritize investments with the highest risk-adjusted returns, focusing on efficient development of our core assets and optimization of our cost structure. We remain committed to a disciplined reinvestment rate and to maintaining a resilient balance sheet. Our capital allocation framework is designed to enhance long-term value creation and sustain competitive cash returns through the cycle.

Outlook

We expect to continue executing our development plans across our core assets, with an emphasis on maximizing capital efficiency, maintaining low leverage and returning cash to shareholders through a combination of our fixed dividend, potential variable dividends and share repurchases, subject to market conditions and Board approval.

Debt Ratings

We receive debt ratings from the major ratings agencies in the U.S. In determining our debt ratings, the agencies consider a number of qualitative and quantitative items including, but not limited to, commodity pricing levels, our liquidity, asset quality, reserve mix, debt levels, cost structure, planned asset sales and size and scale of our production. Our credit rating from Standard and Poor’s Financial Services is BBB with a stable outlook. Our credit rating from Fitch is BBB+ with a stable outlook. Our credit rating from Moody’s Investor Service is Baa2 with a stable outlook. Any rating downgrades may result in additional letters of credit or cash collateral being posted under certain contractual arrangements.

There are no “rating triggers” in any of our contractual debt obligations that would accelerate scheduled maturities should our debt rating fall below a specified level. However, a downgrade could adversely impact our interest rate on any credit facility borrowings and the ability to economically access debt markets in the future.

In addition to the fixed quarterly dividend, we may pay a variable dividend or complete share repurchases. Each quarter’s free cash flow, which is a non-GAAP measure, is computed as operating cash flow (a GAAP measure) before balance sheet changes less capital expenditures. The declaration and payment of any future dividend, whether fixed or variable, will remain at the full discretion of our Board of Directors and will depend on our financial results, cash requirements, future prospects and other factors deemed relevant by the Board.

Revenue Recognition. EOG presents disaggregated revenues by type and geographic area to provide a meaningful depiction of the nature, amount, timing and uncertainty of revenue and cash flows. Disaggregated revenue information for the years ended December 31, 2024, 2023 and 2022 is presented in the consolidated statements of income and Note 11. EOG has determined that disaggregation of revenues by product type (crude oil and condensate, natural gas liquids (NGLs) and natural gas) and by geographic areas defined as operating segments provides the most useful information to understand the nature and risks of EOG’s revenue streams.

Revenues are recognized for the sale of crude oil and condensate, NGLs and natural gas when control of the product transfers to the customer, which occurs at the point in time when the product is delivered to a third-party purchaser at a delivery point specified in the contract. EOG’s performance obligations are satisfied at a point in time (as opposed to over time), and revenue is recognized in the amount of consideration to which EOG expects to be entitled in exchange for transferring the product to the customer. The transaction price is based on the contractual price, which is usually a market-based price, and adjustments for quality, location differentials and other factors may be made as specified in the contract. Contract durations are typically less than one year and therefore EOG applies the practical expedient of not disclosing the transaction price allocated to remaining performance obligations for contracts with an original expected duration of one year or less.

For certain arrangements, EOG may sell volumes of crude oil and condensate, NGLs and natural gas at the wellhead or at a point prior to the processing of raw production. In other arrangements, EOG may retain control of the product through the processing stage and recognize revenue when control transfers to a customer after processing. EOG evaluates whether it is the principal or an agent in such transactions. When EOG is the principal in the sale of products, revenues and expenses are presented on a gross basis. When EOG is an agent, revenues are presented net of the amounts due to the principal.

EOG records contract assets or contract liabilities when either party to the contract has performed but both parties have not fully completed their obligations. EOG does not have any significant contract assets or contract liabilities as its contracts generally provide for payment within a short period of time after delivery. EOG also records balances of accounts receivable from contracts with customers as trade receivables and evaluates expected credit losses on such receivables in accordance with ASC 326. See Note 11.

Revenue Recognition

Upstream Revenues

Upstream revenues include the sale of oil, gas and NGL production; gathering, processing and marketing revenues; and other revenues. Revenue is recognized when performance obligations are satisfied, which is generally when production is delivered and control has transferred and collectability of the revenue is probable. The price received for oil, gas and NGL production is generally a market-based price. Gathering, processing and marketing revenues are recognized gross when the Company is acting as principal and net when acting as an agent. Oil, gas and NGL sales are presented separately from such revenues in the consolidated statements of comprehensive earnings.

Accounts Receivable

Accounts receivable are recorded at the invoiced amount and do not bear interest. The Company maintains an allowance for credit losses based on historical experience and expected credit losses, which is recorded as a reduction to accounts receivable with a corresponding charge to other operating items in the consolidated statements of comprehensive earnings. The Company monitors credit quality by reviewing aging, collection experience and creditworthiness of counterparties. The Company considers accounts receivable past due when they are not collected in accordance with contractual terms.

Contract Balances

The Company does not have significant contract assets or contract liabilities as its performance obligations are typically satisfied at a point in time and payment is generally due shortly after control transfers. The Company has elected the practical expedient not to disclose information about remaining performance obligations that have original expected durations of one year or less.

Executive Overview

 We are a leading independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company with operations focused onshore in the United States. Our portfolio of assets provides multi-year production growth and opportunities to enhance returns through disciplined capital allocation and operational excellence. We maintain a balanced approach to investment across our core development programs and high-return exploration opportunities to ensure sustainable, capital-efficient growth, providing a deep inventory of opportunities for years to come.

 On September 27, 2024, we acquired the Williston Basin business of Grayson Mill for total consideration of approximately $5.0 billion, subject to customary post-closing adjustments. The acquisition allows us to efficiently expand our operated position in the Williston Basin, adding high-quality inventory and infrastructure synergies. We funded the transaction with a combination of cash on hand, borrowings under our commercial paper program and the issuance of senior notes. We also issued approximately 37.3 million shares of common stock as part of the consideration.

 Our strategy is to deliver sustainable free cash flow through the cycle by focusing on capital discipline, cost structure improvements and portfolio optimization. We prioritize high-return projects, optimize development plans to maximize value and continuously improve drilling and completion efficiencies. We maintain investment flexibility and will adjust our activity based on commodity price outlooks and market conditions.

 Market Conditions. Commodity prices and service cost inflation remain key drivers of our financial performance. Oil prices were volatile during the three-month period ended March 31, 2025 compared to the prior-year period, influenced by global supply-demand dynamics and geopolitical events. Natural gas prices remained challenged due to elevated storage levels and milder winter weather, which affected pricing across our operating regions. We continue to mitigate price risk through a combination of firm transportation, basis hedges and, where appropriate, commodity derivatives.

 Outlook. For the remainder of 2025, we plan to invest in development activity that we expect will sustain oil production volumes and improve capital efficiency. We will continue integrating the acquired Williston Basin assets, expect to capture synergies from shared infrastructure, and remain focused on maintaining a strong balance sheet and investment-grade credit metrics. We will also evaluate opportunities for portfolio high-grading through targeted acquisitions and non-core divestitures.

 Non-GAAP Measures. We use certain non-GAAP financial measures, including free cash flow and field-level cash margin, to evaluate our performance and allocate capital. These measures are not defined by GAAP and should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for GAAP measures. Refer to “Non-GAAP Measures” for definitions and reconciliations.

 Definitions. Unless otherwise noted, references to “Devon,” the “Company,” “we,” “us” and “our” refer to Devon Energy Corporation and its consolidated subsidiaries. “Boe” means barrel of oil equivalent. “NGL” means natural gas liquids. “DCF” means discounted cash flow. “Matterhorn” refers to Matterhorn Express Pipeline, LLC and, as applicable, its subsidiaries.

The increase (decrease) in our capital expenditures across the basins was impacted by well activity, service costs, and project timing. Capital expenditures were lower in the Delaware Basin due to optimization of development activity and cost efficiencies. Eagle Ford capital decreased year over year, primarily due to a reduction in drilling and completion activities. The Anadarko Basin capital increased, reflecting continued development of high-return inventory.

We expect to continue allocating the majority of our capital to high-return development opportunities in the Delaware Basin. Additionally, we will selectively invest in infrastructure and midstream projects that support growth and improve overall margins. The timing of capital expenditures will depend upon commodity prices, service availability, and project readiness.

We expect our 2025 capital expenditure budget to be approximately $4.0 billion to $4.4 billion, excluding acquisitions and divestitures. The range reflects optionality in our program to flex activity with commodity prices and to support our objectives of funding the capital program within operating cash flow and maintaining a strong balance sheet.

We plan to allocate capital to projects with the best returns within our portfolio, including continued development and delineation of our acreage in the Delaware Basin and high-return opportunities in the Rockies and Eagle Ford. We expect to fund our capital program with operating cash flow and cash on hand. We may access the capital markets, as necessary, to maintain liquidity and flexibility.

Our capital program prioritizes maximizing free cash flow and returns to shareholders through our fixed-plus-variable dividend framework and share repurchases. We will continue to evaluate our capital allocation based on market conditions and business performance.

Our 2024 capital investments included development drilling, facilities, and infrastructure projects to support production growth and improve operating efficiency. We also incurred capital related to midstream infrastructure to improve processing capacity and reduce flaring.

The increase in our capital expenditures in 2024 primarily reflects higher activity levels in certain core areas and inflationary impacts on service and equipment costs. These increases were partially offset by efficiency gains and optimization of development plans.

We expect to fund our capital expenditures primarily with cash provided by operating activities. We may also utilize cash on hand and our credit facility, as needed. We will continue to focus on maintaining a strong balance sheet and investment-grade credit metrics.

Acquisitions and Divestitures

During 2024, we executed certain acquisitions and divestitures that impacted our asset base and future development plans. These transactions support our strategic objectives by high-grading our portfolio, increasing scale in core areas, and improving capital efficiency.

We continually evaluate our asset portfolio to identify opportunities to divest non-core properties and to acquire assets that enhance our inventory and returns. The timing and amount of future acquisitions and divestitures will depend on market conditions and strategic fit.

The primary drivers of changes in capital expenditures were the timing of development activity and costs for materials and services. We also incurred capital for facilities and infrastructure to support current and future production.

We actively manage our capital program to adjust to changing market conditions and to achieve our financial and operational goals. Our capital planning process considers commodity price outlook, service availability, project economics, and organizational capacity.

Contractual Obligations

Tax Contingencies

As we are regularly audited by tax authorities, we have and will continue to have tax positions under audit or subject to audit. The outcome of these audits or effective settlement of these issues is difficult to predict. The resolution of these positions could result in increases or decreases to our recorded tax liabilities, which could impact our effective tax rate. We recognize interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits as a component of income tax expense.

We have established reserves where appropriate for these matters. The timing of resolution of these matters is uncertain and could span multiple periods. Our tax positions are based on interpretations of applicable tax laws and regulations and are subject to change as laws and interpretations change. We believe our tax positions are reasonable and will be sustained upon examination; however, the outcome of audits could differ from the positions taken and may require adjustments.

We intend to continue to work cooperatively with tax authorities and to resolve open matters as efficiently as possible. We also monitor and evaluate legislative developments and administrative guidance that could impact our tax positions and overall tax profile.

EOG records asset retirement obligations for legal obligations associated with the retirement of long-lived assets, primarily plugging and abandonment of wells and removal of related facilities. AROs are recognized at fair value when incurred and are subsequently accreted to their estimated settlement value. Revisions to estimates may occur due to changes in expected timing and cost of abandonment activities and changes in reserve lives resulting from drilling and development activities or commodity price fluctuations. Accretion expense is recognized over the remaining useful life of the related assets.

Leases
Devon’s right-of-use operating lease assets are for certain leases of office facilities, field offices, drilling rigs and equipment, vehicles, and other assets. Our right-of-use finance lease assets are related to real estate. During 2023, Devon's operating lease assets were primarily impacted by new leases for drilling rigs and compression equipment, as well as the renewal of existing office facility leases. Lease liabilities represent the present value of the Company’s future lease payments, discounted using the Company’s incremental borrowing rate as the rate implicit in the lease is not readily determinable.

Operating leases typically include options to renew and termination options at the Company’s discretion. Lease terms include such options when they are reasonably certain to be exercised. Certain lease agreements contain variable lease payments, which are expensed as incurred and are not included in the measurement of lease liabilities. Variable lease payments include amounts that depend on an index or rate, such as the Consumer Price Index, or on usage or performance. Devon does not separate non-lease components from lease components and accounts for the combined components as a single lease component.

EBITDAX and Field-Level Cash Margin

To assess the performance of our assets, we use EBITDAX and Field-Level Cash Margin. We compute EBITDAX as net earnings before income tax expense; financing costs, net; exploration expenses; DD&A; asset impairments; asset disposition gains and losses; non-cash share-based compensation; non-cash valuation changes for derivatives and financial instruments; restructuring and transaction costs; accretion on discounted liabilities; and other items not related to our normal operations. Field-Level Cash Margin is computed as oil, gas and NGL revenues less production expenses. Production expenses consist of lease operating, gathering, processing and transportation expenses, as well as production and property taxes.

We exclude financing costs from EBITDAX to assess our operating results without regard to our financing methods or capital structure. Exploration expenses and asset disposition gains and losses are excluded from EBITDAX because they generally are not indicators of operating efficiency for a given reporting period. DD&A and impairments are excluded from EBITDAX because capital expenditures are evaluated at the time capital costs are incurred. We exclude share-based compensation, valuation changes, restructuring and transaction costs, accretion on discounted liabilities and other items from EBITDAX because they are not considered a measure of asset operating performance.

We believe EBITDAX and Field-Level Cash Margin provide information useful in assessing our operating and financial performance across periods. EBITDAX and Field-Level Cash Margin as defined by Devon may not be comparable to similarly titled measures used by other companies and should be considered in conjunction with net earnings from operations.

Estimated fair values ascribed to assets acquired can have a significant impact on future results of operations presented in Devon’s financial statements. A higher fair value ascribed to a property results in higher DD&A expense, which results in lower net earnings. Fair values are based on estimates of future commodity prices, reserve quantities, development costs and operating costs. In the event that future commodity prices or reserve quantities are lower than those used as inputs to determine estimates of acquisition date fair values, the likelihood increases that certain costs may be determined to not be recoverable. For additional information regarding our critical accounting policies and estimates, see our 2024 Annual Report on Form 10-K . Non-GA AP Measures We utilize “core earnings attributable to Devon” and “core earnings per share attributable to Devon” that are not required by or presented in accordance with GAAP. These non-GAAP measures are not alternatives to GAAP measures and should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for analysis of our results reported under GAAP. Core earnings attributable to Devon, as well as the per share amount, represent net earnings excluding certain non-cash and other items that are typically excluded by securities analysts in their published estimates of our financial results. Our non-GAAP measures are typically used as a quarterly performance measure. Amounts excluded relate to asset dispositions, non-cash asset impairments (including unproved asset impairments), deferred tax asset valuation allowance, fair value changes in derivative financial instruments and restructuring and transaction costs. We believe these non-GAAP measures facilitate comparisons of our performance to earnings estimates published by securities analysts. We also believe these non-GAAP measures can facilitate comparisons of our performance between periods and to the performance of our peers. Term Loan

In December 2024, we entered into a $1.0 billion delayed draw term loan credit agreement with Toronto Dominion (Texas) LLC, as administrative agent, and certain other lenders and issuing banks (the “Term Loan”), which consists of a $500 million Tranche A Term Loan and a $500 million Tranche B Term Loan. The Tranche A Term Loan matures two years after funding, and the Tranche B Term Loan matures three years after funding. Borrowings under the Term Loan can be prepaid without penalty. As of December 31, 2024, we had no borrowings outstanding under the Term Loan and $1.0 billion of available commitments.

In January 2025, we borrowed $500 million under the Tranche A Term Loan to partially fund the closing of the FME acquisition and $500 million under the Tranche B Term Loan to partially fund the closing of the Avant acquisition.

Borrowings under the Term Loan bear interest at a rate per annum equal to, at our option, either (i) a term SOFR plus a 0.10 percent credit spread adjustment for all tenors or (ii) a base rate, plus an interest rate margin which ranges from 0 to 75 basis points for base rate loans, 100 to 175 basis points for Tranche A SOFR Term Loans and 112.5 to 187.5 basis points for Tranche B SOFR Term Loans based on our credit rating. The ticking fee on the average daily amount of the Tranche A commitments and Tranche B commitments is calculated at annual rates ranging from 10 basis points to 25 basis points based on our credit rating.

The Term Loan includes certain customary covenants, including the maintenance of a maximum leverage ratio of no more than 3.0 to 1.0 as of the last day of any fiscal quarter until such time as we have no other debt (other than our Credit Agreement) in a principal amount in excess of $75 million outstanding that has a financial maintenance covenant based on a leverage ratio, at which time the Term Loan requires maintenance of a ratio of total net debt to capitalization of no more than 65 percent (with all calculations based on definitions contained in the Term Loan).
