We returned $ billion to shareholders in 2024 through a combination of our fixed and variable dividends and share repurchases. We continue to target returning up to 70% of our free cash flow to shareholders, with the balance allocated to high-return reinvestment in our business and strengthening our balance sheet.

We expect to fund our 2025 capital program primarily with cash generated from operations, supplemented by cash on hand. Our capital program is flexible and may be adjusted based on commodity prices, service costs and other factors. We may also opportunistically access the capital markets or utilize asset sales to fund our activities and manage our leverage.

The timing and amount of future dividends and share repurchases, if any, will be at the discretion of our Board of Directors and will depend on, among other things, our future results of operations, financial condition, cash requirements and availability, contractual restrictions and other factors that our Board of Directors deems relevant. We may from time to time seek to retire or purchase our outstanding debt through cash purchases or exchanges for equity or debt securities, in open market purchases, privately negotiated transactions or otherwise. The amount of any such transactions could be material.

For additional information regarding our liquidity and capital resources, see “Liquidity and Capital Resources,” “Risk Factors” and the consolidated financial statements included in Item 8. “Financial Statements and Supplementary Data” in this report.

STRATEGY
Coterra is a premier U.S.-focused exploration and production company with positions in three prolific, oil and liquids-rich basins – the Permian Basin (Delaware), the Anadarko Basin and the Marcellus Shale. Our strategy is to deliver sustainable returns to shareholders by maintaining capital discipline, focusing on capital efficiency and margins, and returning meaningful cash to shareholders while maintaining a strong balance sheet. The following strategic priorities will help drive value creation and long-term success.

Generate Sustainable Returns. Our premier assets across multiple basins provide a deep inventory of high-return drilling opportunities. We prioritize investments that are expected to generate attractive full-cycle returns at conservative commodity price assumptions. Our capital program is designed to be flexible and resilient across commodity price cycles. We target maintenance-level capital spending that supports stable to modest growth in production and free cash flow.

Capital Allocation. We allocate capital to opportunities that meet our return thresholds and align with our strategic objectives. We evaluate projects on the basis of risk-adjusted returns, capital efficiency, and the potential to enhance our portfolio. We regularly high-grade our inventory and optimize our development plans to maximize value. Our capital allocation also includes investments in infrastructure to support efficient operations and reduce costs.

Shareholder Returns. We are committed to returning capital to shareholders through a combination of our fixed dividend, variable dividends and share repurchases. We believe this balanced approach provides flexibility to return cash to shareholders while maintaining the ability to invest in high-return projects and strengthen our balance sheet. Since the inception of our share repurchase program, we have repurchased shares of our common stock, and as of December 31, 2024, we had remaining authorization of approximately $ billion under our share repurchase program.

Balance Sheet Strength. We maintain a conservative financial profile with a focus on liquidity and low leverage. We seek to preserve financial flexibility to invest across commodity cycles and to take advantage of opportunities as they arise. Our goal is to sustain an investment-grade credit profile and maintain ample liquidity through cash on hand, cash flow from operations and availability under our credit facilities.

Operational Excellence and ESG. We are committed to safe and responsible operations. We focus on continuous improvement in operational efficiency, cost management and capital productivity. We also prioritize environmental stewardship, including emissions reductions, water management and land restoration, as well as community engagement and governance practices that support long-term value creation.

Portfolio Optimization. We continually assess our portfolio to identify opportunities to capture value through disciplined acquisitions and divestitures. We target assets that fit our strategic and financial objectives and divest assets that are non-core or lower-return. In 2024, we executed portfolio actions to improve our capital efficiency and focus on our highest-return opportunities.

Technology and Innovation. We leverage technology, data analytics and innovation to improve drilling and completion performance, optimize production and enhance capital efficiency. Our technical teams work across disciplines to apply best practices and rapidly implement improvements.

Risk Management. We proactively manage risks to our business, including commodity price volatility, operational risks, regulatory and legal risks and environmental risks. We use hedging strategies to protect a portion of our cash flows and returns and maintain a robust insurance program. We also conduct ongoing scenario and sensitivity analyses to inform decision-making and capital allocation.

Human Capital. Our people are critical to our success. We invest in talent development, diversity and inclusion, and fostering a culture of accountability, collaboration and innovation. We strive to attract and retain top talent by offering competitive compensation, comprehensive benefits and opportunities for professional growth.

Governance. Strong corporate governance underpins our strategy and supports long-term value creation. Our Board of Directors provides oversight of our strategy, risk management and capital allocation. We align management incentives with shareholder interests through performance-based compensation metrics focused on returns, free cash flow, capital efficiency and ESG performance.

Business and Industry Outlook

In 2024, Devon marked its 53rd anniversary in the oil and gas business and its 36th year as a public company. We generated $6.6 billion of operating cash flow in 2024 as a result of the strength of our portfolio of assets and our operational execution. Our portfolio benefited from the acquisition of Grayson Mill that allowed us to efficiently expand our oil production and operating scale while capturing a meaningful runway of highly economic drilling inventory. The transaction created immediate value within our financial framework by delivering sustainable accretion to earnings and free cash flow. Operating cash flow in 2024 remained consistent with 2023, despite a decline in commodity prices, due to operational outperformance, capital efficiency gains and the positive contributions from our Grayson Mill acquisition.

We remain committed to continuing our track record of industry leading return of capital to our shareholders, underpinned by low capital reinvestment rates and a disciplined, returns-driven strategy which is designed to be successful through economic cycles. In 2024, we returned approximately $2.0 billion of cash to shareholders through cash dividends and share repurchases, and will continue to prioritize this shareholder return strategy in 2025.

In 2024, WTI oil prices averaged $75.79 per Bbl versus $77.62 per Bbl in 2023, reflecting a downward trend as oil prices remained volatile even with continued capital discipline by global oil producers. Oil is expected to remain volatile in 2025 due to geopolitical risks to supply, forecasted stronger non-OPEC supply, and improving global demand growth expectations. Henry Hub natural gas prices fell in 2024, averaging $2.27 per Mcf compared to $2.74 per Mcf in 2023. For 2025, natural gas prices are expected to increase compared with 2024 prices due to increased demand, driven by rising LNG exports, strong powerburn as well as discipline from natural gas producers. Our 2025 cash flow is partly protected from commodity price volatility due to our current hedge position that covers approximately 30% of our anticipated oil and gas volumes. In order to further insulate our cash flow, we continue to examine and, when appropriate, execute attractive regional basis swap hedges to protect price realizations across our portfolio.

Our commitment to capital discipline and capital efficiency remains unchanged with our 2025 capital program. Similar to 2024, the majority of our 2025 capital, or approximately 55%, is expected to be focused on our highest returning oil play, the Delaware Basin. Our Williston Basin assets will receive additional capital allocation through 2025 as we work to develop the newly acquired Grayson Mill assets. The remainder of our 2025 capital will continue to be deployed to our other core areas of Eagle Ford, Anadarko Basin and Powder River Basin. Our 2025 capital is expected to be approximately 7% higher than 2024 primarily due to increased activity in the Williston Basin. Due to our strategy of spending within cash flow, we expect to continue generating material amounts of free cash flow for 2025.

12. Risk Management Activities
Commodity Price Transactions. EOG engages in price risk management activities from time to time. These activities are intended to manage EOG's exposure to fluctuations in commodity prices for crude oil, NGLs and natural gas. EOG utilizes financial commodity derivative instruments, primarily price swap, option, swaption, collar and basis swap contracts, as a means to manage this price risk.

During 2024, 2023 and 2022, EOG elected not to designate any of its financial commodity and other derivative contracts as accounting hedges and, accordingly, accounted for these financial commodity and other derivative contracts using the mark-to-market accounting method. Under this accounting method, changes in the fair value of outstanding financial instruments are recognized as gains or losses in the period of change and are recorded as Gains (Losses) on Mark-to-Market Financial Commodity and Other Derivative Contracts, Net on the Consolidated Statements of Income and Comprehensive Income. The related cash flow impact is reflected in Cash Flows from Operating Activities. Asset Retirement Obligations
EOG's asset retirement obligations (ARO) primarily represent the present value of estimated future costs to plug and abandon wells and remove equipment and facilities associated with oil and gas producing activities upon the retirement thereof. The ARO also includes similar obligations to decommission and remove equipment and facilities related to midstream assets. EOG records the initial estimated fair value of AROs in the period in which they are incurred.

EOG computes the fair value of its AROs using inputs that require the use of significant judgments and estimates and are, therefore, classified within Level 3 of the fair value hierarchy. Such inputs include estimates of future plug and abandonment and decommissioning costs. Accretion expense is recognized over time as the discounted fair value of the AROs is accreted to the settlement value. EOG has elected to account for AROs for certain midstream assets under an alternative method pursuant to which the AROs are recognized in earnings ratably over the underlying assets' estimated useful lives. See Note 1 to the Consolidated Financial Statements for a more complete discussion of EOG's accounting policy related to AROs.

Generally, the timing and amount of future cash flows associated with AROs are based on the estimated economic lives of the underlying assets and historical plug and abandonment and decommissioning costs adjusted for expected future inflation and changes in regulatory requirements and industry practices. EOG's estimates of AROs are subject to change due to changes in technology, industry practices and regulations, as well as changes in the timing and amount of the estimated future cash flows. EOG periodically reviews its AROs for changes in estimates. Changes in the estimated costs, timing of, or assumptions underlying the expected settlement of AROs are recognized by adjusting the carrying amount of the ARO and the related asset. For assets accounted for under the alternative method, such changes are recognized ratably over the assets' remaining useful lives.

EOG's AROs associated with midstream assets are primarily related to gathering and processing facilities and pipelines located in the United States. EOG's AROs associated with oil and gas producing activities are primarily related to wells and related equipment and facilities located in the United States and Trinidad. EOG expects to incur significant cash outflows to settle AROs in the future as wells and midstream facilities are retired. The estimated cash outflows for AROs could change materially in the future due to changes in the estimated economic lives of the underlying assets, changes in the scope and timing of abandonment and decommissioning activities, changes in regulatory requirements or industry practices, or other factors beyond EOG's control. EOG's policy is to mitigate the potential financial impact of ARO cash outflows through continued investment in new wells and midstream facilities that extend the lives of existing infrastructure and through periodic review and optimization of its abandonment and decommissioning programs.

EOG's AROs are discounted using credit-adjusted risk-free rates that reflect the risk associated with the future cash flows. The discount rates used to measure AROs at initial recognition and subsequent measurement dates may differ depending on changes in market conditions and company-specific factors. EOG believes that its estimates and assumptions related to AROs are reasonable; however, actual results could differ from those estimates and assumptions and such differences could have a material effect on EOG's financial position, results of operations and cash flows.

EOG is not aware of any material environmental liabilities associated with its AROs beyond those recorded in the Consolidated Balance Sheets. EOG's operations are subject to extensive environmental regulation and enforcement by federal, state and local governmental authorities. EOG has policies and procedures in place to comply with applicable environmental laws and regulations; however, changes in such laws and regulations or changes in their interpretation or enforcement could result in increased costs or liabilities in the future. EOG cannot predict the ultimate cost of compliance with environmental laws and regulations, which are subject to change and may become more stringent over time.

EOG continues to monitor developments in the legal and regulatory environment that could affect its AROs, including potential changes in bonding requirements, decommissioning standards and financial assurance obligations. EOG also evaluates opportunities to reduce the environmental impact of its operations and to improve the efficiency of its abandonment and decommissioning activities through technological innovation and collaboration with industry partners and regulators.

EOG's ARO estimates include assumptions regarding plug and abandonment and decommissioning costs that could be affected by inflationary pressures, labor market conditions, supply chain constraints, and other macroeconomic factors. EOG uses historical cost data and current market trends to develop its estimates and adjusts those estimates as necessary based on actual experience and changes in market conditions. Despite these efforts, EOG's ARO estimates are inherently uncertain and may change over time as new information becomes available.

EOG's AROs are managed by a multidisciplinary team that includes representatives from operations, engineering, finance, legal and environmental departments. This team is responsible for developing and implementing policies and procedures related to AROs, monitoring compliance with applicable laws and regulations, and coordinating abandonment and decommissioning activities across EOG's operations. EOG's Board of Directors and senior management receive periodic updates on the status of AROs and related risks and opportunities.

EOG believes that its ARO management practices are consistent with industry standards and best practices and that it has adequate resources to fulfill its obligations as they become due. Nonetheless, EOG could be required to incur significant additional costs in the future if new laws or regulations are enacted or existing laws or regulations are interpreted or enforced in a manner that requires more extensive abandonment and decommissioning activities, if technological advances result in new decommissioning methods or standards, or if other unforeseen events occur that affect the timing or amount of ARO cash outflows.

EOG's AROs are not collateralized and do not contain covenants or other restrictions that could impact EOG's liquidity or capital resources. EOG believes that it has sufficient liquidity and access to capital to fund its AROs as they become due and that its AROs do not have a material adverse effect on its financial position, results of operations or cash flows.

EOG will continue to evaluate its AROs and update its estimates as necessary to reflect changes in the underlying assumptions and circumstances. EOG believes that the estimates and assumptions used to measure its AROs are reasonable and appropriate; however, actual results could differ from those estimates and assumptions and such differences could be material.

EOG's AROs are included in Accrued Other Liabilities and Other Liabilities on the Consolidated Balance Sheets. Accretion expense related to AROs is included in Depreciation, Depletion and Amortization and other operating expenses in the Consolidated Statements of Income. Cash outflows related to AROs are included in Net Cash Provided by Operating Activities and Net Cash Used in Investing Activities in the Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, depending on the nature of the activities. EOG's AROs do not affect compliance with any of its debt covenants.

EOG will continue to monitor its AROs and make adjustments as necessary to ensure that it is properly accounting for its obligations and maintaining compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

Commodity Derivative Contracts
EOG utilizes financial commodity derivative contracts to manage certain risks associated with commodity price volatility. EOG's primary objective in executing commodity price risk management activities is to protect cash flows expected to be used to fund capital expenditures, dividends and share repurchases. EOG does not enter into derivative transactions for speculative purposes.

EOG's commodity derivative contracts may include collars, swaps and basis swaps for crude oil, natural gas liquids (NGLs) and natural gas. These contracts are intended to reduce the effect of price changes on a portion of EOG's future production by providing price certainty for a portion of EOG's anticipated sales volumes. EOG's commodity derivative contracts expose it to credit risk in the event of nonperformance by counterparties; however, EOG believes its counterparties are creditworthy and monitors their financial condition. EOG also enters into master netting arrangements with its counterparties to mitigate credit risk by allowing for the net settlement of derivative assets and liabilities in the event of default or other termination events.

EOG recognized gains and losses on its commodity derivative contracts in the Consolidated Statements of Income under the line item "Net (Gains) Losses on Commodity Derivative Contracts." The fair value of EOG's commodity derivative contracts is estimated using industry-standard valuation models that incorporate inputs such as forward commodity prices and discount rates. These inputs are primarily observable in active markets and, therefore, EOG's commodity derivative contracts are generally classified within Level 2 of the fair value hierarchy. Certain credit risk adjustments based on EOG's and its counterparties' credit risk are classified within Level 3.

EOG does not designate its commodity derivative contracts as hedges for accounting purposes. As a result, changes in the fair value of EOG's commodity derivative contracts are recognized currently in earnings. Cash settlements on commodity derivative contracts are reflected in Net Cash Provided by Operating Activities in the Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows. EOG's policy is to limit the notional amount of commodity derivative contracts to a portion of its forecasted production volumes for the relevant periods.

EOG's outstanding commodity derivative contracts are exposed to margin requirements and collateral postings pursuant to agreements with certain counterparties. EOG may be required to post cash or letters of credit as collateral to secure its obligations under these agreements. EOG actively manages its collateral and liquidity to meet such requirements. EOG's master netting arrangements and collateral agreements provide for the offset of derivative assets and liabilities in the event of a counterparty default or other termination events.

EOG continually evaluates its commodity derivative strategy in light of market conditions, its capital program and its overall risk management objectives. EOG may enter into additional commodity derivative contracts, modify existing contracts or terminate contracts to manage its exposure to commodity price volatility and to support its capital allocation priorities. EOG's commodity price risk management activities are subject to the oversight of management and the Board of Directors and are designed to align with EOG's long-term strategic objectives.

EOG's commodity derivative positions at December 31, 2024, along with the associated fair values and maturities, are summarized in the table above. Future changes in commodity prices could result in significant changes in the fair value of EOG's outstanding commodity derivative contracts and the associated gains and losses recognized in earnings. EOG does not expect its commodity price risk management activities to eliminate all exposure to commodity price volatility, but believes that these activities help to mitigate the impact of adverse price movements on its financial position and results of operations.

Asset Retirement Obligations
Devon's asset retirement obligations (ARO) represent the present value of estimated costs to plug and abandon wells and to dismantle and remove related equipment and facilities at the end of their productive lives. ARO is recognized when a legal obligation is incurred and is initially measured at fair value, which is the discounted present value of the estimated future cash outflows expected to be required to settle the obligation. The associated asset retirement costs are capitalized as part of the carrying amount of the related long-lived assets and are depreciated over the assets' useful lives. The ARO liability is accreted over time as the discounted fair value is accreted to the settlement value.

Devon calculates its ARO using various inputs that require the use of significant judgments and estimates. These inputs include estimates of plug and abandonment costs, the expected timing of these costs, the economic lives of the underlying assets and the credit-adjusted risk-free rates used to discount the expected cash flows. Devon's ARO estimates are subject to change due to changes in technology, industry practice, regulations, commodity prices, inflation and the Company's development plans. The ARO is reviewed at least annually and adjusted to reflect changes in estimates, with the corresponding adjustment made to the carrying amount of the related assets or recorded in earnings for certain midstream assets accounted for under the alternative method.

Devon uses credit-adjusted risk-free rates to discount expected future cash flows related to ARO. The discount rates used reflect the risks associated with the expected timing and amount of the future cash outflows. Devon is subject to environmental laws and regulations that may require the Company to incur significant costs to maintain compliance or to remediate environmental contamination. The Company uses financial commodity derivatives primarily to reduce its exposure to volatility in commodity prices for a portion of its forecasted oil and natural gas production. The Company does not enter into derivative transactions for speculative purposes and, as of December 31, 2024, did not have any derivatives with embedded leverage features.

 Accounting for Derivatives
The Company recognizes all derivatives on the balance sheet at fair value. The accounting for changes in the fair value of derivatives depends on whether the derivatives are designated as cash flow hedges or not designated as hedges. For derivatives designated as cash flow hedges, the effective portion of changes in fair value is recorded in Accumulated other comprehensive income (loss) and subsequently reclassified into earnings in the same period or periods during which the hedged transaction affects earnings. Any ineffective portion of a hedging relationship is recognized in earnings immediately. For derivatives not designated as hedges, changes in fair value are recognized in earnings in the period of change.

As of December 31, 2024, the Company had not designated any of its derivatives as hedges for accounting purposes. Accordingly, changes in the fair value of the Company's derivatives are recognized currently in earnings within Other (income) expense in the Consolidated Statements of Operations.

 Fair Value Measurement
The Company estimates the fair values of its derivative instruments using industry-standard models that incorporate inputs such as forward commodity prices, interest rates and credit risk adjustments. These inputs are primarily observable and, therefore, the Company's derivatives are generally classified within Level 2 of the fair value hierarchy. The Company evaluates the credit risk of its counterparties, as well as its own credit risk, in determining the fair value of its derivatives and records credit valuation adjustments as necessary.

 Offsetting of Derivatives
The Company enters into master netting agreements with its derivative counterparties that allow net settlement of derivative assets and liabilities in the event of default or certain other termination events. The Company also has collateral arrangements with certain counterparties that require the Company or the counterparty to post cash or letters of credit as collateral to secure obligations under the derivative agreements. As of December 31, 2024, the Company had posted collateral with certain counterparties and had received collateral from other counterparties, which are reflected as restricted cash on the Consolidated Balance Sheets.

 Credit Risk
The Company is exposed to credit risk in the event of nonperformance by its derivative counterparties. The Company monitors the creditworthiness of its counterparties and limits exposure to any single counterparty. The Company believes its counterparties are creditworthy and that the risk of material nonperformance is low.

 Gains and Losses on Derivatives
Gains and losses on derivatives not designated as hedges are recognized in earnings within Other (income) expense in the period in which they occur. The following table summarizes the gains and losses recognized on derivatives for the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2023 (in millions):

| Total Gains (Losses) on Derivatives| | $ | 207 | | $ | 16 |

 Objectives and Strategy
The Company's objective for entering into commodity derivative contracts is to manage its exposure to commodity price risk and to provide a more predictable cash flow stream to support its capital program and shareholder returns initiatives, including dividends and share repurchases. The Company regularly evaluates its derivative positions and may adjust its strategy as market conditions and the Company's operational outlook change.

 Additional Information
The use of derivatives involves exposure to both market risk and credit risk. Market risk is related to potential changes in the value of derivatives due to changes in commodity prices. Credit risk relates to the potential inability of counterparties to perform under the terms of the derivative contracts. The Company actively manages these risks through established policies, procedures and oversight.

The Company's derivative activities are subject to the oversight of management and the Board of Directors. The Company has established risk limits and controls designed to monitor and manage its exposure to market and credit risk. The Company believes that its risk management policies and procedures are appropriate for its business and that the use of derivatives helps to reduce the volatility of its cash flows and earnings.

The Company may, from time to time, enter into additional derivative contracts or terminate or modify existing contracts to manage its exposure to commodity price risk and to support its capital program and other corporate objectives. Changes in commodity prices, market volatility and the Company's operational outlook could impact the level and types of derivatives used.

The Company's derivative positions as of December 31, 2024, and the related fair values, are included in the accompanying Consolidated Financial Statements and notes thereto.

Oil and Gas Producing Activities
The following disclosures are made in accordance with Financial Accounting Standards Board Accounting Standards Update No. 2010-03 "Oil and Gas Reserve Estimation and Disclosures" and the United States Securities and Exchange Commission's (SEC) final rule on "Modernization of Oil and Gas Reporting."

Oil and Gas Reserves. Users of this information should be aware that the process of estimating quantities of "proved," "proved developed" and "proved undeveloped" crude oil, natural gas liquids (NGLs) and natural gas reserves is complex, requiring significant subjective decisions in the evaluation of available geological, engineering and economic data for each reservoir. The data for a given reservoir may also change substantially over time as a result of numerous factors, including, but not limited to, additional development activity; evolving production history; crude oil and condensate, NGLs and natural gas prices; continual reassessment of the viability of production under varying economic conditions; and improvements and other changes in geological, geophysical and engineering evaluation methods. Consequently, material revisions (upward or downward) to existing reserve estimates may occur from time to time. Although reasonable effort is made to ensure that reserve estimates reported represent the most accurate assessments possible, the significance of the subjective decisions required and variances in available data for various reservoirs make these estimates generally less precise than other estimates presented in connection with financial statement disclosures.

Proved reserves represent estimated quantities of crude oil, NGLs and natural gas, which, by analysis of geoscience and engineering data, can be estimated, with reasonable certainty, to be economically producible from a given date forward from known reservoirs under then-existing economic conditions, operating methods and government regulations before the time at which contracts providing the right to operate expire, unless evidence indicates that renewal is reasonably certain, regardless of whether deterministic or probabilistic methods are used for the estimation. The proved natural gas reserves reported are inclusive of natural gas consumed in operations.

Proved developed reserves are proved reserves expected to be recovered under operating methods being utilized at the time the estimates were made, through wells and equipment in place or if the cost of any required equipment is relatively minor compared to the cost of a new well.

Proved undeveloped reserves (PUDs) are reserves that are expected to be recovered from new wells on undrilled acreage, or from existing wells where a relatively major expenditure is required for completion or recompletion. Reserves on undrilled acreage are limited to those directly offsetting development spacing areas that are reasonably certain of production when drilled, unless evidence using reliable technology exists that establishes reasonable certainty of economic producibility at greater distances. PUDs can be recorded in respect of a particular undeveloped undrilled location only if the location is scheduled, under the then-current drilling and development plan, to be drilled within five years from the date that the PUDs were recorded, unless specific factors (such as those described in interpretative guidance issued by the Staff of the SEC) justify a longer timeframe. Likewise, absent any such specific factors, PUDs associated with a particular undeveloped drilling location shall be removed from the estimates of proved reserves if the location is scheduled, under the then-current drilling and development plan, to be drilled on a date that is beyond five years from the date that the PUDs were recorded. EOG has formulated development plans for all drilling locations associated with its PUDs at December 31, 2024. Under these plans, each location will be drilled within five years from the date the associated PUDs were recorded. Estimates for PUDs are not attributed to any acreage for which an application of fluid injection or other improved recovery technique is contemplated, unless such techniques have been proved effective by actual projects in the same reservoir or an analogous reservoir, or by other evidence using reliable technology establishing reasonable certainty.

When circumstances indicate that proved oil and gas properties may be impaired, EOG compares expected undiscounted future cash flows at a depreciation, depletion and amortization group level to the unamortized capitalized cost of the group. If the expected undiscounted future cash flows, based on EOG's estimate of (and assumptions regarding) significant Level 3 inputs, including future crude oil, NGLs and natural gas prices, operating costs, development expenditures, anticipated production from proved reserves and other relevant data, are lower than the unamortized capitalized cost, the capitalized cost is reduced to fair value. Fair value is generally calculated using the Income Approach described in the Fair Value Measurement Topic of the ASC. In certain instances, EOG utilizes accepted offers from third-party purchasers as the basis for determining fair value.

During 2023, proved oil and gas properties with a carrying amount of $ 59million were written down to their fair value of $ 15million, resulting in pretax impairment charges of $ 44million.

During 2022, proved oil and gas properties with a carrying amount of $ 146million were written down to their fair value of $ 26million, resulting in pretax impairment charges of $ 120million

During 2021, proved oil and gas properties with a carrying amount of $ 27million were written down to their fair value of $ 7million, resulting in pretax impairment charges of $ 20million.

EOG utilized average prices per acre from comparable market transactions and estimated discounted cash flows as the basis for determining the fair value of unproved and proved properties, respectively, received in non-cash property exchanges. See Note 10.

Fair Value of Debt. At December 31, 2023 and 2022, respectively, EOG had outstanding $ 3,640million and $ 4,890million aggregate principal amount of senior notes, which had estimated fair values of $ 3,574million and $ 4,740million, respectively. The estimated fair value of debt was based upon quoted market prices and, where such prices were not available, other observable (Level 2) inputs regarding interest rates available to EOG at year-end.

Natural Gas Sales Linked to Brent Crude Oil . In February 2024, EOG entered into a 10-yearagreement, commencing in 2027, to sell 180,000MMBtud of its domestic natural gas production, with 140,000MMBtud to be sold at a price indexed to Brent Crude Oil (Brent) and the remaining volumes to be sold at a price indexed to Brent or a U.S. Gulf Coast gas index. As such, this agreement will be accounted for as a derivative beginning in the first quarter of 2024 (effective upon the execution of the agreement) using the mark-to-market accounting method. Lease and well expenses include expenses for EOG-operated properties, as well as expenses billed to EOG from other operators where EOG is not the operator of a property. Lease and well expenses can be divided into the following categories: costs to operate and maintain crude oil and natural gas wells, the cost of workovers and lease and well administrative expenses. Operating and maintenance costs include, among other things, pumping services, produced water disposal, equipment repair and maintenance, compression expense, lease upkeep and fuel and power. Workovers are operations to restore or maintain production from existing wells.

Each of these categories of costs individually fluctuates from time to time as EOG attempts to maintain and increase production while maintaining efficient, safe and environmentally responsible operations. EOG continues to increase its operating activities by drilling new wells in existing and new areas. Operating and maintenance costs within these existing and new areas, as well as the costs of services charged to EOG by vendors, fluctuate over time.

Lease and well expenses of $401 million for the first quarter of 2025 increased $5 million from $396 million for the same prior year period primarily due to increased operating and maintenance costs in the United States ($14 million) and Trinidad ($5 million) and increased lease and well administrative expenses in the United States ($4 million), partially offset by decreased workover expenditures in the United States ($19 million).

GP&T costs represent costs to process and deliver hydrocarbon products from the lease to a downstream point of sale. GP&T costs include operating and maintenance expenses from EOG-owned assets, fees paid to third-party operators and administrative expenses associated with operating EOG's GP&T assets. EOG pays third parties to process the majority of its natural gas production to extract NGLs.

GP&T costs of $440 million for the first quarter of 2025 increased $27 million from $413 million for the same prior year period primarily due to increased GP&T costs related to increased production in the Permian Basin and Utica, as well as increased third-party fees in the Utica, partially offset by a decrease in GP&T costs related to lower third-party fees in the Eagle Ford.

DD&A of the cost of proved oil and gas properties is calculated using the unit-of-production method. EOG's DD&A rate and expense are the composite of numerous individual DD&A group calculations. There are several factors that can impact EOG's composite DD&A rate and expense, such as field production profiles, drilling or acquisition of new wells, disposition of existing wells and reserve revisions (upward or downward) primarily related to well performance, economic factors and impairments. Changes to these factors may cause EOG's composite DD&A rate and expense to fluctuate from period to period. DD&A of the cost of other property, plant and equipment is generally calculated using the straight-line depreciation method over the useful lives of the assets.

DD&A expenses for the first quarter of 2025 decreased $61 million to $1,013 million from $1,074 million for the same prior year period. DD&A expenses associated with oil and gas properties for the first quarter of 2025 were $72 million lower than the same prior year period. The decrease primarily reflects an adjustment to DD&A recorded in 2024 ($117 million) primarily related to natural gas production used by EOG's domestic gathering systems. In addition, increased production ($49 million), primarily in the United States, also contributed to the variance. DD&A expenses associated with other property, plant and equipment for the first quarter of 2025 were $11 million higher than the same prior year period primarily due to an increase in expenses related to GP&T assets and equipment.

G&A expenses of $171 million for the first quarter of 2025 increased $9 million from $162 million for the same prior year period primarily due to increased professional services costs and information systems costs.

Interest expense, net of $47 million for the first quarter of 2025 increased $14 million compared to the same prior year period primarily due to the issuance in November 2024 of the $1,000 million aggregate principal amount of 5.650% Senior Notes due 2054.

Ifplans for addit management determines future development activities and the determination of proved reserves are unlikely to occur, the associated suspended exploratory well costs are recorded as dry hole expense and reported in exploration expense in the consolidated statements of comprehensive earnings. Otherwise, the costs of exploratory wells remain capitalized. At December 31, 2024, all material suspended well costs have been suspended for less than one year.

Similar to the evaluation of suspended exploratory well costs, costs for undeveloped leasehold, for which reserves have not been proven, must also be evaluated for continued capitalization or impairment. At the end of each quarter, management assesses undeveloped leasehold costs for impairment by considering future drilling plans, drilling activity results, commodity price outlooks, planned future sales or expiration of all or a portion of such projects. At December 31, 2024, Devon had approximately $1.9 billion of undeveloped leasehold costs. Of the remaining undeveloped leasehold costs at December 31, 2024, none is scheduled to expire in 2025.

Reserves

Our estimates of proved and proved developed reserves are a major component of DD&A calculations. Additionally, our proved reserves represent the element of these calculations that require the most subjective judgments. Estimates of reserves are forecasts based on engineering data, projected future rates of production and the timing of future expenditures. The process of estimating oil, gas and NGL reserves requires substantial judgment, resulting in imprecise determinations, particularly for new discoveries. Different reserve engineers may make different estimates of reserve quantities based on the same data. Our engineers prepare our reserve estimates. We then subject certain of our reserve estimates to audits performed by a third-party petroleum consulting firm. In 2024, 89% of our proved reserves were subjected to such an audit.

The passage of time provides additional information which may result in revisions to previous estimates to reflect updated information. In the past five years, annual revisions other than price to our proved reserve estimates, which have been both increases and decreases in individual years, have averaged approximately 3% of the previous year’s estimate. However, there can be no assurance that more significant revisions will not be necessary in the future. For example, revisions may be driven broadly by economic factors such as significant changes in operating costs, or they may be more focused such as in a given area or reservoir. The data for a given reservoir may change substantially over time as a result of numerous factors, including, but not limited to, additional development activity, evolving production history and continual reassessment of the viability of production under varying economic conditions.

Valuation of Long-Lived Assets

Long-lived assets used in operations, including proved and unproved oil and gas properties, are depreciated and assessed for impairment annually or whenever changes in facts and circumstances indicate a possible significant deterioration in future cash flows is expected to be generated by an asset group. For DD&A calculations and impairment assessments, management groups individual assets based on a judgmental assessment of the lowest level (“common operating field”) for which there are identifiable cash flows that are largely independent of the cash flows of other groups of assets. The determination of common operating fields is largely based on geological structural features or stratigraphic condition, which requires judgment. Management also considers the nature of production, common infrastructure, common sales points, common processing plants, common regulation and management oversight to make common operating field determinations. These determinations impact the amount of DD&A recognized each period and could impact the determination and measurement of a potential asset impairment.

Management evaluates assets for impairment through an established process in which changes to significant assumptions such as prices, volumes and future development plans are reviewed. If, upon review, the sum of the undiscounted pre-tax cash flows is less than the carrying value of the asset group, the carrying value is written down to estimated fair value. Because there usually is a lack of quoted market prices for long-lived assets, the fair value of impaired assets is typically determined based on the present values of expected future cash flows using discount rates believed to be consistent with those used by principal market participants. The expected future cash flows used for impairment reviews and related fair value calculations are typically based on judgmental assessments of future production volumes, commodity prices, operating costs and capital investment plans, considering all available information at the date of review. The expected future cash flows used for impairment reviews include future production volumes associated with proved producing and risk-adjusted proved undeveloped reserves, and when needed, probable and possible reserves.

Besides the risk-adjusted estimates of reserves and future production volumes, future commodity prices are the largest driver in the variability of undiscounted pre-tax cash flows. For our impairment determinations, we utilize NYMEX forward strip prices and

If we choose not to develop our PUD reserves, or if we are not otherwise able to develop them successfully, we will be required to remove them from our reported proved reserves. In addition, under the SEC’s reserves reporting rules, because PUD reserves generally may be recorded only if they relate to wells scheduled to be drilled within five years of the date of booking, we may be required to remove any PUD reserves that are no longer planned to be developed within this five-year time frame. Delays in the development of our PUD reserves, decreases in commodity prices and increases in costs to drill and develop such reserves may also result in some projects becoming uneconomic.

Strategic determinations, including the allocation of capital and other resources to strategic opportunities, are challenging, and our failure to appropriately allocate capital and resources among our strategic opportunities may adversely affect our financial condition and reduce our growth rate.

Our future growth prospects depend on our ability to identify optimal strategies for our business. In developing our business plans, we considered allocating capital and other resources to various aspects of our business including well-development (primarily drilling and completion), reserve acquisitions, exploratory activity, corporate items and other alternatives. We also consider our likely sources of capital. Notwithstanding the determinations made in the development of our 2025 plan, business opportunities not previously identified periodically may come to our attention, including possible acquisitions and dispositions. If we fail to identify optimal business strategies or fail to optimize our capital investment and capital raising opportunities and the use of our other resources in furtherance of our business strategies, our financial condition and growth rate may be adversely affected. Moreover, economic or other circumstances may change from those contemplated by our 2025 plan, and our failure to recognize or respond to those changes may limit our ability to achieve our objectives.

Our ability to sell our oil, natural gas and NGL production and the prices we receive for our production could be materially harmed if we fail to obtain adequate services such as gathering, transportation and processing.

The sale of our oil, natural gas and NGL production depends on a number of factors beyond our control, including the availability and capacity of gathering, transportation and processing facilities. We deliver the majority of our oil, natural gas and NGL production through gathering systems and pipelines that we do not own. The lack of available capacity on these systems and facilities could reduce the price offered for our production or result in the shut-in of producing wells or the delay or discontinuance of development plans for properties. Third-party systems and facilities may be unavailable due to market conditions or mechanical or other reasons, and in some cases the resulting curtailments of production could lead to payment being required where we fail to deliver oil, natural gas and NGLs to meet minimum volume commitments. In addition, construction of new pipelines and building of required infrastructure may be slow. To the extent these services are unavailable, we would be unable to realize revenue from wells served by such facilities until suitable arrangements are made to market our production. Our failure to obtain these services on acceptable terms could materially harm our business.

Moreover, these availability and capacity issues are likely to occur in remote areas with less established infrastructure, such as our Permian Basin properties where we have significant oil and natural gas production. Such availability and capacity issues may result in increased basis differentials, which became more divergent in 2024 in part due to constrained pipeline capacity and oversupply in certain geographic areas. At times, such basis differentials have been significant enough to result in negative spot market pricing in certain areas, such as the Waha Hub in the Permian Basin during 2024. Any of these availability or capacity issues could negatively affect our operations, revenues and expenses. This could result in wells being shut in or awaiting a pipeline connection or capacity, which would adversely affect our results of operations and cash flows.

Acquired properties may not be worth what we pay to acquire them, due to uncertainties in evaluating recoverable reserves and other expected benefits, as well as potential liabilities.

Successful property acquisitions require an assessment of a number of factors beyond our control. These factors include estimates of recoverable reserves, exploration and development potential, future commodity prices, operating costs, production taxes and potential environmental and other liabilities. These assessments are complex and inherently imprecise. Our review of the properties we acquire may not reveal all existing or potential problems. In addition, our review may not allow us to assess fully the potential deficiencies of the properties. We do not inspect every well, and even when we inspect a well, we may not discover structural, subsurface or environmental problems that may exist or arise.

There may be threatened or contemplated claims against the assets or businesses we acquire related to environmental, title, regulatory, tax, contract, litigation or other matters of which we are unaware, which could materially and adversely affect our production, revenues and results of operations. We often assume certain liabilities, and we may not be entitled to contractual indemnification for pre-closing liabilities, including environmental liabilities, and our contractual indemnification may not be effective. At times, we acquire interests in properties on an “as is” basis with limited representations and warranties and limited remedies for breaches of such representations and warranties. In addition, significant acquisitions can change the nature of our operations and business if the acquired properties have substantially different operating and geological characteristics or are in different geographic locations than our existing properties.

Capital Resources and Liquidity
Cash Flow

The primary sources of cash for EOG during the three-year period ended December 31, 2024 were funds generated from operations and, to a lesser extent, funds from investment and financing activities. The primary uses of cash for EOG for the same period were exploration and development expenditures; dividend payments to stockholders; repurchases of treasury stock; net cash paid for settlements of financial commodity derivative contracts; and debt repayment.

Net cash provided by operating activities of $12,143 million in 2024 decreased $2,329 million as compared to 2023 primarily due to a decrease in cash receipts from oil, natural gas liquids and natural gas sales and a decrease in net cash provided by components of working capital and other assets and liabilities, partially offset by a decrease in cash paid for income taxes. The decrease in cash receipts from oil, natural gas liquids and natural gas sales was due to a decrease in wellhead revenues of $2,995 million. The decrease in net cash provided by components of working capital and other assets and liabilities was primarily due to the collection in 2023 of cash collateral posted for financial commodity derivative contracts during 2022.

Net cash provided by operating activities of $14,472 million in 2023 increased $1,187 million as compared to 2022 primarily due to an increase in cash receipts from oil, natural gas liquids and natural gas sales and a decrease in cash paid for income taxes, partially offset by a decrease in net cash provided by components of working capital and other assets and liabilities. The increase in cash receipts from oil, natural gas liquids and natural gas sales was due to a decrease in accounts receivable, partially offset by a decrease in wellhead revenues of $1,470 million. The decrease in cash paid for income taxes was primarily due to a decrease in income taxes paid in cash related to prior years. The decrease in net cash provided by components of working capital and other assets and liabilities was primarily due to the collection in 2022 of cash collateral posted for financial commodity derivative contracts during 2021, partially offset by a change in the timing of payments related to production costs.

Net cash used in investing activities of $7,061 million in 2024 increased $1,540 million as compared to 2023 primarily due to an increase in cash capital expenditures of $1,711 million, partially offset by an increase in proceeds from asset sales of $180 million. The increase in cash capital expenditures was primarily due to increased drilling activity and higher costs. The increase in proceeds from asset sales was primarily due to the sale of certain non-core assets in 2024.

Net cash used in investing activities of $5,521 million in 2023 increased $1,582 million as compared to 2022 primarily due to a decrease in proceeds from asset sales of $1,071 million and an increase in cash capital expenditures of $602 million. The decrease in proceeds from asset sales was primarily due to the sale of certain non-core assets in 2022. The increase in cash capital expenditures was primarily due to increased drilling activity and higher costs.

Net cash used in financing activities of $8,179 million in 2024 increased $2,553 million as compared to 2023 primarily due to an increase in repurchases of treasury stock of $1,995 million and an increase in dividend payments to stockholders of $581 million, partially offset by a decrease in debt repayment of $23 million. The increase in repurchases of treasury stock was due to the timing of share repurchases. The increase in dividend payments to stockholders was due to the increase in the regular quarterly dividend rate and special dividends paid in 2024.

Net cash used in financing activities of $5,626 million in 2023 increased $1,309 million as compared to 2022 primarily due to an increase in repurchases of treasury stock of $1,271 million and an increase in dividend payments to stockholders of $346 million, partially offset by a decrease in debt repayment of $337 million. The increase in repurchases of treasury stock was due to the timing of share repurchases. The increase in dividend payments to stockholders was due to the increase in the regular quarterly dividend rate and special dividends paid in 2023.

EOG’s cash flows are highly dependent on commodity prices and the Company’s ability to manage cost structure and capital program. EOG attempts to maintain flexibility in its capital program by avoiding commitments that could force expenditures during periods of low commodity prices, and regularly adjusts its capital program in response to changing economic conditions.

EOG periodically uses financial commodity derivative instruments (derivative instruments) to manage certain price risks. EOG accounts for derivative instruments used to manage price risks under Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) Topic 815, “Derivatives and Hedging.” EOG does not enter into derivative instruments for trading purposes. EOG’s primary objective in using derivative instruments is to protect its cash flows, liquidity and capital program.

During 2024, EOG recognized a net cash outflow of $227 million for settlements of financial commodity derivative contracts as compared to a net cash outflow of $249 million for 2023 and a net cash inflow of $762 million for 2022. At December 31, 2024, EOG had outstanding financial commodity derivative contracts, which consisted of natural gas price swaps and three-way collars, with notional volumes totaling 790,000 MMBtud for 2025. See “Financial Commodity and Other Derivative Transactions” below and Note 11 to Consolidated Financial Statements for additional information.

EOG regularly reviews its liquidity requirements and alternative uses of cash. As of December 31, 2024, EOG maintained a strong financial and liquidity position, including $7.1 billion of cash and cash equivalents on hand, a $2.0 billion unsecured revolving credit facility (Senior Credit Facility) that matures on December 2, 2027, and no outstanding borrowings or commercial paper. EOG’s Senior Credit Facility is available for general corporate purposes, including commercial paper backstop, and contains customary representations, covenants, events of default and other terms and conditions. EOG is in compliance with all covenants under the Senior Credit Facility as of December 31, 2024.

EOG’s financial condition, results of operations and liquidity can be affected by various risks and uncertainties, including commodity price fluctuations, changes in supply and demand, inflationary pressures, labor availability, geopolitical events and natural disasters. EOG’s ability to access capital markets on favorable terms, or at all, may be affected by these and other factors. EOG believes that its sources of liquidity are adequate to meet its short-term and long-term cash requirements, including its capital program, dividends, share repurchases, debt service and other obligations.

EOG’s Board of Directors has authorized a share repurchase program, under which EOG may repurchase up to $15.0 billion of its outstanding common stock. The share repurchase program does not have a prescribed expiration date and may be modified, suspended or terminated at any time at the Company’s discretion. During 2024, EOG repurchased 28.8 million shares of its common stock for an aggregate purchase price of $3,076 million. At December 31, 2024, the remaining authorization under the share repurchase program was $6,412 million.

In February 2025, EOG’s Board of Directors declared a regular quarterly cash dividend of $0.91 per share, payable on April 30, 2025 to stockholders of record as of April 17, 2025. The declaration and payment of any future dividends are at the discretion of EOG’s Board of Directors and will depend on the Company’s financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, capital requirements and other factors.

Financial Commodity and Other Derivative Transactions

EOG periodically utilizes derivative instruments to manage exposure to commodity price risk and to protect cash flows and the capital program. EOG’s derivative instruments generally consist of swaps and three-way collars for natural gas. EOG does not designate derivative instruments as hedges for accounting purposes under ASC Topic 815; therefore, changes in the fair value of these instruments are recognized in earnings in the period of the change.

The fair value of EOG’s derivative instruments is based on quoted market prices, adjusted for credit risk, or estimates using industry-standard valuation models. The fair value of EOG’s derivative instruments is sensitive to changes in forward market prices for commodities, as well as to changes in interest rates and credit risk of the Company and its counterparties.

EOG is exposed to credit risk in the event of nonperformance by counterparties to derivative instruments. EOG manages this risk by selecting counterparties based on their creditworthiness, monitoring their financial condition, and entering into master netting arrangements and, in some cases, collateral arrangements. EOG does not expect any counterparty to be unable to fulfill its obligations under its derivative instruments.

EOG’s derivative positions are presented on a net basis in the Consolidated Balance Sheets when a master netting arrangement or collateral arrangement exists with a counterparty. The net presentation also considers cash collateral posted or received by EOG. EOG presents the fair value of derivative instruments as current or noncurrent based on the timing of expected cash flows.

EOG’s derivative instruments are not intended for speculative purposes and EOG does not hold or issue derivative instruments for trading purposes. The primary objective of EOG’s derivative program is to reduce the potential negative effects of commodity price volatility on cash flows, liquidity and the capital program, thereby assisting in the execution of the Company’s business strategy.

EOG’s derivative instruments may limit the potential benefits of increases in commodity prices because losses on the derivative instruments may offset a portion of the increases in sales prices received. EOG’s derivative instruments may also expose the Company to potential cash settlement obligations and other financial risks.

EOG’s derivative program is subject to various risks, including changes in market conditions, the availability of counterparties, and legal and regulatory developments. EOG monitors and manages these risks as part of its overall risk management program.

EOG’s derivative instruments are recorded at fair value in the Consolidated Balance Sheets, with changes in fair value recognized in the Consolidated Statements of Income. Cash flows related to derivative instruments are included in operating activities in the Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows in the period in which they occur. See Notes 11 and 12 to Consolidated Financial Statements for additional information regarding EOG’s derivative instruments and fair value measurements.

Cash Management and Liquidity Outlook

EOG’s cash management strategy focuses on maintaining adequate liquidity to fund its capital program, dividends, share repurchases, debt service and other obligations, while preserving financial flexibility and minimizing the cost of capital. EOG’s liquidity sources include cash on hand, cash flows from operations, and, when necessary, access to the capital markets and bank credit facilities. EOG may also consider asset sales, joint ventures and other transactions to enhance liquidity.

At December 31, 2024, EOG had $7.1 billion of cash and cash equivalents on hand and no outstanding borrowings under its Senior Credit Facility. EOG’s liquidity position provides financial flexibility to pursue its business strategy, including reinvestment in the capital program, dividends, share repurchases and potential acquisitions.

EOG believes that its sources of liquidity are adequate to meet its short-term and long-term cash requirements. However, the adequacy of liquidity sources could be impacted by various factors, including commodity price volatility, changes in economic conditions, regulatory developments, and other risks and uncertainties. EOG will continue to monitor its liquidity position and adjust its capital program and other activities as necessary to maintain financial strength and flexibility.

Other

EOG’s cash flows are also impacted by changes in working capital and other assets and liabilities. Working capital changes are influenced by the timing of cash receipts and payments, commodity price movements, and other factors. EOG actively manages working capital to optimize liquidity and support operations.

EOG’s capital structure consists of a mix of equity and debt. EOG seeks to maintain a strong balance sheet with low leverage to support financial flexibility, reduce risk and enhance shareholder value. EOG may adjust its capital structure over time in response to changes in market conditions, business opportunities and other factors.

EOG will continue to evaluate its capital program and other uses of cash in light of market conditions, commodity prices, and business objectives. EOG’s long-term strategy is to generate sustainable shareholder value by maintaining a strong balance sheet, investing in high-return projects, and returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

EOG recognizes all derivative instruments in the Consolidated Balance Sheets as either assets or liabilities and measures those instruments at fair value. The fair value of the derivative instruments is determined using quoted market prices or, when such prices are not available, using estimated discounted cash flows based upon forward commodity prices.

The fair value of EOG’s derivative instruments is affected by changes in commodity prices and the volatility of those prices. Gains or losses resulting from changes in the fair value of derivative instruments are recognized currently in the Consolidated Statements of Income.

EOG may enter into derivative instruments for a portion of its anticipated production and may complement those instruments with options or other instruments to manage exposure to price risk. The extent of EOG’s derivative program may vary from time to time depending on market conditions, EOG’s outlook for commodity prices and other factors.

The increase in repurchases of treasury stock was due to the timing of share repurchases. The increase in dividend payments to stockholders was due to the increase in the regular quarterly dividend rate and special dividends paid in 2022.

EOG’s cash flows are highly dependent on commodity prices and the Company’s ability to manage cost structure and capital program. EOG attempts to maintain flexibility in its capital program by avoiding commitments that could force expenditures during periods of low commodity prices, and regularly adjusts its capital program in response to changing economic conditions.

EOG periodically uses financial commodity derivative instruments (derivative instruments) to manage certain price risks. EOG accounts for derivative instruments used to manage price risks under Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) Topic 815, “Derivatives and Hedging.” EOG does not enter into derivative instruments for trading purposes. EOG’s primary objective in using derivative instruments is to protect its cash flows, liquidity and capital program.

During 2023, EOG recognized a net cash outflow of $249 million for settlements of financial commodity derivative contracts as compared to a net cash inflow of $762 million for 2022 and a net cash outflow of $1,071 million for 2021. At December 31, 2023, EOG had outstanding financial commodity derivative contracts, which consisted of natural gas price swaps and three-way collars, with notional volumes totaling 1,000,000 MMBtud for 2024. See “Financial Commodity and Other Derivative Transactions” below and Note 11 to Consolidated Financial Statements for additional information.

EOG regularly reviews its liquidity requirements and alternative uses of cash. As of December 31, 2023, EOG maintained a strong financial and liquidity position, including $5.4 billion of cash and cash equivalents on hand, a $2.0 billion unsecured revolving credit facility (Senior Credit Facility) that matures on December 2, 2027, and no outstanding borrowings or commercial paper. EOG’s Senior Credit Facility is available for general corporate purposes, including commercial paper backstop, and contains customary representations, covenants, events of default and other terms and conditions. EOG is in compliance with all covenants under the Senior Credit Facility as of December 31, 2023.

EOG’s financial condition, results of operations and liquidity can be affected by various risks and uncertainties, including commodity price fluctuations, changes in supply and demand, inflationary pressures, labor availability, geopolitical events and natural disasters. EOG’s ability to access capital markets on favorable terms, or at all, may be affected by these and other factors. EOG believes that its sources of liquidity are adequate to meet its short-term and long-term cash requirements, including its capital program, dividends, share repurchases, debt service and other obligations.

EOG’s Board of Directors has authorized a share repurchase program, under which EOG may repurchase up to $15.0 billion of its outstanding common stock. The share repurchase program does not have a prescribed expiration date and may be modified, suspended or terminated at any time at the Company’s discretion. During 2023, EOG repurchased 27.1 million shares of its common stock for an aggregate purchase price of $2,781 million. At December 31, 2023, the remaining authorization under the share repurchase program was $9,488 million.

In February 2024, EOG’s Board of Directors declared a regular quarterly cash dividend of $0.91 per share, payable on April 30, 2024 to stockholders of record as of April 17, 2024. The declaration and payment of any future dividends are at the discretion of EOG’s Board of Directors and will depend on the Company’s financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, capital requirements and other factors.

Financial Commodity and Other Derivative Transactions

EOG periodically utilizes derivative instruments to manage exposure to commodity price risk and to protect cash flows and the capital program. EOG’s derivative instruments generally consist of swaps and three-way collars for natural gas. EOG does not designate derivative instruments as hedges for accounting purposes under ASC Topic 815; therefore, changes in the fair value of these instruments are recognized in earnings in the period of the change.

The fair value of EOG’s derivative instruments is based on quoted market prices, adjusted for credit risk, or estimates using industry-standard valuation models. The fair value of EOG’s derivative instruments is sensitive to changes in forward market prices for commodities, as well as to changes in interest rates and credit risk of the Company and its counterparties.

EOG is exposed to credit risk in the event of nonperformance by counterparties to derivative instruments. EOG manages this risk by selecting counterparties based on their creditworthiness, monitoring their financial condition, and entering into master netting arrangements and, in some cases, collateral arrangements. EOG does not expect any counterparty to be unable to fulfill its obligations under its derivative instruments.

EOG’s derivative positions are presented on a net basis in the Consolidated Balance Sheets when a master netting arrangement or collateral arrangement exists with a counterparty. The net presentation also considers cash collateral posted or received by EOG. EOG presents the fair value of derivative instruments as current or noncurrent based on the timing of expected cash flows.

EOG’s derivative instruments are not intended for speculative purposes and EOG does not hold or issue derivative instruments for trading purposes. The primary objective of EOG’s derivative program is to reduce the potential negative effects of commodity price volatility on cash flows, liquidity and the capital program, thereby assisting in the execution of the Company’s business strategy.

EOG’s derivative instruments may limit the potential benefits of increases in commodity prices because losses on the derivative instruments may offset a portion of the increases in sales prices received. EOG’s derivative instruments may also expose the Company to potential cash settlement obligations and other financial risks.

EOG’s derivative program is subject to various risks, including changes in market conditions, the availability of counterparties, and legal and regulatory developments. EOG monitors and manages these risks as part of its overall risk management program.

EOG’s derivative instruments are recorded at fair value in the Consolidated Balance Sheets, with changes in fair value recognized in the Consolidated Statements of Income. Cash flows related to derivative instruments are included in operating activities in the Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows in the period in which they occur. See Notes 11 and 12 to Consolidated Financial Statements for additional information regarding EOG’s derivative instruments and fair value measurements.

Cash Management and Liquidity Outlook

EOG’s cash management strategy focuses on maintaining adequate liquidity to fund its capital program, dividends, share repurchases, debt service and other obligations, while preserving financial flexibility and minimizing the cost of capital. EOG’s liquidity sources include cash on hand, cash flows from operations, and, when necessary, access to the capital markets and bank credit facilities. EOG may also consider asset sales, joint ventures and other transactions to enhance liquidity.

At December 31, 2023, EOG had $5.4 billion of cash and cash equivalents on hand and no outstanding borrowings under its Senior Credit Facility. EOG’s liquidity position provides financial flexibility to pursue its business strategy, including reinvestment in the capital program, dividends, share repurchases and potential acquisitions.

EOG believes that its sources of liquidity are adequate to meet its short-term and long-term cash requirements. However, the adequacy of liquidity sources could be impacted by various factors, including commodity price volatility, changes in economic conditions, regulatory developments, and other risks and uncertainties. EOG will continue to monitor its liquidity position and adjust its capital program and other activities as necessary to maintain financial strength and flexibility.

Other

EOG’s cash flows are also impacted by changes in working capital and other assets and liabilities. Working capital changes are influenced by the timing of cash receipts and payments, commodity price movements, and other factors. EOG actively manages working capital to optimize liquidity and support operations.

EOG’s capital structure consists of a mix of equity and debt. EOG seeks to maintain a strong balance sheet with low leverage to support financial flexibility, reduce risk and enhance shareholder value. EOG may adjust its capital structure over time in response to changes in market conditions, business opportunities and other factors.

EOG will continue to evaluate its capital program and other uses of cash in light of market conditions, commodity prices, and business objectives. EOG’s long-term strategy is to generate sustainable shareholder value by maintaining a strong balance sheet, investing in high-return projects, and returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

We may from time to time seek to repurchase or retire our outstanding debt through cash purchases and/or exchanges for equity or debt, in open market purchases, privately negotiated transactions or otherwise. Such repurchases or exchanges, if any, will depend on prevailing market conditions, our liquidity requirements, contractual restrictions and other factors. The amounts involved may be material.

We may also seek additional debt financing to fund a portion of our capital program and other expenditures as and when needed or deemed appropriate. Additionally, subject to market conditions, securities law limitations and approvals of our board of directors, we may pursue issuances of equity or equity-linked securities from time to time for general corporate purposes.

We also periodically evaluate various asset portfolios and acquisition opportunities. Such transactions are intended to maximize stockholder value but may impact our liquidity in future periods depending on the size of any transaction, the consideration paid or received, the timing of the closing of a transaction and the fluctuating commodity price environment. Non-Recurring Fair Value Measurements. The initial measurement of asset retirement obligations at fair value is calculated using discounted cash flow techniques and is based on internal estimates of future retirement costs associated with property, plant and equipment. Significant Level 3 inputs used in the calculation of asset retirement obligations include plugging costs and reserve lives. A reconciliation of EOG's asset retirement obligations is presented in Note 6.

When circumstances indicate that proved oil and gas properties may be impaired, EOG compares expected undiscounted future cash flows at a depreciation, depletion and amortization group level to the unamortized capitalized cost of the group. If the expected undiscounted future cash flows, based on EOG's estimate of (and assumptions regarding) future crude oil, NGLs and natural gas prices, operating costs, development expenditures, anticipated production from proved reserves and other relevant data (all Level 3 inputs as defined by ASC 820) are lower than the unamortized capitalized cost, the capitalized cost is reduced to fair value. Fair value is generally calculated using the Income Approach described in ASC 820. In certain instances, EOG utilizes accepted offers from third-party purchasers as the basis for determining fair value.
